The *Smṛtyarthasāra* composed by Śrīdharācārya:
[1] Gaṇeśa, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśa, Ambā, Aṅga, Yama, the world-protectors, and Guha;
I salute Durgā, Manu and the other progenitors, as well as the commentators and my constant gurus. || 1 ||
By the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha and Śrīkara Ācāryas, [this was compiled] from the various scattered Smṛti scriptures found within the Śruti, Smṛti, and Purāṇas in manifold ways.
For the sake of assisting the practitioner, the gaps in the Smṛtis have been diligently filled by the Purāṇas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Vedas with their auxiliary sciences (Vedāṅgas).
When the wish-fulfilling cow, the blazing ocean, and the celestial trees and creepers had appeared, it was proclaimed by Śambhu, Draviḍa, Kedāra, Lollaṭa, and others. (4)
I shall expound the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, as elucidated by commentators in the various *smṛtis* of Manu and others, for the sake of achieving its easy practice. (5)

If the direction is not specified, it should be the eastern quarter; likewise, if the north or the northeast is not mentioned, that is intended. And when standing or being upright is not specified in ritual acts, one should remain seated.
If the specific limbs of the agent are not mentioned, then they shall be the right limbs;
however, in the case of something contemptible, the left hand is used, while the right hand is used for what is not contemptible.
All ritual action should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin) and in a clockwise direction;
this is accomplished through mental clarity, truthful speech, austerity, and the act of bathing.
Having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and ensured one's own purity, one should perform the rite;
if one realizes that the rite has been performed incorrectly, one should perform it all over again.

But if the primary act is not performed, it must be performed again along with its constituent parts; however, if a subsidiary part is omitted, one should perform the expiation, but not the ritual act itself.
"He who, though capable of following the primary rule, acts according to a secondary rule, does not obtain its fruit in the hereafter; so say the Śruti and the Smṛti. (11)
One should practice dharma with effort through deed, mind, and speech;
however, one should not practice even that which is dharma if it leads away from heaven or is despised by the world.

Whether it be much or little, for whomever the ritual action prescribed by his own *gṛhya-sūtra* has been impelled, when that much of the meaning of the scripture has been performed, everything is considered done. (13)
In all Vedic rites, that which is prescribed in every Śākhā is appropriate for everyone;
likewise, among those Vedic rituals, the Smārta rules common to them should be adopted.

The practices established by tradition, those arising from one's birth, region, and family, as well as the customs of the village, are to be adopted provided they do not contradict the sacred injunctions. || 15 ||
The duties of the ages (yugas) are to be adopted everywhere as is appropriate:
that which is accomplished in ten years in the Kṛta age is achieved in a single year in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, that [result] is achieved in a month; in the Kali age, it is achieved in a single day and night.
Procreating a son with the husband's younger brother and entering the forest-dweller (vānaprastha) stage of life [are permitted]. 17.
The remarriage of a girl to another after she has been given away, embarking on sea voyages, and the carrying of a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). || 18 ||
Setting out on the Great Journey, the cow and the animal, the drinking of wine, licking the Agnihotra ladle, and the consumption of what has been licked—these [are forbidden]. || 19 ||
Furthermore, regarding marriages with girls of a different caste among the twice-born, there was conduct dependent upon Vedic study, as well as the reduction of sin. (20)
After the collection of the bones, there is indeed the touching of the limbs;
this is the prescription for penance for Brahmins that ends with death.

Association with evildoers, the slaughter of an animal for the sake of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and the formal adoption of a son other than one who has been given as an *aurasa*—these are [prohibited]. (22)

The initiation for a sacrificial session (satra-dīkṣā), the expiation for theft and other mortal sins (mahāpātaka), and the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the purpose of worshipping an image, along with its associated duties. || 23 ||

Association with women who have committed offenses against men of their own caste—even if those women have been purified—as well as officiating at a sacrifice for a Śūdra (śāmitra) and the selling of Soma by Brāhmaṇas; || 24 ||
The wise declare that these practices—long-term celibacy, the human sacrifice, and the horse sacrifice—are to be avoided in the Kali age. (25)

[3] There are four social classes (*varṇa*): the Brahmins (*vipra*), the Kṣatriyas, the Vaiśyas (*viṭ*), and the Śūdras. Among them, the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are the twice-born (*dvija*) and the thrice-born (*trija*). Their first birth is from their mother; the second birth is from the *upanayana* (initiation); and the third, supreme birth is at the consecration for a sacrifice (*yajña-dīkṣā*). For women, marriage takes the place of the *upanayana*. For the twice-born, the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) and ending with the *preteṣṭi* (funeral rite) must be performed with sacred formulas (*mantra*). In that regard, the sacraments (*saṃskāra*) are as follows:

The sixteen principal *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites) that are mandatory are: *garbhādhāna* (conception), *puṃsavana* (male-impregnation), *anavalobhana* (prevention of miscarriage), *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair), *jātakarma* (birth-rite), *nāmakaraṇa* (name-giving), *niṣkramaṇa* (first outing), *annaprāśana* (first feeding of solid food), *caula* (tonsure), *upanayana* (initiation), *sāvitrīvratavedamahāvratāraṇyavratāni* (the vows of the Sāvitrī, the Veda, the Great Vow, and the Forest Vow), *godānika* (shaving of the beard), *snātaka* (graduation), and *vivāha* (marriage). Among these, *garbhādhāna* should be performed during the fertile period (*ṛtu*). The period of fertility lasts from the onset of menstruation for sixteen nights. *Puṃsavana* should be performed before the movement of the fetus, in the third or fourth month. *Anavalobhana* is performed in the fourth month. *Sīmantonnayana* is performed in the sixth or eighth month. When a son is born, the father, having bathed, should perform the *vṛddhiśrāddha* with gold at night, during the two twilights, or during an eclipse; he should then perform the *jātakarma*, including gifts and other rites, for the destruction of sins and for the propitiation of Prajāpati. If the birth occurs during a period of impurity (*āśauca*) caused by another event, one should perform the *jātakarma* and subsequent rites after that impurity has ended. However, if the birth occurs during an impurity caused by a death, one should perform them at the end of that specific death-impurity. *Nāmakaraṇa* should be performed either immediately after the *jātakarma*, on the twelfth day, or on another auspicious day. *Niṣkramaṇa*—which consists of showing the moon, showing the sun, or saluting the gods—should be performed on the twelfth day, or in the third or fourth month. *Annaprāśana* should be performed in the sixth or eighth month, or when the first tooth has appeared. *Caula* should be performed in the first or third year, as this is the widely accepted view, or according to family custom. These *saṃskāras* must be performed according to local custom for the destruction of the sins of the seed and the womb. For women, these rites are without fire-offerings (*ahoma*) and should be performed silently (*tūṣṇīm*), except for marriage, which is accompanied by mantras. If these rites are delayed beyond their time, one should perform a *vyāhṛti-homa* and then proceed. For the omission of each of these, a *pādakṛcchra* penance is required; for the *caula*, an *ardhakṛcchra*. If the omission is intentional and not due to an emergency, the penance is double. Before initiation (*upanayana*), children are not considered impure even when eating the remnants of others' food; they may act, speak, and eat as they please, except for *mahāpātakas* (great sins). Upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste, they must bathe with their clothes on. Before *annaprāśana*, they require only sprinkling with water (*abhyukṣaṇa*); before *caula*, they require only sipping water (*ācamana*); some say that after that, they must bathe. Children should not recite mantras, except for those used for offering the *svadhā* oblation to their parents.

Now, the initiation (*upanayana*): the initiation should be performed for Brahmins and the other classes respectively in the eighth, eleventh, or twelfth year from conception or from birth. If the strength of the auspicious planets, such as Jupiter and Venus, is not obtained, it may be performed for Brahmins and the others respectively starting from the fifth year up to the sixteenth, the twenty-second, and the twenty-fourth. Beyond this, they become *vrātyas*, fallen from the *Sāvitrī*. For them who have not performed the penance (*prāyaścitta*), the initiation, teaching, officiating at sacrifices, marriage, and so forth must not be performed. The heavy penance for *vrātyas* will be described later.
Among those who are eunuchs, blind, deaf, paralyzed, dull-witted, stammering, or lame;
among those who are hunchbacked, dwarfed, afflicted by disease, or have withered limbs or deformed members.
For those who are intoxicated, mute, lying on their side, lacking sense faculties,
or even for those whose virility is destroyed— among these, the sacramental rites (saṃskāras) should be performed as is appropriate.

Some say that those who are mute or insane are not to be consecrated (*saṃskārya*), because they lack eligibility for ritual acts and thus do not incur the state of being an outcast (*pātitya*). Their offspring, however, are to be consecrated, according to the Vedic revelation: "One born of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Brāhmaṇa is indeed a Brāhmaṇa. Others say they are to be consecrated. The teacher performs at least the *homa* (oblation). As for the initiation (*upanayana*), it consists of leading [the boy] to the presence of the teacher according to the prescribed rule, or leading him to the presence of the fire, or the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*. Other auxiliary rites should be performed according to one's ability. And marriage is the acceptance of a girl; this is another auxiliary rite.

The legitimate son of the body (aurasa) and the son born of the wife (kṣetraja)—these two are entitled to perform the sacramental rites and are heirs to the inheritance. Likewise, the legitimate son of the body, the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), the son born of the wife, and the son secretly born (gūḍhaja).

The son of an unmarried girl, the son of a remarried woman, the given son, the bought son, the made son, the son who has offered himself, the son born of a pregnant bride, and the son cast off; these follow in order.
The one who offers the funeral ball (piṇḍa) is the inheritor of their share; in the absence of each preceding one, the next succeeding one takes it.
These twelve types of sons are to be consecrated with sacramental rites among the twice-born.

Some say that the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* born of twice-born men are to be consecrated; others say that the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* are those born of an adulterer, [the former] when the husband is alive and [the latter] when he is dead.
Now, the rule for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*):
Cotton, linen, cow-hair, hemp, bark, grass, and so forth—
whichever is available— should be worn as the sacred thread by the twice-born.
In a clean place, being pure himself, he should draw a cord at the base of the joined fingers;
having carefully tripled that [measurement] by ninety-six [units].
Having thoroughly washed it three times with water not containing the *abliṅga* formula, and having wound it upwards,
one should wrap it three times counter-clockwise while reciting the *Sāvitrī*.
Then, having wound it clockwise so that it is even with nine threads,
and having wrapped it three times and tied it firmly, one should bow to Hari, Brahmā, and Īśvara.
[5] One should wear it with the mantra: "The sacred thread is the supreme purifier" (PārG 2.2.10).
If the cord should have hair on it, one should then remove that hair.
One should lift that [food] up with water consecrated ten times with the Sāvitrī mantra;
if it has fallen apart, or has gone down, or has been touched by a dog, one should discard it after eating.
Or alternatively:
that which reaches the waist when held at the spine or at the navel should be worn as the *upavīta*; it should be neither too long nor too short.
It should never be worn above the breasts or below the navel;
for a student it may be one, but for a graduate there may be many.
The Self-Existent One has declared that unwashed cloth, free from mechanical processing, is suitable for a garment;
in the absence of such cloth, a third upper garment is likewise desired.
When the sacred thread (brahmasūtra) rests on the right shoulder, one is in the *yajñopavīta* position;
when it rests on the left shoulder, one is in the *prācīnāvīta* position; and when it hangs from the neck, one is in the *nivīta* position.
For the purpose of the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta), one should use a garment or a triple-stranded cord during ritual acts;
for all castes, a rope made of kuśa grass, muñja grass, or woolen fibers may also be used.
Thus ends the rule for the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*).
As for the skins of the Brahmin and the other classes, they are those of the black antelope, the Ruru deer, and the goat;
or else a pair of unwashed garments, or even a single white garment.

The girdle made of muñja grass should consist of three strands, twisted from right to left, and its knots should be as many as the years [of the wearer's age]. In the absence of muñja grass, however, it should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balvaja grass.
The staffs for all [initiates] should be made from sacrificial trees, such as the *pālāśa* and others;
specifically, they may be made of *pālāśa*, *bilva*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, *vetasa*, or *khadira*.
Bamboo, Udumbara, and Aśvattha wood are prescribed for Brahmins and the other [castes] respectively;
these should be measured by the length of the hair, the forehead, and the tip of the nose, respectively, by the twice-born.
Smooth items should always be worn; one should wear a loincloth and a waist-string.
The loincloth should be an unwashed one, or it may be a torn piece joined with strips of cloth.
One should wear the sacred thread, the deerskin, the girdle of muñja grass, and the staff.
If these are lost or damaged, one should take new ones with the appropriate mantra and cast the damaged ones into water.

[6] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, he is one who has reached the ultimate goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge. What are the four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—unbroken, untorn, unblemished, unmottled, freeing, praised by the wise, ungrasped, leading to concentration. [6]

Immediately after the *upanayana*, for three nights, twelve nights, or a year, the student (*brahmacārī*), eating food free from pungent vegetables and salt while sleeping on the ground, shall observe the vow of initiation. At the conclusion of every such vow, he should discard his previous sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) and put on new ones; however, there is no fixed rule regarding the discarding of clothes. He must daily perform his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), and the libations (*tarpaṇa*). Wandering for alms at the house of an irreproachable Brahmin with the permission of his teacher, and eating according to the prescribed rules for meals, he should observe the vow of a student for twelve years, five years, or until he has mastered the Vedas. He should serve his teacher for the sake of acquiring the sacred sciences (*chandas*). For all the Vedas, the vow of a year-long study begins with the *upākarma* ceremony. During this time, until his formal graduation (*samāvartana*), he must avoid women, honey, meat, leavings of food, sour substances, stale food, betel, brushing the teeth, sitting on a seat between the thighs (*avasakthika*), sleeping during the day, using an umbrella or sandals, perfumes, garlands, unguents, ointments, collyrium, playing in water, gambling, dancing, singing, instrumental music, idle chatter, and slanderous speech. With the exception of one thing—eating honey and meat when ill—he may consume the leavings of his teacher. However, these are strictly forbidden at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*). After the vow of initiation, the *Sāvitrī-vrata* and the *Āraṇyaka-vratas* ending with the *upākarma* are observed in the same manner. The *upākarma* should be performed when the herbs have grown, on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, or on the fifth lunar day of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism *Śravaṇa*, or on the fifth day joined with the asterism *Hasta*. Alternatively, it may be performed on the full moon of Bhādrapada, under *Śravaṇa* or *Hasta*, or on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, according to local custom. If the asterism *Śravaṇa* is divided, the first four *ghaṭikās* (the portion belonging to *Abhijit*) must be avoided. When there is a conflict between lunar days (*tithi-gaṇḍa*), the lunar day that extends into the sunrise and is sufficient for the performance of the rite should be taken. If *Śravaṇa* is incomplete, a time joined with *Dhaniṣṭhā* that is sufficient for the rite should be taken, but not one joined with *Uttarāṣāḍhā*. Under other asterisms beginning with *Hasta*, a time extending over sunrise in the bright fortnight or sunset in the dark fortnight that is sufficient for the rite should be taken. If obstacles such as birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) arise, or if the herbs have not yet grown, the rite should be performed on any day in the months of Śrāvaṇa or Bhādrapada, avoiding eclipses and solar transits (*saṃkrānti*). There is neither omission nor postponement of the rite. One should provide and wear new girdles (*mauñjī*) and sacred threads, and likewise a new waist-cord and garment. From the *upanayana* until the end of the *upākarma*, the *Sāvitrī-vrata* is observed; to complete it, one should feed Brahmins and relatives according to one's means. Then follows the year-long vow for each Veda, and subsequently the *Āraṇyaka-vratas*, with shaving the head at each vow. At the conclusion of the vows, alms should be brought for the meal. If there is a breach of these vows, one should perform three, six, or twelve *Prājāpatya* penances according to the degree of the offense and begin the vow again. Immediately thereafter, or during the northern solstice (*udagayana*) on an auspicious day in the bright fortnight, one should begin the private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). In the forenoon, having worshipped Gaṇeśa, Sarasvatī, one’s chosen deity, the teacher, and the supreme teacher; having honored the students and married Brahmin women and received their blessings; and holding *darbha* grass as in the *brahmayajña*, they should recite the *Praṇava*, the *Vyāhṛtis*, and the *Sāvitrī*. Having begun the study with the *Praṇava*, having read a little, and having concluded with the *Praṇava*, they should say, "May there be a pause," touch the ground, and bow to the teacher and the elders. From the following day onwards, having bowed to Gaṇeśa and the others, they should perform both the commencement and the conclusion with the *Praṇava*. Those whose caste or conduct is doubtful should not be taught. The student (*brahmacārī*), having performed the twilight prayers and the fire-ritual, should attend upon the teacher, saluting those older than himself by clasping their feet and bowing to those who are simply elders. "Attending upon" (*upasaṃgrahaṇa*) consists of saying, "I, Devadatta Śarmā of such-and-such lineage, salute you, sir," touching the ears, grasping the teacher’s right foot with the right hand and the left foot with the left hand, and bowing the head. In a simple salutation (*abhivādana*), there is no grasping of the feet, though there may be a touch of the feet. After saying, "May you be long-lived, gentle Devadatta," the response should be, "O [Name] Śarmā," or simply, "May you be long-lived, gentle one. Now, the teachers, the mother who suckled him, the father, grandfathers and so forth, the mother’s parents, the provider of food, the protector from fear, the preceptor (*ācārya*), the initiator (*upanetā*), and the instructor of mantras and sciences—their wives also—are to be attended upon by one who has completed his studies (*samāvṛtta*). If the teacher is a child or of equal age, one should behave toward him as toward a teacher. Maternal uncles, paternal uncles, fathers-in-law, and maternal and paternal aunts, even if younger, should be greeted by rising and saluting. Sub-teachers (*upādhyāya*), officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), elder brothers, and the wives of all these, as well as maternal and paternal aunts of the same caste and the wife of a brother, are always to be saluted.
Upon returning from a journey, one should greet women who are kinswomen by birth;
having returned from a journey, one should ask a Brahmin about his welfare and a king about his health.
Having approached a Vaiśya, one should say "well-being" (kṣema); and toward a Śūdra, "health" (ārogya).
One who has been initiated must not be addressed by name, even if he is younger.
One should address those worthy of honor with the terms "bhoḥ," "bhavat," or by their names;
one should address the wife of another who is not one's senior as "sister" (ambā).

A *śrotriya* who is three years senior [in Vedic study] is to be saluted. Relatives who are three years senior, as well as others born of one’s own kin, those advanced in knowledge, and those of good conduct, are always to be saluted—even if they are only slightly older. [One should avoid saluting] a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a woman who has killed her husband, a woman who has caused an abortion, a heretic, an outcast, a *vrātya*, a perpetrator of a mortal sin (*mahāpātakin*), and a rogue.
One should not offer salutation to an atheist, a gambler, a thief, or an ungrateful person;
nor to a man who is intoxicated, negligent, insane, running, or impure.
One should not offer salutations to someone who is yawning, stretching, brushing his teeth, having oil applied to his head, or in the midst of bathing.

One should not offer salutation to one who is engaged in the sacrifice of recitation (japa), standing in water, or carrying sacrificial fuel, flowers, kusha grass, fire, a water-pot, the arghya offering, or alms-food.
Having saluted these twice-born men, he becomes pure after a day and a night.

In the case of saluting a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the penance for a Brāhmaṇa is as follows; in the case of saluting a Śūdra, it is three nights; but in the case of washermen and the like, it is a Kṛcchra;

and in the case of Cāṇḍālas and the like, it shall be a Cāndrāyaṇa—this is the opinion of the author of the Saṃgraha. Upon seeing an image of a deity or seeing an ascetic (yati) bearing the triple staff (tridaṇḍin), [one should perform the same].
If one does not perform a salutation, one is purified by fasting;
furthermore, all beings are always to be saluted in all circumstances.
Greeting, salutation, as well as the return greeting, and the expression of a blessing should be spoken by those who are to be saluted; however, one who is of equal age should merely bow in return.
Women who are aged by years are to be honored, for they belong solely to their husband;
thereafter, he should study the Vedas as instructed by his teacher during his private recitation.
Now the days unfit for study shall be declared: by studying on forbidden days, Yama himself cuts short one's wisdom, lifespan, progeny, fortune, celibacy, prosperity, and splendor.
Out of fear that the power of his mantra might be exhausted, Indra strikes with his thunderbolt;
furthermore, at the end, he will certainly become a brahmarākṣasa and fall into hell.

On the eighth, fourteenth, and full-moon days, as well as on the first day of the lunar fortnight, there is always a suspension of study for a full day and night. The same applies to the *aṣṭakā* festivals. Furthermore, on the twelfth lunar day when the moon is in conjunction with the asterisms of Indra (*Jyeṣṭhā*), Śravaṇa, Maghā, or Bharaṇī, as well as on those lunar days that bear specific epithets, study is suspended. It is traditionally taught that the second day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, the tenth day of the bright fortnight in Āśvina, and the fourth and twelfth days of Māgha are such "epitheted" days.

On the twelfth days of the months of Śrāvaṇa (the month of lying down) and Māgha (the month of rising), on the second days near the full moons of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Phālguna, on the Pretadvitīyā at the end of the dark fortnight, and during all extraordinary portents, there is no study for the remainder of the day. Also, during great calamities, on the Mahānavamī, on the Rathasaptamī, and on the anniversaries of the Yugas;

on the third day of the bright fortnight in Vaiśākha, the thirteenth day of the fortnight of the departed (Pretapakṣa), the ninth day of the bright fortnight in Kārttika, the new moon in Māgha, and the full moon.
These are declared to be the beginnings of the Yugas, which cause what is given to be inexhaustible;
some say that all the beginnings of the Manvantaras are days unfit for study.
The ninth day of the bright fortnight of Āśvayuja, the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Kārttika,
the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, and the third day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada.
The tenth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, the seventh of the bright fortnight of Māgha,
the eighth of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the sixth and the full moon day.
The new moon of Phālguna, the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of Pauṣa, as well as the full moons of Kārttika, Phālguna, Caitra, and Jyeṣṭha; likewise, the fifteenth day of Jyeṣṭha.
And these occasions, such as the beginning of a Manvantara, cause what has been given to become inexhaustible.

One must abstain from study for a day and a night (*ahorātra*) upon following or attending to a corpse, or when seeing a corpse in the sky. Having accepted an invitation to a *śrāddha* feast, or having studied the *Āraṇyaka*, one must abstain for a day and a night, as well as during the time of the abodes and enjoyments of humans, gods, and *nāgas*. Some say this lasts until the end of a dream. Upon eating at a *nava-śrāddha* (recent funeral feast), however, the abstention lasts until the food has been digested; the same applies to eating food from a family in a state of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka*). At a *mahā-ekoddiṣṭa* (great single-offering rite), the abstention is three nights, or until the scent and stain have vanished. Upon the death of a "great guru" (*mahā-guru*), it is twelve nights; upon the death of a non-*sapiṇḍa* relative who is a guru, it is three nights. For a teacher (*ācārya*) or a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), it is a "bird-night" (*pakṣiṇī*). The same applies to a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) of equal learning. For the wife, son, or pupil of an *ācārya*, the abstention is a day and a night. Upon the outbreak of fire, or upon the death of a cow or a Brahmin, it is three nights. The same applies to officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those for whom one sacrifices (*yājya*), and those related by birth. Upon completing the Veda or at the first formal sessions (*saṃsthā*), there is abstention for that day and night, and the next day is also a period of non-study. During an eclipse, however, the abstention lasts through the night; if the release occurs at night, it is three nights; if the release occurs during the day, it is three days. At the *upākarma* and *utsarga* ceremonies, it is three days. At the solstices (*ayana*) and equinoxes (*viṣuva*), it is a "bird-night. During all portents such as thunderclaps, earthquakes, and the fall of meteors, there is non-study for the duration of the event. In the case of a fire outbreak or unseasonable rain, the same applies. Rain falling between the asterisms beginning with Ārdrā and ending with Jyeṣṭhā causes immediate suspension of study; otherwise, it causes suspension for the duration of the event. If there is thunder at the evening twilight, the suspension lasts until sunrise. If there is thunder after midnight or at midnight, the suspension lasts for the duration of the event. But if there is thunder at the morning twilight, the suspension lasts for a full day and night. If crows, owls, dogs, rats, frogs, or similar creatures pass between [the teacher and pupil], if it is during the day, the suspension lasts until the end of the day; if at night, until the end of the night. If a cow, horse, buffalo, domestic animal, woman, or *śūdra* passes between, the suspension is a day and a night, as is the case with a dog or a cat. If a wild cat, snake, mongoose, or five-toed beast passes between, it is three nights. If a wild horse, jackal, monkey, washerman, or similar person passes between, it is twelve nights. If a donkey, boar, camel, *caṇḍāla*, a woman in childbirth, a menstruating woman, or a corpse passes between, it is one month. If a hare, ram, dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), or similar being passes between, it is six months. In the case of an elephant, rhinoceros, crane, lion, tiger, a great sinner, or an ungrateful person passing between, there is no study for a year.
When the teacher or the disciple is engaged in private recitation or formal exposition, and [an obstacle] intervenes,
there may arise mental anguish, physical illness, impediments, death, or sin for both the teacher and the disciple.

There is no study on auspicious days or in an auspicious house. For those belonging to the same *sapiṇḍa* or *gotra*, there is no study from the time of a marriage, the tying of the sacred girdle (*mauñjībandha*), a consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), or the completion of a rite (*udyāpana*) until the end of the month in which the cleansing (*mārjana*) occurs. At a sacrifice, for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) or the teachers (*ācārya*), there is no study until the conclusion of the *anubandhyā* animal sacrifice; furthermore, if the following day is a non-study day (*anadhyāya*), there is no study during the first watch of the preceding night. When two non-study days occur consecutively, there is no study during the last watch of the second night; some say that when two non-study days occur consecutively, there is no study during the last watch of the first day. [There is no study] when the sound of a dog, a jackal, a donkey, an owl, the *Sāman* chants, or an arrow is heard; nor in the vicinity of impurity, a corpse, a *Śūdra*, an outcaste (*antya*), a cremation ground, or one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*).
In an impure place, or when one is personally impure; during a downpour of lightning and thunder;
after eating while the hands are still wet; while inside water; at midnight; or during an excessive windstorm.
During a rain of dust, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, during the fears of twilight or mist,
while running, when there is a foul odor, or when a learned man has arrived at the house.
Traveling on a donkey, a camel, a carriage, an elephant, a horse, or a boat; climbing a tree or a mountain—these thirty-seven occasions are known as temporary interruptions for study.
In the presence of all foul odors, during a meal, in assemblies,
at the time of anointing and bathing, and during great perspiration or excessive trembling.
In cases of obstructing cows or Brahmins, in the presence of all [prohibited] sounds, and during the rows of a Śrāddha feast,
[one should avoid] the Śālmali, Madhūka, Kovidāra, and Kapittha trees.
These are known to be immediately effective when performed in the shade of a *śleṣmātaka* tree,
as well as always on the fourteenth day, the eighth day, the festival days (*parvan*), and the first day of the lunar fortnight.
There is a suspension of study for those of dull intellect during the intervals between [the recitation of] the Vedas,
as well as for those prone to forgetfulness and those who have mastered many Vedic recitations.
However, on days other than the fourteenth, the eighth, festival days, and the first day of the lunar fortnight,
one should study the Vedāṅgas, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and the Dharmaśāstras.

Those who know the rules regarding the suspension of study understand that the period lasting for three muhūrtas at either sunrise or sunset constitutes a "day" and a "night" during which study is prohibited.
[11] Some say that in a certain region, the period of non-study lasts only as long as those nāḍīs of that day; it does not persist into another day.
They say that for vows such as fasting (upavāsa), the lunar day (tithi) is likewise [the determining factor];
and on the fourth day, at the sight [of the moon] during the first watch of the night within nine nāḍīs.
One should not study during the first part of the night on the seventh or thirteenth lunar days;
if these days fall before midnight, one must not study during that portion of the first watch of the night.
Then, for the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, the *sāvitrī*, and the *śiras*,
[these are required] in obligatory rites, occasional rites, vows, and likewise in sacrifices and ritual performances.

Furthermore, it is traditionally taught that there are no forbidden days for study when rites performed for specific desires have commenced; likewise, it is traditionally taught that there is no forbidden day for the recitation of mantras used in the worship of deities.
Now follows the ritual of dismissal (utsarjana).

Then, having studied for three and a half months or six months, he should perform the *utsarjana* (concluding rite) and the *tarpaṇa* (libation) outside the village at the edge of water, together with his pupils, on the day of the *rohiṇī* asterism in the month of Pauṣa, or on the *aṣṭakā* of Pauṣa, Māgha, or Phālguna; or on the first day (*pratipad*) of the bright fortnight, or on another day, or on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*). If he has studied for a year, the *utsarjana* may or may not be performed on the day of the *upākarma*; however, the *tarpaṇa* must certainly be performed. Likewise, having brought both the Vedic studies and the vows to completion, or having observed the vow of celibacy without breach—or having performed the penance if there was a breach—he should honor his teacher and, with his permission, return home (*samāvṛtta*) and marry.
Thus ends the section on the student life (brahmacāri-prakaraṇa). Now, marriage:
[he should marry] one who is pure on the mother’s and father’s sides, suitable, and endowed with good qualities.
Free from chronic illness and devoid of contagious diseases or physical deformities.
She who is not a sapinda on the father’s side beyond the seventh person,
nor on the mother’s side beyond the fifth, and who is not born of a family sharing the same rishi-ancestry (ārṣagotra).
A wise, steadfast, twice-born man should marry a maiden who has not been wed by another, who has brothers, and who is younger than himself, according to the order of the castes.
One should marry according to the path of dharma and according to the rules among the Brahma and other forms of marriage;
some [authorize] the daughter of a maternal uncle, the daughter of a paternal aunt, and so forth.
In some regions, they perform marriages even by contracting the limits of sapinda relationship;
having bathed and being well-composed, one may both give and receive [in such a marriage].
[12] The Brāhma marriage is when a girl, adorned according to one's means, is given after being invited;
the Daiva marriage is said to be the giving of a daughter to the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
When the gift of a maiden occurs upon the giving of a pair of cattle, that is the Ārṣa form;
it is the Prājāpatya form because of the giving with the words, "May you two perform dharma together."
The Āsura [form] arises from the taking of wealth; the Gāndharva, from mutual agreement;
the Rākṣasa, from abduction by force; and the Paiśāca, from the deception of the maiden.

The Brāhma, Daiva, Ārṣa, and Prājāpatya forms are righteous; the Āsura, Gāndharva, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca are unrighteous. Among these, the four intermediate ones belong exclusively to the Brāhmaṇa; the Rākṣasa belongs exclusively to the Kṣatriya; and the other three belong to all [classes]. In the Brāhma and subsequent forms, the fire-oblation (*homa*) is prescribed first, followed by the acceptance of the maiden. In the Āsura and subsequent forms, the acceptance of the maiden should take place first, and the fire-oblation afterwards. The father, grandfather, brother, a kinsman of the same lineage (*sakulya*), one born of the same *gotra*, the teacher (*guru*), maternal grandfather, and maternal uncle are the relatives authorized to give away the maiden in due order.
In the absence of a giver such as a father, however, a maiden may choose her own husband;
she should wait for five seasons once the groom has departed after paying the bride-price.

Even when the betrothal has already been performed, the girl should be given to another after ten months have passed; and if the groom has gone to another country, she should be given to another after waiting for three seasons. Even when the betrothal has already been performed, the girl should be given to another.
If the other [bridegroom] dies, she should likewise be given to another before the seven steps;
some say she should be given away when the husband dies even before union with the man has occurred.
Some say that if she has not been seen during her season, the girl may be given away again;
others say that she may be given away again until conception has occurred.
These practices are to be performed by a wise person according to place and time;
however, they are not for one who lacks noble birth or good character, for a eunuch and the like, nor for one who is fallen.

One may take back a maiden who has been given in marriage by those afflicted with epilepsy, those engaged in improper occupations, those who are diseased, or those wearing the garb of ascetics; likewise, one may take her back if she was married to a man of the same lineage.
A girl who has not been consecrated with the mantra-rites may be given to another suitor;
and a defiled girl must be avoided and given to yet another suitor.
Otherwise, however, one who misappropriates it is liable to punishment and must pay the expenses along with interest;
but for those who are blind, afflicted by disease, and so forth, marriage may take place as is appropriate.
In the event that their marriage is impossible, then the youngest among them may marry.
Among those who are eunuchs, blind, deaf, paralyzed, dull-witted, stammering, or lame;
among those who are hunchbacked, dwarfish, afflicted by disease, withered-limbed, or deformed in their members.
There is no fault in marrying after the fact if the elder brother is one whose virility has been destroyed, is intoxicated, is lying on his deathbed, is impotent, or is mute or insane.
In the case of a paternal uncle’s son, a stepbrother, or the sons of another’s wife and so forth,
there is no defect such as "parivēda" (the younger brother marrying before the elder) regarding marriage, the establishment of the sacred fires, sacrifice, and other such rites.
If he is permitted by his elder brother, there is no fault in marrying before him;
however, even if permitted by his father, he should never perform the marriage ceremony [if the elder brother has not consented].

The hand should be taken in marriages with women of the same caste; however, in the marriage of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya woman should take hold of an arrow, a Vaiśya woman should take hold of a goad, and in a marriage with a Śūdra woman of higher caste, she should take hold of the hem of his garment. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.62; Manu Smṛti 3.44cd)
For from those of the same caste, born of women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage;
through blameless marriages, sons increase the progeny. From Brahmins, a Mūrdhāvasikta is born of a Kṣatriya woman, and from a Vaiśya woman... [Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.90]...from a Brahmin.
From a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra mother, an Ambaṣṭha is born, or he is called a Niṣāda or a Pāraśava.
From a Kṣatriya father and Vaiśya or Śūdra mothers, the sons Māhiṣya and Ugra are traditionally declared.
From a Vaiśya father and a Śūdra mother, a Karaṇa is born; this is the rule recorded for wives who have been duly wedded.
These sons born in the direct order (anuloma), born of twice-born men, are to be consecrated with sacraments;
likewise, those born of the Mūrdhāvasikta and other such castes are also considered twice-born.
From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehika;
and from a Śūdra, one born is a Caṇḍāla, excluded from all religious duties.
From a Vaiśya on a Kṣatriya woman is born a Māgadha, and from a Śūdra, a Kṣattṛ.
A Vaiśya woman indeed gave birth to an Āyogava son from a Śūdra;
furthermore, a Rathakāra is born from a Māhiṣya father and a Karaṇī mother.
These and others are those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), who are excluded from the duties of the twice-born.
[14] After marriage, having established the sacred fires and performing the Agnihotra sacrifice,
one should perform the Darśa, Pūrṇamāsa, Āgrayaṇa, and Soma sacrifices in their proper sequence.
In every way, the first Soma sacrifice must be performed by the twice-born,
even if it yields its fruit only after providing the sacrificial fee with whatever components are available.
For the pacification of great defects such as being a *vrātya* or a wicked *brāhmaṇa*,
one should offer a ewe, a black antelope skin, and other items at Kurukṣetra during a solar eclipse.
Even after accepting [gifts] from a Caṇḍāla, one may perform sacrifices that are obligatory;
furthermore, having performed the domestic fire-ritual (*aupāsana*) and offering oblations, one should carry out the household rites.
In the Ardhādhāna rite, there is great merit consisting of both the domestic (gārhya) and the Śrauta fires.
Upon the birth or death of a relative, a woman attains oneness with her husband regarding the funeral cake, the lineage, and the period of impurity.
If another wife of the same caste exists, one should not have her perform religious duties;
among wives of the same caste, according to the rule of dharma, no other may act without the eldest.
She who carries out his commands, is skillful, bears sons, is beloved, and pure—[cf. YDh 1.76].
She should be employed in religious duties and should never be superseded by another wife under any circumstances.
One who is capable, devoted, pure, and skillful should be appointed to religious duties;
however, one who is impure, unchaste, a Śūdra woman, or defiled should be dismissed.
A woman who drinks liquor, is diseased, deceitful, barren, wasteful of wealth, speaks unpleasantly,
bears only daughters, hates her husband, or whose children die, may be superseded by another wife.
A householder, moreover, may maintain six fires, five fires, or four fires.
There may be two or three fires, or even a single fire; however, one must never be without a fire under any circumstances.
One should perform domestic rites in the *aupāsana* fire; however, for one who has performed the *sarvādhāna*, they are to be performed in the common (*laukika*) fire.
Smārta rites are to be performed in the common fire, while Śrauta rites are to be performed in the sacrificial fires (*vaitānika*).
Now follows the determination of the *gotra* and *pravara*:
here, the determination of the *gotra* and *pravara* is described directly:
Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Atri, and Gautama.
Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Agastya are the sages who establish lineages;
their offspring are considered to be the *gotras*.
Where the persistence of a single entity is observed, whether by way of being selected or by way of its mere existence, that is called its *gotra*.
Baudhāyana has declared that there are two ways [of determining kinship]: having many sages in common, having a single *pravara* in common, and having identical *pravara*s.
By means of the forty-nine most excellent categories established by the Sage,
we shall express all the infinite lineages after having classified them.

The descendants of Jamadagni, Vatsa, Bida, and Ārṣṭiṣeṇa do not intermarry with one another due to the identity of their *pravara*; furthermore, the first two [groups] do not intermarry because they share the same *gotra*.
The Maitrāyaṇīyas, Vaineyas, and Śunakas, though originating from a single common ancestor,
have all abandoned their respective groups and should carry out the funeral rites together with their distant relatives.
The seven lineages of Bhṛgu have been described; now the groups of Aṅgiras will be told:
the Gautamas, the seven Āyāsyas, and likewise the Śāradvatas as another group.
From Dīrghatamas came the Komaṇḍas and the Kāreṇupālayas;
and the Vāmadevas and Auśanasas do not differ [in lineage] because their ancestral seers (gotrarṣi) are one.
The Bharadvājas, the Kapayas, the Gargas, and the Raukṣāyaṇas—
though these four are Bharadvājas, they did not intermarry due to their common lineage.
Some say that the Kevalāṅgirasas, Viṣṇuvṛddhas along with the Kaṇvajas,
Hārītas, Rathītaras, and Mudgalas are one due to the identity of their *pravara*.
Having each abandoned their own group, all should marry with those both higher and lower;
thus the Aṅgirases are said to be of three kinds, as are the Saṃkṛtis.
Because the Saṃkṛtis belong to two lineages and because they share the same lineage and the same *pravara* with the four types of Vasiṣṭhas, they should not intermarry with those of their own group.
Among these, the four— the three beginning with Ātreya, the Bhūtaka, and the Gaviṣṭhira,
as well as the Mudgala— do not intermarry because of their identity of *gotra* and identity of *pravara*.
The three groups of Kaśyapas— Nidhruvas, Rebhas, and Śāṇḍilas—
should not intermarry with one another due to their identity of lineage and identity of ancestral sages (pravara).
There is no lineage connection between the Vasiṣṭhas and the Kāśyapas, nor with the Laugākṣis;
however, the statement regarding the Vasiṣṭhas applies daily to the scope of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.
[16] Vasiṣṭhas, Kuṇḍinas, Upamanyus, and Parāśaras—
these four groups known as Vasiṣṭhas do not intermarry with one another due to their identity of lineage.
The Kuśikas, the Rohitagaṇas, the Raukṣakas, the Kāmakāyanas, the Katas, the Dhananjayas, the Ājas, and the Aghamarṣaṇapūraṇas.
The ten groups of Viśvāmitras are those born of Indra, Kauśika, and Jā;
they should not intermarry because of their common gotra and, in some cases, because of the identity of their pravara.
The three lineages— the Agastyas, the Sāmbhavāhas, and the Somavāhas—
should not intermarry with one another because they share both a common *gotra* and a common *pravara*.
Forty-nine classes are well-known and recorded by the sages;
other lineages that are not well-known are included right here within these very groups.
The Dhanañjayas should not marry women of the Viśvāmitra and other such lineages;
likewise, the Vāmarathyas and others are the sons of the daughters of Atri.
Likewise, Jātūkarṇya with the Vasiṣṭhas and Atris,
Bharadvāja with Śuṅga, and Śaiśira of Viśvāmitra’s lineage.
One born in the field [of another] is said to have two ancestral lineages (gotra), such as Śauṅgaśaiśiri;
because they are born from Viśvāmitra and Bharadvāja, there is no genealogical continuity for those born from that union.
There is no lineage connection between the Kapilas and the Bharadvājas or the Viśvāmitras;
therefore, those who share the same *gotra* and *pravara* as one's preceptor must not be married by people of the Kṣatriya or Vaiśya castes.

Brahmins who are ignorant of their own lineage and so forth may, through gifts and other means, obtain preceptors born of another lineage; likewise, those whose guru’s lineage is unknown may do the same.
The prohibition against marrying those of the same *pravara* applies to both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas;
however, because they do not know their *pravara*s, one may marry women born of other *gotra*s who differ from one's own *pravara*.
Thus, while the matter of marriage within one's own lineage remains settled,
if someone, through ignorance, goes ahead and marries such a girl;
One is purified by the vow for violating the Guru’s bed; the child born of that union shall become an outcaste.
Having abandoned such enjoyment, one should protect [the woman] as if she were one’s own mother.
O son of Kaśyapa, through ignorance, the fetus is purified by three lunar [days];
thus, with great effort, this determination of the *pravara* for the Great One has been made.

[17] The descendants of Jamadagni, as well as those of Vatsa, Bida, and Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, are performers of the five-fold division (pañcāvattin); all others are performers of the four-fold division (caturavattin).
When the ritual for marriage has been spread out and the time for the fire-oblation (homa) has arrived,
what do the officiating priests do upon seeing that the bride has reached her menses?
Having bathed that maiden and honored her according to the prescribed rule,
and having offered the oblation for one engaged in the rite, the ritual procedure then proceeds.
Alternatively:
If the bride becomes menstruating when the marriage-homa has already commenced,
the couple shall remain for three nights on separate beds, seats, and meals.
"On the fourth day, having both bathed well, they should perform the wedding oblation (vivāhahoma) in that fire according to the prescribed rule"— such is the compendium of the Smṛtis.
At the wedding, the husband and wife shall remain celibate for three nights;
the bride, being adorned, shall likewise share the same bed, seat, and meal as her husband.
A twice-born man should by all means avoid betel, approval, the fire-oblation, and the meal in connection with marriages that are contrary to dharma.
In the case of the Āsura form of marriage, there should be a fast; in the Gāndharva forms, a three-night fast;
and likewise, in the Rākṣasa and Paiśāca forms, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

In the sacraments beginning with conception (garbhādhāna), as well as in sacrifices, charitable works, and agriculture, the Vṛddhi-śrāddha must first be performed; at the commencement of any rite, the Svastivācana should be recited.
The elder ancestors, however, partake in the *vṛddhi-śrāddhas*;
at the conclusion of the *cūḍā* fire-sacrifice, the younger ancestors partake.
The Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas, existing in three states and able to assume forms at will—
whether as children, youths, or the aged— are remembered as the refuge of the Pitṛs.
The Rudras are known as the refuge of the pretas, and Yama is the end-maker (Antaka). For those who have died without having received the sacraments, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are the refuge.
A gift given to those living beings who have no one to depend upon does not truly reach them;
however, once the funeral rites have commenced, the marriage must certainly take place even during a period of impurity.
In a sacrifice, the commencement is the selection [of priests]; in a vow or a long-duration session (sattra), it is the formal resolve;
in marriage and similar rites, it is the Nāndī-śrāddha; and in a funeral rite (śrāddha), it is the preparation of the cooked food.
According to the Smṛti, the invitation marks the commencement of a Śrāddha;
however, when [the rites] are performed for groups, there should be only a single worship of the Mothers.
The Vṛddhi-śrāddha should follow the same ritual procedure (tantra), but the fire-oblations (homa) should be performed separately.
[18] Now, the daily practice is being described:

Having risen at dawn here, having mentally bowed to one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) and recalled the duties for that day, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and other rites. Regarding that, one should perform the voiding of urine and feces as follows: taking wood from a tree not used for sacrifice, or dry sticks, clods of earth, grass, leaves, and so forth, covering the head, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) in the *nivīta* fashion hanging down behind the neck, and—if one is wearing only a single garment—placing it over the right ear; then, having looked toward the cardinal directions and having interposed the wood or other materials [between oneself and the ground], and either observing silence or restraining speech, and having sequentially performed the closing of the nostrils, one should void urine and feces facing north during the day and at the two twilights, and facing south at night.
On ground ploughed by a plow, in water, on a funeral pyre, on an anthill, on a mountain peak,
in a temple, on a riverbank, on darbha grass, or on a grassy meadow.
While walking or standing, one should not discharge feces or urine under trees providing shade, on a path, in a cow-pen, in water, or on ashes, nor should one do so in fire.
Facing these— the wind, fire, the sun, stars, cattle, the moon, the twilights, water, women, and the twice-born— one should not discharge feces or urine.
All prohibitions indeed do not apply in cases involving threats to life or disease;
moreover, one may wipe away impurities located on the lower part of the body with wood or similar materials.

One should not discharge [urine or excrement] on a carriage road, at a crossroads, at a sacred bathing place, in a cremation ground, on cow dung, in water, on a plowed field, in a garden, among living beings, or on a sacrificial ground.
One should not wipe away impurity with bulbs, roots, fruits, or charcoal.
Thus concludes the rule for the evacuation of urine and feces.
Now follows the rule for purification:
Effort toward purity must always be made; the twice-born is said to have purity as his root.
For one devoid of purity and right conduct, every ritual action is fruitless.
Purity is said to be twofold: external and internal.
External purity is traditionally defined as being through earth and water, while internal purity is the purification of one's disposition.
Having withdrawn the penis and stood up,
he should diligently perform purification with earth and drawn-up water to remove both odor and residue.
[YDh 1.17] [He should not take earth] from within water, from a temple, from an anthill, or from a place where mice dwell.
And five kinds of earth should not be taken: that which has been used for purification, and that which has been cast away.
One should avoid earth from roads, chariot tracks, or cremation grounds that is dusty or impure;
one should not collect earth that is free of insects, charcoal, and bones, yet is full of pebbles.
One should not take earth from the outer edges of ponds, wells, or tanks;
rather, earth located within the water beyond the wrist-level mark should be taken.
This rule applies specifically to forest-dwellers; for those living in villages, they know that food may be brought from elsewhere.
Regarding urine:
one application of clay should be made to the penis, three applications of clay to the left and right hands, and two applications of clay to both hands; the quantity of clay is manifold.
For the purification after urination, the amount of clay should be equal to three joints of the thumb, or the size of a handful of dust,
or the size of a fresh *āmalaka* fruit; for semen,
it is remembered that the amount should be double that of urine, and triple for sexual intercourse.
Regarding the excrement:
five applications of earth are prescribed for the anus, ten are remembered for the left hand, and seven are to be given to both hands; such is the measure of earth for defecation.
The first is said to be the measure of half a prasṛti, and each subsequent one is half of the preceding.
Some say that the measure of clay is half a handful, then half of that, and again half of that, respectively.
[This applies] for a householder living at ease during the day.
Alternatively, there are three handfuls of earth— measuring one *prasṛti*, half a *prasṛti*, and a third of a *prasṛti*—
or else three *prasṛti*s each, applied separately to the feet and the hands.
This is the standard of purity for householders; it is double for students, triple for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics.
Whatever purification is prescribed for the day, half of that is declared for the night;
half of that is said for one who is ill, and half of that for one on a journey.
For women, Śūdras, and others who are incapable, as well as for children prior to initiation,
one should perform purification sufficient to remove odor and stains, rather than according to a fixed number.
Then, one should wash the feet and hands with each type of clay individually.
Thus ends the rule for purification. [20] Now follows the rule for sipping water (ācamana).

There, having washed his hands and feet, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*), having placed his feet on clean ground, with his waistband and topknot tied, and having recollected the lotus-eyed one (*puṇḍarīkākṣa*) as his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), he should take water that is natural, free from foam and bubbles, with his hand whose fingers are joined; leaving out the thumb and the little finger, he should look at the remainder and, being composed, drink it three or four times through the *brahmatīrtha*. He may drink using the *kāyatīrtha*, the *daivatīrtha*, or the *pitryatīrtha*, but never the *pitryatīrtha*. Having drunk and washed his hands, [having contracted them to the corners of the lips and wiped his mouth twice with the root of the joined fingers where there is no hair], he should wipe his mouth once with the joined fingers and wash his hands. He should sprinkle his feet, head, and body, or alternatively, after touching the region of the mouth with the joined fingers including the hair, he should wash his hands and touch his nostrils with the thumb and forefinger; he should touch his eyes or ears with the thumb and ring finger; he should touch his navel with the thumb and little finger, his heart with the palm, his head with all the fingers, and the roots of his arms with the tips of all the fingers. At every interval between these, he should touch water. In case of extreme incapacity, having drunk three times and sprinkled his hands, he should touch his ears.
The twice-born are purified by water reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively;
Śūdras and others are purified when the water merely touches the lips once.
One should not sip water from rain-showers, nor from water that is warm without a [prescribed] reason.

The *kāya*, *pitrya*, and *brahma* *tīrthas* are located at the base of the little finger, the forefinger, and the thumb respectively; the *daiva* *tīrtha* is at the tip of the hand, and the *saumya* and *āgneya* *tīrthas* are in the middle of the hand. One should perform the daily fire-oblations (*nityahoma*) involving the offering of parched grain (*lāja*) and other oblations associated with the *nirvapaṇa* rite using the *kāya* *tīrtha*. One should perform rites pertaining to the gods (*daivika*), such as worship, the casting of offerings (*bali*), sprinkling water (*paryukṣaṇa*), cleansing (*mārjana*), eating, and the daily fire-oblations, using the *daiva* *tīrtha*. Rites pertaining to the ancestors (*paitṛka*) should be performed with the *pitrya* *tīrtha*. One should perform the touching of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the tasting of curd, the tasting of new grain, the taking up of wine (*surāgrahaṇa*), and rites pertaining to the gods (*daivika*) using the *saumya* *tīrtha*. One should perform the formal acceptance of gifts (*pratigraha*) using the *āgneya* *tīrtha*.
Thus ends the rule for sipping water (ācamana). Now, the occasions for sipping water:

Upon touching leavings, upon splashing water for the feet, upon loosening the topknot, and upon the removal of the sacred thread, one should sip water after having ascended and descended from water; and in all cases of doubt, one should sip water. Upon touching a beard that has entered the mouth, upon touching body hair, upon touching with the tongue something stuck between the teeth, upon walking on a road, upon touching oily substances or the claws of five-toed animals, upon weeping, at the conclusion of purification after voiding feces, urine, or semen, after drinking or licking, after spitting out what was stuck between the teeth, upon approaching a deity, one should sip water twice. [21] After bathing, after drinking or licking, after spitting, after sleeping, after passing wind, after changing clothes, after applying oil, and after eating sacrificial oblations (havir), one should sip water twice.
In eating, in offering oblations, in giving gifts, in receiving offerings,
and in drinking water during the three junctions of the day, one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) twice— once before and once after.

If one touches something impure while engaged in Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) while holding a cloth, one should touch it, place it on one's lap, and then, together with that cloth, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) to become pure. Alternatively, having placed it down and performed *ācamana*, one should sprinkle the cloth and other items with water. If one is touched by something impure while holding food, drink, or the like, one should place it down, perform *ācamana*, and then sprinkle it with water. However, if one is unable to protect the food and so forth, one should touch it, place it nearby, and then perform purification and *ācamana*. While serving food, if one touches something impure, one should set down the food vessel, perform *ācamana*, sprinkle water over it, and then serve. If, while serving, one becomes impure through urine or similar waste, one should set down the food and other items, perform purification, sprinkle the food and other items with water, touch fire or the sun, and then serve. If dust is seen during the serving, the food touched by it must be discarded. If the kitchen is touched by a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), an outcast (*patita*), or others, it must be abandoned. If it is touched by a washerman (*rajaka*) or similar person, however, it should be washed with water and then touched by fire or the sun. This also applies when one is touched by someone impure, speaks with a woman or a *śūdra* who is impure, or sees someone who is untouchable.
During the recitation of mantras dedicated to the ancestors, during self-proclamation, during the ritual sprinkling (prokṣaṇa),
upon the emission of downward wind (flatus), upon shouting, upon anger, and upon sneezing;

Upon touching a cat or a mouse, when laughing, when spitting, when speaking untruth, and upon conversing with or seeing those of the lowest castes, one performing a ritual act should sip water (ācamana). The same applies upon seeing a dog, a crow, or similar creatures.
If not performing a ritual act, in the aforementioned cases, one should touch the right ear.

During the performance of rites, upon touching fire, a cow, a Brahmin, a woman, or fallen hair and nails, or when the lower garment (nīvī) slips, one should touch water; or one should touch moist grass, cow dung, the earth, or medicinal herbs; or one should touch the ear. However, upon touching mucus, blood, pus, or sweat, one should wash [the hand] and then touch water and so forth. In times of distress, as a substitute for the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) required as a limb of occasional rites, touching the ear may be performed for the sake of mental purification. Fire, sacred fords, the Vedas, Varuṇa, the Sun, the Moon, and Vāyu—these deities always reside in the right ear of a Brahmin.
After performing recitations, burnt offerings, and acts of giving, as well as the offering of rice-balls, water, and fire to the ancestors,
one must perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in all rites dedicated to the ancestors.

[22] One should not sip water (ācamana) while touching anything that should not be touched; nor while seated on a seat made of wood-boards or the like; nor on a three-legged stool; nor on a seat intended for another purpose; nor on a seat used for eating after one has finished eating. One should not sip water while on another seat, nor while lying down, nor while in a vehicle, nor while wearing sandals, nor while sitting on one’s haunches; nor in an improper place; nor standing on the tips of one’s toes; nor while bent over; nor while standing; nor while walking; nor without bowing; nor with a distracted mind; nor while looking about; nor while laughing; nor while weeping; nor while talking; nor while naked; nor while wearing only a single garment; nor with joined palms; nor while touching another person; nor with the left hand; nor with the hands outside the knees; nor with the feet crossed; nor with the feet outstretched; nor in a bound posture; nor with something tied around the neck; nor with the head wrapped; nor having worn the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) or the upper garment in any other manner. In such cases, having adjusted them correctly, one should sip water again. If the sacred thread is lost, one should sip water after wearing another cord or cloth as the sacred thread. One should not drink with the right hand while *kuśa* grass or other *darbha* blades rest in the left hand. One should not drink water touched by the nails of the hand; that is as defiled as liquor (*surā*). One should avoid *dūrvā* grass from afar when it is rendered impure by the remnants of sipping water and the like.

One should not sip water using one's fingers, nor from an improper part of the hand, nor while making a sound; nor should one sip water that has not been inspected, that is not of a natural state, or that is hot without a specific reason.
Having lifted the vessel with the left hand, one should not drink from it with the right;
[the vessel] may be made of gold, silver, copper, bamboo, bilva-wood, stone, or leather.
With vessels made of bottle-gourd and wood, with coconut shells and kapittha fruits, with grass and wood, with water-holders, and with earthenware concealed by other materials.
Having lifted [the vessel] with the left hand, one should sip water while speaking, provided that another person is not available;
in that case, the water contained in an earthenware vessel is not defiled.
Water from a sacred ford (tīrtha) remains pure at all times even when contained in a water-jar or similar vessel.
One should perform the washing of the feet, bind the topknot and the waist-knot, and wash the sacred thread (upavīta).
One who has not sipped water is always impure, even if a ring is bound around his neck or head;
therefore, having purified his hands, he should respectfully sip water for the sake of ritual action.
Whether holding merely a blade of *kuśa* grass or even a blade of *darbha*,
one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) with the syllable *oṃ* or with the *vyāhṛtis*.

Whether it be performed with the Sāvitrī mantra or whatever rite is to be done without mantras, one should not discard the kuśa grass that has been cut according to the rules; otherwise, one should discard it.

Other *darbha* grasses should be discarded, but one should not discard *dūrvā* sprouts. One should not sip water (*ācamana*) using the water remaining from washing the feet. Nor should one sip water using the water remaining from a previous sipping; if one must sip water, one should do so after pouring out the water onto the ground. One should not perform ritual acts with the water remaining from a sipping, nor with the water remaining from offerings to the fire. If one should perform them, one should pour out the water onto the ground, set the water vessel right there, and having drawn it up again, perform the ritual acts. Now follows the exception regarding the sipping of water:

When a medicine that is not oily has been eaten, or when something oily or bound with a plaster has been consumed, one should not rinse the mouth after the meal; however, for the sake of purification, one should do so after eating betel nuts and similar items.
Nor in other unwholesome foods, nor in fragrant ingredients,
nor in betel-leaf, areca nut, burnt offerings, or the smearing of oil after a meal.
One should not perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana) after eating raw food consisting of sugarcane stalks, fruits, roots, leaves, flowers, sesame seeds, as well as bark, grass, or wood.
In the case of the honey-mixture (madhuparka), in Soma sacrifices, in the oblations of the vital breaths (prāṇāhutis),
in water, and in all offerings made directly from the mouth, a twice-born man does not become impure by remnants.

Like a tooth, that which adheres to the teeth is pure if its taste is not perceived; it is impure upon contact with the tongue. In that case, there is the touching of the ear. However, what remains in the mouth is pure. As for anything else, one should touch the ear while sipping water (*ācamana*), or when [the substance] has moved from its place, or while swallowing or discarding it. Alternatively, there is the touching of the ear once it has been swallowed. But if it is discarded, one must perform *ācamana*.
If the perception of taste is impossible, however, double *ācamana* is prescribed.
As for anything else remaining in the mouth, once *ācamana* has been performed, only the residue [remains].
One should cleanse the mouth with effort, and the teeth with gentle care;
for there is great sin in injuring the teeth, and they know blood to be equal to liquor.
When this has been done, whatever remains is never a fault;
the paste remaining on the lips and beard is pure if it persists after being washed.
Minute droplets originating from the mouth are pure for oneself and for others;
however, large droplets are pure only if they do not fall upon the body.
If [water] falls upon a limb, one should wash it and perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) if it belongs to another;
however, they should perform the ritual sipping even if drops fall upon what is not a limb.
Those born from the mouth through the study of the Vedas are always pure;
likewise, a beard that has entered the mouth is pure provided it does not touch the body.
Upon touching another person, one becomes pure by touching the ground and sipping drops of water;
likewise, one who stands in knee-deep water and performs the ritual sipping (ācamana) does not incur any fault.
Seated in water that reaches up to the knees, one should sip water;
having sipped water in the water, one is purified within, whereas sipping water outside [the water] effects purification externally.
One who has sipped water while standing outside is indeed pure in all circumstances;
one standing in water is pure for water-related rites, and one standing on dry land is pure for land-based activities.
But one who stands between both [water and dry land] and has sipped water attains purity;
neither with a dry garment in water, nor with a wet garment on dry land.
One should never perform acts such as sipping water (ācamana) with the knee outside [the garment].
Thus ends the section on sipping water (ācamana). Now follows the procedure for cleansing the teeth (dantadhāvana):

In the morning, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth for the sake of purification. Facing either the east or the northeast, raising the right arm, and sitting with the hands between the knees, one should brush the teeth while remaining silent, using a twig from a bitter, astringent, pungent, fragrant, thorny, milky, or shrubby tree or creeper that has been washed. In this regard, the wooden stick should be free of wounds, soft, undamaged by insects, fire, or water, twelve or eight finger-breadths long, as thick as the tip of the little finger, and prepared by cutting it at the middle joint.
The cleansing of the teeth is prescribed, as well as the tongue-scraper.

Among the Kṣatriyas and others, there is a reduction of one finger-breadth [at each stage]. For women, it is four finger-breadths. And for all, according to some, [it is the same]. The mantra for cleaning the teeth:
"O Lord of the Forest, grant us long life, strength, fame, splendor, progeny, cattle, wealth, sacred knowledge, wisdom, and intelligence."

Having washed and broken it, one should discard it. In this regard, the following are recommended for use as tooth-sticks: *khadira*, *garāka*, *ketakī*, *karavīra*, *kuṭaja*, *asana*, *arka*, *sarja*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *bilva*, *āmra*, *kadamba*, *karañja*, *vrajīva*, *veṇu*, *plakṣa*, *māṣaka*, *badarī*, *śirīṣa*, *kovidāra*, *pālāśa*, *śāka*, *vṛkṣa*, *śikhaṇḍin*, *priyaṅgu*, and *tamāla*. One should avoid *śālmali*, *ariṣṭa*, *bhavya*, *kiṃśuka*, *pīlu*, *bibhītaka*, *guggulu*, *ūkāprakumba*, *yaṣṭi*, *tinduka*, *madhūka*, *iṅguda*, *dhattūra*, *pāribhadra*, *amlīkā*, and so forth. One should not perform the cleansing of the teeth with bricks, wood, or stones.
Dadhi, nīla, dhava, mocā, kadamba, iṅguda, and tinduka;
Bandhūka, mallikā, rājaka, kārpāsa, and likewise śrīhara;
as well as udumbara, vaṭa, kramuka, śiṃśipā, aśvattha, and śāgra.
[25] If one cleanses the teeth with *kuśa* or *kāśa* grass, one should look at a cow; otherwise, one is not pure. [One should avoid] the *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *kāca*, *śleṣmātaka*, and *palāśa* trees.
The nirguṇḍī, śiṃśapā, aśoka, kadamba, kuṭaja, and vaṭa trees are both prescribed and prohibited; therefore, they are considered optional.

One should avoid the *palāśa* flower, vegetables, the *śiṃśipā*, cotton, the *damayantī*, the *śālmalī*, the *śirīṣa*, the *śamī*, the *lakṣmaṇā*, the *karañja*, the *vaṭa*, the *arka*, the *bakula*, the *pārijāta*, the *nirguṇḍī*, the *sūcīmukha*, and thorny trees; some say one should also avoid those that are foul-smelling, pungent-smelling, sweet, split, having bark, poisoned, or dried upright. Furthermore, regarding the seat, the bed, the vehicle, sandals, and the cleaning of the teeth—the *palāśa* and the *aśvattha* are to be avoided in all contemptible acts.
At a Śrāddha rite, at a sacrifice, during a religious observance, when the husband has gone abroad,
as well as during indigestion, at a wedding, during a fast, and during vows.
On the first lunar day, the new moon, the sixth, and especially on the ninth.

The cleaning of teeth with a tooth-stick (*dantadhāvana*) should be avoided. On the eighth, fourteenth, and full-moon days, one should avoid women, oil, and tooth-sticks, especially on Sundays, during the *vyatīpāta* yoga, on one's birthday, during the solar transits (*saṃkrānti*), and on the *nandā* tithis. On the sixth, first, fourteenth, eighth, and festival (*parvan*) days—especially on the new moon and the ninth—one should avoid oil massage, women, meat, and tooth-sticks.

In the absence of a tooth-stick or on prohibited days, purification of the mouth is achieved by twelve mouthfuls of water. Alternatively, one may clean the teeth with grass, leaves, water, or even with the fingers—excluding the index finger.
Firmness of the teeth is also attained by using the middle finger, the ring finger, and the thumb.
This is the procedure for cleaning the teeth.
Now, the procedure for bathing:
Having cleansed his teeth and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), one should perform the bath according to the rules.
All rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti for human beings have their root in the bath.
But a man who has not bathed is unfit for rites such as recitation and fire-oblations.
For a man habituated to bathing, there are ten qualities: beauty, splendor, strength, purity,
longevity, health, and freedom from greed.
It destroys bad dreams, and it is austerity and wisdom.
Through bathing, there shall be clarity of self, and the gods will always be favorably disposed;
likewise, good fortune, prosperity, happiness, nourishment, merit, knowledge, fame, and fortitude.
Great sins, misfortune, calamity, and evil thoughts—
bathing at dawn, especially so, removes grief, suffering, and the like.
Bathing at dawn and at midday is prescribed for forest-dwellers and householders;
for an ascetic, bathing three times a day is required, while for a student of sacred knowledge, it is once a day.

Or all [the members of the family] may perform it together at once; if they are unable, they may do so without the water libation. Furthermore, for all social classes, bathing must be performed preceded by purification.
For the twice-born, [the rite] should be accompanied by mantras; for women and Śūdras, it should be without mantras.
However, for Śūdras, the ritual act is recorded as being performed with the mantra "namas" (salutation).
One should not perform libations, sipping of water, recitation of mantras, sprinkling, and other such rites while wearing dry clothes in water or wet clothes on land.

In the case of the Brāhma-baths, the offering of water to the Sun (sūryārghya), the recitation of prayers (japa), the concluding rites (utsarjana), the libations (tarpaṇa), water-offerings (jala), sacrifices (iṣṭi), and burnt offerings (homa),
one does not incur fault by performing them with dry materials while standing in water.
Bathing is said to be of two kinds, distinguished as that of Varuṇa (vāruṇa) and the other (itarat).
Of these, the vāruṇa is primary, while the other is indeed secondary.
The Āgneya, Vāruṇa, Brāhma, Vāyavya, Divya,
and Sārasvata— these six types of bathing are traditionally recorded therein.
The fire-related bath is said to be with ashes, while that with water is called the Varuṇa bath;
the Brāhma bath consists of the *Āpo hi ṣṭhā* verses, and that is also remembered as the Mantra bath.
The *mārjana* consists of [the recitation] by quarters, by half-verses, and by whole verses; it is performed with that [water] over three verses.
