One should hold the water contained in the hand upon one's head, [reciting] the *brāhma* [mantra].
That which is remembered as the *brāhma* [bath] is equal to the *vāyavya* bath through the dust of cows;
the *divya* bath with the waters of heat and rain is remembered as being equal to bathing in the Gaṅgā.
That which is attained through the speech of Sarasvatī, the goddess of the learned, is known as Sārasvata;
likewise, the bath consisting of divine sacred sites is proclaimed by the Guru and the Ācāryas.
The speech of the learned is indeed more purifying than bathing at all sacred fords;
however, upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste, one must perform the Vāruṇa rite alone.
The Vāruṇa bath consists of that performed for a specific desire, that which removes impurities, and the ritual bath;
the others are to be understood according to their appropriateness in view of place, time, and other factors.
One should bathe facing the current of the water during the *mārjana* and *aghamarṣaṇa* rites;
at other times, one should face the sun, or at night, face either the east or the north.
One should perform the twilight prayer at the beginning of the twilight, as well as during the first and last watches of the night;
it is obligatory, occasional, optional, a constituent part of a ritual act, and a means of removing impurities.
The ritual bath (kriyā-snāna) is likewise the sixth; thus the sixfold bath is proclaimed.
It is indeed obligatory at midday, while for some it is also prescribed in the morning.
In the case of ascetics, those observing vows, celibates, performers of fire-sacrifices, students, and practitioners of austerities,
when there is defilement by food-leavings and the like, or contact with those who are untouchable;
Bathing on occasions such as the transit of planets is occasional (naimittika);
bathing for the sake of prosperity (puṣyasnāna) and the like is optional (kāmya), as prescribed by the rules of the astrologers.
That bath which is prescribed as a constituent part of the ritual for performing sacrifices and works of public utility is called *snāna*;
that which consists of the removal of impurities preceded by anointing with oil is also called *snāna*.
The very act of bathing at a sacred ford is called the ritual bath (*kriyā-snāna*);
however, one who is unfit for it should perform the bath merely by immersing himself and then sipping water according to the rules of purification.
Having washed away the remnants of food, one who is still impure from eating should likewise perform a bath;
one should not immerse the head in very little water, nor should one plunge into a small pool.
In the ritual bath, one should immerse the head; this applies to other lakes as well. The bath may take place before sunrise, after it, or even at the time of Saṃgava.
A brief bath in the morning is prescribed for the purpose of performing the fire-oblation and other rites;
this should be performed at rivers, streams, natural pools, excavated pits, and springs.
It is recommended at natural lakes, especially at sacred fords (tīrtha),
or at a step-well, a well, or a pond, whether belonging to another or consisting of warm water.
One who is always ill should always perform the morning bath with warm water alone.

There, having washed his feet and face, recollecting the *praṇava* and the *sāvitrī*, tying his topknot, and sipping water (*ācamana*), he should wash the bank, lay down *darbha* grass and other items, and with *darbha* in hand, having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and bowed to the water, he should enter while facing east with palms joined in reverence. Having wiped away perspiration and so forth, bathed, and sipped water twice, he—with *darbha* in hand—should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the water-deity hymns beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and stir the water while performing the *aghamarṣaṇa*. (Having bathed again and sipped water twice,) he should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the waters, or not. Then, wringing out the end of his garment, touching water, putting on two garments as lower and upper robes, and wringing out the bathing cloth, he should sip water and perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*).
Regarding the midday bath, however, there is this distinction:
the midday bath may be performed either briefly or in detail.
Here, the procedure for the brief version will be stated according to the *Smṛtisaṃgraha*.

There, having performed the purification rites and sipped water twice (*dvir-ācamya*), one should bow to Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, and one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). Having placed earth, *darbha* grass, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), rice grains, and sesame seeds upon a washed bank, one should divide the earth into three parts. Smearing the area below the navel with one portion and washing it off, one should bathe, sip water twice, and sprinkle the earth while reciting *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. Showing it to the sun with both hands while reciting *tat savitur vareṇyam*, one should smear the area above the navel with another portion while reciting *syonā pṛthivi bhava* or *dyāvāpṛthivī śāntā*. Then, sprinkling the head with the mantras “*āpo asmān mātaraḥ*,” “*idam āpaḥ pravahata*,” and “*sumitryā na āpa oṣadhayaḥ*,” and pouring out the remainder outside with “*durmitryās tasmai santu*,” one should wash the residue of the earth while reciting “*yo ‘smān dveṣṭi yaṃ ca vayaṃ dviṣmaḥ*. Having remembered the Gaṅgā at the bathing place (*tīrtha*) and bowed to Varuṇa with the mantra “*hiraṇyaśṛṅgaṃ varuṇaṃ prapadye*,” one should mentally fashion the bathing place as four cubits in size and turn the water clockwise. One should stand in river water reaching up to the knees, or sit elsewhere if it is not so deep. After bathing and rinsing the body, one should bathe again, sip water twice, and perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with verses addressed to the Waters (*abdaivata*) or Varuṇa, which possess signs of purity, cleanliness, and sanctity. Stirring the water three times with the mantra “*idaṃ me gaṅge*,” one should submerge oneself and perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite. While submerged, covering the ears, eyes, nose, and mouth with the thumbs and fingers, one should repeat the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra six, eight, twelve, or twenty-four times.
One should recite the three-verse hymn beginning with "ṛtaṃ ca," or the verse beginning with "drupadām";
or one should recite the syllable Om, and likewise meditate upon Viṣṇu, Śiva, and Sūrya.

Then, having immersed oneself three, five, seven, ten, or twelve times, and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice while still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libation of water (tarpaṇa). Then, having emerged from the water, one should wring out the edge of the bathing garment on the bank with the mantra: "To those who have been born in our family...

Thereafter, discarding the wet bathing garment and putting on two clean garments—either cotton or linen, white or dyed with mineral pigments—one should wash the calves and feet, perform the ritual sipping of water twice, and apply the vertical sectarian mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) using clay from the Gaṅgā or other sacred sites.
Thus ends the section on bathing.
[29] Now follows the procedure for the Brahmayajña and the libation (tarpaṇa): with the left hand supporting [the right], one should perform it with the right hand.
Or alternatively, the libation may be performed with both the right and left hands.
In the ancestral rite (śrāddha), at the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa), at marriage, and in giving, water is offered with one hand;
however, in the libation (tarpaṇa), it must be offered with both hands, and not otherwise.
Having placed sesame seeds in the left hand, one should offer libations into the midst of the water;
never on dry land, nor on a garment, nor on the bank, nor in a vessel, nor on the root of a hair.
One should offer handfuls of water on dry ground for those who have died in an unnatural manner.

Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), facing east, one should satisfy the gods with white sesame seeds using the *daiva* (divine) *tīrtha*. Wearing the sacred thread around the neck (*nivītī*), facing north, one should satisfy the *ṛṣis* with variegated sesame seeds using the *kāya* (body) *tīrtha*. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), facing south, one should satisfy the teachers, the ancestors, and the *pitṛs* with black sesame seeds using the *paitrya* (ancestral) *tīrtha*. Alternatively, one may satisfy the gods and the *ṛṣis* with pure water, and all the ancestors with sesame seeds; or satisfy them all with all three substances. Or else, one may offer unbroken rice grains (*akṣata-taṇḍula*) for the gods, sesame seeds for the *ṛṣis*, and sesame seeds for the ancestors. One should give one handful (*añjali*) for each of the gods, two for each of the *ṛṣis*, and three for each of the ancestors, using the mantras prescribed by one's own tradition. Alternatively, one may recite: "I satisfy those gods who are Brahmā and the others; I satisfy the gods of *bhūḥ*; I satisfy the gods of *bhuvaḥ*; I satisfy the gods of *svar*; I satisfy the gods of *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. "I satisfy those *ṛṣis* who are Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and the others; I satisfy the *ṛṣis* of *bhūḥ*; I satisfy the *ṛṣis* of *bhuvaḥ*; I satisfy the *ṛṣis* of *svar*; I satisfy the *ṛṣis* of *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. "I satisfy those ancestors who are Soma accompanied by the *pitṛs*, Yama, the Aṅgirasas, the Agniṣvāttas, the Kavyavāhanas, and the others; I satisfy the *pitṛs* of *bhūḥ*; I satisfy the *pitṛs* of *bhuvaḥ*; I satisfy the *pitṛs* of *svar*; I satisfy the *pitṛs* of *bhūr-bhuvaḥ-svar*. Thereafter, one should satisfy the father and others individually. One should also satisfy the mother and others, the maternal grandfather and others, the maternal grandmother and others, paternal uncles and their wives, elder brothers and their wives, maternal uncles and their wives, gurus, teachers, preceptors, friends, relatives, kinsmen, those who have provided wealth, and those who have supported one, as well as their wives.

In the absence of sesame seeds, the libation for the ancestors (pitṛtarpaṇa) may be performed with gold, silver, copper, darbha grass, sesame seeds, and water; or it may be done by means of a sword or a pearl held in the hand.
When possible, one should not perform [the rite] with water alone;
nor should one whose father is living perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with black sesame seeds.
On the seventh lunar day, on Sundays, and on the days of one’s birth-star, libation with sesame seeds is forbidden inside the house; it should be performed outside.
[30] There is no libation with sesame seeds in an auspicious house or on an auspicious day, nor during a marriage, an initiation, or a tonsure ceremony, according to their respective order.

Some say that the libation with sesame seeds (*tilatarpaṇa*) should not be performed for a year, half a year, or even half of that; others say it should not be performed during a month when an auspicious occasion (*vṛddhi*) occurs.

On specific lunar days (tithis) and at special sacred sites (tīrthas), as well as always for one who has died, the sapinda relatives should offer rice-balls (piṇḍas); however, in this case, they should do so excluding the funeral rice-ball (pretapiṇḍa).
They should indeed offer [the śrāddha] at the Pitṛyajña sacrifice and at Gayā;
some ancient authorities say that the anniversary of death is equal to Gayā.

Restrained, one should satisfy the ancestors at sacred fords with sesame seeds for the sake of the śrāddha, uttering their names and lineages, while they manifest in the forms of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas.
The festival of lamps (Dīpotsava) should be observed on the fourteenth day, as well as the libation to Yama;
this should always be performed even on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight known as Kṛṣṇāṅgāra-caturdaśī.
To Yama, the King of Dharma, to Death, to the Ender,
to Vaivasvata, to Time, and to the Destroyer of all beings.
Salutations indeed to Audumbara, Dadhna, Nīla, Parameṣṭhin,
Vṛkodara, Citra, and Citragupta.
These fourteen mantras should each be accompanied by the word "namas";
with each one, they should offer three handfuls of water mixed with sesame seeds.
It should be performed either with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin) or with it over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin);
for Yama possesses both a divine and a paternal nature.

Then one should wring out the bathing garment. One should not wring it while it is folded three times; nor should one wring it in water; nor should one spread it out with its ends pointing toward the south. Having bathed and while still wearing wet clothes, if one voids feces or urine, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and bathe again.
One should not place the upper garment below, nor the lower garment above.
One should never wear a garment that is entirely black or entirely red.
A woolen cloth, a hempen garment, a deerskin, a meditation-band, or an upper garment;
or else, another sacred thread (yajñopavīta) may serve as the second [garment] here.
Having bathed, one should not wring out the hair, nor should one squeeze water from the limbs;
one should never shake out the garment, nor should one shake out the hair.
[31] Having bathed, one should by no means wipe one's limbs with the bathing cloth;
one should not wipe one spot with another, nor should one smear one spot with another.
Having bathed, one should not brush the teeth nor wipe the mouth with a cloth;
one should not perform a clay-bath at night, nor on a Tuesday or a Sunday.
Neither cow urine nor cow dung should be used for purification during the two twilights; at night, purification is not achieved by cow dung.
During the day, purification is by means of water, cow dung, and cow urine; at night, it is by means of water and ashes.
One should draw out five or three lumps of earth from the waters of others;
one may bathe when defiled by offspring, but not for the sake of daily rites during the dead of night.
The "great night" (*mahāniśā*) consists of two *ghaṭikās* during the middle watch of the night.
During the great night, there should be no performance of rites for obligatory (*nitya*), optional (*kāmya*), or occasional (*naimittika*) purposes.
One who has not yet bathed should first bathe at night with warm water;
one should not reject water, nor should one revile it, but rather remember other sacred bathing places while at a sacred bathing place.
One should not bathe after a festival has ended, nor after a rite for auspiciousness has been concluded,
nor after escorting friends and kinsmen, nor after having worshipped one's chosen deity.
On the anniversary of death, on the day of one's birth-star, on the first and ninth lunar days,
when performing a śrāddha on another day, and during solar transits and eclipses;
On Sundays, on the seventh lunar day, on the fourteenth, the eighth, the eleventh, the full moon, the sixth, and especially on the new moon;
One should avoid anointing with oil, sexual intercourse, meat, and the use of a tooth-stick;
nor should one bathe with hot water at other times except for a specific reason.
One should avoid ritual bathing for the sake of specific desires using the warm water of others; one should not bathe in a river after sunset, especially during the middle watch of the day.
One may bathe after kindling a fire, or in great bodies of water such as lakes and rivers,
on occasions such as an eclipse, a solar transit, a marriage, a death, or a birth.
Acts such as bathing and giving gifts should be performed at night during optional vows;
having bathed in a river, one who knows the Dharma should not praise another river.

In the event of touching that which is untouchable, neither the bath nor the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite nor the libation (*tarpaṇa*) [is required]; both husband and wife remain impure when they have engaged in sexual union.
Upon rising from bed, the woman becomes pure, but the man remains impure;
however, during sexual intercourse in the fertile period, he should bathe for fear of conceiving a child.
And because that [impurity] does not exist outside of the proper season, purification is like that for urine and feces;
women are not considered impure by the menstrual flow caused by disease.
The details regarding touching outcasts (cāṇḍālas) and others will be explained separately.
Upon following a corpse, bathing is prescribed, and the consumption of clarified butter is an alternative option.
Where a man must bathe with his clothes on,
there a woman who is bathing her head will always suffer from diseases of the head or will have matted hair.
If one is unable [to bathe], one should never bathe in cool water in a beautiful house on an auspicious day; nor should one who seeks heat do so.

When bathing with water drawn from a source, the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) must be performed. There may or may not be the recitation of the *aghamarṣaṇa* mantra. As for the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with water, it may or may not be performed. However, the libation on dry land (*sthalatarpaṇa*) should be performed by throwing unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings into another vessel containing water, or into a pit filled with water. It should be performed on a patch of ground covered with sacrificial grass (*barhis*), not on ground without grass, nor on impure ground. Now follows the procedure for the oil massage bath (*abhyaṅgasnāna*): all lunar days (*tithis*) are always prohibited for an oil massage.
One should avoid the second [alternative] precisely because of the twofold fault of being seen and unseen.
Mustard oil, fragrant oil, and oil scented with flowers—
even oil mixed with other substances— is never defiled.
In prohibitions concerning oil massages, sesame oil is what is forbidden;
however, the prohibition of massage applies even to mustard oil and other such oils.
Anointing with oil is what constitutes "sneha" (oleation), such as mustard oil and the like;
there is no prohibition against using oil for food, for that [prohibition] applies specifically to anointing.
The word *taila* is a well-established conventional term for the oil of sesame seeds (*tilasneha*); it is not merely etymological.
Therefore, it applies even to products derived from sesame, such as oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) and sesame sweets (*tilamodaka*).
And no prohibition whatsoever arises regarding *śaṣkulī* (fried cakes), *kṛsara* (rice and peas), and the like;
for the word "oil" (*taila*) is applied to mustard seeds and such things because they resemble its function.
For one who performs an oil massage on the days of the weekdays, there is distress, luster, short life, wealth, poverty, ill health, and the fulfillment of all desires respectively.
Misfortune and widowhood result from the Guru and Śukra being in the two opposing houses;
likewise, [an initiation] on a forbidden day or weekday, at night, or for one who is ill, is prohibited.
Oil mixed with other substances never becomes defiled;
however, one who has bathed his head with oil should not touch any part of his body with it.
In every case, for the sake of the obligatory daily rites, one should certainly bathe at some time,
even if only once, using either earth or warm water.
Thus ends the procedure for bathing. Now follows the procedure for the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*):
"One who neglects the twilight devotions is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts."
Whatever action one performs, one does not experience its fruit.

There, having washed his feet and hands and performed *ācamana* twice, he should perform the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) on his head with water and *darbha* grass while reciting the *mantras* beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā," which have the waters as their deity; then, having sprinkled himself and drunk water while reciting "sūryaś ca," he should perform *ācamana* twice. At evening time, however, he should drink water while reciting "agniś ca. Then, having performed *ācamana* twice and again performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the water-mantras, he should sprinkle himself and offer three handfuls of water consecrated by the *gāyatrī* as an *arghya* offering to the Sun. In an impure place, one should avoid performing the ritual sprinkling with a stream of water.
One should perform [the ritual] with water held either in a vessel or in the left hand.
Then, having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should recite the *Gāyatrī* while standing and facing east until the sun is seen;
in the evening, one should recite it while seated and facing west until the stars appear.
A celibate student and a householder should each recite it one hundred and eight times.
A forest-dweller and an ascetic should recite it more than a thousand times;
or, in times of distress, one should recite the Goddess twenty-eight or eight times.

Holding darbha grass in his hand until the oblation is completed, he should rotate the Goddess either by hand according to the stated number while standing upon the darbha, or else by means of rosary beads.
With beads made of gold, silver, copper, crystal, and likewise gems;
with those originating from ariṣṭa, putrajīva, indrākṣa, and conch shells.
The rosary may also be made of rudrākṣa seeds, lotus seeds, knots of kuśa grass, or gems;
it should consist of one hundred and eight beads.
Whether with fifty-four or twenty-seven repetitions of the labial [syllable], the whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is superior; the mental recitation (*mānasa*) is indeed even better than that.
That which is whispered recitation (*upāṃśujapa*) is soundless, with the tongue moving and the lips closed;
whereas mental recitation (*mānasa*) is said to have the tongue and lips motionless.

One should not recite with the gaze directed downward, nor with the mind on something else, nor with the feet crossed or hands placed over them; one should not recite with legs outstretched, nor while leaning against something, nor when lazy or impure.
Nor while walking, nor while speaking, nor while looking to the side;
nor without counting [the breaths], nor without *darbha* grass, nor without having tied his topknot and his girdle.
Withdrawal of the mind, purity, silence, reflection on the meaning of the mantra,
freedom from distraction, and lack of despondency are the causes for the successful accomplishment of japa.

At the conclusion of the recitation (*japa*), one should worship the Sun with solar mantras in the morning, or with mantras dedicated to Varuṇa in the evening. Alternatively, at both times, one may worship with mantras addressed to Jātavedas, Viṣṇu, or Rudra. Having paid homage to the quarters and the deities of the quarters, one should offer salutations to Sandhyā, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, Sarasvatī, and to all the deities. Such matters should be performed according to one's own traditional custom. Then, having again paid homage to the Sun, remaining silent and taking fire and water in secret, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) according to the prescribed rule.
Thus ends the procedure for the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana). Now follows the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa):
in the fire-oblation, the primary officiants are the sacrificer, his wife, his son, and his daughter.
An officiating priest, a pupil, a teacher, a brother, a sister's son, and a son-in-law.

That substance which has been offered by these [officiants] is itself considered *dhuta* (purified). The wife and the daughter may offer the oblation themselves, excluding the ritual sprinkling (*paryukṣaṇa*).
However, when the husband and wife are not present, the offering must be made by the officiant or others.
If it should occur out of sight of both [the giver and the recipient], the offering is rendered useless;
the giver must be present in proximity as the one who performs the dedication and relinquishment.
In the absence [of the sacrificer], however, the wife shall be the one who performs the dedication and the renunciation;
in the absence of the wife, however, the Adhvaryu shall do so with her authorization.
One who performs the *prasava* rite on a cart that has not been prepared without obtaining permission shall not observe a fast while traveling abroad; rather, his wife shall maintain the vow.
Or, at all times, the sacrificer, being pure, should offer facing that direction;
for the morning oblation, the time is until the end of the *saṃgava* period, or likewise before sunrise.
In the evening, once the sun has set, the time for the fire-oblation (homa) lasts for nine nāḍikās;
it should be performed when the fire is well-kindled with abundant dry fuel and is free of smoke.
An offering must be made into a fire that is crackling with glowing embers, and never otherwise;
when the fire turns clockwise and its smoke is auspicious, it brings success to the ritual action.

Having swept around the fire, strewn grass around it, and sprinkled water around it, one should then adorn it with perfumes and flowers. Having cast a fuel-stick [into the fire] and, once the fuel-stick is well-ignited, having moved it more than a finger’s breadth away, one should offer the complete oblation (*haumya*) in the temple of the deity using the *devatīrtha* part of the hand, whether with the *kāya* or *saumya* portion. Then, having again cast a fuel-stick, performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), swept around the fire, and sprinkled water around it, one should give the remains of the offering to a Brāhmaṇa and bow down. Milk, curd, barley-gruel, clarified butter, boiled rice, unhusked rice, Soma, meat, oil, and water—these ten are for the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Perhaps there should be a sacramental rite for them in the domestic fire, like the Agnihotra, but devoid of mantras;
or else, they should be sprinkled three times with water, and their meat should not be offered in the domestic fire.
Śāli, śyāmāka, nīvāra, vrīhi, godhūma, yāvaka,
as well as yava, anala, and priyaṅgu— the rice grains of these are to be used for the oblation (homya).
Priyaṅgu, wheat, śyāmāka, rice, and barley may be used for the oblation according to their generic form;
however, sesame seeds must indeed be used in their actual physical form.
A liquid substance should be offered with the *sruva* ladle, while a solid oblation should be offered with the hand;
for rice and barley, one hundred oblations are prescribed.
That food, doubled in size, is a morsel shaped like a peacock’s egg;
however, a ball of food the size of a hen’s egg is designated as a *piṇḍa*.
The portion for the *avadāna* should be the size of a thumb-joint, or even smaller than that;
however, the clarified butter for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering should be measured at four finger-breadths.
Alms consist of a single mouthful; four mouthfuls constitute an *agra*;
and multiplying that *agra* by four is called *hantakāra*.
Almsfood is either abundant or excellent; each preceding type is four times [the size of] the following.
Human food is twice that, as is a *śarāva* measure and a vessel.
Or alternatively:
one *prastha* of grain is prescribed for sixty-four oblations;
half that amount should be used for sesame seeds, and half of that again for clarified butter.
[36] Now, regarding the fuel-sticks (*samidh*): the fuel-stick is produced from *palāśa*, *khadira*, *aśvattha*, *śamī*, or *udumbara*.
Others know that apāmārga, arka, dūrvā, and kuśa grasses [are used].
The fuel-sticks should be made with their bark intact, straight, smooth, and of equal length;
they are recommended to be ten finger-breadths long, or likewise twelve finger-breadths.
Freshly cooked, cut evenly, rounded like the index finger,
unsplit, without double-prongs, and free from the defects of worms.
One should avoid those that are burnt, emaciated, or obese, as well as those that are short or long.
Or alternatively: "The fuel-stick, the purifier, and the Veda—these three are measured at one span (prādeśa);
the fuel-wood (idhma) should be made double that length, and the enclosing-stick (paridhi) is traditionally said to be triple."
According to the Smṛti tradition, the fuel-stick is one span long, and the enclosing stick is remembered as being twice that length.
Now, the procedure for *darbha* grasses:
*kuśa*, *kāśa*, barley, *dūrvā*, *uśīra*, and *kandura*;
wheat, rice, and *muñja*—these are the ten radiant *darbha* grasses.
On the new moon day of the month of Nabhas, one who is pure should collect darbha grass;
that grass, being of unexhausted potency, may be employed again and again.
The mantra for uprooting *kuśa* grass and *darbha* grass: O Darbha, born together with Viriñci, produced from the creation of Parameṣṭhin, dispel all my sins; may you bring me well-being.
Having thus recited the mantra, one facing either the east or the north should then extract [the tooth],
cutting it once with the mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*.
For rites for the ancestors, auspicious green blades with uncut tips and non-dried tips should be used;
for rites for the gods and for recitations such as japa, those that are rootless should be employed.
Kuśa grass with seven blades is recommended for rites dedicated to the gods and those dedicated to the ancestors;
the two purifiers (pavitraka) should be fresh, with tips intact, and one span in length.
The purifier for a Brāhmaṇa consists of four blades of Darbha grass;
it is prescribed that there shall be one fewer blade for each successive social class, in due order.
[37] Or it may be for all [the deities]; it should be purified by two [mantras], whether knotted or not.
For rites of pacification (śāntika), it should be made with three [mantras], and likewise for rites of enrichment (pauṣṭika) with five.

In the case of malevolent rites (abhicāra), some say it should be performed with four [fingers]; others say it should be done without desire. Accompanied by a pavitra and darbha grass, one should perform the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) as a limb of the rite.
That [water] shall not be considered *ucchiṣṭa* (leavings); however, one should avoid the leavings of that person who has eaten.
This applies to those by whom the offering of the *piṇḍas*, the *śrāddha*, or the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors has been performed.
The discarding of those *darbha* grasses that have been used for excrement, urine, and so forth is prescribed;
likewise, those situated within the waist-knot (*nīvī*) and those always remaining on the sacrificial ground must be discarded.
One should not drink with the right hand while the *darbha* grass remains in the left;
however, there is no fault for one who drinks using a cup or similar vessel as a support.
One should never sip water using the *brahmagranthi* (the sacred thread knot) nor with *dūrvā* grass,
during bathing, giving gifts, recitation, fire-offerings, Vedic study, or the libations to the ancestors.
One should keep the hands together with sacrificial grass (*pavitra*) or *darbha* blades, and not otherwise.
In the absence of *kuśa*, however, *kāśa* grass may be used; *kāśa* is traditionally considered equal to *kuśa*.
In the absence of *kāśa* grass, other *darbha* grasses should be taken as appropriate;
one should not cut them while they are wet, nor should one cut them at night or during the two twilights.
In the absence of darbha grass, one should perform the ritual with gold, silver, copper, or gems.
Thus concludes the procedure for gathering darbha grass. Now, regarding the sacrificial grass (barhis): one should take grass made of kāśa; if that is not available, one may use kuśa.
Śara, anuja, vāśa, bāla, mauñja, arjuna, and ikṣu.
When fragrant tejanā wood, dūrvā grass, and even the milky trees are available,
one may take sacrificial grass (barhis) as desired from among all types of grass.
Wise men avoid grass that is thorny, has a long stalk, is black-rooted, or is foul-smelling; others also avoid grass that is white at the tip or red at the base.
In the absence of *kuśa* grass, others say that leaves, creepers, and medicinal herbs may be used;
among these, the *bandhūka* and *śūkara* are desired, provided they are free from the *parivyādhaka*.
One should especially use thick darbha grasses, or alternatively, kāśa, kuśa, śara, balvaja,
puṇḍarīka, barley, rice, or even common grasses.
[38] Now, regarding the fuel: the fuel should primarily be made of *pālāśa* or *khādira* wood; in the absence of these, other woods may be used.
It should be made from śamī, vaṭa, or udumbara wood, or from aśvattha wood if those are unavailable.
In particular, fuel should be prepared from all types of forest trees;
however, one should avoid these trees: the *kovidāra* and the *vibhītaka*.
Having avoided the *kapittha*, the *āmalaka*, the *rājavṛkṣa*, the *śākadruma*, as well as the *nīpa*,
the *nimba*, the *karañja*, the *tilaka*, the *śālmalī*, and even the *śleṣmātaka*,
any other tree may be taken.
Now, regarding the ladles and other implements: the *agnihotrahavaṇī* may be made of either *vaikaṅkata* or *pālāśa* wood;
the *juhū* is made of *pālāśa*, the *upabhṛt* of *aśvattha*, and the *dhruvā* of *vaikaṅkata*.
Alternatively, all the offering-ladles (sruk) for these [deities] should be made from other trees;
or all the ladles should be made of *śamī* wood, or all of them may be made from the *bhūrja* tree.
In the absence of those, ladles made from other sacrificial trees may be used according to availability;
however, the *śamyā*, the *prāśitra* vessel, and the *mekṣaṇa* should be made of *khadira* wood.
The pestle should be made of khādira wood and the mortar of palāśa;
or both may be made of vāruṇa wood, or if those are unavailable, they may be made from other trees.
The cups (camasa) are prescribed as being made from Palāśa, Vaṭa, or other trees;
however, if they are not of Aśvattha or Vāraṇa wood, the vessel for the Iḍā offering here must be made from another tree.
In the absence of the primary substance, however, a similar substance is substituted;
and as long as something similar exists, that very thing should be taken.
There is no substitute for a rite performed for a specific desire, but there is one for obligatory and occasional rites;
however, some authorities maintain that even in the case of a rite for a specific desire, a substitute is permitted after the ritual has already commenced.
There can be no substitute for the mantra, the master, the deity, the fire, or the ritual action;
nor is there a substitute for the place and the time—for in the case of the two fire-drills, the fire itself is that [substitute].
The wise declare that the fire-drill (araṇi) is mounted upon the fuel-stick (samidh);
for the absence of one thing is not accepted as a substitute for another absence.
Nor should any prohibited substance ever be substituted;
however, that substance which is unfit for the consumption of those learned in the Vedas may be accepted without fault.
[39] Nowhere may a substitute be used for the substance intended for the act of oblation;
however, some say that where there is an optional substance already resolved upon, it may be used.
In the absence of that [primary substance], a similar one should be taken, but not another conceptual substitute;
for when the primary substance is unavailable, one acts with the intention of using a representative.
For one who employs a substitute, that very substitute is indeed to be accepted when the primary object is obtained;
however, if the primary object is obtained once the substitute has been taken up, [the substitute is abandoned].
In that case, disregarding the primary [meaning], one should conclude by means of the secondary [meaning] alone,
provided that some primary [word] has been employed, even if it is used figuratively.
If one who employs another substance— whether of the same class or of a different class—
should first obtain [the desired result], [then that other substance is the cause].
Even though there is no difference in their being appropriated, one should abandon the former and resort to the latter;
when the primary [appropriation] is absent, that which was appropriated as secondary perishes.
In that regard, the primary simile is to be accepted, not the secondary one;
for even if it is unsuitable for the conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the primary one alone is indeed taken.
But another substitute that is fit for the ritual action is not accepted;
for even if such a thing is obtained, no regard is paid to it when the primary object is incapable of performing the function.
Having taken what is suitable, one employs that which is capable [of the task],
provided that a primary substance sufficient for both [the purpose and the quantity] is available.
The adoption of wild rice (nīvāra) is not for the sake of the large size of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa),
since there remain other substances such as black rice (kṛṣṇavrīhi) when the ritual is being performed.
Even though it is not black, rice is to be accepted; it is not non-rice merely because it possesses the quality of blackness.
Likewise, [a tree] is recognized by its effects, its forms, its leaves, its sap, its flowers, and even its fruits.
It should always be taken with perfumes and flavors; in the absence of the preceding, each subsequent one is used.
Rice, barley, śyāmāka, or nīvāra may serve as the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Bamboo, barley, juice, tubers, roots, fruits, water, truth, or sacrificial oblation— one should perform these according to availability.
When there is a failure of the sacrificial oblation, another substitute should be known as the truth;
one should relinquish one's own truth by aiming it toward the primary deity.
[40] Or rather, other similar items may also be accepted, such as mere grain;
however, mung beans, varaka beans, kodrava millet, and kodra rice are not to be accepted under any circumstances.
Or, in the absence of rice and barley, one may accept herbs that possess husks and grains, provided they are free from *ānuka* and *kodrava*.
That which is produced in villages belongs to those of the village, and that which is born in the forest belongs to those of the forest.
In the absence of barley, however, wheat may be used, and after that, bamboo-grains and the like.
According to the statement in the *Chandoga-gṛhya-sūtra*, one should offer as oblation, in the event of the absence of sacrificial materials,
either the fruit of a tree suitable for sacrifice or pure water.
Just as milk may never be available for the purpose of the Agnihotra oblation,
then rice, barley, or even another herb should be taken.
Wild forest herbs, tree fruits, and water—these are to be taken in order for the performance of the fire-oblation; in the absence of each preceding one, each subsequent one is to be used.
In their absence, one should offer with faith the truth of one's own self.
For the purpose of the oblation, cow’s ghee should be taken; in its absence, that of a buffalo;
or goat’s ghee; and if even that is unavailable, oil itself shall be taken directly.
In the absence of oil, that which is produced from oil—that is, originating from sesame—should be taken.
In the absence of that, oil from *atasī*, safflower, or mustard seeds, or tree oil should be taken; in the absence of each preceding one, the next subsequent one is to be used.
In its absence, the wise man should prepare a paste from any one of barley, rice, or śyāmāka, mixing it with water, and employ it for the purpose of ghee.
Among vegetable oils, one should avoid those derived from the *puṃnāga*, the neem, and castor;
or, among animal fats, one should successively avoid cow’s ghee, goat’s ghee, buffalo’s ghee, and so forth.
In the absence of that, the milk of cows and other animals is prescribed in due order;
in its absence, curd is to be taken; and in its absence, oil is desired.
Where clarified butter and such things for the purpose of ointment and so forth are never to be obtained,
there one will disregard milk and other substances and take oil directly.
Where curd is primary, even there it may be [substituted] by milk in its absence;
in the case of goats and so forth, [milk or curd is used], but if that is unavailable, then cow's ghee.
[41] In the continuum of cause and effect, that which is the primary producer should be accepted [as the cause]. For this very reason, in the absence of ghee, one first takes curd and then milk.
If any other sacrificial oblations (havis) whatsoever are available,
clarified butter (ājya) should be used in all cases, according to the opinion of the sage Bharadvāja.
If it is impossible to perform a rite that is mandatory during its primary time, it must be performed even during its secondary time; for in this context, the secondary time is also of such a nature.
The evening oblation should not be performed until morning, nor the morning oblation until evening; one should not let a *pārvaṇa* sacrifice lapse beyond the next *pārvaṇa*.
One must certainly perform the sacrifice first with *śyāmāka*, *vrīhi*, or barley, each at its own proper time; however, there is no transgression of the *āgrayaṇa* in this case.
Thus, for a subsequent rite,
the secondary time (gauṇa-kāla) is that which follows its own primary time and precedes the primary time of the preceding rite.
In all cases, one should perform the enjoined rite during the secondary times;
having offered oblations with the Vyāhṛtis as an expiation, one should then proceed with the rite.
If the primary means cannot be obtained at the primary time,
let even a secondary means be employed by resorting to that primary time.
One should not wait for a secondary time out of greed for the primary substance,
as long as a collection of offerings belonging to a single fortnight continues to pass by.
Because of the injunction for daily oblations throughout the fortnight, having offered those, one should sacrifice with the *Tantumatī* [offering];
thus, due to the displacement from its own time, a certain secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) is determined.
Now, another secondary period is also described due to decline:
one who has fallen into various calamities such as illness or disease, or even one who has gone upon a journey.
Even when there is the loss of one's kingdom, a lack of wealth, or while living in the house of a teacher,
and when other such circumstances have arisen;
One should perform the combined Agnihotra sacrifices as far as possible;
for among these various occasions, that which is mentioned here refers to one specific case.
One should understand that all this has been set forth regarding all the signs,
whether they be the oblations for the fortnights in their entirety or even the oblations not belonging to the fortnights.
[42] One should offer the oblation there after having combined [the portions]; this application is now described:
one should draw up [the milk] on the first day of the lunar fortnight, in the evening, in the event of an emergency, or on another day.
Indeed, for as many days as there are prior to the day of the fast (aupavasathya),
for that many days one should perform the fourfold ladling-out (catur-unnayana).
In the case of a constant *sruk* ladle that is accompanied by another vessel,
one should either make another *sruk* larger or pour [the contents] into it.
There is one fuel-stick, a single oblation, and only one wiping;
the attendance should be performed once; the remainder is held to follow the original model.
In the same way, in the subsequent cases as well, one performs the offerings combined: from the day of fasting until the morning offering, one offers all the morning offerings together once.
By means of the application of superimposition, one superimposes what is not there;
thus it is with other practices where misfortune arises.
In the same way, when a calamity occurs on any day prior to the Upavasatha,
that very calamity is accepted as the limit for the condensation of the fire-oblations.

Therefore, having begun at some point, one may combine into a single fortnight all the *homa* offerings equal in number to those [missed], whether they be few or many, as if they occurred during a time of calamity.
Thus, there may be a complete or partial compounding of those oblations belonging to one side,
but not of those situated on the other side.
On the day preceding the sacrifice (upavasathya), the evening oblation (sāyaṃ-homa) should be performed separately;
likewise, on the day of the sacrifice (yajaniya), the morning oblation (prātar-homa) should be performed separately.
If, for whatever reason, one finds oneself devoid of all fasting,
then even that evening *homa* is combined with the previous ones.
If the offense does not depart by that much, and even after another fortnight,
then a separate reconciliation must indeed be performed once again in that case.
But a mutual compounding of those situated in different categories is not enjoined.
Thus, when one has fallen into distress, one should act in this manner toward each category.
In the third subsequent fortnight, one should not perform the ritual union;
however, if a calamity should somehow persist for a long time, one may do so.
One should perform the fortnightly oblation continuously for as long as one lives;
in this matter, the limit is indeed misfortune itself, not the completion of a series of fortnights.
[43] Now, another method of combining is explained: both the evening and morning fire-oblations, however, may be combined at the evening time.
In the event of an offense, one should offer there either one or two fuel-sticks;
because the evening oblation is primary, its ritual procedure (tantra) is prescribed for that occasion.
One should perform four oblations; three and two are the evening oblations, and two are the morning oblations. Now, in the evening homa, if there is but a single fuel-stick—
If the second [offering] has been prepared as fuel, it should be offered in the morning;
one should wipe [the ladle] twice, as in the evening oblation, and likewise twice in the morning oblation.
The attendance (upasthāna) should be performed once; the remainder shall be as in the original rite.
Some, having offered two oblations, lie down and close their eyes.
Having thus interrupted [the sequence], one should then perform two oblations;
in the event of a teacher's misfortune, all [the remaining rites] should somehow be combined together in the morning.
Considering that a calamity may last for a long time, if a sacrificial offering is performed for a fortnight and, in the interim, the calamity should somehow depart;
At each appropriate time, the oblation should again be performed according to the rule or not;
however many [oblations] are combined here, all of them begin in the evening.
Rites such as the morning fire-oblation (*prātarhoma*) have their conclusion at the end of the morning period, but they do not begin in the morning;
however, if a calamity should arise in the morning, [they may be performed then].
Likewise, one combines [the offerings] at the forenoon, afternoon, and other such occasions, as well as on an auspicious occasion;
however, if there is a fear of the death of an Agnihotrin during the night in the bright fortnight, [one acts accordingly].
Having offered the evening oblation, he should then immediately offer the morning oblations as well,
if there should be a fear of the death of the Agnihotrin during the dark fortnight.
One should offer all the oblations in this fortnight using what remains from the previous sacrifice;
and one should perform the New Moon sacrifice (darśeṣṭi) if that sacrifice has not already been performed.
For each of the principal deities individually,
he offers oblations of ghee taken four times with both the *puro'nuvākyā* and the *yājyā* verses.
One should offer oblations in this manner; otherwise, they are offered everywhere except in times of calamity.
Now, if there should be a suspicion of the husband’s death during the middle of an *iṣṭi* or an *ayana*:

Having taken together in a single vessel four portions of clarified butter for each of the remaining deities of the sacrifice, along with the sacrificial ladles (camasa), according to their respective numbers.

One should offer oblations with the *puronuvākyā* and *yājyā* verses as before; likewise, during the interval between the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, there may be apprehension regarding the death of the master.
There, until the end of the final joint [of his life], he performs the Agnihotra sacrifices without exception,
as well as many Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices at that very time.
One should perform here the remaining seasonal festivals of the four-month period;
in the absence of an animal, one should offer a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) dedicated to the deity of the animal sacrifice.
Or he may prepare *āmikṣā*, or even perform a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*);
if one who has maintained the sacred fires dies during the dark fortnight, he should do so at that time.
Then, one should offer all the remaining oblations; thus says Āśvalāyana.
Others, however, should perform the New Moon sacrifice (darśeṣṭi) at that very time, provided the deceased died during the dark fortnight.
They desire the morning oblation for a deceased person on a night during the bright fortnight;
whatever rule applies to one who maintains the sacred fires (āhitāgni) also applies to one who maintains the domestic fire (aupāsanika).
Thus the Śāṭyāyanaka Brāhmaṇa declares;
however, in this regard, one should perform the twilight rites (saṃdhyā), the iṣṭi sacrifice, the caru oblation, and the fire offering throughout one's entire life.

A twice-born man should not abandon [the daily rites] even during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka); by abandoning them, he would go to a lower state. He should perform the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) constantly, except during the period of impurity itself.
One should not neglect one's own duties, whether they be daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), or otherwise;
for by the omission of one's own duty, one falls within a year, unless there is an emergency.
If one’s own religious duties are neglected due to atheism, falling [from one's status] is recorded as occurring within a month;
purification for that occurs only through a twelve-year vow, and not otherwise. Upon seeing such a person, one should look at the sun; upon touching them, one should bathe with one's clothes on.
By conversing with him or laughing with him, one becomes equal to him in a year;
by eating his food, one becomes so immediately; and by sharing a bed or a seat, one becomes so instantly.
Thus concludes the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa).
Now follows the procedure for the worship of the deities:
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Īśāna, Sūrya, Agni, and Gaṇādhipa.
One should worship Durgā, Sarasvatī, Lakṣmī, or Gaurī daily.
The deities reside in the waters, in fire, in the heart, in the sun, on the sacrificial ground, in images,
in the Śālagrāma stone marked with the discus, in paintings, and in ritual hand-gestures (mudrās).
[45] Gold, gems, cows, and Brahmins are always present;
[one should worship them] with the Puruṣasūkta, or with the Gāyatrī, or with the Praṇava.
Or, with the permission of the Guru, he should worship using the mantras that possess their specific characteristics;
or it may be done by means of the names of the deities, ending in the dative case and accompanied by the word "namaḥ."
Invitation, the seat, water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya),
water for sipping, bathing, another sipping, a garment, another sipping, and the sacred thread.
One should prepare water for rinsing the mouth (ācāma), scents, flowers, incense, and lamps;
then, having offered the food oblation (naivedya), water for rinsing the mouth once more, and having bowed and offered praise, one should dismiss [the deity].
And for the Śūdras, the worship of deities shall indeed be performed by name;
all should perform it through the path of the Āgamas, following the tradition of the gods.
No one should worship any deity whatsoever in a manner taught by a guru that is outside the Veda, even if they desire to propitiate that deity.
With every possible means and effort, he should satisfy the Brahmins and the cows;
having thus performed the worship of the gods, he should diligently honor his teachers.
Having cast flowers and prostrated, and having performed daily giving according to one's ability,
one should pay homage to the elders and perform the auspicious rite.
A Brahmin, fire, the sun, water, a cow, gold, a king, and clarified butter are remembered as auspicious.
One who maintains the sacred fires, a tawny cow, one who performs long sacrificial sessions, a performer of sacrifices, a giver of pure food, and the ocean [are also auspicious].

One perfected in knowledge, one perfected by austerity, one who lives a hundred years, one who is righteous, and one who is pure—these remove sins; one should always look upon them and bow to them as well.
A wise person should always look at the morning upon waking upon yellow pigment, sandalwood, gold, a drum, a mirror, a gem, ghee, the sun, a teacher, and a brahmin.
In the morning, one should apply to the head black *brāhmī*, *dūrvā* grass, sandalwood, *śaṅkhapuṣpikā*, white mustard seeds, and *priyaṅgu*.

One should not look at these in the morning: a most wicked person, an unfortunate person, a blind person, a naked person, or one whose nose has been cut off; having seen them, one should look at the sun.
Thus concludes the procedure for the worship of the deities.
Now follows the midday ritual.

Having performed the midday bath, one should regularly perform the midday rites (*mādhyāhnika*). Therein, having washed the feet or [the hands], having sipped water twice (*dvir-ācamya*), and having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) with the *apohiṣṭhā* verses, one should drink water with *darbha* grass in hand while reciting "May the waters purify the earth," then sip water twice again, and once more perform the ritual sprinkling with the *apohiṣṭhā* verses. Having sprinkled oneself with water, one should offer an oblation (*arghya*) to the Sun once with the *gāyatrī*, circumambulate to the right, touch water, worship the Sun with the verse "The swan dwelling in purity" (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*), and worship Him further with "Upwards that [Sun]" (*ud u tyam*) and "The bright [light]" (*citram*). Then, having bowed and touched the ground, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and recite the *gāyatrī* as before. Again, having bowed to the Sun, one should perform the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*) and the other subsequent rites.
The sacrifice to Brahman, the sacrifice to the gods, the sacrifice to beings, followed by the sacrifice to the ancestors and the sacrifice to men— these are proclaimed as the five sacrifices.
The sacrifice to Brahman is the private recitation of scripture; the sacrifice to the gods consists of the fire-oblation;
the sacrifice to the spirits is declared to be the bali offering, which follows from the food remaining after the oblation has been made.
The sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*) consists of giving food and other offerings with the words "Svadhā to the ancestors";
the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*) consists of giving gifts intended for humans, such as guests and others.
Now follows the Brahmayajña.

There, having washed his feet and sipped water twice, sitting facing east upon *darbha* grass whose tips point eastward, with *darbha* blades in hand and forming the *brahmāñjali* with the *pavitra* blades within, he should recite the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *sāvitrī* verse—first foot by foot, then half-verse by half-verse—and then recite the nine [syllables] along with the *kuśa* blades. Having uttered the *praṇava*, he should study an *ṛc*, a *sūkta*, an *anuvāka*, or a *yajus*, a *sāman*, the *sāvitrī*, or the *itihāsa* and *purāṇa*, using either a low or a medium tone. Having said "Obeisance to Brahman" three times, he should begin from the end and conclude with "Oṃ Tat Sat. In a village, he should study mentally. Then, according to the procedure prescribed in his own *śākhā*, he should offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods, the seers, and the ancestors; or else he may act according to custom with the verses beginning "Those gods who are headed by Brahmā," and so forth. Then, having wrung out his garment and sipped water, and taking some pure water, he should go home and perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice.
Now, as for the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*):
the householder begins the rite known as *vaiśvadeva* during the day;
it is intended for the proper consecration of both the food and himself.

Having kindled either the *aupāsana* fire or another fire, having swept around it, and having sprinkled water around it; having thrown unbroken rice grains, perfumes, and flowers in the cardinal directions and toward the fire; having adorned it; and having offered as is customary an oblation of cooked sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) soaked in ghee or mixed with condiments; and having again swept around it, he should sprinkle water around it. [47] Now follows the offering of the bali-oblations.

Having sprinkled a pure place with the remnants of the *devayajña* offering, one should perform [the rites] there. Now follows the *pitṛyajña*: there, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should give the remnants of the *bhūtabali* offering together with water, saying, "Svadhā to the ancestors. Then, in the same manner, one should place food with water outside the dwelling on the ground for dogs, *caṇḍālas*, outcasts, spirits, and crows. These—the *devayajña*, *bhūtayajña*, and *pitṛyajña*—are called the *vaiśvadeva*.
One should avoid all that is unfit for sacrifice (*ahaviṣya*) during the *vaiśvadeva* rite;
or rather:
*kodrava*, chickpeas (*caṇaka*), black gram (*māṣa*), lentils (*masūra*), and horse-gram (*kulitthaka*).
One should avoid all alkaline substances and salts during the Vaiśvadeva offering.
Or rather, there exists no such thing as an oblation of alkaline substances or salt in that manner.

Likewise, for sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) that has been touched by another's food, one should offer it after pushing aside the hot ashes toward the north; thus it becomes both offered and unoffered in the fire. A woman should not perform the offering. Or, if she should offer it upon embers containing ashes, it is not considered sacrificial food (*ahaviṣyaka*). Then, having sipped water, she should perform the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*). Having honored guests and others therein, wearing the sacred thread around her neck (*nivītī*), she should give to the humans beginning with Sanaka, saying "Hanta! Or she may discard the food as the first portion, as the *hantakāra*, or simply with the word "Hanta. In every case—
Food and likewise water should be given to the ancestors and to human beings;
the utterances svāhā, vaṣaṭ, and namas are for the dwellers of heaven.
The utterance *svadhā* is prescribed for the ancestors, while *hantakāra* is remembered as the offering for men;
in the absence of cooked food or when traveling abroad, one may offer rice grains or herbs.
One should employ milk, curd, or ghee, or even bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth, in the sacrifice to the gods and other rites; or, in times of distress, one may use water in place of water.
Liquid offerings should be poured with the *sruva* ladle, while solid oblations are offered by hand.

A *snātaka* or a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) who maintains a separate kitchen must perform the *vaiśvadeva* rite; a woman or a child may cause it to be performed. One should never eat food that is devoid of both the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the first-portion offering (*agra-dāna*).
But whatever is performed by even one among those who are undivided or reunited;
If all rites such as the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña) have been performed in a worldly fire for any purpose, then even after consuming sugarcane,
water, fruit, roots, betel, milk, or medicine,
the ritual acts of bathing, giving gifts, and so forth must still be performed.

"One should perform the *śrāddha* day by day with food and water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits; other *śrāddhas* may be performed according to one's devotion. Thus ends the section on conduct (*ācāra*) in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
When the wish-fulfilling cow, the blazing ocean, the wish-granting tree, the creeper, and so forth have appeared,
[the doctrine] has been proclaimed by Śambhu, Draviḍa, Kedāra, Lollaṭa, and others.
I shall expound the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, as set forth by the commentators Manu, Atri, Yājñavalkya, and others, for the purpose of facilitating its easy practice.
Now, the procedure for the śrāddha is described:

In that regard, *śrāddha* is first of all twofold: *pārvaṇa* and *ekoddiṣṭa*. The *pārvaṇa* is performed with reference to three [ancestors]; the *ekoddiṣṭa* is performed with reference to one. That, moreover, is threefold: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*). Among these, the obligatory is performed day by day, on the new moon, the *aṣṭakā* days, and so forth; the occasional is performed on occasions such as the birth of a son; the optional is for those seeking rewards, performed on specific lunar days, asterisms, and so forth. Furthermore, it is fivefold: the daily *śrāddha*, the *pārvaṇa śrāddha*, the *vṛddhi śrāddha*, the *ekoddiṣṭa*, and the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. Regarding this, the site for the *śrāddha* should be auspicious, free from bones, hair, phlegm, and the like, cleared, sloping toward the south, and smeared with cow dung.

Now, the times for *śrāddha*: the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), the *aṣṭakā* days, occasions of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the solstices (*ayana*), the equinoxes (*viṣuvat*), the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṃkrama*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the "elephant's shadow" (*gajacchāyā*), eclipses, the beginnings of the ages (*yugādi*), and the beginnings of the *manvantaras* (*manvādi*). Likewise, there are other times such as when one is in a distinguished place like Gayā, at a special time such as the anniversary of a death (*mṛtāha*), or when there is an abundance of materials and worthy Brahmins, or whenever one feels a personal inclination; these and others are the [appropriate] times.

Now, the Brāhmaṇas who are worthy of being fed are those previously known for their recitation, endowed with learning and study, experts in the study of the Vedas, knowers of Brahman, those who have mastered the *trimadhu*, the *trisuparṇa*, and the *trināciketa* sections; those who are priests for the *jyeṣṭhasāman* or those for whom they act as officiating priests, and so forth. Alternatively, a daughter’s son, a sister’s son, a son-in-law, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a pupil, a relative by marriage, a kinsman, one established in ritual action (*karmaniṣṭha*), one established in austerity (*taponiṣṭha*), one who maintains the six fires, the five fires, the four fires, the three fires, or the single fire; a student of the Vedas, an ascetic (*yati*), a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), and others such as these are highly commended.

[49] Now, those who are prohibited: one who is diseased, one with deficient limbs, one with redundant limbs, one-eyed, deaf, a eunuch, one whose virility has been lost, an adulterer, the husband of an adulteress, one with a bald head, one with naturally black teeth, one with deformed nails, one with skin disease, one who has shed his hair, the son of a remarried woman, a *kuṇḍa* or a *golaka*, one who eats forbidden food, one who eats from the genitals, one who teaches for a fee, one who learns for a fee, a defiler of maidens, one accused of a crime, a betrayer of friends, a slanderer, a seller of Soma, an elder brother whose younger brother marries before him, the younger brother who so marries, the giver or officiating priest of either of them, one who abandons mother, father, son, wife, or teacher for no reason, the husband of a remarried woman, a thief, a gambler, a temple-priest (*devalaka*), one corrupt in action, one who abandons prescribed duties, and one who performs prohibited acts—these and others are to be avoided. In all cases, if a praiseworthy person is unavailable, one who is merely free from these prohibitions may be accepted. In the daily *śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* and the domestic offering (*gṛhabali*) must be performed first. In the *darśa-śrāddha*, the *vaiśvadeva* may be performed either before or after.

(The Vaiśvadeva rite is to be performed at the beginning for the anniversary of an ancestor's death, at the end for the anniversary of one's own death, in the middle for the new moon, and during the Mahālaya festival; it is to be performed in its fourfold form once the guests have sipped water.)
The domestic offering (gṛhabali), however, is indeed performed afterwards. In all other śrāddhas, everything must be done afterwards.
Now, the pārvaṇa śrāddha of the new moon (amāvāsyā) is described—

And that rite is to be performed for the ancestors (pitṛs) and the maternal ancestors (mātāmahas). On the day before or on that very day, being self-restrained, one should invite the restrained Brahmins, saying, “May a moment be granted for the śrāddha. Having summoned them, asked if they have arrived well, and upon their reply, “We have arrived very well,” one—wearing two unwashed white garments free from burns, indigo-dye, or holes; having sipped water twice; facing east on a circle of cow-dung consecrated with *kuśa* grass, barley, and perfumes; wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*)—should wash the feet of the Vaiśvadeva Brahmins while facing the sun. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should wash the feet of the Brahmins intended for the ancestors on a circle consecrated with *kuśa*, sesame, and perfumes. Having himself sipped water twice, he should cause those who have also sipped water twice to sit down. There, for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva, he should seat two Brahmins facing east on smooth, four-legged, pure seats—free from cracks, woodworms, or burns—either on Nepalese woolen blankets (*nepālakambala*), on grass mats, or on wooden stools. He should seat three Brahmins facing north for the sake of the ancestors. Or else, he may seat one Brahmin for each of the two groups. The same applies to the maternal ancestors and others. Alternatively, the Vaiśvadeva rite may be performed as a single common procedure (*tantra*). Then, having scattered *kuśa* grass and sesame seeds outside the house, and sitting on *kuśa* grass facing east near the Brahmins, he should bow to his chosen deity, to Gayā, to the gods and others, to the Vasus and other ancestors, and to Janārdana. At the proper time, such as *kutapa*, he should perform two breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) with mantras. Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*): “By your permission, I shall perform this Pārvaṇa Śrāddha at this time for my fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, together with their wives; for my maternal grandfathers, maternal great-grandfathers, and maternal great-great-grandfathers, together with their wives; belonging to such-and-such gotras; whose nature is that of the Vasus, Rudras, and Ādityas. Having scattered sesame seeds all around, saying, “The Asuras and Rākṣasas are struck down,” he should sprinkle water with the verse beginning, “May they rise up” (*udīratām*). For everything pertaining to the gods, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), he should proceed clockwise, starting with an even number [of items], with the tips of the *darbha* grass pointing north, ending toward the north, and facing north himself. Then, having given water into the hands of the Brahmins for the sake of the Vaiśvadeva, he should place straight *kuśa* blades on the seats to the south, accompanied by barley, saying, “This is the seat for the Viśvedevas.”
One should offer a seat upon the seats, but never directly into the hand of the twice-born.

Then, having again offered water, one should invite them once more, saying: "May the moment for the rite for the gods (daiva) be granted. The Brahmin should say: "Om, so be it. Then the performer should say: "May your honor partake. Then the Brahmin should say: "I shall partake. Such is the traditional teaching (smṛti) of the author of the *Granthasaṃgraha*.
Furthermore, the genitive case is used for the words *akṣayya* and *āsana*, while the accusative is used in the invocation (*āvāhana*).
In the case of giving food, the dative case should be used; for the remaining [objects], the nominative case is prescribed.
Thus is the tradition of the author of the Ślokasaṃgraha.

Alternatively—throughout [the rite], one should employ only the dative case, with the exception of the invocation (*āvāhana*). Furthermore, one should repeatedly offer water at every step. Then, holding barley in his hand, he asks, "I shall invoke the *Viśvedevas* belonging to Purūravas and Ārdrava"; being permitted by them with the reply, "Invoke them," he invokes them with the two verses beginning, "O Viśvedevas, come hither. Having placed the barley from the right foot to the end of the head [of the Brahmins], and having worshipped them with these two verses, "O Viśvedevas, hear this my call; may the highly fortunate ones come," he scatters barley on the ground near them, spreads *kuśa* grass, and places two vessels made of gold, other precious metals, stone, clay, or *palāśa* leaves, etc., containing a single substance and separated by two *kuśa* tufts (*kūrca*). Having poured water into them with the verse, "May the divine waters be for our aid," and having thrown barley into them with the verse, "Barley art thou, king of grains," and having thrown perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having announced, "Svāhā! This is for you," he places a *kūrca* with its tip pointing eastward in the hand of the Brahmin and gives the *arghya* water into his hand with the verse, "The celestial waters which, together with milk... and the formula, "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*. Then, using the ritual formulas beginning with, "O Viśvedevas, this is your perfume," he should present the perfume and other offerings. The performer should apply fragrant unguents such as sandalwood, saffron, camphor, agallochum, and *padmaka*. After giving the perfume, the performer should anoint them with his hand holding *darbha* grass, but he must not anoint them with his hand while the *darbha* is still held in it. As for the Brahmin, he may anoint himself; this rule does not apply to him. Then, flowers such as the *jātī*, *mallikā*, white *yūthikā*, *campaka*, saffron, and *jāti*, as well as fragrant leaves like *maruvaka*, should be given. One should avoid those with pungent odors, those without odor, those that have withered, those that are not white, those that are not fragrant, those grown on thorny plants, and those such as *arka*, *dhattūra*, *śirīṣa*, *kāñcanāra*, *tulasī*, and *bilva*. Then, when available, incense made of guggulu, sandalwood, agallochum, *sarala*, and so forth, mixed with ghee and honey—or all types combined—should be offered. One should avoid incense made from animal parts or blown upon by the breath of the hand. Then, one should offer a lamp with ghee, sesame oil, or another non-prohibited substance. One should avoid lamps made from fat or marrow. Then, one should give a covering of white, pure, unwashed cloth with its fringes intact, or its value if unavailable; or, in its absence, an upper garment (*uttarīya*) or a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*); or, if unable, anything at all. Then the performer should say, "May the worship be complete. They should reply, "It is complete. The performer should say, "May you say, 'May there be the fulfillment of the resolve' (*saṃkalpasiddhi*). The Brahmins should reply, "May there be the fulfillment of the resolve. Regarding the seat and other items, the Brahmins should say: "May the seat be yours" (*svāsanam*); "May the *arghya* be yours"; "Good perfume"; "Beautiful flowers"; "Fine garland"; "Excellent incense"; "Excellent lamp"; "Excellent light"; "A fine covering. Such is the tradition of the *Saṃgrahakāra*.
Now, the rite for the ancestors—

Wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), facing south, he should perform the rites for the ancestors in a counter-clockwise direction, beginning with the odd-numbered generations and ending toward the south. In the ancestral rites (*pitrya-upacāra*), either the singular or the plural may be employed. For the junior ancestors, the singular alone is used. Having given water into the hands of the Brahmins representing the ancestors, he should place double-folded *kuśa* grass blades along with sesame seeds upon the seats, saying: "This is the seat for the fathers; this is the seat for the grandfathers; this is the seat for the great-grandfathers"—or "This is the seat for the father; this is the seat for the grandfather; this is the seat for the great-grandfather"—or "This is the seat for the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather"; or "This is the seat for the fathers, the grandfathers, and the great-grandfathers. He should offer these on his left side. The same applies to the maternal ancestors (*mātāmaha*). Then, having invited them with the words, "May you accept the invitation for the *śrāddha*," and holding sesame seeds in his hand, he asks the Brahmins, "Shall I invoke the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers? or "Shall I invoke the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather? Having been permitted by the Brahmins with the word "Invoke," he invokes them with the two verses beginning with *uśantas tvā*. He places the sesame seeds from the head down to the right foot, and worships them with the verse *āyantu naḥ pitaraḥ*. Having performed the same for the maternal ancestors, he scatters sesame seeds on the ground near the fathers. Then, upon *kuśa* grass placed in three vessels made of silver or other materials (as previously described) and covered with *kuśa* tufts, he pours water with the verse *saṃ no devīr abhiṣṭaye*. He throws sesame seeds with the mantra *tilo ‘si somadevatyaḥ*, and after throwing perfumes, flowers, and so forth, he announces, "Svadhā-arghya! Having placed a *kūrca* (tuft of grass) in the hand of the Brahmin, he says, "O divine waters... and gives the *arghya* water in order: "Father, this is your *arghya*; grandfather, this is your *arghya*; great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*," or using the dative case. He pours the *arghya* water flowing from their hands into the vessel for the ancestors and, on *kuśa* grass with tips pointing south, turns the vessel face-down, saying, "You are the place for the ancestors. Having turned it face-down, he places the *pavitra* strainers from the *arghya* vessels on top of it and scatters sesame and flowers. He must not move that vessel until the conclusion of the rite. The same applies to the maternal ancestors. If [three vessels] are unavailable, one vessel with three *pavitra* strainers should be used. No modification (*ūha*) of the mantras *uśantas tvā*, *āyantu naḥ*, and *tilo ‘si* should be made. Some say that the invocation occurs at the end of the offering of the vessels for both the gods and the ancestors. Then, using the formula "Father, this is your perfume; O fathers, this is your perfume," he should give perfume, garlands, and white flowers. He should avoid making a sectarian mark (*puṇḍra*) on the forehead and avoid placing a garland on the shoulder. He should offer incense, lamps, light, and coverings. When the sequence of items—seat, invitation, invocation, *arghya*, unbroken rice, perfume, incense, lamp, and covering—is followed for both the gods and the ancestors, there is an increase in progeny. If the sequence follows the individual sections (*kāṇḍānusamaya*), only the performance of the rules is achieved. Then he should perform the rites up to the formal declaration of intent (*saṃkalpa*). Now, having made a square mandala with cow dung and drawn a mystical diagram (*yantra*) upon it, he places the vessels for the gods made of gold or similar materials, and for the ancestors made of silver or similar materials—or other vessels rubbed with gold or silver, excluding those made of clay—upon the mandala. Having poured water into them, wiped them with his hand, and rinsed them, he should wash them again with water. Then, the oblation (*homa*) is performed either in the fire or in the hand. For one without a sacred fire, it is in the hand alone. There, taking food smeared with ghee and ghee itself, he asks, "I shall perform the oblation in the fire," and being permitted with "Do so," he approaches the *aupāsana* fire. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*), he sweeps around the fire, sprinkles water, and wearing the thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), silently places fuel wood (*idhma*) into the fire. Having spread a base of ghee with the *mekṣaṇa* ladle and the *sruva* spoon, he places two portions of food; if he is a performer of the five-fold division (*pañcāvattī*), he places three. Having again sprinkled ghee over them with the *sruva* and taken the portions, he offers two oblations with the two mantras: "To Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, svadhā, obeisance! To Agni Kavyavāhana, svadhā, obeisance! Having cast the *mekṣaṇa* into the fire, he should pour the remains of the oblation into the ancestral vessels. One who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) or has performed the *sarvādhāna* sacrifice should offer in the *dakṣiṇāgni* or in the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors. In the absence of fire, the oblation is in the hand. In a hand-oblation, there is no fuel wood, *mekṣaṇa*, or request for permission from the Brahmin. After sweeping and sprinkling around the hand of the Brahmin representing the ancestors, he spreads a base with the left hand, takes the portion with the right, sprinkles ghee over it, and offers it. Sweeping and sprinkling are performed once more. The same applies to the maternal ancestors. In that case, one who maintains the sacred fire should consume what was offered in the hand, rinse his mouth, and sit down. Alternatively, having placed it in a vessel and rinsed his mouth, he may sit down. If there is no fire, he should not eat what was previously offered; he should eat only at the time of the meal. In funeral *śrāddhas* (*preta-śrāddha*), he should throw it into the fire. This concludes the initial oblation. Then, having spread a base starting with the gods, he himself, his wife, or others appointed should serve excellent sacrificial food first. They should not serve with unwashed hands or with iron vessels. There is no fault if it is served through the intervention of grass or leaves.
Now, the sacrificial foods (haviṣya):

Rice, *śāli*, barley, wheat, *priyaṅgu*, mung beans, black gram, millet, wild rice, and so forth; *kālaśāka*, *mahāśāka*, *droṇaśāka*, pure meat, large-scaled fish and the like; sugarcane, plantain, jackfruit, *āmlātaka*, mango, date-palm, rose-apple, *gostanī*, grape, *priyāla*, *āmalaka*, coconut, cucumber, eggplant, *cirbhaṭa*, *pāleya*, and excellent sweet fruits such as the jujube and others; cardamom, ginger, fresh ginger, asafoetida, black pepper, long pepper, *madhūka*, molasses, sugar, candied sugar, camphor, rock salt, *mānasa* salt, honey, cow’s milk, curd, and clarified butter—these and similar items are recommended. From these ingredients, one should serve in abundance rice, soups, milk-rice, cakes, various edibles, drinks, and so on.
