As for asafoetida, ginger, long pepper, and black pepper, they should be used in the *śrāddha* for the purpose of seasoning the food, but not in their raw form.
Then he spoke of the objects of the senses:

One should avoid *kodrava*, *caṇaka*, *masūra*, *kulattha*, *pulaka*, *rājamāṣa*, red *vidala*, *māṣa*, and *āḍhakī* with their husks; black *yāvanāla* and black grains other than *mudga*, *māṣa*, and *tila*; *upodakī*, *tulasī*, black *atasī*, *śigru*, leaf-vegetables of large mustard, black mustard, and vegetables with a foul odor; and *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *polaka*, and the like. Especially to be avoided are *vṛntāka*, the two types of *bṛhatī*, *alābu*, *gāndhārikā*, *markaṭikā*, *kapittha* roots, *bilva* fruits, *kāñcanālaka*, *kapittha-kanaka*, *karañja*, *karavanda*, *kaliṅga*, and bamboo shoots. Food requested under the pretext of being for the ancestors (*pitṛ*), food brought as a bride-price (*śulka*), and all items such as black cumin, *śatapuṣpī*, salt from saline soil, wild game, buffalo milk, curds, and ghee are considered unwholesome. However, if wholesome food is unavailable, that which is not prohibited may be accepted. Then, having served the food on the plate, one should place *kuśa* grass and barley in the plate for the gods (*daiva*), sprinkle water around the plate, consecrate it with the mantra "The earth is your vessel," recite the verse "Hither come the gods," and place the thumb of the twice-born guest in the food while saying, "O Viṣṇu, protect the sacrificial offering. Having declared, "The Viśvedevas are the deities; this food is the oblation (*havis*); for the sake of the *āhavanīya* fire, this is the earth, the food of Gayā, and the Brahman; the eater is the Brahmin, who is Gadādhara (Viṣṇu)," one should renounce the food with barley-water, saying, "To the Viśvedevas, this food has been served and will be served until satisfaction; it is not mine. One should then worship with the verse "Those gods who... Next, in the plate for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should place sesame seeds and *kuśa* grass, sprinkle water around the plate, consecrate it with "The earth is your vessel," and with the verse "This Viṣṇu... say, "O Viṣṇu, protect the ancestral offering (*kavya*"). Placing the thumb [in the food], one declares, "The Pitṛs are the deities; this food is the ancestral offering (*kavya*). Or, saying, "To the father in the form of Vasu, to the grandfather in the form of Rudra, to the great-grandfather in the form of Āditya, and to the Pitṛs in the form of Vasus," one renounces the food with sesame-water, saying, "This food has been served and will be served until satisfaction; it is not mine. One should then worship with the verse "And those Pitṛs who are here... No modification (*ūha*) of the words should be made here. The same applies to the maternal ancestors. If there is a guest, one should honor him like a god, renounce the food to his own chosen deity or to Śiva, worship with "Those gods who...", and mutter the mantras beginning with "To the deities and the Pitṛs, sevenfold Svadhā in the Daśārṇas... After giving the *apośana* water, one should recite the *praṇava*, the *Gāyatrī*, and the *Madhumatī* verses, and say, "Om Tat Sat; enjoy as you please. Then the Brāhmaṇas should eat silently before the *prāṇāhuti* (the first breath-offering), without lifting the plate from the ground, and avoiding noise from the mouth or fickleness of hand and so forth. Alternatively, they may eat by placing the plate on earthenware bowls or small dishes, either before or after the *prāṇāhuti*. Out of fear of spilling food, touching dust with the feet, or stepping over it, they should never place the plate on a tripod stand (*yantrikā*) or similar supports, nor should they offer the ritual ball (*bali*). Then, whatever oblation (*havis*) is pleasing to the eater, the performer, and the Pitṛs should be given. Until they are satisfied, one wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*upavītī*) should cause them to hear the *Rakṣoghna* and *Pitrya-pavitra* mantras preceded by the *praṇava*, and then mutter the *praṇava* and *Gāyatrī*. Then, taking various kinds of food, saying the *praṇava*, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should cause them to hear the verse "The wind is honey" and the verse "They have eaten, they have rejoiced. Having asked, "Are you satisfied? and receiving the reply, "We are satisfied," one should pour sesame-water with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the ancestors) on *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south in the presence of the Brāhmaṇas of the divine and ancestral rites, near the remains of the meal. Reciting "Those who were burnt by fire, those not burnt by fire, the living ones... one should scatter food mixed with sesame and pour sesame-water, then perform the ceremonial sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, having given water for rinsing the mouth (*gaṇḍūṣa*), one should set aside some food of all kinds for the *piṇḍa* offerings. Having asked, "What shall be done with the remainder of the food? and being permitted by them, "Let it be eaten with those we desire," or if they take it themselves, one should offer the *piṇḍas* either in the case of a fire-sacrifice (*agni-homa*) near the fire, or in the case of a hand-sacrifice (*pāṇi-homa*) near the Brāhmaṇas, according to the procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. That procedure is as follows: On a spot of ground smeared with cow-dung, one should draw two lines with the edge of a wooden sword (*sphya*), a piece of *khadira* wood, or a *darbha* blade, ending toward the south, using the mantra "The Asuras are struck down," etc. Having sprinkled water and spread *barhis* grass there, one should pour sesame-water with the *pitṛ-tīrtha* on the locations for the *piṇḍas* along the western line with the three mantras beginning "May the Pitṛs be purified. Along the eastern line, one should pour water with the mantras beginning "May the maternal grandfathers be purified. Saying, "This is for Devadatta Śarman, and for those who follow you here," one should place the *piṇḍas*—this food in the form of *piṇḍas—is for the father, not mine—with the palm turned away, mixing them with sesame. Then, having consecrated the six *piṇḍas* all at once with the mantra "O Pitṛs, come here," one should turn to the left, face north, sit without exhaling as much as possible, and upon turning back, consecrate them again with "The Pitṛs have rejoiced," etc., and then exhale. Then, having smelled the remains of the *piṇḍas* and washed the hands, one should pour water on the *piṇḍas* as before. Giving oil on the *piṇḍas* with "O Devadatta Śarman, be anointed," and collyrium with "O Devadatta Śarman, apply eye-salve," one should give a garment, a fringe, or a tuft of wool with "This is your garment, O Pitṛs," etc. If the person is over fifty years old, one may give hair from one's own chest. Then one should worship the *piṇḍas* as the forms of the Pitṛs with the mantra "Salutation to you, O Pitṛs," etc., and the three verses beginning "We call the mind hither."
One should give the food-balls to cows, horses, or Brahmins, or else cast them into fire or water.

Except for the pouring of the *arghya* water, the modification (*ūha*) of the word "father" (*pitṛ*) should not be performed. Or, having offered the rice balls (*piṇḍa*) according to the procedure prescribed in one's own *śākhā*, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) and then offer water for sipping. Then, having poured water into the hands of the Brahmins and having successively thrown barley and sesame seeds into them, one should discard those [seeds], throw back in seeds along with unbroken rice grains (*sākṣata*), address them by their lineage and name, and request, "May the lineage increase. When they respond, "May there be well-being; may the lineage increase," one should accept the proffered blessings, move the vessels, and sip water. One who is uninitiated (*anupanīta*) or a woman should not move the vessels. Then, having said, "Say 'May there be well-being' for the Viśvedevas and the ancestors," and when they have said, "Oṃ, may there be well-being," one says, "May there be inexhaustibility (*akṣayya*) for the Viśvedevas and the ancestors. When they have said, "May there be inexhaustibility," one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, such as land, gold, silver, and so forth. Then, when they have said, "May the sacrificial fees protect us; may there be much to give," they respond in the same way. Having been authorized by the words, "I shall cause the *svadhā* to be recited; let it be recited," one says, "Let the *svadhā* be spoken for the ancestors. When they have responded, "May there be *svadhā*," one should sprinkle water on the ground. When they have said, "May the *svadhā* be accomplished," they respond, "May the *svadhā* be accomplished. When it is said, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," they respond, "May the Viśvedevas be pleased. When it is said, "May the ancestors be pleased," they respond, "May the ancestors be pleased. Then, having turned the face-down vessel upward, placed the purifiers (*pavitra*) upon it, and thrown unbroken rice grains and flowers into the hands of the Brahmins, one should dismiss the Brahmins, starting with those representing the ancestors, while reciting "In every battle... (*vāje vāje vata*) and "Arise, O ancestors! (*uttiṣṭhata pitaraḥ*) using a blade of *darbha* grass. Then, at the place where the feet were washed, having circumambulated clockwise with the verse "May the strength of the sacrifice come to us" (*āmā vājasya*), facing south, and when the guests have requested, "May our givers increase and may our food be abundant," the donor should accept the blessings when they have used these two verses or the words "As you have commanded" (*yuṣmad-ākhyāta*) and replied, "So be it. Having prostrated and gratified them, saying, "Today my birth has become fruitful," and having caused them to say, "May everything be complete," one should say, "Forgive me. Following them as far as the entrance of their residence, when they say, "Rest," one should circumambulate them again, return, and perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites with another meal or with the remnants of the *śrāddha*. Together with his loved ones, he should eat the remnants of the *śrāddha*. From the invitation onwards, and that night, he should remain celibate (*brahmacārī*). But the eater should avoid eating again, traveling, teaching, studying, sexual intercourse, giving gifts, receiving gifts, and performing fire-sacrifices (*homa*). Thus the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* has been written down according to the opinion of Sarvasaṃgrahakāraka. Uninitiated persons, women, and *śūdras* should have the *śrāddha* performed by a priest, or they themselves may perform it without mantras by means of name and lineage, or with the two mantras: "Salutation to the gods" (*namo devebhyaḥ*) and "Salutation, *svadhā* to the ancestors" (*svadhā namaḥ pitṛbhyaḥ*).
Wherever the ancestors are worshipped, there the maternal grandfathers must also be worshipped without distinction; by failing to do so, one goes to hell.

Thus is the *kāma-śrāddha*. In that, Dhūri and Locana are the Viśvedevas; the oblation (*homa*) is offered either in the fire or into the hand. The occasional (*naimittika*) śrāddha is likewise. In that, Kāma and Kāla are the Viśvedevas. The *iṣṭi-śrāddha* and the *ruci-śrāddha* are likewise. In those, Kratu and Dakṣa are the Viśvedevas. Now, the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*—

In that [Nāndīśrāddha], two Brahmins each—or an even number according to one’s ability—should be engaged for the Viśvedevas, for the sake of the maternal ancestors (mother, etc.), for the paternal ancestors (father, etc.), and for the maternal great-grandfathers with their wives. The *darbha* grass should be rootless. Wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*), facing east, he should offer to those facing north; or facing north, he may offer to those facing east. Under no circumstances should he offer while facing south. Barley is used in place of sesame seeds. For the Nāndī-devas in the Nāndīśrāddha, he should say: "May a moment be granted. They respond: "Om, so be it; may you both receive it," and so forth. In the rite for the paternal ancestors as well, there is a *pavitraka* made of two blades of *kuśa* grass. In the rite for the paternal ancestors, the rule of pairing begins with the "Joyous-faced" (*nāndīmukha*) invocation. Barley is scattered with the mantra: "Thou art barley, whose deity is Soma"; in place of *svadhā*, the word "puṣṭyā" (for nourishment) is used. In place of "svadhā namaḥ," the words "svāhā namaḥ" are used. The offering of the *arghya* water is announced with "svāhārghyaḥ. Fragrance and other items should be offered twice each, saying: "May the Joyous-faced Fathers be pleased. The ritual services are performed clockwise, ending toward the north. The oblation (*homa*) is offered either in the fire or into the hand. The oblation is offered out of order: "To Agni Kavyavāhana, svāhā! To Soma Pitṛmat, svāhā! The throwing of the stirring-spoon (*mekṣaṇa*) follows the same procedure as the oblation. He should cause the mantras that destroy demons and the Indra-peace mantras to be recited. In place of the verses beginning with "madhu vātā," he should cause the five verses beginning with "upāsmai gāyata naraḥ" to be recited, or other honey-related mantras. At the end, he should cause the verse beginning with "akṣann amīmadanta" to be recited. When they have sipped water, he should smear the ground with cow-dung where the meal was taken, spread *darbha* grass with tips pointing east, and offer two *piṇḍas* each for every individual from the remains of the food mixed with clotted butter (*pṛṣadājya*), curd, and jujube fruits, following the divine portion. The addition of curd to the clarified butter constitutes the divine *pṛṣadājya*. The rest is like the *Pārvaṇa* rite. In this case, there is either the omission of the *piṇḍas* alone, or the omission of the *piṇḍas* and everything else.
Now, regarding the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, the *Mitākṣarā* states:
"The Lord of Yoga has taught that the *ekoddiṣṭa* is to be performed every year on the anniversary of death. Likewise, another *smṛti* says:
"Every year, however, the honoring of one's mother and father must be performed."
One should perform the śrāddha without feeding the deities and should offer only a single piṇḍa.

In this regard, all *śrāddhas* are of three kinds: *nava-śrāddhas*, *nava-miśras*, and *purāṇas*. Among these, the *nava-śrāddhas* are those prescribed from the day of death up to the eleventh day. Those prescribed from the eleventh day until the end of the first year are the *nava-miśras*. After that, they are called *purāṇas*. In all *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, there is no portion for the gods (*daiva*). There is one person to be addressed, and only one Brahmin; or alternatively, an odd number of Brahmins. There is one vessel and one *pavitra* (strainer). With the remnants of the meal, a single *piṇḍa* (funerary cake) is to be offered. In a *purāṇa-ekoddiṣṭa*, everything is like a portion of the *pārvaṇa* rite, excluding the portion for the gods, but performed with the recitation of mantras. The oblation (*homa*) is performed in the hand with two mantras. In the *nava-miśra* rites, the invitation is given during the day. From the invitation onwards, there is no private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). Mantras containing the word "Father" (*pitṛ*), or the words "Svadhā" and "Namaḥ," are omitted. All actions such as the scattering of sesame seeds (*tila*) are to be done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). Having silently presented the *arghya* water and invoked [the deceased], one gives the *arghya* by name while addressing the *preta* at the end of the mantra, and then offers perfumes (*gandha*) and other items. Into the hand, one offers a single oblation with the formula, "To the *preta*, Svāhā. In *nava-śrāddhas*, one should avoid incense, lamps, the word "Svadhā," the word "Father," the word "Anu" in the *piṇḍa* offering, the silent recitation (*japa*), and the pouring of water over the head (*abhiśravaṇa*). At the place where the food is made inexhaustible, one should say, "May he attend [to the food]. The response is likewise. One should dismiss them with, "Be pleased. The reply is, "We are pleased. Some say that in the *nava-miśra* rites, everything is accompanied by mantras. However, in a *nava-śrāddha*, everything must be done without mantras. One should not omit the name or the word "preta. The invitation is to be given immediately. One should avoid incense, lamps, and eating the remnants of the *śrāddha*. Having performed the *nava-śrāddha*, one should bathe. Everything else is like the *pārvaṇa* rite. Or, the *nava-śrāddhas* may be performed on the eleventh day. In that case, the first one is combined with the *ekoddiṣṭa*. In that context, many sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) should be given, such as clothing, ornaments, vehicles, beds, seats, food, sandals, shoes, umbrellas, and so forth, for the sake of the *preta*. In the section dedicated to the *preta* within the Rudra-group, it is like the *nava-śrāddha*. But in the section dedicated to Rudra, one should worship the Brahmins while wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītin*) and feed them. Like the dedication to the *preta* in the form of Rudra, the *śrāddha* should include a water-pot (*udakumbha*) and sesame seeds, and a fee should be given everywhere, especially in the *preta-śrāddha*.
Now, the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite—

In that rite, there are three mandalas: two Brahmins for the gods (*daiva*), one for the deceased (*preta*) position, and three for his father and the others (*pitrya*). In case of inability, there shall be one Brahmin each for the gods, the deceased, and the ancestors. Kāma and Kāla are the Viśvedevas. The worship of the gods is exactly as before. For the sake of the deceased, there is one vessel; for the sake of his father and the others, there are three. Having filled the vessel for the ancestors according to the *pārvaṇa* rite—with the deceased’s portion being like the *ekoddiṣṭa* mixed with nine parts—one should add perfumes and other offerings. Having placed the vessels right there, and having asked, "Shall I join the vessel of the deceased with the vessels of the ancestors?", and being permitted with the words, "Do so," one should cast the *kuśa* grass from the deceased's vessel into the ancestral vessels. Leaving a small amount of water along with the *kuśa* in the deceased's vessel, one should sprinkle it into the ancestral vessels with the two mantras beginning with "ye samānāḥ samanasaḥ. The *arghya* for the deceased is from the remainder of the deceased's vessel. Having given the *arghya* from that vessel for the ancestors and completed the rites up to the covering, one should offer food separately for each ancestor; or else, one may offer a single oblation into the hand of the deceased on the head, or not at all. The oblation for the ancestors is performed either in the fire or into the hands with the two mantras. One should place the remnants of the oblation into the hands of the ancestors. That food should not be eaten before the formal meal. One should eat it together with the food intended for the meal. Having offered one *piṇḍa* dedicated to the deceased and having offered three *piṇḍas* for the ancestors, one should ask, "Shall I join the *piṇḍa* of the deceased with the *piṇḍas* of the ancestors? and being permitted with the words, "Do so," one should divide the *piṇḍa* of the deceased into three parts and place them upon the *piṇḍas* of the father and others with the previously mentioned mantras. All subsequent rites, such as the recitation of mantras, are like the *pārvaṇa*. One should conclude everything right there. If the participants touch one another during the Śrāddha meal—
Having eaten that food and abandoned it, one should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.

If it is sprinkled with remnants [of another's meal], one should wash it, eat it, bathe, and then mutter it two hundred times. In the case of eating food containing remnants, one should mutter it two thousand times. It is the same for the Mothers;
however, there is this distinction:

If a woman dies without a son, her husband should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite together with his own mother and others. If she was born of an *āsura* or similar marriage and is a "son of an appointed daughter" (*putrikāputra*), he should perform the offering of the mother’s *piṇḍa* and other rites using the *gotra* of that father alone. If she was born of a *brāhma* or similar marriage, he may perform it using either the father’s *gotra* or the mother’s *gotra*. In the case of *anvārohaṇa* (the widow ascending the funeral pyre), if they ascend the same pyre or die on the same day, a separate *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for the woman need not be performed; what is done for the husband is also done for the wife. However, if she dies on a different day, the son, having placed *kuśa* grass between the *piṇḍas* of his own father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother by means of one of those fathers. In all cases, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the wife is performed with the husband alone; association with the father-in-law is prohibited. Some say the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is with three ancestors. A "son of an appointed daughter" born of an *āsura* or similar marriage performs it with the maternal grandfather and others. This being so, the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather must be performed regularly on the anniversary of death and other occasions. One born of a *brāhma* or similar marriage performs it with the father alone. While the father is alive, he should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* with the grandfather and others, or with the mother and others. For those killed by Brahmins and the like, for those who have not performed penance, for lifelong celibates (*brahmacārins*), and for those without offspring, there is no *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*; for them, only the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite is always performed. For those who die out of the natural order of succession, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* may be performed with the intervening ancestors or not at all. Some say the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* applies to all. If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed before the end of a year, one should perform the *sodakumbha-śrāddha* every day or every month—just like the annual death-day *śrāddha*—until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is reached, or alternatively, from the eleventh day onwards, perform those sixteen *śrāddhas* just like the annual death-day *śrāddha*, and then perform a *pārvaṇa-śrāddha* and feed many Brahmins for the sake of releasing the deceased from the year-long state. The annual death-day *śrāddha* should be performed by sons according to custom as either an *ekoddiṣṭa* or a *pārvaṇa*. The day of death is the specific lunar day (*tithi*) in the specific fortnight and month of the moment of death. For husbands, wives should always perform the *pārvaṇa* rite. For one who died on the new moon (*darśa*) or during the fortnight of the dead (*pretapakṣa*), the *pārvaṇa* alone is performed annually. For ascetics (*yatis*) carrying the triple staff (*tridaṇḍin*), there is no state of being a *preta* at all. On the eleventh day, only the *pārvaṇa* should be performed. If death occurs before the taking of the staff, one should cremate the body according to the rules of one's own *śākhā* and perform the water-offering, *piṇḍa*-offering, *preta-śrāddha*, *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, and other rites. For *Śūdras*, however, the entire *preta-śrāddha* should be performed on the twelfth day without mantras, or after a month has passed. For one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the funeral rites such as cremation and the death-day *śrāddha* are performed until the end of the third fortnight; thereafter, they are performed only on the actual day of death. For one who has maintained the fires (*āhitāgni*), the funeral rites and death-day *śrāddha* begin from the cremation and continue until the end of the third fortnight; after that, only on the day of death. For everyone, the *śrāddha* should be performed only on the day of death. During the *aṣṭakās* and at Gayā, the *śrāddha* for mothers, fathers, and paternal uncles along with their wives is performed separately, yet together with their consorts. There, the ritual procedure belongs to the gods (*daivatantra*), and the order begins with the fathers. Even if there are multiple mothers, they should be joined in one place; the rest is as before. In a rite for prosperity (*vṛddhi*), it is said that there is no consort, the women come first, and the ritual belongs to the gods. At the death-day *śrāddha*, the *śrāddha* for the fathers should be performed on the father’s death-day, and not with their wives. At the mother’s death-day, the *śrāddha* for the mothers should be performed, and there is no inclusion of the fathers in that *śrāddha*. (In a rite for prosperity, the mothers are primary; in the *anvaṣṭakā*, they are in the middle; at Gayā and elsewhere, they are at the end. When the death-days of father and mother coincide, the *śrāddha* for father and mother should be performed separately, not together with their wives. There, having first completed the father’s *śrāddha*, one should then perform the mother’s *śrāddha*. If the death-days of both parents coincide and they were cremated together, the mother’s *śrāddha* is still separate. However, the father’s *śrāddha* and the mother’s *śrāddha* should be completed in sequence at the same time and with the same cooking. If the death-days coincide and they ascended the same pyre, the mother’s *śrāddha* is separate; there, the ritual belongs to the gods, followed by the fathers and then the mothers. If there are multiple mothers, they are performed separately in sequence. There is unity in the timing, the cooking, and the external performance. If they ascended different pyres, everything is performed separately. This sequence applies even when the death-day *śrāddha* is an *ekoddiṣṭa*. Except for the *aṣṭakās*, Gayā, and rites for prosperity, the *śrāddha* is performed with the wives. For maternal grandfathers in these cases, it is also with their wives, except on their own death-days. In those cases, all are performed separately. The same applies to paternal uncles, heirs, brothers, maternal uncles, gurus, and teachers. During the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) and the *mahālaya*, the *śrāddha* for all ancestors should be performed. There, the *śrāddha* for the mothers is recommended separately. For maternal grandfathers, it is with their wives. The *śrāddha* should be performed for gurus, teachers, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, officiating priests (*upādhyāyas*), brothers, friends, those who supported him, those who gave him wealth, sons, disciples, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), and others, as well as their wives. It should be performed especially for those without sons. In that case, there is a single cooking; the *vaiśvadeva* ritual is common, and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) and *piṇḍas* are also common. The same applies to the fortnightly *śrāddha*. On the thirteenth day of that fortnight, the *śrāddha* for a single group should not be performed
At Mahālaya, at a Gayā-śrāddha, on the anniversary of the death of one's mother or father,
or when the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite has been performed for any deceased person whatsoever;
Even after having performed his marriage, one should always perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa-nirvapaṇa);
and at a sacrifice, as well as at Gayā, they should indeed offer the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛ-yajña).

In all *śrāddhas* except for the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, when the detailed *pārvaṇa* procedure is not possible, it should be performed by the method of *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) alone. The *saṃkalpa* procedure consists of whatever is prescribed for the *pārvaṇa* rite as far as possible, excluding the invocation (*āvāhana*), the water-offering (*arghya*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). When there is an absence of food, an absence of twice-born guests, while traveling abroad, upon the birth of a son, in the absence of a wife, in the absence of the sacred fires (*agni*), in the absence of a cook, when the wife is menstruating, in times of distress, at a holy pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), during an eclipse, at a time when eating is forbidden, on the anniversary of a death, in another type of *śrāddha*, in a medical extraction (*saṃgraha*), at night, during the sun’s passage into a new sign (*saṃkrānti*), for a woman whose husband is deceased, or for a *śūdra*—in these cases, one should always perform an *āma-śrāddha* (a *śrāddha* with raw food). In that case, having performed the rites up to the end of the clothing offering, one should discard the raw food—either quadrupled or equal in amount—along with the ritual implements, give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and conclude the rite. There is no fire-oblation or rice-ball offering in this; nor is there a formal recitation for well-being (*svastivācana*). When the aforementioned causes such as lack of food exist, a *hema-śrāddha* (a *śrāddha* with gold) may be performed instead. Specifically, in the cases of the birth of a son, being without a wife, being abroad, lacking the sacred fires, at a *tīrtha*, in distress, or in a medical extraction, in a *hema-śrāddha* they may or may not perform the invocation, the water-offering, the domestic cooking, the fire-oblation, and the rice-balls. At the end of the clothing offering, one should discard gold—eightfold, fourfold, twofold, or equal in weight—along with a sacrificial fee, and conclude as before. When multiple causes such as lack of food exist, the *śrāddha* intended by *saṃkalpa* must be performed. In that case, if the material or a Brahmin is not available, one should make a *saṃkalpa* according to one's ability regarding materials such as silver, gold, land, clothing, wealth, or grain, dedicating them to the ancestors. The monthly *śrāddhas* on the anniversary of death should be performed with cooked food whenever possible; however, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* must under all circumstances be performed with cooked food.
Now follows the procedure for the time of the Śrāddha rite:

In that regard, on the day for which a specific rite is prescribed, one should perform both the commencement and the conclusion of that rite during its designated *ghaṭikās* (time-units), particularly in the case of the *śrāddha* for the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*). If this is impossible, one may perform either the commencement or the conclusion. When the day is divided into fifteen parts, the eighth *muhūrta* is called *kutupa*. The *śrāddha* should be performed during the five *muhūrtas* beginning with *kutupa*, but not in the evening, nor at night, nor in the morning. The five divisions of the day consist of three *muhūrtas* each: morning (*prātaḥ*), forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*), midday (*madhyāhna*), afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), and evening (*sāyāhna*). A *śrāddha* performed in the morning on account of a birth (*vṛddhi*) is highly commended. In the forenoon, the *āmāśrāddha* and *hemaśrāddha* are performed; at midday, the *ekoddiṣṭa*; and in the afternoon, the *pārvaṇa*. On the day of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *pārvaṇa* is also permitted even in the evening. The same applies to the preceding days.
Now, the [calculation for] deficient lunar days (khaṇḍatithi) is stated:

The new moon (*amāvāsyā*) on which the moon is visible is called *sinīvālī*; that on which the moon has disappeared is designated as *kuhū*. If the new moon is not pierced by the fourteenth day (*bhūta-viddhā*), it should be accepted provided it extends into the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). If it is pierced by the fourteenth day, one should abandon that day and accept the lunar day (*tithi*) on the following day that extends into the afternoon. When the new moon is perceived after midday, it becomes pierced by the fourteenth day. In the case of an extreme decrease in the lunar day, if the new moon is absent in the afternoon of the following day, then the *sinīvālī* pierced by the fourteenth day, extending into the evening (*sāyāhna*), should be accepted. In cases of a decrease less than that, the *sinīvālī* pierced by the fourteenth day and extending into the afternoon should be accepted by all. Alternatively, those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) should accept *sinīvālī*, while those without fires (*niragnika*), as well as women and Śūdras, should accept *kuhū*. In the case of an extreme increase in the lunar day, one should abandon the *sinīvālī* pierced by the fourteenth day and accept the *kuhū* that extends into the afternoon. In cases of an increase less than that, one should abandon the *sinīvālī* pierced by the fourteenth day and accept the *kuhū* that extends into midday. If both extend into midday and the lunar days are equal, either may be accepted according to preference. Alternatively, those with fires should accept *sinīvālī*, while those without fires, women, and Śūdras should accept *kuhū*. Or else, *kuhū* should be accepted by everyone. Regarding the *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* sacrifices and the dates for ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the acceptance of increase or decrease in the lunar day applies only there and not elsewhere. On the anniversary of death (*mṛtāha*), only the lunar day that extends into the afternoon should be accepted; the afternoon was given to the ancestors by the Self-Existent One, not the time of sunset. [62] Even if it extends for only three *muhūrtas*, in the case of an increase, the subsequent day should be accepted; if the days are equal, either the preceding or the subsequent may be taken; but in the case of a decrease, only that which extends for three *muhūrtas* past sunset should be accepted. If it is impossible to perform the *śrāddha* on the following day due to birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) or other obstacles, the preceding day, even if it only reaches sunset, should be accepted. Some say that in all cases the day pierced by the preceding one should be accepted, but those learned in many *smṛtis* and logic do not accept this. If it is impossible to perform the *śrāddha* on the previous day due to birth-impurity or other obstacles, the subsequent day, which extends from sunrise and provides sufficient time for the ritual, should be accepted. Even in that case, if the materials for the *śrāddha* on the anniversary of death are unavailable or if it is prevented by some other obstacle, it should be performed immediately upon the removal of the cause. In the event of an obstacle such as birth-impurity, it should be performed after that impurity has ceased. Alternatively, it may be performed on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*) or on the new moon (*amāvāsyā*). Or it may be performed in the next month on that same day. When the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite arrives and an obstacle occurs, it should be performed in the next month on that same day. The sixteen *śrāddhas* must be performed at their proper times. If an obstacle arises due to an impossibility, they should be performed immediately upon the removal of the cause. A monthly *śrāddha* interrupted by an obstacle should be performed on that same day in the subsequent month. If the date of death is unknown but the month of death is known, the new moon of that month should be accepted. If the month of death is unknown but the date is known, that date in the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Bhādrapada, or Māgha should be accepted. If neither the date nor the month of death are known, the date and month of departure should be accepted. If the date and month of departure are unknown, the date and month when news of the death was heard should be accepted as before. If the date and month when news of the death was heard are unknown, the month of cremation should be accepted as before. Or, in all cases where death occurred in the dark fortnight, the new moon should be accepted; if in the bright fortnight, the full moon (*pūrṇamāsa*). If the date of death is entirely unknown, the new moon of the month of Māgha should be accepted. Even for one who did not go abroad, if the date and month of death are entirely unknown, it should be done in this very manner. For specific *śrāddhas* prescribed for the beginnings of Yugas or Manvantaras, etc., the lunar day that extends from sunrise in the bright fortnight should be accepted; in the dark fortnight, that which extends until sunset. Performance in the forenoon is recommended for the bright fortnight, and in the afternoon for the dark fortnight. Even for *śrāddhas* prescribed under a specific asterism (*nakṣatra*), the day of the asterism that extends from sunrise in the bright fortnight should be accepted; in the dark fortnight, the day of the asterism that extends until sunset should be accepted.
Now, the transits (saṃkrānti) are described:

In all *saṃkrāntis*, it is taught that during the eight *ghaṭikās* on both sides [of the transit], the fruit—whether seen or unseen—is declared. Among these, the *saṃkrānti* of Cancer (*karkaṭa*) is the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*). During the southern solstice, the first thirty *ghaṭikās* are meritorious for bathing, giving, *śrāddha* rites, and so forth. Likewise, in the cases of the "steps of Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇupada*), the first sixteen *ghaṭikās* are meritorious. The transits of Taurus, Scorpio, Aquarius, and Leo are the "steps of Viṣṇu. The transits of Libra and Aries are the equinoxes (*viṣuva*). Therein, ten *ghaṭikās* before and four *ghaṭikās* after are meritorious. In the cases of the "mouths of the six-eighths" (*ṣaḍaśītimukha*), sixteen *ghaṭikās* after are meritorious. The transits of Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces are the "mouths of the six-eighths. The transit of Capricorn is the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*). During the northern solstice, forty *ghaṭikās* after are meritorious; [some] say that forty *ghaṭikās* before are also meritorious. When the transits occur prior to midnight, the preceding day is meritorious; therein the ritual enjoyment (*bhoga*) should be performed. When the transits occur at midnight, both days are highly meritorious; therein the ritual enjoyment should be performed. Alternatively, during eclipses, *saṃkrāntis*, marriages, deaths, or festivals of prosperity (*vṛddhi*), bathing, giving, and so forth should be performed even at night. Likewise, one should accept the conjunctions (*yoga*) such as *vyatīpāta* when they coincide with times such as *kutu-pa*, as well as the lunar phases (*karana*) such as *viṣṭi*.
Thus concludes the determination of the times for *śrāddha* in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.

Now, the determination of the *parvan* (lunar phases) is stated: when the *parvan* is complete, there is the *anvādhāna* (preparation); the sacrifice (*yāga*) takes place on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipad*). A distinction is stated regarding the *khaṇḍaparvan* (defective lunar phase): the full moon is twofold—the *Anumati*, with a waning moon, and the *Rākā*, with a full moon; the new moon is also twofold—the *Sinīvālī*, with the moon visible, and the *Kuhū*, with the moon invisible.
Rākā and Anumati are the two full-moon nights, so named because of the moon being visible during the night and by day;
Kuhū and Sinīvālī are likewise remembered as the two dark fifteenth days (new moons), when the moon has vanished from view.

The time for the sacrifice is to be understood by adding the increase or decrease of the subsequent lunar day (tithi) to the preceding day, based on the primary lunar day. If the conjunction (*saṃdhi*) of the first lunar day (*pratipat*) occurs before the sun’s turning point (*āvartana*) or exactly at the turning point, the sacrifice is performed on that very day. If the conjunction occurs after the turning point, the sacrifice is on the following day. The last quarter of the final day of the *parvan* and the first three quarters of the *pratipat* constitute the time for the sacrifice. If the conjunction occurs during the afternoon suitable for the morning ritual, the fourth quarter of the *pratipat* on the following day is the time for the sacrifice, provided the conjunction was not in the forenoon. In this regard, the twofold division of the day is the same for both previously mentioned types of *parvan*. A specific rule for the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) will be stated later. If the *parvan* conjunction occurs before the turning point, it may be a "same-day" (*sadyaskāla*) rite or not; however, if the conjunction occurs before the turning point but after the *saṅgava* period, it is definitely a *sadyaskāla* rite. Some say that the entire full moon day is the day of sacrifice, or that when the *parvan* falls on the same day, it is a *sadyaskāla* rite. In the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is never a *sadyaskāla* nature; some say that applies only to the modified rites (*vikṛti*). Furthermore, regarding the full moon, this is the distinction: when the days are extremely long and the lunar day decreases, even if the fourth quarter is absent near sunrise, the *parvan* conjunction can still occur in the forenoon. In that case, on the day of the forenoon conjunction, the sacrifice is performed on the following day to avoid the conflict. [64] On the new moon (*amāvāsyā*), however, if the *parvan* conjunction occurs in the afternoon or later, the sacrifice must be performed on the following day even if the moon is visible. If the conjunction occurs in the forenoon, one should offer an oblation with the mantra "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā" and give a staff to a Brahmin as an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) on the day the moon is seen in the west. If the moon is seen in the east while performing the sacrifice, one should perform the *abhyuditā-iṣṭi* mentioned in the Taittirīya, or an oblation with the *manasvatī* verse, or an oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*. If the moon is seen in the west after the fire has been prepared (*anvādhāna*), one should complete the sacrifice on the following day and then perform the *pathikṛt-iṣṭi*. In that rite, there is a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Pathikṛt, a cake on eleven potsherds for Indra Vṛtrahan, and a cake on eight potsherds for Agni Vaiśvānara; a bow with an arrow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). This is the *pathikṛt-iṣṭi* mentioned in the Vājasaneyaka. Alternatively, the archetypal deities should be worshipped again, or an oblation with the *manasvatī* verse, or an oblation with the *vyāhṛtis* should be made. Even if the time for the morning sacrifice spans two days, the morning sacrifice is performed only on the day of the forenoon conjunction. In every case, the conjunction itself is the factor determining the postponement or advancement of the sacrifice, not the increase or decrease of the lunar day. The seventeenth lunar day is prohibited for the preparation of the fire (*anvādhāna*), but not for the sacrifice itself. When the archetypal sacrifice has begun, the modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) should be performed on the same day. If the conjunction is before the turning point, one should complete the archetype and then perform the modification. If the conjunction is after the turning point, one should complete the modification and then begin the archetype. If the *parvan* is not available, the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice should be performed during the bright fortnight under an auspicious asterism (*devanakṣatra*). The time for the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña* is when the moon is not visible in the east during the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Viśākhā.
Thus concludes the determination of the lunar festivals (*parvan*).

Now follows the determination of the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*): on the eleventh day, a fast (*upavāsa*) must be observed. For householders who have sons, this is to be done only on the bright fortnight (*śukla*) eleventh day, not on the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa*) eleventh day. On the dark fortnight eleventh day, one may perform fasting, eating unasked food (*ayācita*), eating only at night (*nakta*), eating a single meal (*ekabhakta*), or giving gifts according to one's capacity; however, under no circumstances should one fail to observe the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*). One who is unable to fast should act in this manner. For householders who are sonless, as well as for ascetics (*yati*), forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), students (*brahmacārin*), those who have completed their studies (*snātaka*), and widows, the fast is obligatory on both the eleventh days.
He who desires union with Viṣṇu, prosperity, long life, progeny, and happiness,
should not eat on the eleventh day of either fortnight.
Thus, for those observing a fast as part of a Vaiṣṇava vow, the Kṛṣṇa (fourteenth) lunar day is not prohibited.
When a fast is obligatory but a Śrāddha occurs on that occasion,
one should perform the fast after having smelled the food offered to the ancestors.

If a *śrāddha* is performed on the eleventh day (*ekādaśī*), one should fast after smelling the remnants of that *śrāddha*. There is no prohibition against fasting on the eleventh day when it coincides with Sunday, a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), and so forth. During great calamities, great festivals, impurity due to birth (*sūtaka*), impurity due to menstruation (*ārtava*), or in cases of incapacity, the vow of the twelfth day (*dvādaśī-vrata*) must not be abandoned. In that case, for a compulsory (*nitya*) observance, one should bathe and perform the fast without the worship of deities. For an optional (*kāmya*) observance, however, having bathed, one should have one’s wife, husband, son, brother, sister, officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), or another person perform the worship and other rites. At the conclusion of the period of impurity due to birth or menstruation, one should give gifts; if the husband or wife gives a gift during the interval, even co-wives may do so for one another. It is the same for other vows. On the days preceding and following the eleventh day, one should eat only one meal. On the previous day, one should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils (*masūra*), excessive ghee, excessive satisfaction, eating a second time, and sexual intercourse. Then, being composed, having bathed in the morning on the eleventh day, one should make the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
Having remained without food on the eleventh day, I shall eat on the following day; O lotus-eyed one, O Acyuta, be my refuge.

Having thus resolved, one should avoid daytime sleep, sexual intercourse, the consumption of betel and similar substances, drinking water more than once, all sensual enjoyments, and conversation with women in their courses, women recently delivered, outcasts, heretics, and those of low birth. However, for virtuous women, the following do not cause defilement during a fast: flowers, ornaments, garments, perfumes, incense, ointments, the cleaning of teeth, and the application of collyrium.

In the event of a lapse in the restraint of speech, one should mutter Vaiṣṇava mantras or meditate upon Viṣṇu. In the event of a lapse in the restraints of mind, speech, and body, one should mutter the *Śārīra-mantra* beginning with "itthādyām. Having purified oneself and worshipped Viṣṇu, one should remain awake before Him or sleep. When the next day has dawned, having worshipped Him again, one should pray:
"O Keśava, for me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, be gracious through this vow;
O Lord, be well-disposed and grant the vision of knowledge."

Having bowed thus, one should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*). One should avoid bell-metal, meat, lentils (*masūra*), honey, greed, falsehood, oil, sesame paste, physical exercise, collyrium, eating a second meal, traveling on a journey, fatigue, sleeping during the day, and sexual intercourse. Otherwise, these would destroy the fruit of the fast and one’s spiritual power. When the Ekādaśī is pure and complete, and there is no Dvādaśī on the following day—whether that Dvādaśī is equal, deficient, or excessive—the fast is observed on the Ekādaśī. When the Ekādaśī is complete and there is some portion of Dvādaśī remaining, and the Dvādaśī extends into the Trayodaśī, then the latter (Dvādaśī) alone should be fasted upon by all. When the Ekādaśī is complete and there is some portion of Dvādaśī, and the Trayodaśī begins at the end of the night, then the former (Ekādaśī) should be fasted upon by householders and the latter by ascetics (*yatis*). (When the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī and some portion of Dvādaśī exists, whether the Dvādaśī extends into the Trayodaśī or not, then the latter alone should be fasted upon by all. When the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī and some portion of Dvādaśī exists, and the Trayodaśī begins at the end of the night, then even at the end of the day, the meritorious latter (Dvādaśī) should be fasted upon by ascetics, but not by householders who desire progeny; rather, it should be fasted upon by householders on the former (Ekādaśī). When the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī and there is no Dvādaśī, but the Dvādaśī exists on the Trayodaśī, then the Dvādaśī alone should be fasted upon. When the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī and the Dvādaśī is equal or deficient, then for those other than ascetics, the fast is on the Ekādaśī pierced by the Daśamī; for ascetics, however, the fast is on the pure Dvādaśī. When the Ekādaśī is pierced by the Daśamī and exists at the end of the night and on the Trayodaśī, whether equal or deficient, then for everyone the fast is on the Ekādaśī pierced by the Daśamī. This Ekādaśī vow is also a vow of Maheśvara according to the *Liṅga*, *Ādi*, and other Purāṇas. On the eighth and fourteenth days, one should perform either a nocturnal meal (*nakta*) or a single meal; the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) and the breaking of the fast should be performed with the name of Tatpuruṣa. Likewise, the Ekādaśī vow is also a vow of Sūrya (*Saura*) like the vow of Maheśvara, according to the *Saura Purāṇa*. The obligatory nature (*nityatva*) is the same everywhere. In this regard, the distinction is as follows: on the sixth lunar day, a fast should be observed, and on a Sunday, a single meal should be taken; the formal resolve should be made in the name of Savitṛ.
Thus concludes the determination of Ekādaśī in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now follows the determination of other lunar days (tithis):
Ekādaśī, Aṣṭamī, Ṣaṣṭhī, Paurṇamāsī, and Caturdaśī.
The new moon day and the third lunar day [are auspicious] for vows such as fasting and the like.

Those [days] pierced by the following [tithi] are meritorious; the remaining ones should be observed as pierced by the preceding [tithi]. In the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), the eighth and fourteenth days are recommended when pierced by the preceding [tithi]; some say this applies to the third and ninth as well. In all cases, for vows, gifts, and so forth, the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) is superior to the dark fortnight. And the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) is superior to the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*). If that is impossible, two *muhūrtas* after sunrise should be taken. For a fast (*upavāsa*), even a single *ghaṭikā* may be accepted.
But if those [tithis] not pierced [by others] cannot be obtained, one should eat only a small amount once of milk, curd, and ghee; thus it becomes a fast.

The Ekādaśī, even if pierced by five muhūrtas [of the previous day], should be observed as a fast; other days [pierced] by half of that [measure] are [to be avoided]. For the Nakta vow, the lunar day (tithi) that extends throughout the evening (pradoṣa) is always to be accepted.

[67] On the day of the fast (*upavāsa-tithi*), the night meal (*nakta*) which serves as a substitute for the fast should be performed. Furthermore, regarding a vow prescribed by the conjunction of a lunar day (*tithi*) and a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the lunar day that extends through the *pradoṣa* period should be accepted. (That very lunar day which is meritorious through its conjunction with a lunar mansion should be accepted for a vow prescribed for it. However, for the vow of the *Śravaṇa-dvādaśī*, the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) that extends through the sunrise should be accepted. In this regard, if the eleventh lunar day (*ekādaśī*) ends on the morning of the twelfth, and the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) occurs during the remainder of the night of the twelfth, then: "It destroys twelve twelfth lunar days if the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) takes place on the thirteenth."

The breaking of the fast (*pāraṇa*) at the end of every lunar day (*tithi*) or asterism (*nakṣatra*), as well as the observances (*niyama*), have already been stated previously. However, on the occasion of a solar transit (*saṃkrānti*), on a Sunday, during an eclipse, on the *vyatīpāta* yoga, and on the eleventh day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇaikādaśī*), a householder who has sons should neither break his fast nor observe a fast. This prohibition applies specifically to those occasions such as the solar transit and so forth, but not to those prescribed for other purposes.
Thus concludes the determination of ordinary lunar days.
Now, the determination of what is to be done and what is not to be done during an intercalary month (malamāsa) is stated:

A month devoid of the sun’s transit (*saṃkrānti*) is an intercalary month (*malamāsa*). In that intercalary month, one must perform obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites that would otherwise entail a fall from grace (*pātitya*) if not performed; such rites include daily bathing, the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), fire-rituals (*agnikārya*), the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), honoring guests, the *agnihotra*, the *aupāsana* fire, burnt offerings (*homa*), the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and *pārvaṇeṣṭi* sacrifices, the *pārvaṇasthālīpāka*, the *piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *amāvāsyā-pārvaṇaśrāddha*, monthly *śrāddhas*, worship of the gods, and regular giving. These obligatory acts must be performed even in the intercalary month. Obligatory acts for which there is no other recourse (*ananyagatika*) are those that must be performed. Those for which there is another recourse (*anyagatika*)—such as the *somayāga*, *paśubandha*, *ādhāna*, *āgrayaṇa*, and *cāturmāsya* sacrifices—are not to be performed in the intercalary month. Likewise, rites prescribed according to the specific month of the performer, such as the *mahālayāṣṭakā*, the ritual of beginning Vedic study (*upākarma*), its conclusion (*utsarjana*), the *śravaṇākarma*, the *āśvayujakarma*, and the *pratyavarohaṇa* sacrifice, are not to be performed in the intercalary month; they must be performed in the subsequent month. Occasional rites (*naimittika*) include those occasioned by pregnancy, such as the *puṃsavana*, *anavalobhana*, *sīmantonnayana*, and *jātakarman* performed according to the month of gestation, along with the auspicious gifts associated with them; rites on lunar or solar eclipses, including bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and *śrāddha* and giving; the *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day of the month of *Maghā*; bathing at sacred sites (*tīrtha*), water-libations, *śrāddhas*, and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*); oblations of barley, rice, sesame, and so forth; purification after death; and the first *śrāddha*, the nine *śrāddhas*, and the sixteen *śrāddhas*, as well as the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and other rites intended to liberate the deceased from the state of a ghost (*pretatva*). Because these occasional rites have no other recourse when the intercalary month arrives, they must be performed. Consequently, while performing the monthly rites until the end of the year, one should not perform them in the intercalary month. (At the end of the year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* and the "liberation of the year" should be done at their proper time; even while performing the monthly rites, one should not do them in the intercalary month. One should certainly perform them in the subsequent month. For those who died in the intercalary month, the annual *śrāddha* (*ābdika*) should be performed in the intercalary month; for others, it should be performed in the subsequent month. When a usurer or a servant dies, one should not avoid the intercalary month. Here, the *vaṣaṭ*-offerings, obligatory and occasional rites, those undertaken for desired ends (*kāmya*), expiatory offerings (*prāyaścitta-iṣṭi*), and *sthālīpāka* homas are to be performed even in the intercalary month. However, even an occasional rite such as the *jāteṣṭi* (offering upon birth) is not to be performed in the intercalary month. After the *ādhāna*, one should not perform the *anvārambhaṇīyeṣṭi* or the first *sthālīpāka* in the intercalary month. Desirable (*kāmya*) sacrifices and homas are not to be performed in the intercalary month. A desirable rite commenced before the intercalary month may be performed once the intercalary month has arrived. If, due to a lack of old grain, one cannot subsist, a sick person may perform the *āgrayaṇa* with *syāmāka* millet in the intercalary month, eat the new grain, and then perform the *vrīhyāgrayaṇa* at the proper time. If the *somayāga* was not performed before the spring festival due to divine circumstances, and if the remaining single festival is defiled by the intercalary month, then even the obligatory *somayāga* should not be performed there; in that case, there is simply a lapse (*lopa*), just as in the case of a wife's menstruation.
Thus concludes the determination regarding the intercalary month.
Now follows the rule concerning what is fit and unfit to be eaten.

One should not eat food that is defiled by preparation (*saṃskāraduṣṭa*), defiled by ritual action (*kriyāduṣṭa*), or defiled by its inherent nature (*svabhāvaduṣṭa*). Food defiled by preparation is that which is devoid of the *vaiśvadeva* offering and other such rites. Food defiled by ritual action refers to a change in the proper order within a single row of diners. Food defiled by its inherent nature includes garlic and the like; as well as *kāliṃdava*, cucumber, *kumbhītaka*, round gourd, *vanyakaṇṭaki*, safflower, red *śigru*, *kovidāra*, *śleṣmātaka*, reed, small white thorny plant, eggplant, and all foul-smelling bulbs, roots, and fruits—all these must be avoided in every way at all times by ascetics and those observing vows. On the eighth day and other such lunar days, one should respectively avoid the skull, entrails, nails, skin, and sesame seeds. Food belonging to one’s own *gotra*, food from artisans, food shaken off by a cloth or by the hand, food smelled, food sneezed upon, and so forth, will be declared inedible in the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Thus ends the rule regarding what may and may not be eaten. Now follows the rule for eating.

Having performed the daily rites (*nityavidhi*), having washed his feet and sipped water twice outside, facing either east or north, wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) and an upper garment, with jewels and gold in his hands if he can afford it, pure, adorned with perfumes, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and garlands, seated comfortably on a smooth four-legged stool made of auspicious wood such as *śrīparṇī* upon the ground with his feet placed thereon, with hands between his knees, silent, and focused on that [act], a Brahmin should eat within a square *gomaya*-maṇḍala at the end of the worship, near a lamp. A Kṣatriya should eat in a triangular maṇḍala; a Vaiśya in a circular one; a Śūdra should eat on a sprinkled [spot]. Then, having placed a clean vessel on a tray or similar support within the maṇḍala, having washed it, and being surrounded by guests, visitors, servants, sons, and others, he should eat in a secluded place food that remains from the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), which was previously prepared, prescribed, measured, seasoned with ghee and other ingredients, and served by his mother, wife, and so forth. Without disparaging that food, with his right hand purified by a *pavitra* (ring of grass) free from the *brahmagranthi* knot, having sprinkled the food with the *Gāyatrī*, consecrated it with the mantra beginning "Oṃ bhūḥ," and offered an oblation (*bali*) on the ground with "I sprinkle thee with truth through the Real; Oṃ, salutation to Citra, salutation to Citragupta, salutation to Yama, salutation to all beings," he should take the *āpośana* water with the mantra "Thou art the spreading of the nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*). Then, eating every morsel with all his fingers, he should offer five oblations ending in "svāhā" for the sake of the vital breaths: "To Prāṇa... to Vyāna... to Udāna... to Samāna..."—these oblations being accompanied by ghee or milk. Avoiding fickleness of speech, hands, and feet, the man should eat the entire morsel including the thumb. Having eaten, he should drink half a mouthful of water with the mantra "Thou art the covering of the nectar" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), pour the other half on the ground outside his hand, discard the *pavitra*, throw it on the ground or into the vessel, wash the remains thoroughly, and sip water twice. Then, having rubbed his hands together, sprinkled them around, and touched his eyes with the thumb, he should touch fire and remember his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*). One should not sip water while remaining on the seat in the dining room, nor drink with joined palms, nor with the *pitṛtīrtha* (the part of the hand used for offerings to ancestors). One should avoid a seat made of cow-dung, clay, or wood from the *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, or *arka* trees; likewise, a seat that is patched, broken, burnt, or bound with iron. One should avoid a broken or cracked vessel, except those made of copper, silver, gold, or stone. One should not eat with dry hands or feet, nor while standing, walking, lying down, bent over, on a bedstead, during the twilight hours, while staying on a bed, nor having placed the vessel thereon. One should not eat placing it on the knee, in the lap, or on the palm of the left hand. One should not eat with children, nor without giving to those who wish to drink. One should not eat without first giving to kinsmen, children, the elderly, or the sick, nor with his wife, except during marriage. One should not eat while wearing wet clothes, nor having made a couch of cloth and such, nor with legs raised, nor with feet resting on a seat, nor facing an intermediate direction, nor in a defiled row. A row is broken by water, grass, fire, ashes, a path, or a pillar. During an eclipse, one should not eat. At that time, there is no impurity due to birth or death (*sūtaka-sūtakitva*). Having then performed bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), sacrifice, and charity, and having performed the "liberation bath" (*mokṣasnāna*), one may eat. During a solar eclipse, one should not eat for four watches (*yāma*) beforehand; during a lunar eclipse, for three watches. If the moon rises already eclipsed, one should not eat during the day beforehand. If the sun and moon have not yet been released and have not reached the sky, one should bathe and eat on the following day.
When the moon has risen while being eclipsed, one should not begin eating during the day.

One should not eat during the two twilights, nor at midnight, nor in houses where fire is absent or which are empty; nor while not wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), nor with the left hand, nor with the back of the hand, nor with only the palm of the hand, nor from a cloth. One should not eat sitting on another's seat. Furthermore, it should be understood that an ascetic (*yati*), a student (*brahmacārī*), one under a vow (*vratī*), and a widow should not eat from a *yantrikā* (a wooden tray) or similar vessels. Then, at the proper time, having performed the evening twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, and the honoring of guests, one should eat surrounded by one's dependents. Regarding the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) at night, there is this distinction: "I sprinkle you with Truth through Right" (*ṛtaṃ tvā satyena pariṣiñcāmi*)—this is for the evening. Then, together with his wife, he should sleep while enjoying fragrant ointments, betel, and so forth. One should not sleep during the twilight, nor in an empty house, a cremation ground, under a solitary tree, at a crossroads, in the temples of fierce deities such as Śiva, the Mothers (*mātṛkā*), Yakṣas, Nāgas, Skanda, Bhairava, and others, nor on riverbanks. One should not sleep upon grain, cattle, gods, Brahmins, fire, or teachers; nor while impure, nor when one is already impure, nor with wet clothes or feet, nor naked. One should sleep with the head toward the east or the south, having bowed to one's tutelary deity, keeping in mind [the deity], and having placed a bamboo staff (*vaiṇava-daṇḍa*) near the bed. Having washed one's feet and performed protective rites (*rakṣā*), one should sleep. One should spend the first watch of the night and the last watch in study (*vidyā*).
Thus ends the section on daily observances (*āhnika*) in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*;
now the purification of substances (*dravyaśuddhi*) is described.

In this regard, feces, urine, semen, blood, fat, marrow, liquor, and wine are causes of extreme defilement (*atyantopahati*). Dogs, jackals, boars, cats, and the like, as well as excrement and so forth, earwax, feces, nails, phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, sweat, and the like, are causes of slight defilement (*alpopahati*). Likewise, contact with a *śūdra* who has consumed leftovers, with twice-born persons during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), with untouchable crows and the like, with untouchable boars and the like, and with animals, is called slight defilement. Similarly, contact with urine, leftovers, or wild animals for a short duration and in a small area is called slight defilement. However, upon contact with those born of the fifth or the lowest castes, such as *caṇḍālas*, with a woman who has recently given birth or one who is menstruating, with outcasts (*patita*), with a dog, with a corpse, or with those who have touched a corpse, extreme defilement occurs. Furthermore, contact with liquor for a short time and in a small area, or contact with leftovers, blood, and the like for a long time, results in extreme defilement due to the corruption of the object.

A vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or iron that has been defiled by feces, urine, a *caṇḍāla*, a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or other such impurities, shall be purified by twenty-one applications of ash and acidic water (*amlodaka*). A vessel of gold, silver, copper, or iron that is merely touched by feces, urine, a *caṇḍāla*, a menstruating woman, or others, provided it is free of stains (*nirlepa*), shall be purified by washing with water; if it has stains (*salepa*), it shall be purified by ash and acidic water. For vessels of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and the like, the process of smelting (*āvartana*) is required. When there is extensive damage, all of them must be melted down and recast. Vessels made of metal are purified by immersion in cow’s urine; if the stain does not depart, they must be recast. Copper that has been defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, or by a *caṇḍāla* and others, is purified by acid and water. In the case of bell-metal and brass (*pittala*), if they are defiled by rinsing the mouth with feces or urine, by washing feet, or by the touch of a *caṇḍāla* and others, they are purified by scrubbing them twenty-one times with ash and then washing them. If the defilement occurred for a short time, purification is by heating and scraping; if for a long time, recasting is required. Alternatively, having buried them in the ground for six months, they may simply be scrubbed; in this regard, the amount of effort should be greater for a greater degree of defilement and lesser for a lesser degree. Thus, for all metallic objects, "recasting" means making them anew; "scraping" means planing. If bell-metal or brass is defiled by the remains of food from cows, horses, or crows, or by the touch of a Śūdra, they are purified by washing with ten applications of ash. If the defilement is of short duration, purification is by ash along with rubbing with salt and oil; if of long duration, recasting is required. Tin, lead, and iron are purified by ash and water. In the case of minor defilement of all metallic objects, purification should be performed as appropriate with cow’s urine, cow dung, earth, ash, acid, and water. For mother-of-pearl, conch-shells, stones, gems, jewels, and aquatic products, if they are merely touched by feces, urine, the remains of food from a *caṇḍāla* and others, purification is by washing with water. If they have stains, purification is by ash and water, or by earth and water. If they are extremely defiled, they are purified by burying them in the ground for seven days and then washing them. There is no fault in breaking vessels made of gold, silver, copper, conch, mother-of-pearl, stone, crystal, and other gems. For objects made of horn, ivory, or bone, if the defilement is minor, purification is by washing with the powder of *bilva* fruit, white mustard seeds, or any one of earth, ash, cow’s urine, or cow dung. If the defilement is extreme, they must be planed; if they are penetrated by the essence of an impure substance, they must be discarded. For vessels made of wood, bamboo, or cane, if the defilement is minor, they are purified by planing; those that are excessively defiled must be discarded. For vessels made of wood-apple, *bilva*, bottle-gourd, or coconut, if the defilement is minor, they are purified by washing and scrubbing with a cow's tail; if the defilement is extreme, they must be discarded. For vessels made of horn, bone, or ivory, and for rare aquatic products, if they are extremely defiled, purification is by planing and washing. For earthen vessels that are slightly defiled, purification is by burning them again. Those defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, or touched by a corpse, a woman who has recently given birth, or a menstruating woman, must be discarded. In large storage jars, an external defect does not defile the interior; in that case, only the exterior is to be washed. Vessels such as the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are purified by washing with water. Sacrificial vessels containing oily substances are purified by washing with hot water. When many vessels are piled together and only one is defiled, purification is to be performed for that one alone, not for those touched by it. For raw bulbs, roots, and vegetables, and for bamboo vessels, clothes, and wood touched by impure things, purification is by washing with water. For clothes that weigh more than what one person can carry, which are thick, numerous, or otherwise touched by a *caṇḍāla* and others—even if they are unwashed or purchased—the purification is by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). In the case of white clothes and threads, twenty items constitute a "plurality" if they are commercial goods, thick, or new; eleven items constitute a plurality for patterned clothes; three items constitute a plurality for those dyed with safflower and the like. Even fewer than these constitute a plurality in the case of commercial goods and new items; even a very small amount constitutes a plurality when pierced by a needle. Purification of those few items is by washing. For unwashed or dirty clothes, whether few or many, and for new clothes or those with fast colors, washing is required for Vedic rites. For a woolen blanket (*āvikakambala*), if the defect is minor, purification is by exposure to the sun's rays or by sprinkling. In the case of feces, urine, and other defects, purification is by washing with earth from an anthill. For silk (*kauśeya*) cloth, if the defect is minor, purification is by sprinkling. If defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, purification is by washing with earth and water. For linen (*kṣauma*) cloth, if the defect is minor, purification is by washing. If defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, purification is by scrubbing with *bilva* powder and washing with water. Cloth associated with indigo (*nīlī*) must be discarded by all four castes according to its nature.
In woolen cloth and silk thread, the defect of indigo-dye is not found.

For a Nepalese blanket (*nepālakambala*) that has suffered slight defilement, sprinkling with water (*prokṣaṇa*) is prescribed. In the case of defects such as contact with urine and the like, purification occurs by rubbing it with the froth produced from *ariṣṭa* fruit and then washing it with water. For cotton beds, pillows, and cloths dyed with safflower (*kusumbha*) and similar substances, if they have suffered slight defilement, they should be dried slightly in the sun. If they are touched by feces, urine, or other impurities, the purified portion must be removed, and then purification follows from drying. The same applies to wool, cotton, silk-cotton (*tūla*), safflower, saffron, flowers, camphor, and resinous exudations. A white cloth touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person becomes pure through washing; if it is defiled by feces and the like, purification occurs by washing it with cow’s urine and cow dung. For items associated with beds, seats, and vehicles, as well as for garments with many hairs, purification is achieved by sprinkling. The purification of skins is the same as that of cloth. However, for new ones, purification occurs when the odor is removed by washing them with a decoction of bitter and dry substances from the *jambu* tree and others, or with water infused with the three myrobalans (*triphalā*).
Even in the case of a new, large, and seamless leather garment,
purification by the aforementioned substances in the prescribed order is declared by the wise to be immediate.
The highest purification of leather is said to be accomplished in twelve days by means of clay, ashes, and decoctions of the three myrobalans (triphalā), each applied for three days.
One *pala* of ash is prescribed, twice that amount of clay;
three times that amount of astringent dyes (*kāṣāya*) is taught, and three times that amount of the three myrobalans (*triphalā*) is prescribed.

In leather vessels, the exterior is defiled, but the interior is not. There, the exterior must be thoroughly washed. Grain that exceeds the weight of one man’s load, even if touched by a *caṇḍāla* or others, becomes pure by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Grain weighing exactly one man’s load becomes pure by washing. Impure grain mixed with earth becomes pure by being husked into rice. If a heap of grain is smeared with urine and such, the smeared portion should be removed, and the remainder becomes pure by sprinkling. If grain is stored in a house and that house is burned, and if a human or animal dies therein, that grain must be discarded. Grain situated underground or within a granary becomes pure by sprinkling. Wet pulses such as mung beans and black gram, if less than a man’s load, become pure by washing; if dry and excessively defiled, they should merely be sprinkled. Grain defiled by *mūra* and similar substances must be discarded. A book touched by a *caṇḍāla* or others should be sprinkled. For leguminous grains (*śimbidhānya*), there is purity by sprinkling when the defilement is slight. Grain that is impure and touched by dust becomes pure by being de-husked. In the case of extreme defilement, it must be discarded. In the case of hard grains, "much" refers to more than a man’s load; for loose grains, "much" refers to a measure of one *droṇa*; for rice, split peas, and the like, "much" refers to half that amount. In those cases, if there is the defect of touch, there is sprinkling. In all cases of defilement by feces, urine, and so forth, having discarded that much, everything should be sprinkled. Loose rice and the like are to be sprinkled everywhere. That which is less than a man’s meal must be discarded. Earth, leather, grass, wood, and the like, if exceeding a man’s load, become pure from wind and sun in the case of slight defilement. Ground soiled by hair, insects, chaff, and the like, becomes pure by sweeping and sprinkling. Ground frequented by dogs, donkeys, camels, pigs, and the like, becomes pure by the treading of cows, sweeping, and sprinkling. If ground is extremely defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, it becomes pure by scraping, the treading of cows, sweeping, and sprinkling. Ground defiled by a woman’s childbirth, defiled by the residence of *caṇḍālas* and the like, defiled for a long time by feces and urine, or defiled for a long time by donkeys, camels, pigs, and the like, becomes pure by removing the earth of that spot, filling it with other earth, and then performing the treading of cows, sweeping, and sprinkling. If that same ground is extremely defiled, it becomes pure by digging it up, burning it with straw fire, filling it with other earth, and then performing the treading of cows, sweeping, and sprinkling. When a house is impure, the plastering of the walls, the scraping of the floor, and sweeping must be performed. Even ground that has been the site of a cremation ground due to being scented for a long time by feces, urine, and so forth, attains purity through the aforementioned method after being washed by rain. When a garden or field becomes a cremation ground and is extremely defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, purity comes from plowing with a plowshare after the rain. In a house where a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya has died, one should discard the earthenware vessels and cooked food located there. The place of death should be smeared with cow dung and purified by the treading of a cow whose mouth has been untouched by goats, or by sprinkling with water mixed with *kuśa* grass and gold while reciting sacred texts. If someone dies in a house due to imprisonment by a king or others, the ground and walls should be well-sprinkled, heated by straw fire, trodden by cows, and exposed to the rays of the sun, according to the previously mentioned rule. Whether in a birth or a death in the house, after the period of impurity (*āśauca*) has passed, purity comes from throwing earth from a pure site and by reciting the *puṇyāha* formula. If a Śūdra or similar person dies in a Brāhmaṇa’s house, the house is impure for ten days. If an unworthy Śūdra dies, the impurity lasts for a month. If a *caṇḍāla*, an outcaste (*patita*), or similar person dies, the impurity lasts for four months. If a washerman or similar person dies, the impurity lasts for two months. In all these cases, at the end of the impurity, purification should be performed as prescribed for the purification of an impure site. If a cat or similar animal dies in a burnt Brāhmaṇa’s house, that house becomes pure by plowing and sprinkling. If a dog, crow, or similar animal dies, the procedure for plowing is the same, with this specific difference. An image defiled by slight contact with iron becomes pure by rubbing with ashes and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). An image made of stone, if defiled by slight contact, becomes pure by being washed with water and earth from an anthill, followed by the *pañcagavya*. An image defiled by feces, urine, village mud, and so forth, should be consecrated with the *pañcagavya* for five days, submerged, thoroughly washed with cow urine, cow dung, and anthill earth, and then purified by re-consecration. For images made of gems, after washing them with the *pañcagavya*, a further washing should be performed.
