Water situated on the ground that possesses its natural smell, color, and taste, even if defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, is pure provided it is sufficient for three cows to drink. If it is less than that and touched by dogs, crows, and the like, it is pure provided it is sufficient for one cow to drink. Pure water brought in a vessel is pure on that very day; therefore, no ritual performance should be done with it on another day. Water in a large vessel exceeding four *droṇas* that is defiled by feces, urine, and so forth, becomes pure by discarding it, washing the vessel, scrubbing it with *kuśa* grass, washing it again, sprinkling it with the *pañcagavya*, and refilling it with water. In small waters such as ponds, wells, and tanks, if the corpse of a dog, cat, or similar animal remains until it decays, that water becomes pure by drawing out all the water, removing the earth, and sprinkling with the *pañcagavya*. In the case of a structure built with stones or bricks, if it is a place for carving, the procedure is burning; otherwise, it is the same. In a wooden structure, there is only washing. In a large body of water, sixty jars of water should be drawn out. In the case of killing small creatures such as mice, thirty jars should be drawn out and cow urine and other substances added. There is no fault regarding the corpse of an aquatic creature in water. If a human corpse remains in the water of a pond or well, purity comes from drawing out a hundred jars of water and adding the *pañcagavya*. This same purification applies even when the corpse of an animal falls into it. In that case, if death occurs in the water, the water is impure for three nights. At the end of the impurity, the previously mentioned purification should be performed. If the water of a pond or well is defiled by shoes, phlegm, semen, feces, urine, blood, fat, marrow, or bone, purity comes from drawing out sixty jars if the water is abundant, or a hundred jars, followed by sprinkling with the *pañcagavya*. If the water of a well or similar source is defiled by impure dust, it becomes pure during the day by the touch of the sun's rays and the wind; at night by the touch of the wind, moon, and stars' rays; and at twilight by the touch of the wind. If the current of a river or the water of a tank is defiled by outcastes, it is pure everywhere except at the place occupied by them.
A *śāṇa*, a *pāṇitala*, a *māna*, a *kuḍava*, a *prastha*, an *āḍhaka*, a *droṇa*, and a *khārikā*— each subsequent measure is four times the preceding one, as previously stated.

If grain or cooked food measured by a *droṇa* is smelled by a cow, or touched by a donkey, a dog, a village pig, a domestic cock, or a crow, one should remove only the portion that was touched. The remainder of the food should be encircled with fire (*paryagnīkṛtya*) and sprinkled with water consecrated once with the *sahasragāyatrī*, or with the *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ* section of the Veda, or with the *śuddhavatī* verses, or with mantras containing words signifying purity (*śuciliṅga*). Having obtained the declaration from a Brahmin, "Let this be pure," it becomes purified. Or, if it has been smelled by the mouth of a goat, it is purified. If that food is rubbed by the saliva of a dog, a crow, or similar creatures, one should remove just that much; the rest should be sprinkled with water from a golden or silver vessel, touched with a firebrand (*ulmuka*), and touched with clarified butter and gold. It is then purified by the Brahmin’s declaration, "Let this be pure. If the aforementioned food is seen to be defiled by nails, hair, feces, urine, or the like, one should remove only what was seen, sprinkle it as before with consecrated water, scatter ashes over it, pour clarified butter upon it, and it is purified by the Brahmin’s declaration, "Let this be pure. In the case of a *droṇa* measure of clarified butter or fresh butter (*navanīta*) defiled by dogs, crows, ants, or the like, one should remove the defiled portion, purify it with a cloth, fill the vessel with more of the same substance, heat the whole in fire, and purify it by sprinkling with water consecrated with the *gāyatrī*. In that regard, for a *droṇa* measure of fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, milk, or curds, if defiled by a crow or similar creature, the purification is the same as for clarified butter. Curds, milk, and buttermilk kept in a Śūdra’s vessel become pure when poured into a twice-born’s vessel. If fresh butter, clarified butter, or honey has been kept in a Caṇḍāla’s vessel, it becomes very pure if heated and then poured into a Brahmin’s vessel. Fresh butter, clarified butter, or honey touched by a Caṇḍāla through negligence is purified by being thrown into water and then retrieved. Regarding grain and cooked food measured less than a *droṇa*, or clarified butter and other liquids measured less than an *āḍhaka*, or buttermilk and other liquids measured less than a *droṇa*: in the event of the aforementioned defilement, they must be discarded except in times of distress (*anāpadi*). In times of distress, however, purification occurs by the previously mentioned rules. If a sauce sufficient for four men to eat is extremely thin, it is purified by pouring more liquid over it. A small amount should be discarded. Molasses, salt, and the like are purified by being encircled with fire. If hair, insects, or the like are seen in food while eating, one should remove that portion, throw water, ashes, or earth into it, and it is purified. If such things touch the mouth, one should spit, drink water, spit again, drink clarified butter, and then eat. If hair or the like remains in the cooking vessel, the food should be discarded; having eaten it, one should fast. Whatever object is suitable for religious duty, exceedingly dear, and extremely difficult to obtain due to place or time—if that is defiled, even if it is small, it is purified by the previously mentioned rule. The mouth of a horse, the mouth of a goat, the mouth of a woman during sexual intercourse, the mouth of a dog during hunting, the mouth of a calf at birth, or the mouth of a bird when fruit falls—these, as well as merchandise, are always pure. Children are pure prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*); a woman is pure prior to marriage. Mice, locusts, mosquitoes, grasshoppers, flies, insects in grain, cows, elephants, horses, goats, parrots, and all living beings dwelling in water are pure by their very nature; they are not defiled even by contact with impure things. The rays of the moon and sun are pure by themselves. Fire is naturally pure, except when it is in contact with a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, impure substances, outcasts (*patita*), low-caste people (*antyaja*), or a cremation ground. Dust blown by the wind is pure, as are things produced by elephants, horses, and chariots. The dust from the feet of cows and dust arising from grain are praised as auspicious. However, dust arising from dogs, village pigs, donkeys, camels, goats, sheep, crows, owls, domestic birds, or brooms—if touched, it makes one unprosperous, shortens life, and is non-meritorious. An object whose defect is unknown is pure by itself. An object whose defect is doubtful is purified by the word of a Brahmin. Touching a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*) is detrimental to life and non-meritorious. (Likewise, touching clothes, hair, water from a jar, dust from censurable birds, or wind—all such things are unprosperous.)
Curd, milk, clarified butter, meat, fragrance, flowers, fish, a bed, a seat, food, and vegetables— these should never be refused anywhere.
Kuśa grass, vegetables, milk, fish, perfumes, flowers, curd, earth, meat, a bed, a seat, parched grain, and water— these should not be refused when offered.
Droplets from the mouth are pure; likewise are drops of water that have touched the ground after rinsing the mouth.
Beard that has entered the mouth is pure, but that which remains between the teeth should be discarded.
If one swallows [the betel] or sips water, there is no fault provided it was not part of the formal ritual;
however, if betel remains in the mouth, or has been discarded, or has been swallowed, one must perform the rite again.
One should neither sip water for purification nor abandon one's current task upon seeing an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, or others of that sort;
however, cows are pure behind their backs, whereas impurities originating from humans are unclean.
And paths are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the winds;
likewise, the mud and water on roads are purified when touched by outcasts, dogs, or crows.
Those built with baked bricks are purified by the wind alone;
likewise, a continuous stream of water is pure as it flows along.
"Water that has been praised by speech, or water that has been released [from a vessel], is always pure even if its source is unknown.
Thus ends the purification of substances in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. Now follows the purification of the body:

Purification for one smeared with impurities occurs through the removal of odor and stain by means of earth and water. One should avoid a *caṇḍāla* and an outcast (*patita*) from a distance; a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*) and a menstruating woman (*udakyā*) should be avoided whenever possible. In an unconfined place, if one comes into proximity with a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or an outcast at distances of four, three, two, or one *yuga* (four cubits) respectively, one must bathe with one's clothes on (*sacaila-snāna*). In a confined place, this applies even within the range of a cow’s tail or a whisk. Depending on the degree of proximity, bathing with one's clothes on must be performed. The same applies when stepping into the shadow of a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*) and others. If one intentionally touches a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or an outcast, one should bathe with one's clothes on and recite the *Abliṅga* mantras, the *Gāyatrī*, or the *Pādonā* and *Ardhapāda* [mantras] in sequence, eight hundred, seven hundred and fifty, and four hundred times respectively. In this context, touching through a cloth is treated as direct contact. For a second person who has touched someone touched by a *caṇḍāla* and so forth, and for a third person who has touched someone touched by that second person, bathing with one's clothes on and the respective half-recitation of the mantra apply everywhere. However, if the intentional touching reaches a fourth person, bathing alone is required. If one unintentionally touches a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or an outcast, one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform the recitation forty-four times, thirty-six times, and eighteen times respectively. For one who unintentionally touches someone touched by a *caṇḍāla* and so forth, bathing with one's clothes on, half the recitation, and a quarter of the recitation apply respectively; for a fourth person, merely sipping water (*ācamana*) is required. Regarding women in their courses, they say that on the second day and subsequent days, after bathing, one should perform the recitation minus a quarter. For those touched by such persons, after bathing, half of the respective recitation should be performed. If one is touched by a *caṇḍāla* and so forth using an unconscious object like a staff, bathing alone is required; for a third person, sipping water; and for objects, sprinkling with water (*prokṣaṇa*). If one intentionally touches a washerman and others, one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform ten recitations. If one intentionally touches someone touched by them, bathing with one's clothes on is required. If one unintentionally touches a washerman and others, bathing with one's clothes on is required. If one touches someone touched by them, bathing alone is required; for a third person, looking at a light (*jyotirdarśana*). If one intentionally touches a person of the fifth caste (*pañcamajāti*), bathing with one's clothes on and five recitations are required; for one touched by him, bathing alone. Upon touching a low-caste *śūdra*, bathing with one's clothes on; upon touching a high-caste *śūdra*, bathing alone. Upon touching a *niṣāda*, bathing with one's clothes on; upon touching someone touched by a *niṣāda*, one should bathe and then sip water. Having touched a corpse, one in a state of impurity due to death, the smoke of a funeral pyre, those who live off divine property, village priests, sellers of *soma*, wood from a sacrificial post or a funeral pyre, or anything inside a cremation ground, or human bones still containing fat or marrow, or vessels containing liquor—one should bathe with one's clothes on, recite the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times, consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*), bathe again, and sip water three times. In all cases of unintentional contact, bathing alone is required. For women, in place of recitation and oblation, the gift of food, grain, a water-jar, and so forth, should be made. Having touched those outside the Veda—such as Śaivas, Śāktas, Pāśupatas, Lokāyatas, atheists, temple-priests, or twice-born men engaged in forbidden acts—as well as one who has fallen from his status (*ārūḍhapatita*), one who has abandoned the sacred fires (*visṛṣṭāgni*), one accused of a crime, a rogue, a eunuch, or a corpse-burner, one should bathe with one's clothes on. If the contact was unintentional, bathing alone is required. When one is asleep during indigestion, or when the sun rises or sets while one is in solitude, or after a bad dream, touching a wicked person, undergoing a haircut, or eating, one should bathe after a *muhūrta* (two hours) has passed, or after vomiting. After sexual intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtu*), one should bathe. Outside the fertile period, proper purification and sipping of water are required. If one has sexual intercourse during the day, or on the eighth or fourteenth lunar days, one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform the penance prescribed in the Smṛtis. If one remains for more than two watches (*yāma*) without performing purification and sipping water after urination, defecation, etc., one should bathe with one's clothes on and perform oblations and recitations with the *Vyāhṛtis*. If one emits semen at sunrise or sunset, one should bathe with one's clothes on, recite "punar manaḥ," and offer oblations of clarified butter with the seven *Vyāhṛtis*, or simply recite them. If unintentional, bathing with one's clothes on is required. Upon the twitching of the eyes or a piercing cry in the ears, bathing with one's clothes on, recitation, and oblations are required. Upon touching carnivorous animals such as dogs, jackals, wolves, donkeys, camels, wild boars, rams, or monkeys above the navel, excluding the hands, one should bathe with one's clothes on. If the touch is below the navel, bathing alone is required. If it occurs at night above the navel, bathing alone is required. If it is below the navel, one should wash the area, sprinkle water, sip water again, and become pure. Upon touching birds such as crows, owls, kites, lice, pigeons, village cocks, or other carnivorous birds above the navel, excluding the hands, one should bathe with one's clothes on. If the touch is below the navel, bathing alone is required. If it occurs at night above the navel, bathing alone is required. Below the navel, one should simply wash the area. If one is touched above the navel by road-dust, mud, water, spittle, and so forth, one should bathe immediately. If the touch is below the navel, washing the area is sufficient. Having been touched by impure substances belonging to one's own or another's species—such as feces, urine, semen, blood, bone-marrow, fat, and the like—or by spiritsuous liquor (*surā*) and intoxicants, one should wash away the odor and stain with earth and water and then bathe. If the touch is above the navel, one should bathe and fast. If the organs are defiled by food remnants, one should bathe, fast, and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). However, upon touching one's own bodily excretions, even above the navel, washing alone is required. Upon touching the bone of a twice-born person while it is still moist with fat, a Brahmin must bathe with his clothes on. If it is dry, bathing alone is required. If it is very old, one becomes pure by sipping water, touching a cow, or looking at the sun. If it is the bone of a non-twice-born person, there is a three-night fast if it is moist, and a one-night fast if it is dry. In the case of a non-human bone, however, only edible food should be avoided. Upon touching the bone or teeth of a five-nailed animal or a corpse, if it is moist, one should bathe and change into different clothes. Upon entering a village during rain where mud and filth are mixed, one should wash the shanks with three applications of earth and the feet with six. There is no fault if the mud and such have dried by the wind. Upon stepping into the shadow of a dog-cooker and others, one should bathe with one's clothes on and drink clarified butter, or "golden water" (*hiraṇyodaka*),
In battle, on the marketplace road, in processions and temples,
during festivals, sacrifices, and pilgrimages, and in times of upheaval for a village or a country;
In the vicinity of large bodies of water, among great crowds of people,
during the outbreak of fire, and in times of great calamity, there is no fault in touching what is normally untouchable.
The sense organ that functions by reaching its object is one that grasps what is touched, while the other sense organs grasp what is not touched;
they describe the objects of these two respectively as "touched" and "untouched."
Thus ends the rule regarding touching and non-touching.
Now follows the rule regarding impurity (aśauca).

Within the first four months of pregnancy, the loss of the embryo alone is called *srāva* (miscarriage). In that case, for *srāva*, there is impurity (*āśauca*) for three nights for the mother during the first four months. Beyond that, for the mother, the period of impurity lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had been in the womb. For those who share the same lineage (*sagotra*) and are *sapiṇḍas*, purification occurs immediately by bathing. Those from whom the lineage branches off are the *kūṭastha*; counting from him, seven generations are *sapiṇḍas*. Beyond them are the *samānodakas*. In the fifth and sixth months, the loss of the embryo alone is called *pāta* (falling). In the case of *pāta*, the impurity for the mother lasts for as many days as the number of months the fetus had been in the womb. For the father and other *sapiṇḍas*, the impurity lasts for three nights. This impurity caused by the loss of the embryo is the same for all social classes (*varṇas*). From the seventh month onwards, the emergence of a full-term fetus is called *prasava* (birth). In the case of birth, the full period of impurity caused by childbirth—lasting ten days and so forth according to each class—applies to everyone. For *samānodakas*, it is three nights. The state of untouchability (*aspṛśyatva*) caused by birth applies only to the mother until the end of her impurity, not to the father; for him, there is no untouchability after bathing. For *sapiṇḍas*, there is never any untouchability at all. A woman who has given birth (*sūtikā*) may engage in normal activities once the impurity of her own class has passed. However, for rites intended for unseen spiritual merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*), a woman who has borne a son is unfit for twenty nights, while one who has borne a daughter is unfit for a month. On the day of a son’s birth, gold, land, cattle, horses, clarified butter, clothing, beds, houses, and so forth—all these may be accepted as gifts. Cooked food (*kṛtānna*) must be avoided. If cooked food is accepted, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance is required. On the day of a son’s birth, one should perform acts of giving (*dāna*). If gold and such items are unavailable, one should make a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) at that time and offer them later. On the first day, the gift of gold and so forth should be made; on the sixth or seventh day, the offering of oblations (*bali*); on the tenth day, the gift of food, and so on, according to local custom. Protection of the lying-in chamber (*sūtikāgṛha*) must be maintained, especially at night. If the death of that infant occurs during the period of birth-impurity, it is said as follows: If the death of the infant or the exit of a lifeless infant occurs after the cutting of the umbilical cord, the full period of impurity caused by birth applies to all *sapiṇḍas* according to their respective classes. For the cause of death, however, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥ śuddhiḥ*). But if the death of the infant occurs before the cutting of the umbilical cord, the impurity for *sapiṇḍas* due to birth lasts for three nights. For the cause of death, there is immediate purification. For the mother, the full impurity due to birth applies according to her class. For the cause of death, there is immediate purification. If the infant dies before the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), burial alone is prescribed; there is no following the corpse (*anugamana*), nor the offering of fire or water, etc. For the relatives (*jñātis*), purification occurs immediately after a bath with clothes on. After that, if death occurs before the eruption of teeth, burial is performed silently, or cremation and the offering of water, etc., may be done. Following the corpse is optional; in the case of burial, there is immediate purification. In the case of cremation, however, it lasts for one day. As for burial, one should wash away the corpse's filth, anoint it with ghee, bathe it, and decorate it according to one's ability with new clothes, threads, perfumes, garlands, ointments, and so forth, and then perform the burial outside the village on clean ground. As for cremation, having similarly bathed and decorated the corpse, the relatives, led by the eldest, should carry it to the cremation ground and perform the rite silently with common fire (*laukikāgni*). The offering of water and so forth is also done silently. In the case of cremation, one should avoid impure fires, fires of *caṇḍālas*, those of women in childbirth (*sūtakī*), outcasts (*patita*), or funeral pyres. From the eruption of teeth until the first year—even for one whose tonsure (*cūḍā*) has been performed—the impurity lasts for one day. In the first year, even for one who has erupted teeth but whose tonsure has not been performed, it is only one day. After the eruption of teeth and until the age of three, for one whose tonsure has not been performed, either burial or cremation should be done. In the case of burial, the impurity lasts for one day; in the case of cremation, for three nights. In this context, following the corpse is optional until the completion of two years; thereafter, it is mandatory. After the eruption of teeth and until the age of three, for one whose tonsure has been performed, cremation is done silently, and the silent offering of water, etc., is done. The three-night impurity is mandatory. After three years, even for one whose tonsure has been performed, until the initiation (*upanayana*), following the corpse is mandatory. Silent cremation, the offering of water, and the three-night impurity are fixed rules that must be observed. In the case of the death of one who is not initiated, the view that the parents observe a ten-day impurity is disregarded. Regarding the impurity for the death of one not initiated, the various classes become touchable (*spṛśya*) after one-third of their own respective periods of impurity have elapsed. Upon hearing of the death of one not initiated, there is no further impurity; there is only a bath. This impurity based on age is the same for all classes. At the end of the impurity, having bathed, one should feed Brahmins preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*). In the case of the death of a maiden, however, for *sapiṇḍas* related within three generations, purification occurs by bathing, provided it is before the performance of the tonsure or up to the time of the tonsure. Among women, *sāpiṇḍya* extends only to three generations as long as they are unmarried. Therefore, before the betrothal (*vāgdāna*), the impurity lasts for one day. Thereafter, before marriage, for both the husband’s side and the father’s side, the impurity lasts for three nights up to three generations. Some say that in the absence of a betrothal, the certainty of marriage is the limit. In this case, for a child under two years, burial is prescribed; thereafter, cremation or treatment like a male is done. All matters regarding untouchability, etc., are exactly as previously stated. After initiation, in the case of the death of a man, and after marriage, in the case of the death of a woman or a Śūdra, one should cremate according to rule and observe full impurity according to class, accompanied by the offering of water and rice-balls (*piṇḍa*). That cremation should be performed with the *kapālāgni* (potsherd-fire) according to the procedure taught in one's own Vedic branch (*śākhā*) for those who are celibate students (*brahmacārin*), those without a sacred fire (*anagnika*), or widowers (*vidhura*), etc. For a householder (*gṛhastha*), it should be done with the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*). For one who maintains the three sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the cremation should be done with the *tretāgni*. That impurity lasts ten days for Brāhmaṇas, twelve days for Kṣatriyas, fifteen days for Vaiśyas, and one month for Śūdras. For Śūdras who are established in good conduct, who serve the twice-born, and who perform the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), the impurity lasts fifteen days. The position that it should be ten nights in the fourth [generation] is refuted.
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and is learned in the Vedas is purified in one day.

These and other such [rules] are disregarded. Furthermore, that period of impurity (*āśauca*) for one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) must begin from the very day of cremation, provided the cremation has been performed according to rule. If one dies while abroad, there is no lapse of duties such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) for sons and others until the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) have been performed according to rule. For one who does not maintain the sacred fires, impurity begins from the day of death. If there is no cremation according to rule for one who does not maintain the sacred fires, the assumption of impurity is optional. If there is no cremation according to rule for one who maintains the sacred fires, there is no impurity at all. The offering of water and fire (*agny-udaka-dāna*) for sons should be performed on the first day, or on the tenth, or after three days, or before the tenth day, or on some day prior to the first *śrāddha* ceremony; it should be done outside the village. The same applies upon the death of a teacher (*guru*). In the absence of the corpse, one should perform the "bone-rite" (*asthi-saṃskāra*). In the absence of bones, having fashioned a substitute body with *palāśa* stalks or *kuśa* grass, one should perform the rite again. In the case of a second rite for one who maintained the sacred fires, the cremation and so forth must be performed just as for an actual corpse, and the full period of impurity must be observed according to caste. If the second rite for one who maintained the sacred fires occurs during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), purification occurs by the remainder of that *sūtaka* alone. If the second rite occurs after the *sūtaka* has passed, then for a son or wife who had not yet assumed impurity, the full period of ten days or more applies; for those who had already assumed impurity, it is three nights. The same applies to a husband regarding his wife’s second rite, and between two wives regarding each other. For *sapiṇḍas* who have not assumed impurity, it is three nights; for those who have already assumed it, there is no further impurity. If a birth or death is known after the first day while one is abroad, purification for sons and others occurs by the remainder of their own respective impurity. If a person of lower caste is a *sapiṇḍa* of a higher caste such as a Brāhmaṇa, the impurity of the higher caste applies. Female slaves, male slaves, and servants become touchable (*spṛśya*) when they have completed a period equal to the master’s impurity while performing the master’s work; however, their eligibility for their own duties resumes only at the end of their own impurity. For those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*), there is no impurity; at the end of that [period], there is merely the washing away of dirt. Having burned the corpse, returning without looking back, they should take a smooth, uncracked stone, go to a large body of water, wash away the bodily filth in that great water, clean their clothes, bathe, and then bathe again with their clothes on. Then, remaining silent and composed, the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* of the same lineage, led by the elders, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*), facing south, shall pronounce the name and lineage of the deceased and, with the left hand placed over the right, release a handful of water mixed with sesame seeds onto the stone once, saying, "May the deceased be satisfied. Having thus offered the water and emerged from the water, standing properly on ground where fresh grass has grown, the family elders should console them with ancient histories, saying: "Grief is fruitless; the tears and phlegm shed by kinsmen fall into the mouth of the deceased; therefore, weeping should not be done; the prescribed rites must be performed. Once consoled, they should wring out their clothes, dry them, and go home with the children first. Standing at the door, composed, they should slowly chew neem leaves, sip water (*ācamana*), and touch fire, water, cow dung, white mustard seeds, *dūrvā* sprouts, a bull, and gems, coral, etc., as available, as prescribed in their own Vedic branch (*śākhā*). Placing their feet slowly on a stone, they should enter the house. On that day, water should be placed in a single earthen vessel in the air or on a shelf, saying, "O deceased, bathe. In another earthen vessel, milk should be placed, saying, "O deceased, drink. Either the chewing of neem leaves or the placing of the vessels should be done. Then, on that day, they should not cook food in that house. They should subsist on purchased food, food brought unasked, or food cooked in another's house, using sacrificial grains (*haviṣya*), but not food cooked in their own house, and avoiding alkaline substances, salt, black gram (*māṣa*), meat, cakes, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Except for children, the elderly, and the sick, everyone else should sleep on the ground, separately, and observe celibacy. Upon the death of a teacher (*guru*), the sons and wife should fast. During a birth-impurity (*jāta-sūtaka*), none of the restrictive rules apply. Upon the death of a "great guru" (*mahāguru*), they should eat food free of alkaline and salt for twelve nights and avoid giving gifts and Vedic study. A father becomes a "great guru" by procreating a son, performing his rites, teaching him the Veda and its meaning, and providing for his livelihood. Then, as long as the impurity lasts, they should offer one handful of water daily. Thus, in ten days, there would be ten handfuls. Alternatively, having increased the handfuls daily according to the number of days of impurity, they should offer them according to the elapsed days. Thus, there would be one hundred handfuls. In this way, one should perform the water-offering for maternal grandfathers and teachers. One may perform the water-offering for friends, married daughters, sisters, etc., nephews, mothers-in-law, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) according to one's desire. The collection of bones (*asthi-saṃcayana*) for one who maintained the sacred fires, or for one who did not, should be performed on the first, second, third, fourth, seventh, or ninth day—whichever is not prohibited—according to the procedure prescribed in one's own Vedic branch. There, three rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) should be offered: one for the spirits dwelling in the cremation ground (*śmaśāna-vāsin*) who died previously; one in the middle for the deceased now; and one to the south for his friends. The bones should be cast into the Ganges, or at another holy ford (*tīrtha*), or in a pure place. Once the collection is done, the castes become touchable after a third, fourth, or fifth part of their own impurity period—that is, after three, four, or five days. They become fit to eat from after ten, twelve, fifteen, or thirty days. A student (*brahmacārī*) should not perform cremation, impurity, water-offerings, etc., for anyone except his father, mother, great guru, teacher (*ācārya*), or sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*) until his own graduation (*samāvartana*). However, he must perform them for his father and others. One who has begun a penance or vow should not perform cremation, etc., until the completion of that vow. Nor should one who is devoid of his own duties perform them; even if performed, it does not stand. In the funeral rites for mother, father, guru, teacher, or sub-teacher, there is no lapse of the vow for the one observing it. He should not eat the food of one in impurity, nor live with those in impurity. If another funeral decoration is required, the initiation (*upanayana*) should be performed. For a disciple whose vow is completed, there is ten-day impurity if the teacher is cremated. Those fallen from their own duties, those fallen through mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*), women who have gone to men of lower caste, those who cause abortion of a Brāhmaṇa fetus, those who kill their husbands, those of a thieving nature, those of contrary conduct, and eunuchs should not perform cremation, water-offerings, etc. Even if performed out of delusion, it does not stand. On the third day, the son of the deceased should offer three rice-balls outside the village in front of a stone, without mantras, using the name and lineage, following the procedure of the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*. On the rice-ball and the stone, he should offer unbroken
Except for the five stars of Dhaniṣṭhā, one should place the five jewels in its mouth;
the performer should offer three oblations, saying, "O Fire, accept the omentum!"
Then the removal [of the body] should be performed; this is recorded as the ritual for one who maintains a sacred fire.
One should simply bury the other [tooth].
Likewise, if a tooth falls out during the three-footed asterisms (the Tri-pāda nakṣatras), one should place a fragment of gold in the mouth and offer it.

When the purification of the corpse is directly perceived, and when repeated purification is required due to circumstances such as being defiled by the remnants of food from above (*ūrdhvocchiṣṭa*), from below (*adharocchiṣṭa*), or from both (*ubhayocchiṣṭa*); or by touching one who is untouchable (*aspṛśya*); or death on a bed (*khaṭvāmaraṇa*); or death while bound (*baddhamaraṇa*)—in these cases, one should undertake a penance of three, six, twelve, or fifteen *kṛcchras*, according to the specific cause and the instruction of a Brāhmaṇa. If one lacks the capacity, one may immediately perform the substitute for the *kṛcchra* by giving a cow, gold, wealth, grain, clothing, or other items, thereby attaining purity at that moment before performing the cremation and subsequent rites. If a capable and devoted son or relative desires the complete purification of a deceased parent who has committed sins, he should perform whichever appropriate penance is prescribed in the section on expiations and then carry out the cremation. Even the performer of the cremation must likewise attain personal purification, as he lacks the inherent qualification [otherwise], before proceeding with the rites. If, having thus purified both the deceased and himself, one performs the cremation out of greed or similar motives, none of it bears fruit; it perishes in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), and both parties certainly fall into hell. One must not perform cremation or any funeral rites for: heretics (*pāṣaṇḍins*); those outside the Vedic fold (*vedabāhya-liṅga*); those who, despite being qualified, have fallen away from their stage of life (*anāśramin*); those who have lost their own duties (*svakarma-hāni-patita*); great sinners (*mahāpātakin*); women who have gone with men of low caste; unchaste women (*kulaṭā*) who have killed a Brāhmaṇa fetus or their husband; and those who intentionally commit suicide by fasting to death, weapons, fire, poison, hanging, or jumping from a height. Nor should one perform cremation, impurity rites, water libations, and so forth for those who die intentionally through pride, anger, or malice caused by Cāṇḍālas, water, serpents, Brāhmaṇas, lightning, fanged animals, horned beasts, or wild animals. Even if performed out of delusion, it does not bear fruit; it simply vanishes into the air. Their bodies should be cast into the Gaṅgā or another great river. The three sacred fires (*tretāgni*) should be cast into water, and the domestic fire (*gṛhyāgni*) at a crossroads. One should burn their sacrificial vessels. If one unintentionally touches these corpses, bathes them, adorns them, carries them, cuts their binding ropes, burns them, sheds tears for them, or speaks of them, one should perform the *mahāsāntapana* penance. If done intentionally, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra*. For each of these acts done unintentionally, a fast (*upavāsa*) is required. For intentional repetition, one should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* as appropriate. There is no atonement for all these categories, including heretics and the rest, if no penance is performed. If it is impossible to perform the penance at that time, then at the end of a year, for the sake of avoiding public reproach, for the sake of purity, and for the sake of eligibility for *śrāddha* and other rites, one should perform the *Nārāyaṇabali* and then the *śrāddha*. Now, if there are sons or others who are deeply detached devotees and capable of performing penance, they should perform two *cāndrāyaṇas* and four *taptakṛcchras* as penance for suicide. Having performed thirty-two *kṛcchras* and having applied the appropriate penance for all those starting with the heretics, they may perform the cremation and the *śrāddha* either immediately, at another time, or within a year, since life is uncertain. "Prāya" refers to the Great Departure (*mahāprasthāna*) or falling from mountains, trees, and the like.
Now, the Nārāyaṇa-bali is described:

On a certain eleventh day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-ekādaśī*), having duly worshipped Viṣṇu and Yama, the son of Vivasvat, one should—recalling the deceased in the form of Viṣṇu and uttering his name and lineage—offer ten funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) mixed with sesame seeds and soaked in honey and ghee upon *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, while facing south. Having worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings, and having completed the ritual up to the disposal of the cakes, one should cast them into a river; one should not give them to the wife or others. Then, on that very night, having invited an odd number of Brahmins and observed a fast, on the following day at midday, one should worship Viṣṇu and perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite according to the prescribed rules, from the washing of the Brahmins' feet up to the inquiry regarding their satisfaction (*tṛpti-praśna*). Having performed the rites from the drawing of lines (*ullekhana*) up to the sprinkling of water (*avanejana*) as in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, one should offer four cakes to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, and Yama along with his retinue. Recalling the deceased together with his name and lineage and invoking the name of Viṣṇu, one should offer the fifth cake. Then, having satisfied the Brahmins who have sipped water (*ācānta*) with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and other gifts, and among them having especially gratified one most virtuous man by thinking of him as the deceased with gifts of cattle, land, gold, and so forth, one should have the Brahmins—who hold sacred grass (*pavitra*) in their hands—cause water mixed with sesame to be given to the deceased. Finally, one should eat together with one's own kinsmen.
But in the case of one killed by a snake, this is the distinction:

For him, the *Nāgavrata* must be performed. Therein, for one year, beginning from the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Bhādrapada or another bright fifth day, a fast (*upavāsa*) must be observed. Alternatively, eating only once on the fourth day and taking a single meal at night (*nakta*) on the fifth, having fashioned a five-hooded Nāga out of wood or clay, one should worship Ananta, Vāsuki, Śaṅkha, Padma, Kambala, Karkoṭaka, Aśvatara, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Śaṅkhapāla, Kāliya, Takṣaka, and Kapila on the fifth day with perfumes, Karavīra flowers, Śatapatra, Jātī flowers, incense, and so forth; thereafter, one should feed Brāhmaṇas with ghee, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), and sweetmeats (*modaka*). At the end of the year, having worshipped in this manner, one should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas and perform the gift of a golden Nāga, the gift of a cow, and other offerings. Or else, on the fifth days of both fortnights, having drawn a Nāga on the ground with flour, having honored it with white flowers and perfumes, and with rice scented with white fragrances, having offered cow’s milk and sweetmeats upon the ground, and having performed the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*), one should say: "Release, release this [person]. On that day, one should eat sweet food. Thus, having worshipped the Nāga according to the rule for a year, when the year is complete, one should perform the *Nārāyaṇabali* and give a golden Nāga and a cow. Then one should perform all rites such as the *Śrāddha*. In the case of death due to negligence caused by Caṇḍālas, cows, Brāhmaṇas, beasts, fanged animals, serpents, fire, water, and so forth, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* and two *Taptakṛcchra* penances, or alternatively, having performed fifteen *Kṛcchras*, all rites such as cremation, impurity (*āśauca*), and the water-libation (*udaka*) must be performed according to the rule. For those such as aged forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) who are unable to perform religious observances, or those afflicted by incurable and severe diseases, intentional self-destruction by means of fire, water, fasting, falling from a mountain, and so forth, is permitted. Having performed their cremation according to the rule, a three-night impurity (*trirātrāśauca*) must be observed; on the second day, the collection of bones (*asthisaṃcayana*); on the third, the offering of water and funeral cakes (*piṇḍadāna*); and on the fourth day, one should perform the *Śrāddha*. The same applies to others who have committed suicide in accordance with the rules. For those killed by consecrated Kṣatriyas and others, by cows, Brāhmaṇas, or outcastes (*antyaja*), or by beasts, fanged animals, etc., or for those who intentionally commit suicide in battle, for heretics (*pāṣaṇḍin*), those outside the stages of life (*anāśramin*), and the fallen (*patita*), there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). During birth-impurity (*jātāśauca*) and death-impurity (*mṛtāśauca*), the obligatory and occasional rites (*nityanaimittika*) such as the *Agnihotra*, *Darśapūrṇamāsa*, and others to be accomplished with the three sacred fires (*tretāgni*) must be performed. Those rites to be accomplished with the domestic fire (*aupāsanāgni*), such as the morning and evening oblations (*sāyaṃprātarhoma*), the *Pārvaṇa-sthālīpāka*, and others, being enjoined by the *Śruti*, must indeed be performed. In the absence of materials, one may omit them; but one should never omit them entirely. Even though they are *Smārta* (based on tradition), rites such as the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, *Śravaṇākarma*, and *Āśvayujīkarma* should be performed by one of a different lineage (*asagotra*) and not omitted. (For those observing vows such as celibacy (*brahmacarya*), when the *Śrāddha* rite is underway, there is no impurity for the performers, the invited guests, or the eaters, provided they abide by some minor restriction, accept what is not forbidden, and are constant givers; for these, as long as the condition lasts, there is no impurity at all. For priests (*ṛtvij*) and others, there is bathing at that time. The sacrificer (*yajamāna*), however, having bathed and sipped water, should perform the dedication and renunciation. All optional (*kāmya*) rites, however, must be avoided. Even though they are *Smārta*, the offering of handfuls of water with the *Gāyatrī* during the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*) must be performed. The ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) may or may not be performed. During a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), there is an abandonment of ritual acts. Or else, restraining the breath and mentally reciting the mantra, having performed the sprinkling and so forth, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* aloud and offer a handful of water. There is indeed an abandonment of the *Smārta* acts such as giving gifts, receiving gifts, the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), daily *Śrāddha*, and Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). However, one must certainly perform the daily bath, purification, sipping of water, and the rules regarding eating, as well as the bath required upon touching the untouchable. One should not eat the food of those in birth-impurity if they are not of one's own kin; for those of one's own kin, there is no fault. Once the birth-impurity is known by either the giver or the eater, one must not eat. If it is unknown to both, there is no fault. In marriages, festivals, and sacrifices, if birth or death impurity occurs in the interval, there is no fault regarding the wealth previously intended for the purpose. (In that case, among prepared foods, others should provide the food. The person in birth-impurity should not touch the givers or the eaters. While the Brāhmaṇas are eating, if impurity occurs in the interval, they become pure after rinsing with water in another house. In all cases of impurity, there is no impurity regarding salt, honey, meat, male plants and fruits, vegetables, wood, grass, water, milk, curds, ghee, oil, medicinal herbs, and skins. One may take these oneself with the permission of the owner. For those engaged in a continuous distribution of food (*annasatra*), there is no impurity regarding uncooked rice and all such trade goods. Impurity caused by contact with a corpse and impurity from following a corpse affect only the one who had contact with the corpse, not his wife, sons, and so forth, nor the objects. And there is no impurity at all for objects whose period of impurity has already passed. For artisans, craftsmen, physicians, female and male slaves, royal messengers, wage-laborers, and manual workers, there is no impurity while engaged in their respective occupations, provided they have bathed immediately. In the absence of other means, there may be touchability in certain cases. However, there is indeed impurity regarding the duties prescribed for themselves. Artisans include carpenters and the like; craftsmen include painters, washermen, and the like. For chosen priests (*ṛtvij*), for those initiated by the *Dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi* and others performing sacrificial rites, for those performing the *Annasatra*, for those observing vows such as the *Kṛcchra* and *Cāndrāyaṇa*, for those engaged in penance as an expiation, and for those observing vows such as celibacy—when the *Śrāddha* rite is underway, for the performers, the invited guests, the eaters, those abiding by some minor restriction, those who cause others to accept what is not forbidden, and the givers—for these, as long as the condition lasts, there is no impurity at all. For students (*brahmacārin*) and ascetics (*yati*), there is never any impurity at all.
The rite of mantra-recitation and the worship of the deity should be performed by men who have received initiation;
for there is no sin nor any birth-impurity for those self-controlled ones.

Immediately after the period of impurity (*āśauca*), all castes (*varṇa*) bathe with their clothes on. Then, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure by touching water with his right hand; a Kṣatriya by touching a vehicle or a weapon; a Vaiśya by touching a goad or reins; and a Śūdra becomes pure by touching a staff. In this manner, the *sapiṇḍas* and *samānodakas* should carry the corpse—adorned with a pair of garments and other ornaments—to the cremation ground. They should not carry the deceased toward the house or the village. Śūdras and outcasts (*patita*) should not carry the grass, wood, or sacrificial offerings for the corpse. They should not burn a naked corpse. When the rites of carrying, bathing, adorning, and burning the corpse of a Brāhmaṇa have been performed for the sake of Dharma, the twice-born (*dvija*) attain immediate purity through bathing with their clothes on; great merit, auspiciousness, and long life result. Even in the case of performing the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) for a masterless deceased person, much merit and longevity increase. When one carries out the rites for a deceased person of a superior caste for the sake of Dharma, purity is attained by bathing with one's clothes on. When one carries out the rites for a deceased person of one's own caste for the sake of Dharma, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on and performing breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). When one carries out the rites for a deceased person of a lower caste for the sake of Dharma, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, eating neem leaves (*nimbapatra*), and so forth, until the end of the entry into the house; then purification is achieved through the *kṛcchra* penance. If one carries out the rites for a deceased person of one's own caste out of affection or similar motives, purification occurs after one day of impurity (*ekāhāśauca*). If, out of affection or similar motives, one carries out the rites for a deceased person of one's own caste and stays in that house, there is impurity for three nights (*trirātrāśauca*). If, out of affection or similar motives, one carries out the rites for a deceased person of one's own caste, stays in that house, and eats its food, purification occurs after ten days of impurity (*daśāhāśauca*). If, out of affection or similar motives, one carries out the rites for a deceased person of another caste, the impurity of that specific caste must be observed. Following a corpse (*anugamana*) should not be performed by Brāhmaṇas and others even for those of their own caste. If one follows a deceased person of a superior caste or a twice-born (*dvijāti*) out of affection or similar motives, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). The consumption of clarified butter is solely for the purpose of purification and does not take the place of a meal. Following a *sapiṇḍa* is indeed prescribed. However, regarding those of a lower caste, it is as follows: if a Brāhmaṇa follows a Kṣatriya, the impurity lasts one day; if he follows a Vaiśya, it lasts a "bird-day" (*pakṣiṇī*, i.e., two days with the intervening night); if he follows a Śūdra, the impurity lasts three nights. Having observed this, he becomes pure by bathing in a river flowing to the ocean, performing a hundred breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*), and consuming clarified butter. For a Kṣatriya following a Vaiśya, the impurity lasts one day; for following a Śūdra, it lasts a "bird-day"; for a Vaiśya following a Śūdra, it lasts one day. The same applies to weeping. If one performs the cremation and other rites for someone who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, the penance is a quarter-*kṛcchra*, and the impurity lasts ten days, three nights, or [one day], depending on the case. For one who is unable [to perform the rites] due to fear of death, purification should be effected through appropriate expiations (*prāyaścitta*) preceded by ritual bathing. If a woman in her menses or afflicted by fever touches another woman in her menses on the fourth day, she should plunge into water with her clothes on, sip water (*ācamana*), and touch [water] ten or twelve times; finally, she should discard her clothes. Then that woman in her menses is pure. By giving gifts according to one's ability and especially by a declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), there is special purification. If a healthy person comes into contact with one who is ill when bathing is required for the latter, the healthy person should bathe ten or twelve times, sipping water after each bath, and then touch the sick person. Then that sick person becomes pure. If a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*) dies, one should take water in a jar, pour the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) into it, consecrate it with the *ṛks* beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and the *vāmadevya*, obtain the permission of Brāhmaṇas for the expiation, and having bathed her with that very water, burn her according to the rules. If a woman in her menses dies, one should wash her, bathe her with the five products of the cow, cover her with another cloth, and burn her according to the rules. In this case too, the previously mentioned permission of Brāhmaṇas must be obtained. Alternatively, having washed away the filth of a woman who has recently given birth or one in her menses and having bathed her, one should burn her like wood, obtain the permission of Brāhmaṇas, and then burn the bones according to the rules. Posthumous impurity (*atītāśauca*) occurs for all castes, including Brāhmaṇas and others, after the completion of their respective periods of impurity—for women after marriage, and for Śūdras after initiation (*upanayana*). That [impurity] lasts three nights if [the news is heard] within three months; a "bird-day" if within six months; and one day if within nine months. Beyond that, purification is achieved by bathing with one's clothes on and offering water. This is the same for all castes. Regarding posthumous impurity, those who are touchable (*spṛśya*) are permitted after one-third of their own period of impurity has passed. There is no posthumous impurity for *sapiṇḍas* in the case of a birth. Upon the birth of a son, the father certainly undergoes a bath. If a person dies in a region within the same country, and the news is heard after the period of impurity has passed, then in that region, having divided twenty *yojana*s or more into three parts, there is impurity for three nights in the first part nearest to oneself; a "bird-day" in the next distant part; and one day in the most distant part. Thus, having considered the place and time, one should adopt whichever results in the lesser impurity; one should not increase the number of days here. If one hears of a death in a foreign land after the period of impurity has passed, the *sapiṇḍas* need only bathe with their clothes on, not for three nights and so forth. Upon hearing of the death of mother or father after ten days, even from a distant land and even after a year has passed, the son should observe the ten-day impurity and so forth, starting from the day the death was heard, and perform the water and rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) offerings. Upon the death of a great teacher (*mahāguru*), even from a distant land, one should observe the impurity and so forth while wearing wet clothes and fasting. The same applies between husband and wife. The same applies to co-wives (*sapatnī*) of the same or higher caste. But if a son hears of the death of a co-wife of a lower caste in a foreign land or at another time, the impurity lasts three nights. The same applies to co-wives of a lower caste. Even after a year has passed, the same applies to co-wives relative to each other. This impurity is the same for all castes. A "foreign land" (*deśāntara*) is defined in various ways in the *Smṛtis*, *Purāṇas*, and *Tīrthakalpas*. Within the period of impurity, a place where the news of a death is not heard beyond a certain distance is a "foreign land. Since traveling more than two *yojana*s is forbidden there, for a Brāhmaṇa subject to ten-day impurity, a "
Eight horizontal barley grains, or three vertical rice grains, are said to be the measure of one finger-breadth (aṅgula);
twelve finger-breadths constitute a span (vitasti).
A *vitasti* is twice an *aratni*; from that, a *kiṣku*; from that, a *dhanus*.
Two thousand *dhanus* make a *krośa*, and four *krośas* make a *yojana*.

For a woman married in her father’s house who gives birth, there is one day of impurity for the parents and others. In that case, if she dies, the impurity lasts three nights. If she dies in another house, it is the same for the parents. If she dies in another village, it lasts for a *pakṣiṇī* (two days with the intervening night). If someone who is not a *sapiṇḍa* dies in the house, it is three nights. For wives and other women dependent on others, it is three nights; for *sapiṇḍas*, it is one day. If the father is absent, it is one day for the *sapiṇḍas*; this is an additional period of impurity when they are present, and less when they are absent. This applies equally to all castes (*varṇas*). Upon the death of parents, for a daughter who has been given away (*putrikā*) in all castes, the impurity lasts three nights. When both birth-impurity and death-impurity occur together, it lasts three nights for those of the same generation. If the maternal grandfather, a guru, a teacher (*ācārya*), a daughter’s son, a father-in-law, a relative, a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), one who performs many sacrifices, a performer of a *kratu*, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), or a person for whom one acts as a priest (*yājya*)—if such qualified persons die in the same village, the impurity lasts three nights. If in another village, it is a *pakṣiṇī*. If they are unqualified, it is a *pakṣiṇī* in the same village and one day in another village. For non-aurasa sons, such as the *kṣetraja*, *dattaka*, and others, it is one day. Regarding the death of a person for whom one acts as a priest, an officiating priest, a daughter’s son, a fellow student, one initiated together, a kinsman of oneself, a kinsman of the father, or a kinsman of the mother; and regarding a father-in-law, a pupil, a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), a learned scholar (*anūcāna*), a teacher’s son, a teacher, a son of a teacher, a master, a friend, a sister’s son; and regarding a mother-in-law, a sister, a maternal grandmother, a mother’s sister, a father’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, the wife of a guru or teacher—it is a *pakṣiṇī* period of impurity if they die in the same village, but one day if in another village. If they are unqualified, even in the same village it is one day, and in another village it is merely bathing. A *guru* is one who teaches the Veda preceded by sacraments prior to initiation (*upanayana*), and one who instructs in the knowledge of mantras. An *ācārya* is one who teaches the Veda preceded by initiation, and one who performs Smārta rites. A *upādhyāya* is a teacher of the Veda or a teacher of a portion of the Veda. An *anūcāna* is a speaker of the Vedāṅgas and a speaker of the true scriptures. A *śrotriya* is one who studies a single branch (*śākhā*) of the Veda.
The sons of one's father's sister, the sons of one's mother's sister,
and the sons of one's maternal uncle are to be known as one's own kinsmen.
The sons of one's father's paternal aunt, the sons of one's father's maternal aunt,
and the sons of one's father's maternal uncle are to be known as paternal relatives (pitṛbāndhava).
The sons of one's mother’s sister, the sons of one's mother’s paternal aunt,
and the sons of one's mother’s maternal uncle are to be known as maternal relatives (mātṛbandhu).

In the case of a fellow religious student (*sabrahmacārin*), the impurity lasts for three nights. A *sabrahmacārin* is one initiated by the same teacher. Upon the death of the king of one’s own country, if the death occurs during the day, the impurity lasts until the end of that day; if the death occurs at night, the impurity lasts until the end of that night. While a corpse remains within a village, the entire village remains under impurity for that duration. For Kṣatriyas and others who have been consecrated for the protection of the earth, there is no impurity. In activities such as sorcery (*abhicāra*) performed for the sake of protecting the earth when those tasks cannot be accomplished by others, there is no impurity for the domestic priest (*purohita*) and similar officials. However, kings and others have no authority over rites specifically prescribed for themselves. There is no impurity for the *sapiṇḍas* of those killed in battle, for the sake of women or Brahmins, for the sake of cows, or by lightning. If one dies later from wounds sustained in battle, or if the lord of a village or the head of a family (*kulapati*) has died, the impurity lasts for one day. Upon the death of a sister who has been married, a brother who has been married, a friend, a son-in-law, a daughter’s son, a sister’s son, a maternal uncle, or his son—if these are of a different caste (*asavarṇa*)—purification occurs immediately through bathing. In cases of very slight relationship, bathing with one's clothes on (*sacaila*) applies equally to all castes. When a wife of one’s own caste or a higher caste dies, the husband’s impurity lasts for one day; for the paramour, it lasts for three nights. For those born of inverse unions (*pratiloma*) who have performed penance (*prāyaścitta*), the rules regarding impurity and so forth must indeed be observed; for those who have not performed penance, there is no impurity at all. For one who has taken refuge with an unchaste woman (*svairiṇī*) and others, the impurity lasts for three nights. If the father is present, the impurity lasts for three nights. If, in the midst of an impurity caused by birth, another impurity of the same duration or shorter occurs, or if an impurity of death shorter than the first occurs, purification is achieved by the remainder of the first alone. If, in the midst of an impurity of birth, an impurity of death of equal or lesser duration occurs, it is not completed by the birth-impurity; purification occurs only through the death-impurity, not the birth-impurity. Conversely, if in the midst of a death-impurity, an impurity of birth of equal or lesser duration, or another death-impurity occurs, purification is by the first alone. If a long-duration impurity occurs in the midst of a short-duration impurity caused by birth or death, purification is by the long-duration impurity alone, not the short-duration one. If a father’s death-impurity occurs in the midst of a mother’s death-impurity, purification is by the father’s impurity alone, not the mother’s. If a mother’s death-impurity occurs in the midst of a father’s death-impurity, one should complete the father’s impurity and observe an additional impurity of one night (*pakṣiṇī*); purification does not occur by the father’s impurity alone. If another death-impurity occurs while only one night remains of the first death-impurity, one should complete the first impurity and then be purified after two nights. If another death-impurity occurs in the fourth watch of that night, purification is by the subsequent three nights alone, not by the remainder of the first. If a death-impurity occurs in the midst of a birth-impurity, the cremation, water-offering, rice-ball offering (*piṇḍa*), and other rites for the deceased must indeed be performed. Some say they should be performed once the death-impurity has passed. When two death-impurities coincide, the funeral rites (*pretakṛtya*) must be performed. When two birth-impurities coincide, the birth-rites (*jātakarma*) and so forth must be performed. In that case, the performer is indeed temporarily pure. When the death of a man and a woman occurs simultaneously and the time for cremation arrives, for those of the same caste and equal status, one should perform the cremation together with the wife, and then perform the water-offerings, rice-balls, and so forth separately, beginning with the husband. However, if the husband dies later, one should first perform the *sapiṇḍana* for the husband and then perform the *sapiṇḍana* for the wife. For wives of different castes who share the same duties, all rites such as cremation must be performed separately. For wives of the same caste who share the same duties, the cremation may be together, but the water-offerings, rice-balls, and so forth must be performed separately, starting with the eldest. For co-wives of different castes and unequal status, the cremation and other rites are separate. When there is inequality of status, everything is separate. In the case of a father and son of equal status whose bodies are to be burned with the *kapāla*-fire, the cremation is simultaneous; the water-offerings and so forth are separate, beginning with the father. For brothers of equal status whose bodies are to be burned with the *kapāla*-fire, the cremation is together; the water-offerings and so forth are separate, beginning with the eldest. For those of unequal status, everything is separate. This applies similarly to the cremation and burial of male children and female children. The practice of *anvārohaṇa* (following the husband onto the funeral pyre) is praised for all classes of chaste women; it destroys all sins of oneself and one’s husband, delivers them from hell, grants many fruits of heaven, bestows longevity, health, sovereignty, sons, and all prosperity until the end of heaven, and eliminates suffering, poverty, widowhood, and the like—so it is heard in the Purāṇas and Smṛtis. In this regard, *anvārohaṇa* is forbidden for a pregnant woman. For a Brāhmaṇī woman, it is equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā*); for a pregnant woman of Kṣatriya or other castes, it is equal to the killing of a Kṣatriya or other caste. A woman of the same caste should ascend the same funeral pyre (*ekacityārohaṇa*) with her husband. A Brāhmaṇī woman should ascend the same pyre and not a separate one. For a Kṣatriya woman or others, if the husband has died in a foreign land, she should ascend a separate pyre. A woman of a different caste should ascend a separate pyre. And that *anvārohaṇa* should be performed thus: having made the resolve, "I shall perform *anvārohaṇa*," and having bowed to the husband, she should ascend the pyre and perform the entire ritual procedure. Or, having made the resolve and the procedure being performed, she should bow to the husband while he is being cremated and enter the fire. A woman who fails to reach the pyre or wavers out of delusion should perform a *Prājāpatya* penance. When cremated together, however, there is unity of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*), the cooking, the time, and the performer in the *śrāddha* and other rites. In all cases, the offering of rice-balls should be performed by a qualified son. In the absence of a son, the husband and wife, or the co-wives, do so among themselves. In their absence, the brother’s son, the brother, the daughter-in-law, the daughter, the daughter’s son, another of the same lineage (*sagotra*), a *sapiṇḍa*, a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*), a friend, a disciple, a teacher, a kinsman, or a relative connected by wealth should offer them.
A father should not give [the Śrāddha] for his son, nor likewise an elder brother for his younger brother;
even out of affection, one should not give it except for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.

The parents are the givers of daughters who have not been given away in marriage; in the absence of others, the parents are also the givers of a daughter already given. The daughter’s son (*dauhitra*) and maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*) are givers to one another; so too is the daughter’s son to the maternal grandmother. The son-in-law (*jāmātṛ*) and father-in-law (*śvaśura*) are givers to each other; the daughter-in-law (*snuṣā*) is the giver for the mother-in-law and others; and two brothers are givers to each other. The teacher (*guru*) and the pupil (*śiṣya*) are givers to one another. In the absence of those mentioned as givers, anyone may act as such. It is known that for one who performs these rites, there is the attainment of all prosperity. On the eleventh day and subsequent occasions, the eldest son or other qualified heir should perform the rites. One who has divided his property or one who has not should alone perform the nine *śrāddhas* and the sixteen *śrāddhas*. However, regarding the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, divided sons who possess wealth should perform it separately on the same day according to their own order of seniority, and not otherwise. From that point forward, they should perform it separately. For a *Śūdra*, the rite is to be performed everywhere without mantras, just as for the twice-born. In all cases where the lineage (*gotra*) is unknown, the rite should be performed using only the name. In the absence of materials such as rice for the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), the rite should be performed with fruit, roots, milk, vegetables, or molasses mixed with sesame seeds. Until the end of the ten-day period of impurity, one should hold iron in the hand. One should cremate a sacrificer who did not maintain the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) using common fire (*laukikāgni*). In the absence of the husband, there is permission even to use a fire from potsherds (*kapālāgni*) for the wife. At the time of cremation, if the fire is extinguished, one should kindle fire by friction using the burnt wood and cremate him. Or, having offered oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) into the common fire with the mantra "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ Svāhā," one may cremate him. One should cast that body into the earth or into water. Having offered the funeral cake (*pretapiṇḍa*) during the ten days and having bathed after eating, a non-*sapiṇḍa* relative must observe a three-night fast, while a *sapiṇḍa* relative must fast. For one who performs the funeral rites intentionally, the penance is double. Prior to the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*), if there is sexual intercourse, a lunar penance (*cāndrāyaṇa*) must be performed; after that, it is required. For others who are impure due to death, there is first a three-night fast and afterwards a fast. If one takes the property of a deceased person without performing the funeral rites, he should perform the penance for killing a person of that same caste. In the case of death in a foreign land, one should cremate the body after performing two *parāka* and eight *kṛcchra* penances. If a person has gone to a distant land and news of him is later received, or if no news is heard at all, then—after performing three *cāndrāyaṇas* or thirty *kṛcchras* for one of middle age (if over twenty years old) or for one of advanced age (if over fifteen years old)—one should fashion an effigy with *pālāśa* twigs or *kuśa* grass and perform the cremation, the period of impurity, and the *piṇḍa-śrāddhas*. If he returns after this has been done, he should be immersed in a vat of clarified butter, undergo the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) beginning with the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*), and then be married to his former wife.
Now follows the sequence for the Śrāddha ceremony:

Regarding that, first, the *navaśrāddha* (the nine-fold funeral rite) is prescribed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and eleventh days. In this regard, the [first] is either postponed to the eleventh day or not. In the case of postponement, the *navaśrāddha* consists of a group of five days beginning from the third day. In the case of non-postponement, since the rites of the eleventh day are optional, it consists of a group of five days beginning from the first. Alternatively, the *navaśrāddha*, designated as a group of three days, should be performed on the first, third, and fifth days, and likewise on the seventh day; one should not perform them on even-numbered days. This *navaśrāddha* may also be performed on the eleventh day. Likewise, the sixteen *śrāddhas* known as the "mixed with the new" (*navamiśra*) should be performed. These are prescribed every month for one year on the anniversary of death: twelve on the twelfth day, one in the third fortnight, one in the deficient sixth month, and one in the deficient year—thus making sixteen. Among these, the first is prescribed as being postponed to the eleventh day. The sequence there is as follows: on the eleventh day, the twelfth day, the second month, the third fortnight, the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth months, the deficient sixth month, the seventh, eighth, ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth months, and finally in the deficient year. Then, on the following day at the end of the year, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* (rite of unification) is performed. On the day after that, at the start of the second year, the annual *śrāddha* (*ābdika*) is performed; at the start of the third year, the recurring annual *śrāddha* (*pratyābdika*). Alternatively, one who maintains the sacred fire (*agnimān*) should perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* before the end of the year, provided that the *piṇḍapitṛyajña* and *pārvaṇaśrāddha* are required, or if the *vṛddhiśrāddha* occurs on the twelfth day or the third fortnight after the ten days have passed, or if an occasion for longevity rites arises, since those are not fixed. That [unification] must be performed only after completing the sixteen *ekoddiṣṭas*. In this context, four types of *śrāddhas* are possible on the eleventh day: the first of the *navaśrāddha*, the last of the *navaśrāddha*, the first monthly *śrāddha*, and the independent *ekoddiṣṭa*. For those who desire success through the performance of the independent *ekoddiṣṭa*, the others are accomplished through its ritual procedure (*tantra*); therefore, the first *ekoddiṣṭa* is called "mixed with the nine. It possesses the characteristics of the *navaśrāddha* and the characteristics of the "mixed with the new," thus possessing both sets of properties. Consequently, what remains is the *navaśrāddha*, and what remains is the monthly *śrāddha*. In the view of performing them separately, the independent *ekoddiṣṭa* should be performed first; however, that too possesses both sets of properties. Then the *navaśrāddha*, and then the monthly *śrāddha*. On the eleventh day, eleven Brahmins are fed, either for the sake of the deceased or for the sake of the eleven Rudras. Because of the dedication to the eleven Rudras, they say it is the "Rudra-group. The release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*) is also highly recommended. In place of the twelfth day, the deficient monthly *śrāddha* occurs for Kṣatriyas and others. Once the collection of bones (*saṃcayana*) has been performed, for the deceased who is going from the world of men to the world of the departed (*preta*), the *pātheyaśrāddha* (provision for the journey) should be performed according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite. Once the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed, for the deceased who is going from the world of the departed to the world of the ancestors (*pitṛ*), the *pātheyaśrāddha* should be performed according to the *pārvaṇa* rite. After that, the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) should be performed. If the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is performed before the end of the year, one should perform the monthly *śrāddhas* separately, either like the *ekoddiṣṭa* or like the *pārvaṇa*, as if they were the *śrāddha* for the anniversary of death. At the conclusion of the monthly *śrāddhas*, the *śrāddha* ending the year and the *puṇyāhavācana* should be performed; such is the sequence.
Now, the procedure for renunciation:
I shall proclaim the entire procedure for renunciation in its proper sequence,
according to the opinion of Govindarāja and the doctrine of Baudhāyana.

One who possesses the sacred fire should perform the sixteen śrāddhas according to the ekoddiṣṭa procedure; however, he should offer them using the pārvaṇa rite while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (savya).
Having performed four *kṛcchra* penances for the sake of purification, one who was not yet a forest-dweller (*āśramin*) becomes fit;
if he is already a forest-dweller, he attains fitness by performing a *taptakṛcchra*.

At the end [of life], one should offer eight śrāddhas: for the gods, for the sages, for the celestial beings, for the ancestors, for the maternal ancestors, for humans, for the elements, and for the self.
Having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he should prepare a staff and a water-strainer; thereafter, he should perform the daily rite according to the prescribed rule.
Then, a twice-born man who maintains no sacred fire should perform [the rite] according to the daily rule;
one who maintains a fire, however, should perform it with reverence in his own fire until its completion.
At the edge of the village, at the boundary of the village, in a fire-sanctuary, or in a temple,
one should cause [the student] to sit down after having consumed this triple mixture of clarified butter, milk, and curd.

In the absence [of water], [he may use] water. "Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī; Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyam. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī; Oṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi. Oṃ svaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī; Oṃ dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. Thus, [he recites] by quarters, by half-verses, or in its entirety. "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī; Oṃ tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt. Having thus led himself from stage to stage of life (*āśrama*) by means of the self, he becomes one with Brahman; so it is known. Then, having kindled the fire in that manner, he should offer the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) preceded by fuel-sticks with "Oṃ svāhā. By this, it is known that the "preparation for Brahman" (*brahmānvādhāna*) has been performed. For one who has not maintained the sacred fires, there is an offering of cooked rice (*caru*) to Vaiśvānara in place of the *iṣṭi*.
[97] For one who has not maintained the sacred fires, the renunciation of the student (*brahmacārin*) is prescribed as being devoid of fire.

Likewise, having consigned the fires into oneself and given all one's possessions to the teacher, one should recite three times in a whisper and three times aloud: "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I have renounced. Thus it is known from the *Triṃśacchati-deva* [text]: "And likewise Kātyāyana [says]:
[He should meditate on the Lord] gentle, adorned with all ornaments, bearing the five weapons."
Having meditated thus in his heart and being authorized by the guru, he should utter the command.

Then, saying "I am silent," he pours out a full handful of water. He takes up his staff, saying, "O friend, protect me. He takes up his sling, saying, "At the end of the footstep, beyond the dust. He takes up his water-strainer, saying, "With that strainer by which the gods [purified themselves]. He takes up his water-pot with the *Sāvitrī* verse. He takes up his sacred vessel (*brahmabhājana*) with all the *vyāhṛtis*. Then, [he recites]: "Upwards that [sun]," "The bright," "That eye," "The swan dwelling in purity," and "Homage to Mitra.
Homage to Savitṛ, the sole eye of the world, the cause of the origin, maintenance, and destruction of the universe.
