To him who consists of the three Vedas, who assumes the nature of the three qualities (guṇas), and whose essence is Virañci, Nārāyaṇa, and Śaṅkara.
Thus one worships the Sun. And so Vyāsa says:
"Having washed the hips with clay outside [the water] while reciting the *praṇava*, one should then perform the bath in a body of water according to the prescribed mantras."

During all three twilights, having offered joined palms (*añjali*), one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with: "Oṃ bhūs, I satiate; Oṃ bhuvas, I satiate; Oṃ svas, I satiate; Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svas, I satiate. Then, when the sun has risen, having offered joined palms with "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svar," one worships the Sun with the mantras: "Upwards that [light]," "The bright," "That eye," "The swan dwelling in purity," "Viṣṇu strode across this," "Threefold the triple heaven," and "Brahman was born. Having circumambulated oneself with the words "Homage to all beings," one should pay obeisance. One should recite three times at the three periods of the day: "Oṃ, we know the Āditya; we meditate upon the thousand-eyed one; may that Sūrya impel us. Now, intending to beg for alms, having worshipped the Sun with the four verses beginning "Up from the darkness," one should enter five or seven houses while observing silence. Then, having murmured, "Thou art full; may I become full," one returns again. Having become pure in a clean place, one should offer four morsels (*piṇḍa*): "Oṃ bhūs, svadhā, homage; Oṃ bhuvas, svadhā, homage; Oṃ svas, svadhā, homage"; the fourth is for all beings (*sārvabhautika*). Having eaten the remainder, one should perform six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). "One becomes fit for becoming Brahman, one becomes fit for becoming Brahman," so said the venerable Baudhāyana. [Cf. BDh 2.17.13–41]
Thus ends the procedure for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) according to the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
[98] Now follows the procedure for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*).

Having gone from the village toward the east or the north, he digs a sacrificial ground (*devayajana*) the size of a staff at the foot of a sacred tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*), on a riverbank, or in a pure place, using the *vyāhṛtis*. Having sprinkled it with the twenty-one *vyāhṛtis*, having spread *darbha* grass and decorated it, he places the corpse [there] with the words: "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering in this pit. He places a staff in the right hand with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this... He places a water-strainer (*śikya*) in the left hand with the verse, "That which is beyond this region... He places a water-purifier (*jalapavitra*) in the mouth with the verse, "With what purifier the gods... He places the vessel for the *brahma* priest in the belly with the *Sāvitrī* verse. He places a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in the private parts with the verse, "The earth by its breadth... He consecrates [the corpse] with the ten *hotṛ*-formulas beginning with "Consciousness is the ladle... There are no further funeral rites (*śeṣasaṃskāra*) here, because they have already been performed previously.
For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the practice of meditation,
no cremation should be performed, nor any ritual impurity observed, nor any water-libation ceremony.
Now, the procedure for cremating renunciants: in a pit dug in the ground—
when the father has passed away and has been renounced by his sons who are nearby.
His cremation must be performed, as well as whatever else is designated as the remaining rites.

Having kindled a fire near him, [the sons] should cause the ascetic to descend into it with the words "Descend," having thus caused him to descend; then his sons, according to the rules for the ancestors, should cremate that fire of his by means of the *agnihotra* ritual, or with the *Sāvitrī* verse or the *praṇava*. By merely immersing oneself in water immediately after touching those who have been cremated, one becomes pure at once. One obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
When the eleventh day arrives, the *pārvaṇa* rite is prescribed;
however, one should never perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite for those who carry the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*).
"The Sapindikarana rite for them must not be performed by the son;
because of the wearing of the triple staff (tridanda), their state of being a deceased person (pretya) has perished—so says the sage Aushanasa."
The *kuṭīcara* should burn [the senses] away; the *bahūdaka* should fill them.
The *haṃsa* should cast them into the water; one should fill the *paramahaṃsa*.
Thus spoke the Blessed Baudhāyana.
Thus [ends] the section on purification in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
In the *Kāmadhenu*, when the ocean has been set ablaze, [one should seek refuge] in the Kalpa-tree, creepers, and so forth.
And it was spoken by Śambhu, Draviḍa, Kedāra, Lolāṭa, and others.
[99] I shall expound the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, as set forth by the commentators Manu, Atri, Yājñavalkya, and others, for the sake of achieving its easy practice.
Now, the expiations are being stated:

In this regard, the ripening of the karma of those who have committed sins for which no expiation has been performed is described as occurring at the end of their experience in hell. One who kills a Brahmin out of ignorance successively enters the wombs of a jackal, a dog, a pig, and a camel. A drinker of spirituous liquor enters the womb of a donkey, a Pulkasa, a Vena, a snake, a bird, a Caṇḍāla, or a Pulkasa. A thief of gold attains the state of a village pig, a worm, an insect, or a moth. One who violates the teacher’s bed successively becomes grass, a shrub, or a creeper. If one kills a Brahmin knowingly, he enters the womb of a dog, a pig, a donkey, a camel, a cow, a goat, a sheep, a deer, a bird, a Caṇḍāla, or a Pulkasa. A drinker of spirituous liquor enters the womb of a worm, an insect, a moth, a bird, or a predatory creature. A thief of gold enters the womb of a spider, a lizard, various animals, aquatic creatures, predators, and Piśācas by the thousands. One who violates the teacher’s bed enters the womb of grass, shrubs, creepers, carnivorous beasts, and those of cruel deeds by the hundreds. And one who associates with such a person undergoes the same fate. Then, upon being born as a human, a killer of a Brahmin suffers from consumption; a drinker of spirituous liquor has black teeth; a thief of gold has deformed nails; and one who violates the teacher’s bed suffers from leprosy. One who associates with them likewise suffers the same. Having stolen another’s wife or property, one becomes a Brahma-rākṣasa in a waterless forest region. One who studies on forbidden days (anadhyāya) becomes a jackal, as does one who accepts many gifts. Having stolen food or a jewel, one suffers from indigestion or becomes extremely poor. A stealer of books containing knowledge or the Vedas becomes mute; a stealer of leafy vegetables becomes a peacock; a stealer of jewels becomes a goldsmith, a bird, or an extremely poor man; a stealer of a deposit becomes childless or poor; a stealer of fragrant scents becomes a muskrat (chuchundarī); a muskrat is a royal rat; a stealer of grain becomes a mouse; a stealer of oil becomes an oil-drinking bird; having stolen another’s property, one becomes various species of animals. Eating the sacrificial oblation (huta-haviḥ) makes one a dog and causes great suffering. Stealing a vehicle makes one a camel; fruit, a monkey; water, a water-fowl, a moth, a bird, or a fish; milk, a crow or a heron; household utensils, a house-stealing insect. Stealing honey makes one a gadfly or an insect; meat, a vulture; a cow, a monitor lizard or a snake; fire, a heron; clothing, a leper or a moth; liquids and salt, a salt-eating insect; metal, a ringworm; the property of cows, gods, or Brahmins, a patient of anemia (pāṇḍurogī); a deposit, one-eyed or childless; a bed, a Buddhist mendicant (kṣapaṇaka). Stealing a conch or a pearl shell makes one a skull-bearer (kapālī); a lamp, an owl; oil, a consumptive; another’s property, a servant of others. Whatever they steal, they are born as creatures of that specific kind, or deficient in its corresponding function. One who approaches a Brahmin woman becomes seedless (impotent). Approaching one’s mother or daughter-in-law makes one suffer from testicular swelling. Approaching a Caṇḍāla woman or a Pulkasi makes one a python; a renunciant woman, a male Piśāca; a Śūdra woman, a long worm; a woman of equal caste, a pauper; a king’s wife, a eunuch. Approaching a cow makes one a frog. Mixing grain [with impurities] makes one have redundant limbs; a slanderer has a foul-smelling nose; a backbiter has a foul-smelling mouth; one who reviles gods or Brahmins has stammering speech; a poisoner or arsonist becomes insane; one who opposes his guru suffers from epilepsy; a cow-killer becomes blind. Abandoning one’s lawful wife to pursue another makes one a creature that shoots sound or suffers from intestinal obstruction. One who eats from a honey-pot becomes a honey-eater; one who lives off women as merchandise becomes a eunuch; one who abandons a wife after marriage becomes unfortunate; one who eats only delicacies becomes a monkey or suffers from wind-obstruction; one who eats forbidden food suffers from goiter; one of cruel deeds becomes a dwarf; a betrayer of friends suffers from consumption; one who reviles his parents has the form of a eunuch; a liar has unstable speech; a false witness has severed shanks and feet; one who obstructs a marriage has a cleft lip; one who threatens another has severed hands; one who voids excrement or urine at a crossroads suffers from dysuria; a defiler of virgins becomes a eunuch; an envious person becomes a mosquito; one who quarrels with his father suffers from epilepsy; one who sells knowledge becomes a "human-deer" (man-mṛga); a seller of the Vedas becomes a leopard; one who begs excessively becomes a water-fowl; one who officiates at sacrifices for those unfit to sacrifice becomes a boar; one who eats without invitation becomes a crow; one who eats here and there becomes a cat; one who burns a thicket becomes a firefly; a thief becomes a bull; a teacher of children has a foul-smelling mouth; one who eats stale food becomes a worm; an envious person becomes a bee; one who extinguishes fire suffers from ringworm-leprosy; a teacher of Śūdras becomes a dog-cooker (śvapāka); a usurer has defective limbs; one who sells what should not be sold becomes a vulture; one who reviles a king becomes a donkey; one who studies on forbidden days becomes a jackal; one who kills fish dwells in a womb. These and other such examples are equivalent to those who do not ascend upwards (to higher realms). Women also, due to these causes, are born as females among those same species. These ripenings of karma from previous births have been shown for the sake of turning present-day sinners toward expiation.
Now, regarding those who commit great sins (*mahāpātakin*):

the killer of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinker of intoxicants, the thief of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—these are the perpetrators of great sins. One who associates with them for a year is the fifth [in this category], as is the one who directly assists the perpetrator, the one who commands, and the one who instructs. The "commander" is the one who solicits; the "instructor" is the one who instigates, whether for his own sake or for the sake of another. (*Whether reviled, beaten, or even deprived of wealth...*)
"He who would give up his life for such a person is declared a slayer of a Brahmin.

[101] The "consenter" is the one who, by means of incitement, threatening, beating, seizing property, and so forth, generates anger; he is the "causal agent" (*nimittakartṛ*). Among those who act upon it, the direct perpetrator and the one who assists him incur a minor fault compared to the instigator (*prayojaka*); less than that, the instructor (*upadeṣṭṛ*); less than that, the one who consents to the instigation (*prayojakānumantṛ*); and less than that, the causal agent. Their penance is likewise proportionate to their respective degrees of fault. Now, the secondary sins (*anupātakas*)—

In that regard, acts equal to the killing of a Brahmin are: the killing of a king or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice; the killing of one who has sought refuge; the killing of a woman in her menses, of a pregnant woman, of a woman not of the same lineage as one's mother, or of a friend whose pregnancy is unknown; falsely accusing or provoking anger toward a Guru or a Brahmin; repeatedly insulting them or falsely persisting in such accusations; backbiting directed at the king; harboring great hatred toward a Guru; reviling the Vedas out of atheism, and the destruction of the Vedas through the study of heterodox scriptures. Now, those acts equal to the drinking of liquor are:

The intentional consumption of garlic, village pigs, mushrooms, village cocks, onions, leeks, and the like; false accusation against a teacher, speaking untruthfully, and acting otherwise [than what was promised]; likewise, crookedness and deceit; speaking falsehoods to the royal court and other such places for the sake of self-exaltation; tasting the mouth of a woman in her courses; the killing of a friend; giving false testimony; abandoning the Vedas and reviling the Vedas; and eating the food of those two [who have abandoned or reviled the Vedas]. Now, the following are equal to stealing gold:

The seizure of a Brahmin’s horse, jewel, human being, woman, land, or cow; and likewise, the misappropriation of a deposit before it has been weighed in gold. Now, those equal to violating the Guru’s bed:

Emission of semen in a daughter-in-law, a sister, a Caṇḍālī, a female friend, a wife, or a girl of the highest caste; likewise, approaching a father’s sister, a mother’s sister, a maternal uncle’s wife, a mother’s co-wife, a daughter-in-law, or a sister—provided they are willing—as well as the wife of a teacher, one’s own daughter, a sister, a paternal aunt, a maternal grandmother, a maternal uncle, a learned Brāhmaṇa (*śrotriya*), a sacrificial priest (*ṛtvij*), a guru, or a preceptor (*upādhyāya*); the wife of a disciple, a woman of the highest caste, a menstruating woman, a woman entrusted [to one's care], a woman who has taken a vow, one established in a religious observance, a woman of the highest caste, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), one who has sought refuge, a mother’s female friend, the wife of a king, a wet-nurse, another mother, a mother’s sister’s friend, or a maternal uncle’s wife—one falls immediately from one’s status like one who violates the bed of a guru (*gurutalpaga*). Likewise, one falls by approaching a woman related through the paternal or maternal line of birth. Theft, atheism (*nāstikya*), abandoning those whose duties must not be abandoned, failing to abandon those whose duties have been abandoned, abandoning those who are fallen (*patita*), and abandoning those who are not fallen—these, along with causing others to commit mortal sins (*pātaka*), are secondary sins (*anupātaka*).
Now, regarding the minor offenses (*upapātaka*):
on this point, Yājñavalkya says: "Killing a cow, being a *vrātya*, theft, and the non-payment of debts."
Not maintaining the sacred fires, selling goods that should not be sold, and superseding a younger brother in marriage.
[102] Receiving instruction for a fee, likewise teaching for a fee,
adultery, causing a younger brother to marry before the elder, usury, and the manufacture of salt;
Killing a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; living by means of censurable wealth;
atheism; the abandonment of religious vows; and the sale of one's own sons.
Stealing grain, base metals, or livestock; officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice;
abandoning one's father, mother, or son; and the sale of a tank or a grove.
Defiling a maiden, officiating at a sacrifice for one who has superseded his elder brother in marriage,
giving a daughter in marriage to that very person, crookedness, and the violation of a vow.
Undertaking actions for one's own sake, consorting with women who drink liquor, abandoning sacred study, the sacrificial fire, and sons, as well as the abandonment of kinsmen;
Cutting down trees for the sake of fuel, living by the slaughter of women or by medicinal herbs, the construction of murderous machines, and the sale of oneself— these are vices.
Service to a Śūdra, friendship with the low-born, consorting with those of inferior birth,
likewise dwelling outside the stages of life (āśramas), and being nourished by the food of others.
Studying false scriptures, claiming authority regarding the original sources [of the law],
and the sale of one's wife— each of these is a minor offense (upapātaka).

The killing of a cow is the destruction of a cow's body. Being uninitiated at the proper time is *vrātyatā*. Stealing is the taking of another’s property, specifically gold belonging to a Brāhmaṇa, or anything less than that. Non-payment of debt is the failure to return gold or other goods once received; it also includes the failure to discharge one's debts to the gods, sages, and ancestors. Not maintaining the sacred fires despite being qualified to do so is another fault. Selling what is not for sale, such as salt and the like, is prohibited. *Parivedana* is the taking of a wife or the establishment of the *agnihotra* by a younger brother while an elder uterine brother remains. *Bhṛtādhyayana* is studying under a teacher for a fee. *Pāradārya* is adultery, defined as approaching a woman other than one's own teacher's wife, but equal to her. *Pārivittya* is an elder brother remaining unmarried while a younger brother marries. *Vārdhuṣya* is living off forbidden interest. *Lavaṇakriyā* is the manufacture of salt. Killing a woman who is not an *Ātreyī* (even if she is not pregnant) is a sin. So too is the killing of a Śūdra, an uninitiated Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya. Living off wealth not sanctioned by the king is a fault. Nihilism (*nāstikya*) is the conviction that there is no world beyond. For a student (*brahmacārin*), sexual union with a woman is a violation of his vow, as is the abandonment of a vow undertaken for the sake of worshipping a deity. Selling children for the purpose of making them slaves, selling tanks, gardens, groves, and the like, or stealing grain and other goods by taking them through force, as well as stealing base metals such as tin and lead, and livestock such as cattle, are all forms of theft. Performing sacrifices for Śūdras and others who are defiled by birth, or for those defiled by their actions such as *vrātyas*, and eating with either of these groups, are likewise sins. Abandoning one's father, mother, or son who have not fallen from their caste is a fault. Defiling a maiden is the tearing of her hymen with a finger or similar object. Acting as a priest for a *parivedaka* (the younger brother who marries first) and giving a daughter in marriage to him are both sins. Deceit toward one who is not a teacher is a fault. Beginning the preparation of food for oneself alone, or enjoying the company of a woman who drinks liquor, are sins. Abandoning the study of the Veda already learned—whether for the sake of maintaining a family or for the sake of learning false sciences—is a fault. Neglecting the consecration and maintenance of the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, or neglecting one's son and kinsmen when one has the capacity to care for them, are faults. Cutting down green trees for the sake of cooking or other visible purposes is a sin. Making one's wife a commodity for profit and living off the proceeds is "living off women" (*strījīvana*), as is living off a woman's dowry. Living by the slaughter of living beings or living by medicinal herbs used for subjugation and the like, operating cruel machines for crushing sesame, sugarcane, and so forth, or operating large-scale industrial machinery, are sins. The eighteen vices include hunting and the rest. Selling oneself, selling one's wife, serving a Śūdra, forming friendships with the low-born, failing to marry within one's own caste, marrying into a lower caste, consorting with women of low birth, or having sexual relations with a common woman, are faults. Remaining without a stage of life (*anāśramitva*) is a sin. Being devoted to the food of others and being nourished by the food of others are faults. Studying the texts of the Cārvākas and others is the study of false sciences. Holding official authority over mines by royal decree, performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), intentionally eating garlic and the like—these and others are secondary sins (*upapātaka*).
Now, those acts designated as causing loss of caste (jātibhraṃśakara):
"Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or intoxicants, dishonesty, and sexual intercourse with a male—these indeed cause loss of caste. [MDh 11.68]
Now, the acts that cause loss of caste (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*): the killing of donkeys, camels, deer, elephants, goats, sheep, fish, snakes, buffaloes, and other domestic or wild animals.
Now, the acts that cause loss of the right to receive gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*):
Accepting wealth from those who are censured, trade, serving Śūdras, living by usury, and speaking untruths. [MDh 11.70] Now, the acts that cause defilement (malinīkaraṇa):

The killing of many worms, insects, aquatic creatures, or fish; eating food accompanied by liquor; the theft of many fruits, fuel, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these and other such sins are designated as miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka). Now follows the penance for mortal sins (mahāpātaka):

Having killed a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally, one should wear hair-cloth, bark, rags, or similar garments; keep matted hair or be shaven; carry the skull-bowl of the Brāhmaṇa he killed as a mark—failing which, the skull-bowl of another—or some other skull-bowl; hold a staff and a banner; subsist once a day on forest-grown food with measured portions in a single vessel; remain self-controlled; bathe at the three junctions of the day; perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) according to rule preceded by mantras; avoid study, teaching, exposition, recitation, officiating at sacrifices, giving, receiving gifts, and so forth; observe celibacy; avoid women, honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping by day, collyrium, ointments, shoes, umbrellas, desire, anger, delusion, joy, grief, despondency, and the like; avoid dancing, singing, and slander; be intent on the welfare of all beings; wander through noble lands, staying in standing or sitting postures as required; dwell near sacred fords (*tīrtha*), or having built a hut in a forest or a holy hermitage, live there, or stay at the edge of a village, in a cow-pen, or at the root of a tree. Having practiced this vow for twelve years, one becomes pure. If he cannot subsist on forest-grown food, he may enter a village for alms. There, standing at the door of a house with a piece of red earthenware or a shallow bowl, he should proclaim his own sin, saying, "I am a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa. Having begged for food from seven houses among the four castes, distinguishing between clean and unclean, he should eat a measured amount only once a day. Having practiced this vow for twelve years, he becomes pure. Alternatively, being self-restrained, he may perform the *prājāpatya* penance continuously for twelve years; by performing three hundred and sixty of these, he is purified. For a second killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the penance is doubled; for a third, tripled; for a fourth, there is no atonement. Or else, for each such sin from the fourth onwards, he should give a thousand cows. If he is destitute, he should enter the fire. Or else, he should perform the aforementioned vows, such as begging for alms and the *kṛcchra* penances, until death; by that, he is purified. In this regard, for those who intentionally assist, instigate, approve, provide the cause, encourage, or otherwise participate in a direct killing—even if not the actual perpetrator—the penance should be inferred as equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, half of that, half of that again, and so on. Or, whether intentional or unintentional, the assistant of the direct perpetrator is purified by performing a penance less by one-quarter (*pādona*). The instigator performs half of that; the approver performs one and a half quarters; the causal agent performs one quarter; and for those such as encouragers, it should be determined by the relative degree of their involvement. If the instigation was without motive, the reviler is virtuous, and the reviled is devoid of merit and has died, then one should perform the vow for one year. Even then, for those assistants and others of the primary perpetrators, it should be determined by their relative degrees. Likewise, punishment should be determined accordingly for encouragers, providers of shelter, and those who consent. For boys under sixteen, for those over eighty, for women, and for the sick, the full penance applies. Or else, before twelve years or after eighty, it is only a quarter; for men under eleven, it is half; for women, only a quarter; and for boys who have not been initiated, the penance is only a quarter, which the father, brother, or a friend equal to them should perform, following the entire penance prescribed in the Kalpas. Beyond that, until sixteen, others may perform it; beyond that, until eighty, they should perform it themselves. When the penance is heavy and no other penance is possible, its performance is established by necessity. For killing a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a Soma sacrifice, the vow is doubled. If unable to do that, one should duly give two thousand cows to worthy recipients. For killing an Ācārya, the vow is for twelve years or a thousand cows. For an Upādhyāya, a teacher of a branch (*aṅga*), or a learned priest (*anūcāna-ṛtvij*), one should perform the twelve-year vow or, beyond that, a thousand cows, reduced by a quarter, a half-quarter, and so on, as determined by the relative degree of the offense. Likewise, for killing a priest or a Guru, one should perform the vow for the duration of one's life, or double, triple, or quadruple that. If unable to do that, having performed the twelve-year vow, one should give a thousand cows. Now, if while performing the twelve-year vow, one protects a Brāhmaṇa or a herd of twelve cows being attacked by thieves or wild beasts by placing oneself between them, even if the twelve years are incomplete, he is purified at that very moment. If he dies while engaged in that act without completing it, he is still purified then. Likewise, by proclaiming his sin to the priests during the final bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a great sacrifice like the Aśvamedha, or in the presence of the sacrificer, and being permitted by them, he is purified upon bathing. Or, during the vow, by protecting a Brāhmaṇa or a cow afflicted by chronic or severe diseases like leprosy with medicines, he is purified then. Or, during the vow, by giving back all the property—a Brāhmaṇa’s land, cows, etc.—that was stolen by thieves, he is purified. If he is engaged in that act and is killed by them, or remains severely wounded and nearly dead, he is purified then even if he lives. Knowing the nature of the killing, members of the four castes should resort to falling from a cliff (*bhṛgupatana*) or entering the fire. Among them, those of the three higher castes who have already performed their first sacrifice (*iṣṭaprathamayajña*) should perform, in order, the Aśvamedha (if a universal monarch), the Svarjit, Gosava, Abhijit, Viśvajit, Trivṛt, or Agniṣṭut sacrifices with small sacrificial fees. If the three castes, possessing sacred fires, commit a mortal sin unintentionally, their sons and descendants should maintain those fires until the fault is exhausted. If intentional, they should cast the domestic and sacrificial fires into water; then, for those performing penances like entering the fire, the same applies if they die along with their belongings. If the killer is learned, virtuous, and destitute, while the victim is devoid of merit, the killer should go to a forest and recite the Veda three times with self-restraint. If capable, he should walk a hundred *yojana*s while reciting the Veda. If the killer is unlearned, destitute, yet virtuous, he should go against the current of the Sarasvatī from Plakṣaprasravaṇa toward the western ocean, eating only sacrificial food. If the killer is devoid of merit but wealthy, he should give to a worthy recipient a house, land, and so forth, sufficient for livelihood; or a house with its furnishings sufficient for livelihood; or, if childless, his entire estate. Having chosen one of these three, one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) should perform the Vaiśvānara sacrifice, and one who does not maintain them should perform the Vaiśvānara *sthālīpāka*. An ignorant, destitute killer of a mere Brāhmaṇa should sleep on the ground, bathe at the three junctions of the day, proclaim his own deed, subsist on alms, and wander among holy hermitages at the confluences of great rivers, cow-pens, mountains, springs, and penance groves, sitting in the *vīrāsana* posture for a full year. At the end, he should give gems, gold, cows, grain, sesame, curd, and clarified butter to Brāhmaṇas. If he merely forms the intention of killing a Brāhmaṇa in his mind but stops himself, he should subsist on water for twelve days and fast for twelve days, and so forth. In other cases where the offenses are equal, there is an option; where they are unequal, a specific arrangement should be devised. The twelve-year penance and others mentioned apply only to a Brāhmaṇa. For a Kṣatriya, it is double; for a Vaiśya, triple; for a Śūdra and others, quadruple. Even there, the specific penance should be understood according to the specific qualities of the killer and the victim. The same applies to Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others
Now, the instruction:

Upon killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a *somayāga*, one should perform the twelve-year vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyāvrata*). If done intentionally, it is indeed doubled, but it does not extend to the penance ending in death (*prāṇāntika*). In that case, the determination depends on caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth. In all cases, regarding the killing of a woman or a eunuch, or an embryo whose sex is unknown; and regarding the killing of an *Ātreyī*—one who is in her menses, of the lineage of Atri, or belonging to the Atri clan—the legal procedure is the same as for the killing of a man. When there is a possibility of the death of the castes during testimony, being a witness while speaking the truth directly, being overcome by anger toward a guru, stealing the deposit of a Brāhmaṇa, violating the wife of a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) and possesses good qualities, or being a destroyer of the *somayāga*—in these cases, one should perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. For those cases where the rule is extended (*atideśika*), the penance is reduced by one-quarter. The extension applies to the penance, but not to the state of being an outcaste (*pātitya*). If a blow with a weapon was dealt for the purpose of killing a Brāhmaṇa or others, but he did not die due to some obstruction, one should still perform the vow for the murder of a Brāhmaṇa etc., reduced by one-quarter. In the case of sexual intercourse [with an unprotected woman], it is half. If there was an attempt, it is one-quarter. Regarding penances equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa: everywhere, the direct perpetrator (*sākṣāt-kartṛ*) performs the full penance; the abettor (*anugrāhaka*) performs one-quarter less; the instigator (*prayojaka*) performs half; the consenter (*anumantṛ*) performs one and a half quarters; and the causal agent (*nimittakartṛ*) performs one quarter. One should understand the relative gradation among those such as the inciter (*protsāhaka*). In all cases, children, the elderly, women, and the sick deserve half the penance even if they are direct perpetrators. One over eighty years of age is "elderly"; under sixteen years of age is a "child. For uninitiated children and girls, the penance is one-quarter. That should be performed by the father, brother, or another friend. Until the end of the twelve years, they should have it performed thus; after that, they should perform it themselves. Everywhere, the determination depends on caste, capacity, qualities, and so forth.
Thus concludes the penance for killing a Brahmin according to the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now follows the penance for drinking liquor (*surāpāna*).

Among those, the primary types of *surā* are *paiṣṭī*, *gauḍī*, and *mādhvī*. Among these, a member of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), as well as a *śūdra* man or woman, shall not drink *surā* under any circumstances, whether born into a *cāturvarṇya* marriage or otherwise. If one knowingly drinks *surā* even once, one becomes pure only through death; having made any one of *surā*, water, cow urine, milk, or clarified butter resemble fire, one should drink it while wearing wet clothes from a vessel of iron, steel, or copper. If one drinks *surā* unknowingly, thinking it to be water, and it merely touches the palate, one should perform the full twelve-year vow for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyāvrata*)—wearing matted hair and clothing of bark or hair, excluding only the specific marks of that penance—and not a quarter-less version. In all cases, for women, children, and the elderly, the penance is half, which is six years. For unmarried girls and those who have not undergone initiation (*anupanīta*), one should perform a quarter, which is exactly three years. If done knowingly, the penance is doubled. If, after drinking, one vomits, one should eat only oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) at night for three years and not eat [elsewhere]. In the case of drinking *surā* where only a small amount has touched the mouth, one should act for one year wearing bark garments, with matted hair, and carrying a banner. If *surā* is drunk for medicinal purposes or due to illness, provided it was done unknowingly, one should perform a quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance or a *cāndrāyaṇa*, and undergo re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*). In childhood, however, the mother, brother, or father should perform that. If done knowingly, one should perform a *taptakṛcchra*, a *parāka*, and a *cāndrāyaṇa* in sequence. If one knowingly eats food whose liquid essence has been touched by *surā*, or urine, feces, semen, a corpse, and so forth, re-initiation must be performed. If one drinks water from a dried *surā* vessel, there should be vomiting, a fast, and the consumption of clarified butter. Having drunk that water if it has stood overnight, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three days. In the case of repeated unintentional drinking, one should drink it for five nights. If one drinks that water intentionally, one should drink it for seven nights. In the case of intentional repetition, however, one should drink *brāhmī-suvarcalā* with milk for twelve nights. If a Soma-drinker unintentionally smells the breath of a *surā*-drinker, he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) in water and consume clarified butter. If intentional, the penance is double in all cases. If he is not a Soma-drinker, he should perform breath-restraints without water and consume what was prescribed, though some say water infused with *kuśa* grass. But for the direct smelling of the scent of *surā*, the *sāntapana* penance prescribed among those acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*) applies. If intentional, it should be understood that the [full] penance is required, and so forth.
Thus concludes the penance for drinking *surā* according to the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. Now follows the penance for drinking *madya*:

In this context, *gauḍī* (molasses-based) and *mādhvī* (honey-based) liquor constitute *surā-madya*. One should know that there are eleven types of intoxicants: *tāla*, *pānasa*, *drākṣa*, *mādhuka*, *khārjūra*, *saira*, *āriṣṭa*, *maireya*, and *nālikeraja*. These intoxicants, by their very nature, must not be drunk by Brāhmaṇas, their women who have not been initiated (*anupanīta*), or unmarried girls. For Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, drinking intoxicants is not a cause for fault. If one drinks *tāla* and other intoxicants out of ignorance, thinking them to be water or the like, the penance is the *taptakṛcchra* and a second initiation (*punar-upanayana*). The same applies to twice-born men (*dvija*) who consume urine, feces, semen, or similar substances. If one drinks *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* out of ignorance, or *tāla* and others out of knowledge, one should perform the *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances, followed by a second initiation and the consumption of clarified butter (*ghṛtaprāśana*). However, if one knowingly drinks *gauḍī* or *mādhvī*, the penance lasts three years with oil-cake (*piṇyāka*) or grain-particles (*kaṇa*); for repeated practice, six years; for excessive and continuous practice, twelve years; and for practice over a long period, one is purified only after dying having drunk liquor that has become red-hot like fire. For *tāla* and other intoxicants, half of these periods should be prescribed. In all cases, half the penance applies to women, children, the elderly, and so forth. For an uninitiated boy or an unmarried girl, a quarter of the penance should be performed by the mother, father, or brother. Regarding substances such as leavings (*lehya*), non-edibles, urine, feces, semen, and discharges, if they merely enter the mouth—compared to *tāla* and other intoxicants—one should drink milk boiled with *udumbara*, *bilva*, *pālāśa*, and *kuśa* grass for six nights. For *gauḍī* and *mādhvī*, the period is doubled. If one unknowingly drinks water from a dry vessel scented with *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *kuśa* roots for three days. If it is done knowingly and repeatedly, one should drink milk boiled with *udumbara*, *bilva*, and *pālāśa* for three days. If it is done repeatedly out of ignorance, one should drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* ghee and milk for five nights. If it is done repeatedly knowingly, one should drink barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) mixed with cow’s urine for seven nights. For excessive and continuous practice, one should take *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* with milk for twelve nights. If one drinks water from a vessel used for *tāla* and other intoxicants, half the penance should be prescribed. In all cases, appropriate adjustments should be made for women, children, and others.
Thus ends the penance for drinking intoxicants in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now, the penance for stealing gold is described:

By the word *steya* (theft) is meant the taking—either in the presence or absence of the owner—by force or by stealth, without the cause of ownership such as purchase and so forth. First, the measurement of gold (*suvarṇa*) is defined: the dust particle visible in a beam of sunlight passing through a window-lattice is called a *trasareṇu*. Eight *trasareṇus* equal one *likṣā*. Three *likṣās* equal one *rājasarṣapa* (black mustard seed). Three *rājasarṣapas* equal one *gaurasarṣapa* (white mustard seed). Six *gaurasarṣapas* equal one *yava* (barley grain). Three *yavas* equal one *kṛṣṇala*. Five *kṛṣṇalas* equal one *māṣa*. Sixteen *māṣas* equal one *suvarṇa*. Having unintentionally stolen a *suvarṇa* of gold from a Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyā-vrata*) for twelve years, excluding the carrying of a corpse’s head as a banner or a skull. Whoever steals the gold of anyone at all must pay eleven times its value and then perform penance. Having stolen a *suvarṇa* of gold from teachers, performers of sacrifices, Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), or righteous Brāhmaṇas, one should shave one's head, smear one's body with clarified butter, and be burned while covered in a heap of dried cow-dung; thus one is purified. For stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa devoid of virtues, one should perform the same for nine years. If the theft was for the sake of protecting a large family in distress, one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for six years or perform a sacrifice such as the *Viśvajit*. Whoever intentionally steals a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, starting from one *suvarṇa*, having confessed his sin to the king and offered an iron staff or one of *khadira* wood, shall be purified whether he dies or lives, being beaten severely with a royal rod with disheveled hair. If the king beats him beyond his capacity, the fault lies with the king. A Brāhmaṇa who has stolen gold should perform the vow alone and not kill himself with the rod; nor should the king kill a Brāhmaṇa, for in killing him, the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa certainly occurs. A learned Kṣatriya who maintains the sacred fires and is righteous, having stolen a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, is purified by the *Aśvamedha* sacrifice. Or, having performed the *Gosava* sacrifice, he is purified. Or, having given gold equal to his own weight, he is purified. In the absence of such wealth and if unable to perform penance, he should give enough money to maintain a Brāhmaṇa along with his family. If a non-Brāhmaṇa steals a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, desiring not to die by the beating of the rod, he is purified by performing the vow for drinking liquor (*surāpāna-vrata*). However, when after the theft he feels remorse and returns it or abandons it, then the penance prescribed by Āpastamba applies: eating only at the fourth meal-time for three years. One who mentally intends to steal gold but stops of his own accord is purified by subsisting on air for twelve days. For acts equal to stealing gold—such as stealing a horse, a gem, a human, a woman, land, or a milch-cow—one should perform half the penance for stealing gold. For stealing gold the size of a *trasareṇu*, one *prāṇāyāma* (breath control). For stealing gold the size of a *likṣā*, three. For stealing gold the size of a *rājasarṣapa*, four or six *prāṇāyāmas*. For stealing gold the size of a *gaurasarṣapa*, the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* mantra eight thousand times. For stealing gold the size of a *yava*, the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* from morning until evening. For stealing gold the size of a *kṛṣṇala*, the *Sāntapana* penance. For stealing gold the size of a *māṣa*, one is purified in three months by eating barley boiled in cow urine. For stealing gold slightly less than the measure of a *suvarṇa*, one is purified in one year by eating barley boiled in cow urine. It has been stated that for stealing a full measure of a Brāhmaṇa’s gold, the twelve-year vow and so forth must be performed. For stealing silver less than the measure of a *suvarṇa*, the *Sāntapana* penance. For stealing silver from four *niṣkas* up to ten *niṣkas*, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance is required. For silver exceeding ten *niṣkas* up to a hundred *niṣkas*, two *Cāndrāyaṇas*. For silver exceeding a hundred *niṣkas* up to a thousand *niṣkas*, three *Cāndrāyaṇas*. For stealing silver exceeding a thousand *niṣkas*, one should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa minus one quarter. For stealing silver, lead, iron, copper, brass, or bell-metal weighing a thousand *niṣkas*, the *Parāka* penance. For stealing these items valued at a thousand *niṣkas* or more, the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa, such as the twelve-year vow, applies. For stealing gems worth four *niṣkas*, the *Sāntapana*. For stealing gems worth more than four *niṣkas* up to ten *niṣkas*, the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. For stealing gems worth more than ten *niṣkas* up to a hundred *niṣkas*, two *Cāndrāyaṇas*. For stealing gems worth more than a hundred *niṣkas* up to a thousand *niṣkas*, three *Cāndrāyaṇas*. For stealing gems worth more than a thousand *niṣkas*, the penance for killing a Brāhmaṇa minus one quarter, such as nine years and so forth. Having stolen a deposit of gold from a non-Brāhmaṇa, one should perform the vow for six years. And for stealing a human, land, or a horse, the six-year vow applies.
Thus ends the expiation for stealing gold according to the Smṛtyarthasāra.
Now follows the expiation for violating the Guru’s bed.

The father is the guru; his wife is called the *gurupatnī*. If one approaches his mother through ignorance, or approaches the co-wife of his mother who is of the same caste (*savarṇā*) or of a higher caste (*uttamavarṇā*), being incited by her, he becomes pure by dying after embracing a red-hot iron woman (*lohastri*) once he has realized his error. Alternatively, he is purified by dying after lying upon a heated iron bed. However, if both parties have incited him, purification comes from embracing while lying on the heated iron bed. If he has incited himself, he shall cut off his own three private parts with his own hand, hold them in his joined palms, and go toward the southwest (*nairṛtī diś*); not looking back and not reflecting on what stands before him, he shall be purified by the end of his life. In the case of unintentionally approaching a woman of the same caste or a woman of a higher caste, the vow for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyāvrata*) must be observed for twelve years. In the case of intentional repetition, one smeared with clarified butter and shaven-headed, staying in the midst of a heap of dried cow-dung (*karīṣa*), shall be purified by dying after having all his limbs, beginning with the feet, set on fire. This same rule applies to the mother even if done intentionally. If one has begun with the mother intentionally but desists before the emission of semen, the penance is twelve years. If unintentionally, it is six years. If one intentionally approaches the co-wife of his mother who is of the same caste and is unchaste (*vyabhicāriṇī*), he should perform three *Cāndrāyaṇa* fasts accompanied by the recitation of the Vedas. If unintentionally, he should perform the *Kṛcchra* for one year. If a Brāhmaṇa intentionally approaches the Kṣatriya wife of his father even once, he must eat only at eight meal-times for three years. In the case of intentional repetition, purification comes from cutting off the testicles, provided the penis is not removed. For one who has begun with the Kṣatriya wife intentionally but desists before the emission of semen—having been incited by her—the penance is three months. For one incited by both, it is a three-month *Atikṛcchra*. If she was incited by him, it is a three-month *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. In those same cases, for one who has begun unintentionally but desists before the emission of semen, or in the case of being incited by the woman, by both, or by himself, the penances are, in order: *Kṛcchra*, *Atikṛcchra*, and *Cāndrāyaṇa*. In the case of the Vaiśya wife of the guru, if he approaches her once intentionally, he should perform the penance for six years. In the case of intentional repetition, purification comes from cutting off half the penis. If unintentionally approached once, it is three years. In the case of extreme repetition, he remains under the vow for as long as he lives. For one who has begun intentionally with the Vaiśya wife but desists before the emission of semen—whether incited by both, by himself, or by the woman—the penances are, in order: *Taptakṛcchra*, *Parāka*, and *Sāntapana*. For one who has begun unintentionally, in the cases of being incited by the woman, by both, or by himself, the penances are, in order: five nights, seven nights, and eight nights of fasting. If a Brāhmaṇa intentionally approaches the Śūdra wife of his guru even once, he should perform the penance for three years. In the case of intentional repetition, it should be done for twelve years. In the case of unintentional repetition, he should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* continuously. For one who has begun intentionally with the Śūdra wife but desists before the emission of semen—whether incited by the woman, by both, or by himself—the penances are, in order: *Atikṛcchra* and *Parāka*. In that same case, for one who has begun unintentionally, the penances are *Kāya*, *Sāntapana*, and fasting for seven nights. In this manner, for the son of a Kṣatriya approaching his Vaiśya mother, the penances of nine years and so forth should be applied to intentional single acts and the like. And for the Śūdra wife, nine years and so forth should be applied. And for the son of a Vaiśya approaching a Śūdra wife, nine years and so forth should be applied. In all cases, "approaching" (*gamana*) is said to mean up until the discharge of the final element (semen). In all cases where one desists before the emission of semen, the penance is twelve years for those ending in death; otherwise, half of what has been stated should be performed. Women indeed possess the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) just as men do. Therefore, for them, when they have proceeded intentionally, the expiation is that which ends in death. When they have proceeded unintentionally, the appropriate penance should be performed as prescribed for men, by applying half of the twelve-year periods and so forth in every case.
Adultery as prescribed for one's own caste, the defilement of a maiden,
and likewise violating the Guru’s bed— these do not apply to women in common with men.
Now, the extreme sins (atipātaka) and secondary sins (anupātaka) are being described:

Having approached a woman who has been married by her own consent (*matyā*)—one who belongs to the same lineage (*gotra*) or the same *pravara*—he shall be purified by performing the penance for violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*). The fetus born of her shall be a *caṇḍāla*. She, as a wife, is to be abandoned in sexual intercourse but must be protected [otherwise]. Having approached one married without her consent (*amatyā*), he shall be purified by three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. The fetus shall be a *kaśyapa*. If he approaches a girl of his own caste (*savarṇa*), a friend’s wife, a sister, a woman of the same lineage, a *caṇḍālī*, a *māgaṅgī*, or his own daughter once unintentionally, he shall be purified by two *cāndrāyaṇas*. If it is intentional and occurs only once, purification comes after a year of *kṛcchra* penance. If he approaches any of these women many times in a single night, he shall perform the three-year penance for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-vrata*). If he approaches any of these on multiple days, he shall perform the penance for killing a Brahmin. If he intentionally approaches one of these over many days, he shall be purified by entering the fire and dying. If he unintentionally approaches a mother’s sister, a father’s sister, a teacher’s daughter, a teacher’s wife, a younger brother’s wife, or his own daughter once, he shall be purified by a year of *kṛcchra*. If he approaches any of these many times in a single day, he shall perform the three-year penance for killing a Brahmin. If he approaches any of these persistently over many days, he shall perform the expiation for killing a Brahmin. If he intentionally approaches one of these once in a single day, he shall perform the six-year penance for killing a Brahmin. If he intentionally approaches any of these over many days, he shall be purified by entering the fire and dying. Having approached a *caṇḍālī*, a *pulkasī*, a woman of the hunter caste (*vyādha*), a sister, a daughter-in-law, a mother’s sister, a female friend, a trusted woman, a female ascetic (*pravrājitā*), a maternal aunt, a woman who has sought refuge, a woman of the inner apartments, a disciple’s wife, an outcaste woman (*patita*), or a woman of the same lineage—he shall be purified by a month-long fast (*māsa-upavāsa*) or a *cāndrāyaṇa* if he withdraws before the emission of semen. If he should approach an unchaste woman among these only once, he shall be purified by a *cāndrāyaṇa*. Having approached an unknown woman once, he shall be purified by a *taptakṛcchra*.
Thus concludes the penance for violating the Guru’s bed according to the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now follows the penance for one who associates with those who have committed mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*).

By engaging in study, teaching, marriage, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, living together, or eating together with these four types of great sinners (*mahāpātakins*), one incurs immediate loss of caste (*pātitya*). By sharing a seat, eating in the same row, sleeping on the same bed, or traveling in the same vehicle with them for one year, one incurs loss of caste. A person who has become an outcast through association with a particular great sinner shall be purified by the penance prescribed for that specific sinner. In place of the penance leading to death (*maraṇāpādaka-prāyaścitta*), there shall be the twelve-year vow for killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā-vrata*). For one whose association with a sinner occurred through ignorance, purification comes from half of the prescribed penance. Through ignorance, in the case of association with the four great sinners for five nights, [the penance is] three nights; for ten nights of association, a *kāyakṛcchra* and so forth; for twelve nights of association, the *sāntapana*; for association lasting a fortnight, ten fasts; for association lasting a month, purification through a *parāka*; for association lasting three months, a *cāndrāyaṇa*; for association lasting six months, two *cāndrāyaṇas*; and for continuous association for slightly less than a year, a *kṛcchra* for six months or the like. For association lasting slightly less than a full year, a *cāndrāyaṇa* for a year. In cases of association with these four, women, children, the elderly, and the sick should perform half of the respective prescribed penances. However, in the case of association with someone who was himself associated with a great sinner, one should perform half of the penance prescribed for that associate.
Thus ends the section on penance for those associated with great sinners (*mahāpātakin*) in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now, the penances for minor sins (*upapātaka*) are stated:

If a Brāhmaṇa kills even a single cow out of ignorance, he becomes pure by fasting for three nights and giving eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh, or by performing twelve *prājāpatya* penances; or he becomes pure by giving twelve cows as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*). If it was done intentionally, however, he should personally perform whatever service is beneficial for the cow—whether in its movement, standing, sitting, or lying down. Protecting it from fear, disease, hunger, thirst, cold, heat, and the like, and refraining from consuming food or drink belonging to himself or others, he should worship the cow at night, remain in the *vīrāsana* posture, and subsist on forest herbs and such for three months. At the end of that period, he should give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh. If he is unable, he becomes pure by giving his entire property. In the case of the *prājāpatya* substitute, the requirement is double that of the unintentional act. If a Kṣatriya kills a single cow out of ignorance, he should follow the cow for its benefit, sleep in the cow-pen, bathe at the three periods of the day, remain self-controlled, and subsist only on the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one month. At the end of the month, he becomes pure by giving a milch-cow, or by performing six *prājāpatya* penances. In the case of the substitute, six cows are to be given. If it was intentional, he should eat a measured amount of sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) free from pungent and salty flavors at every fourth mealtime, bathe in cow-urine for two months, and then become pure. In the case of the *prājāpatya* substitute, the requirement is double. If a Vaiśya kills a single cow out of ignorance, he should perform acts beneficial to the cow and so forth, perform an *atikṛcchra* penance continuously for one month, and at the end of the month, he becomes pure by giving a milch-cow, or by performing five *prājāpatya* penances. In the case of the substitute, he should give four cows. If it was intentional, having killed a single cow, he must perform all of that twice over. If a Śūdra kills a single cow out of ignorance, he should perform acts beneficial to the cow and so forth, perform a *prājāpatya* penance continuously for one month, and at the end of the month, he becomes pure by giving a milch-cow. In the case of the substitute, he should give four cows. If it was intentional, he becomes pure by wearing a wet cow-hide, living in the cow-pen for six months, and drinking barley-gruel (*yavāgū*). In the case of the *prājāpatya* substitute, both requirements are doubled. If one kills a single cow belonging to a learned (*śrotriya*) Soma-sacrificer who is not intentionally seeking it, he should perform acts beneficial to the cow and so forth, subsist on herbs and such for one year, and at the end of the year, give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh. Or, by eating only what is fit for a cow for six months, he is purified. If it was intentional, he should perform acts beneficial to the cow and so forth, shave his head, subsist on herbs, and perform this for three years. A wealthy man should perform the aforementioned vow while tending a hundred cows. If a wealthy man, lacking merit but possessing wealth, kills a *kapila* cow intended for a Homa sacrifice—one that is pregnant, has much milk, and possesses qualities such as good conduct and youth—belonging to a learned Soma-sacrificer who is extremely destitute and has a large family, he becomes a slayer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*). He must perform a vow twice as severe as that for killing a Brāhmaṇa. Alternatively, performing acts beneficial to the cow and so forth, carrying a staff and a girdle of *muñja* grass, eating dry, salt-free food at the sixth mealtime, reciting the *Gomatī* hymn or the *Praṇava*, and chanting the Veda, he should give a thousand cows at the end of two months. If it was out of ignorance, the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa is to be performed for three years, followed by the gift of one hundred and eleven cows (one hundred cows plus a bull), provided she was not pregnant. If the killing was intentional, he should perform acts beneficial to the cow and so forth, shave his head, subsist on herbs, and perform this for three years. If he kills her with a wooden stick, there is a hundred *sāntapana* penances and the gift of ten thousand cows over three years and so forth. If with a clod of earth, a *kāya* penance. If with a stone, a *taptakṛcchra* preceded by a vow, and at the end of the vow, he should feed the Brāhmaṇas and give them thirty cows and a bull. Having killed a young cow, one very old, very emaciated, or diseased, he should perform half of the previously mentioned vow, feed the Brāhmaṇas, and according to his ability, give gold and sesame seeds. When a cow is killed within one year, he performs a quarter-vow; within two years, a half-vow; within three years, three-quarters; thereafter, a full *kāya*. Regarding the killing of a pregnant cow, it is said: if the fetus has been produced, a quarter-vow; if it is firm, a half-vow; if fully developed, three-quarters; if conscious, the cow-vow is doubled. If many people kill one cow out of ignorance, each should perform a quarter of the stated vow. If two are killed, they perform a half; if many, three-quarters. If it was intentional, each must perform a full *kṛcchra*. If many are killed by a single act such as confinement, the vow is doubled. If a physician kills one cow through false medicine out of ignorance, the vow is doubled. If an unlearned person gives medicine with the intent to help out of ignorance, the vow is a quarter. In cases of confinement and the like, where the agents are indirect, the penalty is a quarter for confinement, a half for binding, three-quarters for yoking, and the whole for causing death. If, after performing confinement and the like out of ignorance, one fails to take precautions against the resulting negligence and the cow dies, one should perform a *kāya* penance, feed the Brāhmaṇas, and give a pair of cows. If death occurs due to negligence in confinement and failure to protect, one should perform a quarter, a half, or three-quarters of the vows, starting from the three-month penance and so forth, respectively. Except in cases of branding, disease, burning, excessive driving, cutting of the nose or tail, blocking by rivers or mountains, excessive burning, excessive taming, being crushed in a crowd, or being bound with strong nooses made of chains, coconuts, hemp, hair, or *muñja* grass, if the cow dies, the penalty is three-quarters. In all cases involving bells, eyes, or ornaments, the penalty is a half-*kṛcchra*. If the cow is nearly dead, one should eat barley-meal, barley-gruel, alms-food, milk, curds, and ghee for half a month respectively, feed the Brāhmaṇas, and give a cow. If one causes a disease that leads to death, one should drink *pañcagavya* for twelve nights. If a horn or bone is broken, or the hide is stripped off, and the cow survives, one should drink barley-gruel for one month. If unable, one should drink milk, curds, or ghee for ten nights. For accomplices, instigators, and others, the degree of fault is proportional as before. If death occurs due to failure to protect or negligence—such as leaving her in water, mud, low or uneven ground, a difficult place, a deserted house, or in confinement; or due to lightning, snakes, wild beasts, tigers, dogs, predators, cold, wind, or hanging—the owner of the cow should perform a *kāya* penance. If he was distracted by other duties, the penalty is half. There is no fault in killing for the purpose of extracting a hidden fetus, or when inserting a knife, stick, hook, or goad for protection, or in confinement and binding for the sake of protection. There is no fault in administering medicine or oil, or in burning, cutting, or piercing the head for the sake of benefit; nor in a village raid, a shower of arrows, the collapse of a house, excessive rain, the falling of a wall, or the burning of another's house or village. If the cow dies while tied up, one should perform a quarter-vow. The female gender is not intended here. The royal fine shall be equal to that. All of this applies only to a Brāhmaṇa killer. For a K
Thus concludes the expiation for cow-slaughter according to the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now follows the expiation for the *vrātya* and other such cases.

In that regard, for the purpose of expiating all minor offenses (*upapātaka*), one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Pañcagavya, a month of milk, a month of the Parāka penance, or the three-month Kṛcchra, in the absence of a specific rule prescribed for a particular case. Regarding the status of a *vrātya*, however, if the time for initiation has passed due to the absence of an initiator (*upanetr*) or other causes, one should have initiation performed after having the person undergo one of the four vows, such as the Cāndrāyaṇa, according to their capacity. If the time has passed outside of an emergency, one should initiate them after having them perform the three-month vow. In that same situation, if some time has elapsed even beyond fifteen years, one should perform the Auddālakavrata. It is as follows: one should subsist on barley-gruel for two months; on milk for one month; on curd-mixture (*āmikṣā*) for a fortnight; on ghee for eight nights; on food obtained unasked for six nights; subsisting on water for three nights; and fasting for one day and night. Alternatively, one may sacrifice with the Vrātyastoma. According to Āpastamba, for one whose father or grandfather was uninitiated, there is a year-long period of Vedic studenthood (*brahmacarya*) according to the three Vedas. For one whose initiation is not remembered back to the great-grandfather and so on, there is a twelve-year period of Vedic studenthood according to the three Vedas; having performed this, the initiation takes place.
Now, the expiation for theft:

In this regard, if a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally steals ten *kumbhas* of grain, or an equivalent amount of rice and so forth, or copper, silver, and the like belonging to another Brāhmaṇa, he shall perform the three-month penance (*traimāsika*). If it is done intentionally or repeated, he shall perform the one-year *kṛcchra* penance. For a Kṣatriya or others who steal, there is a reduction of one-quarter for each quarter [of the caste]. If a Brāhmaṇa steals the property of a Kṣatriya, he shall perform the six-month penance; for the property of a Vaiśya, the three-month penance; and for the property of a Śūdra, the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. The same should be inferred for subsequent cases as well. A *kumbha* is a measure of five thousand *palas*. For a Brāhmaṇa who steals the house, field, land, deposits, silver, diamonds, gems, men, horses, women, or the water from wells, ponds, and reservoirs—each obtainable for two hundred and fifty *paṇas*—his penance is equal to that for stealing gold. For the property of a Kṣatriya and others, the penances are the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, half of that, a quarter, and so on. For one who steals substances such as tin and lead which have little utility, worth two hundred and fifty and fifteen and a half *paṇas*, the penance is the *Sāntapana*. For one who steals food, drink, and the like sufficient for a single meal, or beds, seats, flowers, roots, and fruits, the penance is consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for a day and night. If it is sufficient for three meals, the penance lasts three nights. For one who steals grass, wood, trees, or dried food, molasses, oil, leather, and meat, when their value is sufficient for three meals, the penance is three nights. For one who steals gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, bronze, or stones, when their value is sufficient for twelve meals, the penance is eating only *kaṇa*-grains for twelve days. For one who steals cotton, silk, wool, cloths made of animal hair, animals with cloven hooves, solid-hoofed animals, ropes, birds, perfumes, or medicinal herbs, when their value is sufficient for three meals, the penance is drinking milk for three days. In all cases, the lightness or heaviness of the penance should be determined according to the smallness or greatness of the stolen object. All materials required for the penance for theft must be given to the owner before the rite is performed.
Thus concludes the penance for theft.
Now, regarding the non-payment of debts:

In this context, "debt" refers to that incurred by oneself, one's father, grandfather, and so forth. One owes a debt to the *ṛṣis* for failing to perform austerities (*tapas*) and the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*); a debt to the gods for failing to perform sacrifices; and a debt to the ancestors for failing to procreate offspring. If these debts are not discharged, one must perform at least one penance from the group beginning with the *Cāndrāyaṇa* according to one's capacity. If it is in every way impossible to do so, then at the end of the year, the *Vaiśvānareṣṭi* sacrifice must be performed. However, if one has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) despite being qualified to do so, there shall be a three-night fast every month for up to one year after the fire-establishment ceremony (*agnyādhāna*). Thereafter, every year, one penance from the *Cāndrāyaṇa* group must be performed; in the absence of an emergency, a three-month penance is required. If the father has not established the fires, has not performed sacrifices, or if the son who was to have sacrificed has failed to do so, the *Vrātyapaśu* sacrifice must be performed. If the *aupāsana* fire is not present, there is a monthly fast for two years, and at the end of the year, one penance from the *Cāndrāyaṇa* group. Alternatively, in the first year there is a *Kṛcchra*, in the second an *Atikṛcchra*, in the third both *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra*, and thereafter a *Cāndrāyaṇa*.
In the sale of goods that ought not to be sold—

For the sale of molasses, sesame, flowers, roots, fruits, or cooked food, one must perform the *saumyakṛcchra*. For the sale of lac, salt, honey, meat, oil, milk, curd, clarified butter, buttermilk, perfumes, skins, or garments, one must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. For the sale of wool, hair, lions, land, slaves, houses, or weapons, one must perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. For the sale of forbidden meat, sinews, bones, horns, or nails, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra*. For the sale of asafoetida, bdellium, yellow orpiment, realgar, collyrium, red ochre, alkali, salt, gems, pearls, coral, bamboo, reeds, or earthenware, one must perform the *taptakṛcchra*. For the sale of groves, tanks, wells, lotus-pools, or one's own meritorious deeds, one shall be purified in one year by bathing at the three periods of the day (*triṣavaṇa*), sleeping on the ground, eating only at the fourth meal-time, and reciting [the sacred syllable] ten thousand times. The same applies to selling goods with deficient measures or weights, or mixing them with inferior items. Other rules stated by Śaṅkha, Likhita, and others should be understood accordingly; where no penance is specified, a *cāndrāyaṇa* or similar penance applies. In cases of non-emergency, a three-month penance is required.
Thus concludes the penance for the sale of forbidden goods.
Now, the supersession of a younger brother by an elder brother—

In that regard, one who has married before his elder brother (*parivettṛ*) should perform one of the penances beginning with the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, give his own married wife to the elder brother, and, having been authorized by him, marry that same woman again. If it was done intentionally, and even there if the father of the girl and others were unaware, he must perform this for one year. He should do so only after subsisting on alms obtained from the house of a Brāhmaṇa. If the marriage was performed with the consent of the girl’s father and others, the penance is three months; or he may perform the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra* penances and then proceed as before. For the one whose younger brother marries first (*parivedya*), however, there are two *Kṛcchras*; for the girl, a *Kṛcchra*; for the giver, an *Atikṛcchra*; and for the officiating priest (*hotṛ*), a *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Similarly, for those who have set up the sacred fires before their elder (*paryāhita*), for those who officiate as priests for them (*parījya*), and for the elder brother himself (*parivitta*), there is a pair of *Kāya* penances. For the one who marries before his elder (*parivettṛ*), the elder brother (*parivitta*), the one who sets up the fires before his elder (*paryādhātṛ*), the one who officiates for him (*pariyaj*), the husband of a younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried (*agredidhiṣūpati*), and the husband of an elder sister whose younger sister is already married (*didhiṣūpati*), they must observe celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year as prescribed by Gautama, and only afterwards may they marry. The husband of the younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried (*agredidhiṣūpati*) should perform a *Kṛcchra* and then marry her. The husband of the elder sister whose younger sister is already married (*didhiṣūpati*), however, should perform the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra*, give her back to the man who first married her younger sister, and—having received permission—marry her again. Alternatively, the husband of the younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried (*agredidhiṣūpati*) should perform a *Kāya* penance and then marry that same elder sister, provided she was later married by another. The husband of the elder sister whose younger sister is already married (*didhiṣūpati*), however, should perform the *Kṛcchra* and *Atikṛcchra*, give his own married elder sister to the man who first married her younger sister, and then marry another woman. When the elder brother remains unmarried while the younger brother marries, the younger is called a *parivettṛ* or *parivividāna*, and the elder is called a *parivitti* or *parivedya*. The same applies to those who divide property before their elder (*parivibhāgavettṛ*) and the elder who is thus divided from (*parivibhāgavitti*). If a younger brother marries while an elder sister remains unmarried, she is the *agredidhiṣū*, and the elder sister is the *didhiṣū*. A teacher who teaches for a fee (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*) and a student who learns for a fee (*bhṛtakādhyāpita*) should, being self-controlled, drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* with milk for three fortnights, or perform one of the penances beginning with the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. The same applies to "offering an inquiry" (*anuyogapradāna*). Inquiry regarding one studying for the sake of excellence—asking, "What are you reading? Have you forgotten it?"—is what is meant by "offering an inquiry. They say that through the habitual practice of such inquiries, one incurs loss of caste (*pātitya*).
Now, regarding adultery:

In this regard, specific penances for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) and similar acts have been stated. For approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman who is merely by birth during her fertile period (*ṛtu*), one must observe the standard vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) for one year. For approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman of the same qualities—such as being a means for performing religious duties—who has reached her fertile period, the penance is two years. For such a wife of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*śrotriya*), it is three years. For a Kṣatriya woman of the same qualities, it is two years; for a Vaiśya woman, one year; and for a Śūdra woman, six months. Similarly, for a Kṣatriya approaching Kṣatriya and other women, the penances are two years, one year, and six months respectively. For a Vaiśya approaching a Vaiśya or Śūdra woman, they are one year and six months. And for a Śūdra approaching another man’s wife who is a Śūdra, it is six months. In the case of repeated intercourse with women who have not belonged to another before, the penance is twelve years. If the repetition involves approaching the same woman, the penance should be reduced by a quarter for each instance. In all cases, if the act is unintentional, half the penance should be applied. For approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman by birth during a non-fertile period, the penance is three months. For Kṣatriya and other women, it is two months and a lunar month (*cāndrāyaṇa*) respectively. For Kṣatriyas and others approaching Kṣatriya and other women, the penance is two months only. If Brāhmaṇas and others unintentionally approach a Śūdra woman, they should respectively perform the gift of eleven cows including a bull, the consumption of *pañcagavya* for a month, and the *kāya* penance for a month. However, if she is a Śūdra woman approached intentionally, the penance is half a *kāya*. If a Brāhmaṇa unintentionally approaches a Śūdra woman who is the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he should perform a *kṛcchra* if she has ceased her religious duties, and an *atikṛcchra* if she has not. The same applies to approaching the wives of twice-born men who have strayed twice or thrice unintentionally. If intentional, the penance is two *kṛcchras*. Even for women of the various castes, upon the fourth instance of infidelity they become wanton women (*svairiṇī*), and on the fifth, unchaste women (*bandhakī*). For approaching wanton women: for a Śūdra woman, one should bathe with one's clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa; for a Vaiśya woman, one should eat only at the fourth meal-time and feed Brāhmaṇas; for a Kṣatriya woman, having fasted for three nights, one should give an *āḍhaka* of barley. For unchaste women (*bandhakī*), however, for a Brāhmaṇa woman one should give something small; for a Kṣatriya woman, a bow; for a Vaiśya woman, a garment; and for a Śūdra woman, a water-pot—a Brāhmaṇa should give these. This penance applies when no pregnancy has occurred. If a pregnancy occurs, one should perform double the specific penance prescribed for that case. In the case of approaching women in the inverse order of castes (*prātilomya*), there is corporal punishment for the man, and the cutting off of the ears and so forth for the woman. If one approaches a woman of the inverse order under the mistaken belief that she is his own wife, the penance for a Śūdra approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman is twelve years. For a Vaiśya and others, there is a reduction of a quarter for each step. For a Śūdra approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman who is excessively unfaithful, the penance is consuming barley boiled in cow-urine. For a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya, it is the *kṛcchra* and *sāntapana* penances. Outcastes (*antyaja*) such as washermen, leather-workers, Bhills, hunters, actors, dancers, basket-makers, fishermen, and Mlecchas—these washermen and others, as well as Kāpālikas—are treated similarly. For unintentionally approaching a washerwoman or other outcaste women, a Brāhmaṇa should perform a *parāka* or a *cāndrāyaṇa*; if intentional, two *cāndrāyaṇas*. For Kṣatriyas and others, there is a reduction of a quarter for each step. In case of repetition, the penance is a *kṛcchra* for one year. If one withdraws before the emission of semen, the *kāya* penance is required. For sexual intercourse with a Cāṇḍāla or other outcaste woman, a heavier penance than that for violating the Guru’s bed is shown in the section on *gurutalpa*. If a pregnancy occurs with a Cāṇḍāla or other outcaste, the penance is half of the twelve-year vow for violating the Guru’s bed. For women also, in approaching a man of their own caste or a higher caste, the same three-year penance and so forth as stated for men should be performed. But in approaching a lower caste, if a Śūdra approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should wrap him in *vīraṇa* grass and throw him into the fire. The Brāhmaṇa woman, having shaved her head, smeared herself with clarified butter, and being naked, should be led along the high road on a donkey; thus she becomes purified. If a Vaiśya does so, one should wrap him in red *darbha* grass and throw him into the fire; the Brāhmaṇa woman should be led as before. If a Kṣatriya does so, one should wrap him in arrow-heads and throw him into the fire; the Brāhmaṇa woman should be led as before. Thus is the penance for a Vaiśya or Śūdra approaching a Kṣatriya woman, and for a Śūdra approaching a Vaiśya woman. Alternatively, for a Brāhmaṇa woman approaching a Kṣatriya, the penance is an *atikṛcchra*; for a Vaiśya, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. For a Kṣatriya woman approaching a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, the penances are half-*kāya*, *kāya*, and *atikṛcchra* respectively. For a Śūdra woman approaching a Śūdra, the *kāya* penance; but for Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya, they are a day-and-night, a three-night fast, and half-*kṛcchra* respectively. There is a special rule regarding pregnancy when a Brāhmaṇa woman approaches a man of the inverse order. If a Brāhmaṇa woman has intercourse with a Śūdra, the penance is a *kṛcchra* and three *cāndrāyaṇas*. With a Vaiśya, a *kṛcchra* and two *cāndrāyaṇas*. With a Kṣatriya, a *kṛcchra* and one *cāndrāyaṇa*. If a Kṣatriya woman has intercourse with a Śūdra, the penance is a *kṛcchra* and two *cāndrāyaṇas*. With a Vaiśya, a *kṛcchra* and one *cāndrāyaṇa*. With a Śūdra, a *kṛcchra* and one *cāndrāyaṇa*. With a Vaiśya, a *kṛcchra*. If the pregnancy is advanced, for a Brāhmaṇa woman: in the case of a Brāhmaṇa fetus, a *parāka*; in a Kṣatriya fetus, a *cāndrāyaṇa*; in a Vaiśya fetus, a *cāndrāyaṇa* and a *parāka*. In the

Thus ends the penance for adultery in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. For one who has married before his elder brother (*parivitti*), the penance is the same as that for the younger brother who marries first (*parivettṛ*). In this case, the *kāya* penance is to be substituted for the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
