Regarding usury, one of the three-month penances, such as the *cāndrāyaṇa*, should be applied according to the caste, capacity, and qualities [of the offender]. The same applies to the manufacture of salt.
Now, regarding the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya—

In this context, for the intentional killing of a woman who has not reached puberty, or of a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, one should perform the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmahatyāvrata*), a three-year vow, a one-year vow, or a six-month vow, respectively. Alternatively, one may give a thousand cows with one bull, a hundred cows with one bull, eleven cows with one bull, or a milch cow together with her calf. For the intentional killing of Kṣatriyas and others who are only slightly established in their conduct, the penances are one-fourth, one-eighth, or one-sixteenth of the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa. For those who are fully established in their conduct, these penances are increased by one part. Being established in conduct (*vṛttasthatva*) consists of possessing qualities such as good behavior, reverence for elders, compassion, purity, restraint of the senses, and benevolence toward living beings. For intentional killing, the penances are six years, three years, or one year. For the killing of a Kṣatriya or others who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), the vows last nine, six, or three years. For the killing of a Kṣatriya or others who are both learned in the Vedas and engaged in a vow (*vratastha*), the penance is ten years. For the killing of a Kṣatriya or others who are learned in the Vedas and engaged in a Soma sacrifice that has already commenced, it is twelve years. For the killing of a Kṣatriya or others who are learned in the Vedas and engaged in a Soma sacrifice, Gautama prescribes a six-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) accompanied by the gift of eleven cows including a bull, or a six-month penance. For the intentional killing of a Kṣatriya or others of bad conduct, the penances are three months, two months, or a *cāndrāyaṇa* fast. For unintentional killing, one should perform a three-night fast along with the gift of eleven cows including a bull, or a month-long consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), or a month-long subsistence on milk. This entire collection of expiations is to be understood as applying when the perpetrator is a Brāhmaṇa. When the perpetrator is a Kṣatriya or others, it should be understood that the penance is reduced by one-quarter for each successive class. In the case of killing Mūrdhāvasiktas and others, the expiation is to be inferred accordingly in each instance. In all cases, the increase or decrease of the expiation should be understood through the increase or decrease of the legal punishment (*daṇḍa*).
Now, regarding the killing of a woman:

In that regard, for the unintentional killing of women of the Brāhmaṇa and other castes born of inverse unions (prātilomya)—that is, wives of Brāhmaṇas and others who have become unchaste—one should respectively give a water-reservoir, a leather bag (dṛti), a bow, a goat, and a sheep. If the act was intentional, penances of six, four, two, and one month should be performed. The same applies to the killing of their sons and so forth. For the killing of those who live by the profession of prostitutes, one should give only a small amount of water. For Kṣatriyas and others who kill Brāhmaṇa women and others of the inverse order through adultery, the penance prescribed for cow-killing should be applied as appropriate. However, for the unintentional killing of Brāhmaṇa women, there is a six-month penance or the gift of ten cows; for the killing of Kṣatriya and other women, the penances are three months and half of those respective periods. If intentional, these are doubled for Brāhmaṇa and other women. Alternatively, for a Vaiśya woman, the gift of a cow is prescribed; for a Śūdra woman, one of the penances such as the Cāndrāyaṇa is sufficient. But for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa woman or others who were instrumental in performing religious rites, the standard vow of celibacy (brahmacarya) lasts six years for a Brāhmaṇa woman, three years for a Kṣatriya woman, one and a half years for a Vaiśya woman, and nine months for a Śūdra woman. In all cases, if the act was unintentional, the penance is halved. The penance for killing an Ātreyī has already been stated.
Now, regarding non-violence toward others:

In that regard, for the killing of a thousand boneless creatures such as lice, mosquitoes, bedbugs, gadflies, and the like, or for the killing of bone-bearing creatures such as lizards and others for whom no specific expiation has been mentioned, one must observe the standard *brahmacarya* vow for six months or give ten cows. If the number exceeds that measure, a greater penance should be prescribed. Furthermore, for the killing of a creature with thin bones, something small should be given; "something" refers to eight handfuls of grain, or "something" refers to a *puṣkala*. Four *puṣkalas* equal a *pūrṇapātra* or an *āḍhaka*. Four *āḍhakas* make a *droṇa*, and four *droṇas* make a *khārikā*. For gold, "something" is one *paṇa*. For the killing of a very minute boneless creature, a *prāṇāyāma* is required. For the killing of larger boneless creatures such as woodworms (*ghuṇa*), one must consume hot barley-gruel (*taptayāvaka*) for three days. For the killing of creatures born from fruits, flowers, food, or liquids, one must subsist on clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for a day and night. For each of the following—cats, iguanas, mongooses, frogs, blue jays, crows, owls, and so forth—one must drink milk for three nights, perform a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance, or travel one *yojana*; or else bathe in a river flowing to the ocean; or recite the *Abdaivata-sūkta*. One should perform each of these for three nights, or give a one-year-old calf. If the act was intentional, the penance is doubled. In case of repetition, the *kāya* penance is required. For the killing of all these together, the *kāya* penance lasts for six months. For an elephant, five dark-colored bulls (*nīlavṛṣa*) should be given. For a horse, a pair of excellent garments. For a camel, a load of *guñjā* seeds or a *suvarṇa-guñjā*. For a donkey, a bull or a one-year-old calf should be given. For a goat, an ox or a bull. The same applies to a ram. For swans, cranes, pigeons, peacocks, ruddy geese, cranes, herons, poisonous birds, *kaṅka* birds, dogs, *kāraṇḍava* ducks, hawks, vultures, and royal birds, a cow should be given. For vultures, crows, owls, doves, roosters, and large-winged birds, a three-year-old calf. For parrots, blue jays, wagtails, quails, and mainas, a two-year-old calf. For small birds such as *ṭiṭṭibhas*, partridges, and *maṅgvāhikās*, a one-year-old calf. For the killing of carnivorous beasts such as tigers, jackals, and monkeys, and for swans, hawks, *kaṅkas*, vultures, water-fowls such as herons, land-fowls such as crows, vultures, and peacocks—for the killing of each of these, a cow should be given. For non-carnivorous deer and similar animals, and for wagtails and similar birds, a heifer should be given. For reptiles, an iron rod with sharp points at both ends should be given. Or else, for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; for a curlew (*krauñca*), a three-year-old calf. For the killing of hermaphrodites among beasts and birds, lead or tin weighing one *māṣa* should be given, or a load of straw. For a pig, a jar of clarified butter. For a partridge, a *droṇa* of sesame seeds. If one is unable to give these items, one should perform a *kṛcchra* or other penance calculated according to the value of the object. Alternatively, if one is unable to give gifts, for the unintentional killing of each of the following—an elephant, a rhinoceros, a horse, a camel, a donkey, a cow, a gayal, a *ṛṣya*, or a buffalo—a *kṛcchra* plus a half is required. For the killing of all of them together, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is required. If intentional, for the killing of each, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is required. For the killing of all together, there is a repetition of the penance. For deer, spotted deer, *ruru*, boars, lions, *gaṇḍa* elephants, leopards, tigers, crocodiles, large fish, sharks, porpoises, and the like—if unintentional, a *kṛcchra* for each; for the killing of all together, two *kṛcchras*. If intentional, for each, the same; for all together, a *cāndrāyaṇa*. For dogs, wolves, monkeys, jackals, wild boars, and the like—if unintentional, three nights for each; for all together, a *kṛcchra*. If intentional, for each, the same; for all together, double. For cats, snakes, pythons, mongooses, frogs, mice, crabs, locusts, *sedhā* insects, iguanas, porcupines, tortoises, rabbits, and the like—if unintentional, a quarter-*kṛcchra* for each; for all together, a *kṛcchra*. If intentional, for each, the same. For swans and the like, if unintentional, a *kṛcchra* for each; for vultures and the like, a quarter-less *kṛcchra*; for parrots and the like, a half-*kṛcchra*. If intentional, for each, the same. For *ṭiṭṭibhas* and the like, a quarter-*kṛcchra*. In cases of killing all together, double that is required everywhere. This applies specifically to the case of a single killer. If there are two killers, half of what is stated for each should apply to each. If there are many killers, for elephants and the like, a *kṛcchra* for each; for deer and the like, three nights; for dogs and the like, two days; for cats and the like, a fast; for *ṭiṭṭibhas* and the like, eating only at night. If the creatures are nearly dead, for unintentional killing of each: for elephants and the like, three nights; for deer and the like, two days; for donkeys and the like, eating at every fourth mealtime; for cats and the like, a fast; for vultures and the like, eating at night; for parrots and the like, a single meal; for *ṭiṭṭibhas* and the like, a *prāṇāyāma* in water. For unknown beasts and birds, three nights. Thus, the rules should be applied to heavy or light cases depending on the place, time, species, strength, qualities, and other factors.
Thus concludes the expiation for violence.
Now follows the expiation for cutting down trees:

For cutting trees, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants that are useful for their fruits, flowers, and so forth, one should mutter the *Gāyatrī* and other *ṛcs* one hundred times, or perform as many repetitions of the *Gāyatrī*. For cutting domestic or wild herbs in vain, one should tend cows during the day and sleep at night only after drinking milk. There is no fault in cutting [plants] for the sake of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and the like, which serve transcendental purposes, nor is there any fault when they serve visible purposes such as tools for agriculture and the like. If a tree stands upon a shrine (*caitya*), a cemetery, a boundary, a holy place, or a temple, or if it is another well-known tree, the recitation of the hundred *ṛcs* is doubled; furthermore, an expiation must be performed according to the prescribed penalty. In all cases, for a Śūdra, instead of the recitation, a fast of two nights or more should be prescribed according to the penalty. In the case of habitual cutting of trees, one of the penances such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa* should be performed.
Thus concludes the penance for cutting down trees.
Now, regarding those bitten by dogs, cats, and the like:

If one is bitten by a dog, wolf, jackal, donkey, camel, village pig, crow, cock, monkey, unchaste woman, carnivorous animal, or a person of the lowest caste (*antyaja*), if he is capable, he must remain for two nights with water below the navel; for one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire, for one night; for a religious student (*brahmacārī*), for three nights. If the bite is above the navel, the penance is doubled; if on the mouth, tripled; if on the head, quadrupled. Alternatively, having bathed in a river that flows into the ocean and performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he may subsist on ghee for one night. For one who is incapable, having performed three breath-restraints in water, he may subsist on ghee for one night. In the case of extreme incapacity, having gone before Brahmins and prostrated, he becomes pure when looked upon by them. In the case of absolute incapacity, he becomes pure by consuming ghee mixed with gold and water. If the bite is slight and below the navel, there is bathing with the *Āpohiṣṭhīya* hymns and so forth, and three breath-restraints; if above the navel, double and so on. If bitten by a cat, mouse, dog, mongoose, horse, goat, buffalo, a low-caste person, or a wild forest animal, there are ten breath-restraints in water; for one slightly bitten, five. For Kṣatriyas and others, the penance is reduced by one-quarter for each successive rank. For a Śūdra, purification is achieved through fasting, the gift of a cow, the gift of a pair of cattle, or breath-restraints without mantras. If a Brāhmaṇī woman is bitten, she becomes pure after bathing and seeing the risen planet and stars. If a woman observing a vow such as the *Kṛcchra* is bitten, she should fast for three nights, eat barley-gruel with ghee, and complete the remainder of her vow. For women of the Kṣatriya and other ranks, it is the same according to their respective status. A menstruating woman bitten by a dog or similar creature becomes pure after fifteen nights of fasting and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). For bites above the navel or on the head, the multiples of two, three, or four should be applied accordingly. If one is smelled by a dog or the like, or licked, or scratched by nails, there should be washing with water and warming with fire. If worms are produced in a wound caused by a dog-bite, a weapon-wound, or the like, one should perform bathing with cow-urine and dung at the three junctions of the day. If this occurs above the navel, one should consume *pañcagavya* for three nights; from the neck upwards, for six nights; but for a wound on the head, for twelve nights. In that regard, for a wound from a dog-bite, this penance for the production of worms is to be performed after the specific penance for that bite. However, for a wound from a weapon or the like, the same rule of consuming *pañcagavya* for three days applies. For Kṣatriyas and others, there is a reduction of one-quarter for each rank. In the case of worms in another type of wound, purification is achieved by fasting, giving gold, and performing a *Kṛcchra* penance. For living by reprehensible means, one of the penances beginning with the *Cāndrāyaṇa* or lasting three months should be performed. "Atheism" (*nāstikya*) is the reviling of Vedic rites; living by that is the practice of atheism. For a single instance of atheism, a *Kṛcchra* is required; for its repetition, an *Atikṛcchra*; for further habituation, one of the penances beginning with the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. In the case of extreme persistence and long-term habituation, one should live for five years on alms in the house of a Brāhmaṇa.
Now, the expiation for the omission of the Brahma priest:

In this regard, a student (*brahmacārī*) of the three higher castes who has taken a wife becomes an *avakīrṇin* (one who has spilled his seed). For such a person, the penance for violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*) or an act equal thereto has been prescribed. However, having approached a woman other than those [specifically forbidden], he should perform a sacrifice to the deities of the Nairṛtas and Rakṣasas using a one-eyed donkey as the sacrificial animal, in the forest at a crossroads during the night, according to the rules of the *pākayajña* and the *paśukalpa* manuals of Āśvalāyana and others. Having donned its skin with the hair turned upward, bathing at the three periods of the day, carrying a red vessel, and proclaiming his deed, he shall become pure after a year by collecting alms from seven houses once a day. If he is unable to do so, he should offer a *caru* oblation to the Nairṛtas, cook it, and perform the fire-sacrifice with the mantras: "Svāhā to Kāma! Svāhā to Nirṛti! Svāhā to the deities of the Rakṣasas! and thus complete the remainder of the *homa*. By performing the water-vow (*ambuvrata*), he shall be purified. This annual vow is to be performed in the case of the wife of a non-learned Śrotriya, or in the case of a Vaiśya woman who is the wife of a Śrotriya. It is also to be performed in the case of a virtuous Kṣatriya woman who is the wife of a Śrotriya, or a Vaiśya woman who is the wife of a Śrotriya; however, in the case of a virtuous Kṣatriya woman who is the wife of a Śrotriya, the vow lasts for two years, and in the case of a virtuous Brāhmaṇī woman, it lasts for three years. An *avakīrṇin* who does so unintentionally shall perform the vow for Brahman-murder (*brahmahatyāvrata*) for six months, wearing clothes of bark, in place of the annual vow. The same applies to a woman who has committed only slight infidelity. In cases of unintentional acts involving two-year vows and the like, the penance is half. In the case of women who are excessively unchaste, or a Śūdra woman, he should bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot. In the case of a Vaiśya woman, he should eat only at every fourth meal-time and feed Brāhmaṇas, and give a load of fodder to the cows. In the case of a Kṣatriya woman, having fasted for three nights, he should give a vessel of clarified butter. In the case of a Brāhmaṇī woman, having fasted for six nights, he should give a cow. One who spills his seed upon cows should perform the *kāya* penance. In the case of a eunuch woman, he should give a load of sesame, lead, and beans. If he intentionally emits semen without sexual intercourse with a woman, the mere sacrifice to the Nairṛtas suffices. The same applies to nocturnal emission during sleep. In the case of seminal discharge during vows such as the *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* where celibacy is prescribed, this same mere sacrifice is required. Upon a nocturnal emission, a student (*brahmacārī*) should bathe, worship the Sun, and recite the verse "Punar mām aitv indriyam" three times. A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) or an ascetic (*yati*) who intentionally breaks their vow of celibacy should perform the *avakīrṇin* vow accompanied by three *parāka* penances. If unintentional, a triple *kṛcchra* is prescribed. If a renunciant (*saṃnyasta*) takes up the maintenance of a domestic fire (*gārhapatya*), he must perform a six-month *kṛcchra*, undergo all purificatory rites beginning with the birth ceremony (*jātakarma*), and then take up renunciation again for purification. For a Kṣatriya in this situation, two *cāndrāyaṇas*; for a Vaiśya, three *kṛcchras*. Alternatively, these may be applied specifically to a Brāhmaṇa, depending on his capacity and whether the act was a single instance or repeated. The same applies to those who have desisted from fasting unto death (*anāśaka*). However, for those who have died through renunciation, or those who perished by water, fire, or hanging, or those who failed in their wandering life or fasting, or those who died by poison, falling, or being struck by weapons, a *cāndrāyaṇa* and two *taptakṛcchras* should be understood as the penance, depending on their capacity and other factors. For one who resolves upon an unscriptural death such as suicide, there is a three-night fast for that duration alone. If wounded by a weapon or the like, a *kṛcchra* is required; if severely wounded, a *cāndrāyaṇa*. For the sons and relatives of one who dies by weapons or similar means, they should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* and two *taptakṛcchras*.

Thus ends the penance for one who has spilled his seed. However, a student (*brahmacārī*) who is not ill, having through negligence failed for seven nights to collect alms or perform the fire-ritual due to being preoccupied with more important duties such as service to the teacher, and having intentionally spilled his seed, shall offer two oblations of clarified butter with these two mantras: "I have spilled, I have spilled; to Kāmakāma, svāhā! I have fallen, I have fallen; to Kāmakāma, svāhā! Then he recites: "May the Maruts sprinkle me, may Indra, may Bṛhaspati."
May this Agni sprinkle me with long life and with strength.

One should worship [the Sun] with this [verse]. In the event of an omission due to distraction, one must perform the penance for a transgressor (*avakīrṇin*). Immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*), if the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) or other items are lost during the period of vows, one should put on another cloth or thread and offer four oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) with verses containing the word "mind" (*manas*), such as *mano jyotiḥ*, and verses containing the word "vow" (*vrata*), such as *tvam agne vratapā asi*. Having offered these, one should wear the sacred thread again according to the prescribed rule. In the following cases, one should offer oblations: eating improper alms-food; when the sun has risen or set while eating; after vomiting; sleeping during the day; seeing a naked woman; sleeping naked; stepping onto a cremation ground; riding horses and similar animals; bypassing those worthy of one's own respect; and omitting the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*). Upon accepting gifts such as jewels, clothing, or cattle, one should recite the *Sāvitrī* mantra eight thousand times. For killing living beings—whether stationary or moving, trees, anthills, domestic animals, or reptiles—one should perform a fire-oblation (*homa*) with the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses. If one eats without wearing the sacred thread, or wears it improperly, or after voiding feces or urine, purification is achieved by reciting the *Gāyatrī* eight thousand times along with breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*). For drinking [impure water], three breath-controls are required. For eating while naked, six breath-controls are required. The same applies to eating or urinating [under such conditions]. If the sacred thread, girdle (*mekhalā*), deerskin (*ajina*), or staff (*daṇḍa*) are lost, one should perform a *vyāhṛti-homa*, perform six breath-controls, and then wear them again. If the twilight rituals (*saṃdhyā*) or the fire-ritual are omitted, one should bathe and recite [the *Gāyatrī*] eight thousand times. If a healthy person eats a single meal without first going out for alms, he should recite [the *Gāyatrī*] one hundred and eight times. There is no fault in eating a single meal after having requested alms. If service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*) and other duties are neglected, one should recite [the *Gāyatrī*] one hundred and eight times. For consuming honey or eating forbidden meat, the *kṛcchra* penance is required. If done intentionally, the *parāka* penance is required. In case of repetition, the penance is doubled, followed by re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) and the completion of the vow. That same [forbidden food] may be given to a physician for medicinal purposes, provided it is the leavings of the teacher. Then, having become free from disease, one should worship the Sun with the verse *haṃsaḥ śuciṣad*. If one performs actions contrary to the teacher’s will, such as disobeying his commands, one becomes pure only after propitiating him through prostration and other means. If a student sent by his teacher for his own sake dies by chance in a region disturbed by fear of thieves, tigers, and the like, or in great darkness at night, the teacher becomes pure by performing three *kṛcchra* penances. In all cases, there is no fault if a person dies while medicine, wholesome food, or effort toward that end was being provided for the sake of health.
Now, regarding false accusation:

A Brāhmaṇa who falsely accuses another Brāhmaṇa of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*) or similar offenses shall become pure by subsisting on water for one month, with his senses restrained, and habitually reciting the *Śuddhavatī* mantras. In the case of accusing a Kṣatriya or others, he should perform the penance with a reduction of half for each successive class. Kṣatriyas and others, when accusing a Brāhmaṇa, should perform twice, three, or four times the respective penance. For a Śūdra, in place of mantra-recitation, there are breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*) without mantras. In the case of accusing someone of a minor offense (*bhūtapātaka*), the penance is half of that; for those who accuse of a secondary sin (*atipātaka*), it is three-quarters; for those who accuse of a grave sin (*anupātaka*), it is half of that; and for those who accuse of a minor sin (*upapātaka*), it is less than that. One who has been falsely accused should perform a *Kṛcchra* penance, or offer a *Puroḍāśa* cake to Agni, or an animal sacrifice to Vāyu. In the case of accusations regarding mortal sins and the like, the penance is reduced by a quarter for each successive degree of severity. If one unintentionally approaches the wife of an elder brother or a younger brother without being authorized, he must perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. If he does so intentionally, he should live for a year on alms at the house of a Brāhmaṇa. If he unintentionally approaches his own wife while she is menstruating once, he becomes pure by consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for three nights. In the case of repetition, the period is seven nights. If intentional and occurring once, it is seven nights; if repeated, it is a *Kṛcchra*. In the case of continuous and habitual repetition, the penance lasts for three years.
Now, the case of mutual contact between women in their menses will be explained.

When two women of the same caste who share the same husband touch each other while menstruating, whether intentionally or unintentionally, they both become pure by bathing immediately. However, if two women of the same caste who are not co-wives, but are related by birth or *gotra*, touch each other unintentionally, mere bathing suffices. If intentional, there must be one night of fasting and the consumption of *pañcagavya*. If they touch women of the same caste who are unrelated, unintentional contact requires purification after bathing at the end of the day or the night; intentional contact requires abstaining from food until purification. If she eats, she must fast every day thereafter, or perform an equivalent gift (*dāna*), or feed a Brahmin, or perform a substitute rite (*pratyāmnāya*). If she intentionally touches outcastes such as *caṇḍālas*, those living on the outskirts, the fallen, corpses, and so forth, she should observe a fast for the first few days and then perform penance. For intentional contact on the first day, it is a three-night fast; on the second, a two-day fast; on the third, a day-and-night fast; and thereafter, eating only at night. If she eats during the first or subsequent days, she should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance, reduced by a quarter for each subsequent day. If she unintentionally touches a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, she becomes pure simply by fasting for that period. If she eats during the first or subsequent days, a substitute rite is required. For intentional contact with washerwomen and others, the penance is like that for touching *caṇḍālas*, but if she eats during the first or subsequent days, she should perform two *kṛcchra* penances, reduced by half for each subsequent day. If she unintentionally touches washerwomen and others, she becomes pure by fasting for that period; if she eats, a substitute rite is required. For intentional contact with dogs, wolves, jackals, monkeys, donkeys, camels, pigs, crows, cocks, five-nailed animals, or those defiled by the remnants of a *śūdra*, she should observe a fast for the first few days and then perform penance. For contact on the first day, it is a two-day fast; on the second, a day-and-night fast; on the third, eating only at night; thereafter, eating only once a day. If she eats during the first or subsequent days, she should perform a *kāya* penance, reduced by a quarter for each subsequent day. If she unintentionally touches dogs and others, she becomes pure by fasting for that period; if she eats, a substitute rite is required. For intentional contact with those touched by *caṇḍālas*, washerwomen, or menstruating women, or with those defiled by low, impure, or filthy substances, or by the remnants of food, she should observe a fast for the first few days. For contact on the first day, it is a fast; on the second, eating only at night; on the third, eating only once a day. If she eats during the first or subsequent days, she must perform fasts of three, two, or one night, or eat only once a day. If she unintentionally touches those who have touched such people, she becomes pure by fasting for that period; if she eats, a substitute rite is required. If she is unable to do so, or if the contact was unintentional, she may bathe immediately and remain pure until the moon is seen; if she is extremely unable, she may bathe and eat during the day. If two menstruating women who are both defiled by food remnants touch each other unintentionally, a Brahmin woman is purified by a *kṛcchra* and a three-night fast, while a Śūdra woman is purified by gifts and fasting. For women of other castes who are not defiled by food remnants, the penance for intentional mutual contact is the same as that for unintentional contact when defiled by food remnants; for intentional contact between those defiled by food remnants, the penance is double. If a menstruating woman touches twice-born men who are defiled by food remnants, she should fast if the defilement is from below (mouth), and for contact from above (head), she should fast for three nights. If a menstruating woman who is eating and defiled by food remnants touches a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, she should observe a fast for the first few days and then perform penance: for contact on the first day, she should consume cow-urine and barley-gruel for six nights; on the second, for four nights; on the third, for two nights; and on the fourth, she should fast. (*In this case, if she eats during the first or subsequent days, she should perform a *kāya* penance followed by a *cāndrāyaṇa*. If a menstruating woman defiled by food remnants touches washerwomen and others, she should remain without eating from the start, and for contact on the first or subsequent days, she should reduce the penance by one day starting from five nights. In this case, if she eats during the first or subsequent days, she should perform a three-night fast followed by a *kāya* penance. For contact with dogs and others, (*she should fast from the start for four nights etc.; if she eats during the first or subsequent days, she should fast followed by a three-night penance. For contact with those touched by *caṇḍālas*, washerwomen, and others,*) she should remain without eating from the start for three nights etc. If she eats during the first or subsequent days, a substitute rite is required. In all cases, if she is unable, she should give gold, or provide food to Brahmins or an equivalent act, and then have them recite, "May she be pure. When a penance has been prescribed and she sees her menstrual blood, she should proceed as follows: having touched a menstruating co-wife and then seen her blood, she becomes pure by bathing immediately. Having touched a co-wife of the same or higher caste and then seen her blood, she should fast for one night. Having touched a woman of lower caste and then seen her blood, she should fast until purification and, if she has not seen her own blood, consume *pañcagavya*. Upon touching a *caṇḍāla*, a woman in childbirth, a corpse, or those attending to them, and then seeing her blood, she should fast until purification and afterwards perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*. Upon touching washerwomen and others and then seeing her blood, she should fast until purification and afterwards perform a *kāya* penance. Upon touching dogs and others and then seeing her blood, it is a three-night fast. Upon being defiled by other untouchables and then seeing her blood, it is a fast. When a state of impurity arises and she sees her blood, in all cases, a woman with young children may eat after performing an ablution; afterwards, a substitute rite for eating may be performed. For a woman observing a *kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa* vow, when a mandatory bath is due and she sees her blood, she should bathe using water poured through another vessel, then sprinkle her limbs with water, wring out her clothes, or put on other clothes, and then continue her vow. During the impurity of a death or birth, if her menses appear in the middle, she should eat without bathing; upon purification, she should fast. If a death or birth impurity occurs during her menses, she should bathe and then eat. If a menstruating woman observes a vow and speaks to another menstruating woman, she should fast. Having touched a menstruating woman and eaten, she should not eat until the time of the menstruating woman's bath. For a woman observing a vow, she should also consume *pañcagavya*. If a menstruating woman is bitten by a dog or similar animal, she should fast for five nights and be purified by *pañcagavya*. There is no loss of the vow if menses appear while a long-term vow has already begun; she should consume sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) and so forth, and perform daily worship and other rites. If she eats without bathing at the time of purification, the penance for intentional contact is a *kāya* penance; for unintentional, a *cāndrāyaṇa*. The remaining rules regarding edible and non-edible foods will be stated later. A menstruating woman should avoid applying collyrium, oil-massage, bathing, walking about, cleaning teeth, cutting nails, handling ropes, manual labor, betel, honey, meat, perfumes, flowers, sleeping during the day, and observing planets or stars. She should eat from her hand, or from an earthenware or metal vessel, and abide by these and other such rules. In all these cases, the bath is to be taken with one's clothes on.
Thus ends the rule regarding a woman in her menses. Now, regarding the sale of children:

therein, for the sale of a daughter, and for the sale of temples, shelters, gardens, groves, lotus-pools, assembly halls, water-stations, and holy bridges, one should perform a Cāndrāyaṇa or similar penance, or alternatively, a three-month penance. In times of distress, a Taptakṛcchra; in extreme distress, a Sāntapana. For the sale of a son, all these penances are doubled. For the sale of an only son, one becomes pure after one year by bathing at the three periods of the day, sleeping on the ground, and eating only at every fourth meal-time. For the sale of a daughter, purification is achieved in half that time.
Now, regarding the officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not sacrifice:

In this regard, one who performs sacrifices for *vrātyas*, one who initiates or teaches *vrātyas*, a priest of the low-born (*hīnayājaka*), one who performs funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) for *Śūdras*, a seller of the Veda, a killer of those seeking refuge (excluding thieves), one who fails to abandon thieves, or one who performs malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) intentionally, shall perform the three penances beginning with the *Kṛcchra* according to the gravity of the offense. For initiating, teaching, or sacrificing for a *vrātya* intentionally, one shall perform the *Uddālaka-vrata*; this has been described among the penances for *vrātyas*. A *vrātya* is one whose initiation has passed its time. An "Ahīna" sacrifice is a sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*) lasting from two days up to twelve days. They say there is a fault even in the non-transgression of the vow (*āvratāvyabhicāre*). For sacrificing out of greed for the funeral rites of Brahmins and others, one shall perform the *Kāya*, *Atikṛcchra*, and *Taptakṛcchra* penances respectively. In case of repetition, double; in case of extreme repetition, triple. For sacrificing for those unfit to be sacrificed for, such as *Śūdras*, if unintentionally, one of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances applies; if unable, a *Kṛcchra*; if intentional, a three-month penance; in repetition, double and so on. It is the same for sacrificing for a younger brother who marries before the elder (*parivedaka*) and others. Studying the Veda during forbidden times—such as on festival days (*parvan*), when a *Caṇḍāla* or similar person is within earshot, or during other interdictions—is a corruption of the Veda (*vedavilava*). Also, questioning one who studies for the sake of excellence by saying, "What are you reading? You have ruined it," is a corruption of the Veda. Upon hearing a *Caṇḍāla* or a fallen person (*patita*), the recitation of the Veda requires a fast. If intentional, a three-night fast; in repetition, a *Kṛcchra*; in extreme repetition, three *Kṛcchras*. For explaining the *Smṛtis* and Dharmaśāstras, half of that. For studying during obligatory interdictions (*nityānadhyāya*), one should mutter the *Svādhyāya* in water as many times as studied, like the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. If unable, one should mutter it like the *Aghamarṣaṇa*. If utterly unable, one should mutter it on land, or mutter another mantra for that duration. For intentional study during each interdiction, a fast; the same applies to studying while impure. The same applies to studying during occasional interdictions (*naimittikānadhyāya*). For that which is difficult to understand, half of that. If a village cock, mouse, frog, or similar creature passes between [the teacher and student], there is a night-fast. If a cow, horse, buffalo, woman, *Śūdra*, or similar being passes between, there is a fast. If a cat, snake, mongoose, or any five-clawed animal passes between, there is a three-night fast and bathing at the three times of day. If a dog, wolf, jackal, monkey, washerman, or similar person passes between during study, a *Kāya* penance. If a donkey, boar, camel, *Caṇḍāla*, a woman recently delivered, a menstruating woman, a corpse, or similar thing passes between, three *Kāyas*. For passing near a white cow, gayal, goat, or those who have abandoned the Veda (*brahmodgata*), atheists, and so on, a three-month penance. For passing near a hare, sheep, dog-cooker (*śvapāka*), and so on, a six-month penance. For passing near an elephant, rhinoceros, crane, tiger, great sinner (*mahāpātakin*), ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*), and so on, during study, one shall perform a *Kṛcchra* for a year and remain without study for that long. In all cases, if intentional, half. Some say there is no penance if one ceases the study immediately upon the passage. For abandoning father, mother, or guru without cause, one of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances or a three-month penance. Additional requirements include eating only at every sixth meal-time for an extra month, or the *Saṃhitā-japa*. For abandoning a son, one of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances or a three-month penance; the same for abandoning a relative. For defiling a maiden of the same caste, a *Cāndrāyaṇa* or a three-month penance. For those of different castes in the direct order (*ānulomya*), a month of milk or a *Kāya*. In the inverse order (*prātilomya*), for a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya, a year-long *Kṛcchra*; for a Śūdra, the same as execution. In extreme repetition, even for a person of the same caste, a year-long *Kṛcchra*. A seller of Soma, a husband of a *Vṛṣalī*, one who abandons a wife married in childhood, a sacrificer for a Śūdra, one who opposes his guru, a drinker of *surā* or other intoxicants, one who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa, a fraudulent dealer, one who deals with outcasts, a betrayer of friends, and one who lives by forgery—if unintentional, a three-month vow; if intentional, a six-month vow; in repetition, one shall perform a year-long *Kṛcchra*. For breaking a vow taken for the propitiation of deities and the like, or for breaking any other vow, or for cooking for oneself, or for consorting with a woman who drinks intoxicants, one of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances or a three-month penance. For abandoning the study of what has been learned due to addiction to vices, it is equal to the sin of killing a Brāhmaṇa. For abandoning the protection of a large family due to addiction to the study of good scriptures and the like, one of the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances or a three-month penance. In extreme distress, a *Kāya* penance for one who has abandoned the Veda.
Now, regarding the abandonment of the sacred fire (agnityāga):

If one abandons the *agni* (sacrificial fires) out of atheism (*nāstikya*), after two months have passed, one should perform the *kāya* penance and then re-establish the fires. After four months, an *atikṛcchra*; after six months, a *parāka*. Beyond six months, one of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; beyond a year, a three-month or two-month penance. However, if the abandonment is due to laziness or similar causes, then upon the lapse of twelve days, there is a three-day fast; upon the lapse of a month, twelve fasts or subsisting on milk. If the abandonment is due to negligence or the like, then for up to three nights, there are twelve light *prāṇāyāmas*; up to six nights, twenty; up to twelve nights, fifty; up to twenty nights, one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*; up to thirty nights, a fast; up to sixty nights, a three-night fast; up to a year, the *kāya* penance; and beyond that, the *kāya* penance for each subsequent year. In all cases, they say that for as long as the fire was not maintained, one should give an equivalent amount of wealth. Upon abandoning the *agnihotra* after a year, one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* and then re-establish the fires. Upon abandonment after two years, a *cāndrāyaṇa*, a *somāyana*, or two *cāndrāyaṇas*. Upon abandonment after three years, a year-long *kṛcchra*, the gift of a cow, and re-establishment of the fires. For those who live by the wives of others, those who live by violence, those who live by medicinal herbs for subjugation and the like, or those who construct machines for the purpose of killing, one of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances applies. The same applies to vices such as gambling and hunting. A liar, a thief, a king’s servant, one who lives by planting trees, a poisoner, an arsonist, one who lives by riding horses or elephants, a stage-player, a dog-keeper, a teacher of Śūdras, the husband of a Śūdra woman (*vṛṣalī*), a bawd, one who lives by the stars, one who lives like a dog, a Brahmin who lives by medical practice, a physician, a temple-priest, a domestic chaplain, a gambler, a drunkard, a forger, and a seller of children, men, or cattle—these and others are those whose food should not be eaten. If one eats their food while desiring to maintain Brahminhood, one should renounce the wealth and perform a three-month penance. For a long period, having renounced wealth, eating at the fourth meal-time, bathing at the three junctions of the day, and practicing for a year, they become pure at the end by offering libations to gods and ancestors and giving daily fodder to cows. A "dog-keeper" (*śvagaṇika*) is one who lives by a pack of dogs. A "bawd" (*bhāṇḍaka*) is one who lives by musical instruments or is a bard. A "dog-liver" (*śvavṛtti*) is a servant. A "Brahmin-liver" (*brahmajīvī*) is one who performs the duties of a twice-born for a fee. In the case of selling oneself or serving a Śūdra, one of the *cāndrāyaṇa* penances or a three-month penance applies. In the case of long-term service to a Śūdra, eating sparingly at the fourth meal-time, bathing at the three times of day, and alternating between standing and sitting postures, they become pure in three years. The same applies to sea-voyages, misappropriating a Brahmin’s deposit, trading in all kinds of merchandise, and lying about land. In friendship with an inferior, one of the *cāndrāyaṇas* or a three-month penance. In breaking a friendship with a non-inferior, one should fast and then drink milk at the breaking of the fast. In consorting with a woman of low birth, one of the *cāndrāyaṇas* or a three-month penance applies if unspecified. In that regard, if a Brahmin unintentionally approaches a previously married Kṣatriya woman, he should perform the *kāya* penance; approaching a previously married Vaiśya woman, a *kṛcchra*; approaching a previously married Śūdra woman, an *atikṛcchra*. A Kṣatriya approaching a previously married Vaiśya woman, a *kāya*; approaching a previously married Śūdra woman, a *kṛcchra*. A Vaiśya approaching a previously married Śūdra woman, a *kāya*. If intentional, one of the *cāndrāyaṇas* applies; the appropriate penance should be applied for Brahmins and others. In approaching a common woman, a female animal, or a prostitute, if unintentional, a *kāya* penance; if repeated, one of the *cāndrāyaṇas*. If intentional, one should drink *kuśa*-infused water once a day for seven nights. If repeated, a three-month penance. Here, there is no repetition of the occasional penance for every single occasion; rather, in the case of intentional repeated intercourse, the duration increases daily for less than a month; thereafter, it increases monthly until a year; thereafter, it increases yearly until the sin is exhausted—one should act thus. In the case of repeated unintentional intercourse, however, what was prescribed for a single act is tripled for three days, fivefold after a month, tenfold after six months, fifteenfold after a year, and twentyfold after three years; beyond that, it should be calculated accordingly. This also applies to the repetition of minor offenses (*upapātaka*). But in the case of repeating a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), what was prescribed for a single act is doubled for the second time, tripled for the third, and for the fourth there is no atonement, and so forth. In the case of approaching a common woman, if the repetition is continuous from the time of birth due to attachment, the vow for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*) applies. One who does not belong to an order of life (*anāśramī*), when an order is impossible, should perform a *kāya* penance for a year and then enter an order; in the second year, an *atikṛcchra*; in the third year, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; beyond that, a *cāndrāyaṇa*. If an order is possible, an *anāśramī* should perform one of the *cāndrāyaṇas* or a three-month penance in the first year; thereafter, a fourfold increase per year should be applied. In being fond of another's cooking, studying false scriptures, holding office in mines, or selling one's wife, one of the *cāndrāyaṇas* or a three-month penance applies.
Thus concludes the section on penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*.
Now, regarding the acceptance of gifts from unworthy persons (*asatpratigraha*):

In that regard, the unacceptability (*asattva*) of a gift arises from the donor being defiled by birth, such as a *caṇḍāla*, or defiled by conduct, such as one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*), or from the place—such as Kurukṣetra—and the time of the acceptance. It is also unacceptability by its very nature (*svarūpataḥ*), as in the case of liquor, wine, a buffalo, a black antelope skin, a black man, a bed used for a corpse, or a two-faced cow, and so forth. In that context, if one who maintains celibacy (*brahmacaryavān*) accepts a ewe or similar items from a fallen person or the like, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, reciting the *Sāvitrī* three thousand times every day and subsisting on milk; after a month, he becomes pure. However, if one accepts forbidden items such as an ewe from a Brāhmaṇa of righteous conduct, or accepts permitted items such as land from a fallen person, the penance is a *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Alternatively, there may be the *Pavitreṣṭi* sacrifice, the *Mitravindā* sacrifice, or the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* a hundred thousand times. In the case of repeated practice, he shall dwell in water for a month, subsisting on milk at every sixth meal-time; at the end of the month, having gratified the Brāhmaṇas with gifts, he becomes pure. This same rule applies when a fallen person or the like accepts an ewe or similar items during the reception of Kurukṣetra and other such occasions. Where nothing is specified regarding the donor, the place, the time, or the object, if the donor, place, time, and object are not otherwise defective, the penance is a *Kṛcchra* for the acceptance of an object valued at twelve *niṣkas*. Thus, in all cases, the increase or decrease of the penance follows the value of the object. When any one of the donor, place, time, or object is defective, the penance increases by one degree. For the acceptance of minor objects such as jewels, clothes, or cows, there is the recitation of the mantra eight thousand times. If it is even less than that, or merely the acceptance of alms, one should utter an auspicious mantra. Every penance must be performed only after renouncing the object. As long as the object remains, there is no entitlement to perform the penance.
Now, the expiation for eating what is forbidden to eat:

Regarding that, if one unintentionally eats once garlic (*laśuna*), onion (*palāṇḍu*), *gṛñjana*, mushroom (*chatrāka*), village pig (*viḍvarāha*), or village cock (*grāmakukkuṭa*)—all of which are inherently impure—one must perform the *sāntapana* penance. In the case of repetition, a *yaticāndrāyaṇa* is required. If it is intentional and done once, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is required; however, in the case of repetition, it is equal to the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*). The same applies to varieties of mushrooms similar to onions, such as *pūlibheda*, *dīrghapatra*, *picchagandha*, *mahauṣadhi*, *paṇyavṛntāka*, *parārikā*, *yavaneṣṭa*, and types of mushrooms like *kabuka*. In the case of repetition, there is a cycle of *cāndrāyaṇas*; in extreme repetition, it is equal to the drinking of liquor. If these are eaten by force or when they are known only to a single person, purification is achieved by reciting the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times, sprinkling drops of water continuously on the head, and fasting. In all cases where vomiting has occurred, half of the prescribed penance is ordained. For those things equal to garlic in smell, color, or taste, the *sāntapana* penance applies. For ascetics (*yati*), observers of vows (*vratin*), and celibates (*brahmacārin*), the *taptakṛcchra* and other such penances apply. In the case of eating the following—*khaṭvā* birds, *kusumbha*, eggplant (*vārtāka*), *kumbhītaka*, drumstick tree (*śigru*), *bhūtṛṇa*, *khukhaṇḍakavaka*, black mustard (*kṛṣṇasarṣapa*), *taṇḍulīyaka*, *nālikā*, coconut, *khaṭvā* vegetables, *kālinda*, *bābaka*, *kumbhīka*, round bottle-gourd (*vartulālābu*), *āraka*, thorny plants (*kaṇṭakī*), red drumstick, *kovidāra*, *śleṣmātaka*, *nālika*, small white *kañcuki*, eggplant, *potikā*, *ketuka*, *khaṭvā* birds, mushrooms (*kavaka*), hemp flowers (*śaṇapuṣpa*), silk-cotton tree (*śālmalī*), and others such as bulbs, foul-smelling excrement-bulbs, roots, and products from incisions in trees, as well as red resinous exudations, semen, feces, urine, curd churned with the hand, and sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) offered by priests outside the Vedic fold—if eaten unintentionally once, there is a fast. In the case of repetition, there is a cycle of penances; if intentional, a three-night fast. In the case of repetition, a *kāya* penance; in extreme repetition, an *atikṛcchra*; and in continuous, unremitting repetition, a *taptakṛcchra* and a second initiation (*punar-upanayana*). Otherwise, one falls [from caste]. If one unintentionally eats *nīlī* (indigo) once, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is required. For a Brahmin, in the case of repetition, there is a cycle of penances; in extreme repetition, there is a fall [from caste]. Eating the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*) or food offerings (*naivedya*) belonging to Śiva or the Sun requires a *cāndrāyaṇa*. In the case of repetition, it is doubled. If intentional and repeated, the *sāntapana* penance applies. This same rule applies to the remains of other deities, except in times of distress (*anāpadi*).
Now, regarding those things that are inherently impure by nature:

For consuming the milk of cows that are in heat (*sandhinī*), those whose calves have died (*syandinī*), those that have not yet passed ten days after calving (*anirdaśā*), or those that have been defiled by impure things (*amedhyasevin*); for the milk of goats or buffaloes within ten days of calving; for the milk of one-hoofed animals (excepting the buffalo) and of wild forest animals (excepting the goat); for drinking curds produced from such milk; and for consuming *śukta* (fermented liquids) other than those derived from curds—[if done] unintentionally, there is a fast (*upavāsa*); [if done] intentionally, a three-night penance (*trirātra*). For unintentionally consuming the milk of sheep, donkeys, camels, monkeys, village pigs, beasts of prey (*śvāpada*), or of two-teated animals (excepting the goat), the *sāntapana* penance is required; [if done] intentionally, the *taptakṛcchra*. In case of repetition, the *cāndrāyaṇa* and a second initiation (*punar-upanayana*) are required. In all cases of re-initiation, shaving, the girdle, the staff, begging for alms, and the specific vows are dispensed with. In case of extreme repetition, there is degradation (*patana*). For a student (*brahmacārin*) and others, the *kṛcchra* or *taptakṛcchra* is prescribed. Curds and their derivatives may be eaten as *śukta*. Among two-teated animals, the milk of goats and wild animals, and among forest animals, that of buffaloes, may be consumed. For unintentionally consuming the milk of a tawny cow (*kapilā*) and similar forbidden milk products, or their derivatives, there is a two-night barley-meal (*yāvaka*) penance; intentionally, a six-night penance; in case of repetition, double that. For eating the flesh of birds other than village pigs, village cocks, and their congeners; for eating the meat of goats, buffaloes, or wild animals; for consuming earth, clods, hair, nails, insects, moths, worms, aquatic creatures, bone, blood, fish, fish-bones, or fish-scales; and for vomiting blood—[if done] unintentionally, a fast; [if done] intentionally, a three-night penance. For eating food cooked in a vessel used for meat, one should drink water boiled with *kuśa* grass for three days. If hair or the like enters the mouth of one observing a vow, one should drink heated clarified butter (*taptaghṛta*) or the juice of *brāhmī*. If food is defiled by flies, hair, etc., at the time of eating, one should immediately touch water; that food should be touched with ashes, earth, or water. If defiled by a bone, there is bathing and the consumption of clarified butter. Upon seeing blood and the like, there is a fast; if seen in the mouth, a three-night penance. If eaten, the juice of *brāhmī*; if in water, *kuśa* water. Even if they are otherwise pure, for the raw meat of snakes, reptiles, rats, cats, lizards, cocks, mongooses, frogs, horned animals, peacocks, carnivorous beasts, poison-eaters, *mudgara*, crabs, porpoises, crocodiles, sharks, fish with snake-like mouths, or birds with horns or beaks, and for eating meat not consecrated for sacrifice (*vṛthāmāṃsa*), or for eating meat when not appointed to do so—[if done] unintentionally, a three-night penance; [if done] intentionally, an *atikṛcchra*. In case of negligence, a fast; if there is vomiting, immediate bathing and the consumption of *pañcagavya*. For eating the meat of village pigs, village cocks, and similar carnivores; humans, apes, monkeys, dogs, jackals, wolves, tigers, lions, beasts of prey, elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, one-hoofed animals, or those with tusks on both sides; crows, cranes, vultures, web-footed birds, partridges, *puṇḍarīka*, *kapiñjala*, *cakrapāda*, *kukkuṭa*, *sārikā*, *kāmacakra*, swans, *plava*, *cakravāka*, *kāraṇḍava*, sparrows, pigeons, *pārāvata*, *pāṇḍu*, parrots, *sārikā*, *sārasa*, *ṭiṭṭibha*, owls, *kaṅka*, red-footed birds, *tittiri*, blue jays, cuckoos, *salahi*, *kuṭaca*, *ārama*, *madgu*, *kalaviṅka*, *krauñca*, hawks, *khañjarīṭa*, woodpeckers, *mūliṅga*, *vāgulā*, and the like; and for the meat of fish, dried meats found in slaughterhouses, and their excrement, urine, semen, blood, fat, marrow, or the leavings thereof—[if done] unintentionally, the *kāya* penance; in case of repetition, the *mahāsāntapana*; [if done] intentionally, the *taptakṛcchra*; in case of further repetition, the *cāndrāyaṇa*; in case of extreme repetition, degradation. For the six types of impurities such as earwax and the rest of these animals, half the penance should be prescribed. For a student and others consuming honey, meat, etc., there is a three-night penance according to common law (*laukika*), or the *kāya* penance, or a second initiation, followed by the completion of the vow. That [food] may be eaten which is intended for a single physician or which is the leavings of a teacher. The urine and other products of cows are pure, as are the leavings of goats.
Now, regarding the consumption of food touched by impurity:

Regarding the consumption of leftovers (*ucchiṣṭa*): if one unintentionally eats the remains left by dogs, birds such as crows, predatory beasts, rats, cats, or mongooses; or if one eats food that has become abundant in liquid, or is infested with hair and the like; or if one eats from a vessel used for offerings to the gods (*devadroṇī*) that lacks the ritual purification of the substance—then, in the case of unintentional eating, one should drink *brāhmī suvarcalā* for one night. In the case of intentional eating, for three nights. If the quantity of the substance is small and the act is repeated unintentionally, an *atikṛcchra* penance is required. If repeated intentionally, the vow is to subsist on barley gruel (*yāvaka*) for a fortnight. However, regarding the leftovers of a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra, a Brāhmaṇa should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for one, three, five, or seven nights respectively. In the case of repetition, this cycle is repeated for each of them. But if one eats these intentionally, one should perform those same purifications beginning with fasting (*śuddhopavāsa*). In the case of intentional repetition, one should perform the *kāya*, *atikṛcchra*, *taptakṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. For the Kṣatriya and others, one should reduce the penance by one-quarter at each stage. If food contained in a vessel is defiled by hair, ants, impure insects, or worms, one should remove that portion with a mantra and sprinkle the remainder with water mixed with ashes, copper, lapis lazuli, gold, silver, and the like, or with cow-hair and *darbha* grass. If the food is in one's hand and thus defiled, one should discard it. If it is in the mouth, one should spit it out and consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*). In the case of consuming human semen, feces, or urine, members of the castes should perform the *taptakṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, *kāya*, and three-night fasts respectively. If done intentionally, they should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*, *taptakṛcchra*, and *kāya* penances, followed by a re-initiation (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). The same applies to the food of *caṇḍālas* and other "outcastes" (*antyajāti*) who are not to be licked or drunk from. Outcastes include the *caṇḍāla*, *śvapāka*, *kṣattṛ*, *sūta*, *vaidehaka*, *māgadha*, and so forth. Regarding the eating of their food, the rule is the same. Having eaten the remnants of the meal of an outcaste, the castes should perform a *yaticāndrāyaṇa*, a *kāya*, half of that, or a quarter of that respectively. But upon eating the actual leftovers of an outcaste, they should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*, a *mahāsāntapana*, a six-night fast, or a three-night fast. In the case of repetition or excessive repetition, the penance is doubled or tripled; in the case of continuous practice, there is loss of caste (*patana*). If one consumes raw grain seized by such persons, the penance is half. Eating their leftovers doubles it; eating together triples it. In the case of intentional repetition, there is loss of caste. Having consumed lamp-soot oil, oil defiled on a road at night, or oil remaining from anointing the body, one should perform a *nakta* (eating only at night) penance. If one drinks what remains after being drunk or what has come out of the mouth, one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* or a *parāka* penance in the case of intentional repetition. If one drinks merely what remains after drinking or drinks with the left hand, the penance is half of that.
Now, regarding the consumption of food touched by impure substances:

In that regard, regarding food or drink containing hair or insects; touched by indigo, lac, sinew, bone, skin, blood, flesh, fat, marrow, liquor, semen, feces, or urine; looked upon by a great sinner (*mahāpāpa*); rendered impure by the leavings of wicked birds or village pigs; smelled by a cow; dried out; stale; cooked for no sacred purpose; or intended for offerings to gods or ancestors, or for *homa*—if one eats or drinks these unintentionally, there is a fast and the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in all such cases. If done intentionally, it is a quarter-*kṛcchra* (or half-*kṛcchra*). If the substance is defiled by bones or other things of unknown origin, the penance is half of that. Regarding the six types of bodily waste such as earwax, the penance is half of this in cases of slight contact; however, in cases of extensive contact, it is double. Furthermore, if the nature of the defilement is recognized, it is a *taptakṛcchra*, and in all cases, a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) is required. Regarding substances defiled by contact, defiled by ritual action, or defiled by their very nature: those defiled by contact include *caṇḍālas*, the lowest castes (*antyaja*), women in childbirth, menstruating women, outcasts (*patita*), corpse-burners, eunuchs, temple-priests (*devalaka*), those who have abandoned the sacred fire, those who have ascended the funeral pyre, those accused of crimes, and others of similar status. Those defiled by animals include dogs, village pigs, donkeys, camels, beasts of prey, five-toed animals, and herds of cattle. Upon seeing someone eating from such persons, one should discard the morsel, wash the internal and external smears from the mouth, and bathe. If one has swallowed even a small amount, there is a recitation (*japa*) of one hundred and eight times. If one has eaten a full mouthful, there is a fast for a "bird-night" (*pakṣiṇī*). If one has eaten the entire meal, it is a three-night fast; if one has drunk water, it is half of that. In the case of dogs and similar animals, one should perform *ācamana*. After eating or drinking, the penance is half of that. If one hears that a *caṇḍāla* or similar person is eating while one is eating, one should stop eating immediately to become pure. If one has already eaten, one should bathe and perform a *japa* of one hundred and eight or observe a fast. If one touches a vessel used for the leavings of a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, it is a *kṛcchra* if it is made of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*), and an *atikṛcchra* if it is earthenware. If it is touched by the leavings of a washerman or similar person, the penance is half of that. Eating food touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person requires a three-night fast; eating food seen by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person requires a fast and *pañcagavya*. Eating from a vessel held in the hand of a *caṇḍāla* or similar person requires a *cāndrāyaṇa*; eating with them is double that; eating their leavings is fourfold. Drinking water released from the hand of a *caṇḍāla* or similar person requires a fast; touching such a person while one is impure from leavings is half of that. Seeing a *caṇḍāla* or similar person while one is impure from leavings, one should fast; touching them requires a three-night fast. If a menstruating woman of lower caste is touched by another menstruating woman, she should not eat until she is purified. If she touches one of equal or higher caste, she may eat after bathing on that very day. If a menstruating woman is touched by a crow or similar bird, or by another menstruating woman, she should fast and consume *pañcagavya*. If it was intentional, she should fast until purified, bathe, and then consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*) for purification. If a menstruating woman is touched by a *caṇḍāla* or the lowest castes, she should not eat until purified. If she has already eaten, she must wait for that many days and then perform the penance once purified: a three-night fast on the first day, two days on the second, one day and night on the third, and thereafter eating only at night. If she sees menstrual blood while in a state of impurity, a young mother may eat after an ablution. If she comes into contact with a death or birth impurity (*sūtaka*) during her period, she should not eat from the time she touches it until the prescribed bathing time. If she eats intentionally, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is required. In the case of contact with a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, if she eats, she should consume cow’s urine and barley gruel (*yāvaka*) for a fortnight or perform a *kṛcchra*. If a *caṇḍāla* or similar person stays in one's house unknown, if one eats their food unintentionally, it is a *kāya-kṛcchra*; if intentional, a *parāka*. If one unintentionally drinks water from a well, pond, or river frequented by *caṇḍālas* or similar persons, one should drink *pañcagavya*. For drinking water directly from a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, it is a *kāya-kṛcchra* or half of that. For drinking water touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, one should consume cow’s urine and barley gruel for three nights. If one is impure from leavings and touches a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, it is a *kāya-kṛcchra*. Alternatively, having recited the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times, one thousand times, or one hundred and eight times, one should drink *pañcagavya* at the end of three nights. For the leavings of raw food, the penance is a quarter. If one is touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person while seated below them in a row of leavings, it is a quarter. If one urinates while touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person, one should fast for three nights or recite the *Jātavedas* hymn. For one who is unable due to lack of intention, a fast is required; for eating, six nights. For eating raw food, three nights or one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. Regarding washermen and similar castes, the same rules as for *caṇḍālas* should be understood. One who is impure from leavings and touches a dog or similar animal, a *śūdra*, wine, or impure things that should not be touched, should fast and drink *pañcagavya*. If one intentionally eats food touched by a menstruating woman, a woman in childbirth, an impure person, an outcast, a *caṇḍāla*, a *pulkasa*, an *avadhūta*, a *kuṇṭha*, a *hastaka*, one with worms, one with leprosy, or a woman with bad nails, or food touched by such impure persons, it is a *kāya-kṛcchra* if intentional, and half if unintentional. If the food contains forbidden substances or hair, one should drink a decoction of *kuśa* grass, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, etc., or *brāhmī*. If one eats food cooked by a *śūdra*, or food contaminated by impure insects, or if one eats while being touched by a *śūdra*, or eats in a row with an unworthy person, or if the server gives leavings, or if one sips water (*ācamana*) while eating, or if one serves food after being reviled, or if one eats in a row of leavings, one should fast and consume *pañcagavya*. If intentional, it is a *sāntapana*. If one eats from a vessel released by the left hand, or if one eats after someone in the same row has risen, it is a *sāntapana*. If one drinks from a well or similar source containing the corpse of a five-toed animal, a donkey, a village pig
Now, regarding the consumption of food corrupted by one's state of mind:

In that regard, food devoid of its natural color and so forth is "defiled in thought" (*bhāvaduṣṭa*). For food defiled in thought, if eaten intentionally, one must fast for three nights; if unintentionally, for half that time. Upon vomiting, one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*). However, if one eats something while suspecting it to be either edible or inedible, one should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*—unseasoned with alkaline salt—for three nights. Alternatively, one may drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* with milk, or a decoction of water boiled with the leaves of *kuśa*, lotus, *udumbara*, *palāśa*, and *bilva*. One should perform a *kṛcchra* penance for three, two, or one year [according to the severity]. In a case of doubt, upon learning the truth, a twice-born man should perform double that penance.
Now, regarding the consumption of food that is spoiled by time:

That which is spoiled by time includes stale food, fermented liquids, and the milk of a cow within ten days of calving, and so forth. In such cases, if consumed unintentionally, one must fast; if intentionally, one must observe the *kāyavrata* for three nights. There is no fault in consuming barley, wheat, milk, curd, products made from flour, foods cooked in oil, or foods smeared with oil, during the month of *māsa* (Mārgaśīrṣa) and others. Having drunk from vessels made of horn, bone, or ivory, or having drunk from bulbs, lotus roots, conch-shells, oyster-shells, or cowrie-shells, or having drunk fresh rainwater—whether at its proper time within three days, or at an improper time within ten days—one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). If done intentionally, one must fast. In the *Saṃgraha*, it is stated that for eating at a new funeral feast (*navaśrāddha*), for food offered by a village priest, during forbidden times caused by eclipses and the like, during the twilight hours (*saṃdhikāla*), too early in the morning or too late in the evening, and for eating parched grain, curd, or flour-meal at night, or for eating food mixed with sesame seeds—in such cases where no specific penance has been prescribed—one should perform one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) or fast intentionally.
Now, regarding the consumption of oyster shells and other such items that are defiled by their qualities:

In that regard, having unintentionally drunk or eaten various impure decoctions or substances tainted by defects, one should fast. If done intentionally, one should consume *yāvaka* (barley gruel) for three nights. There is no fault in using sour gruel (*kāñjikā*) mixed with fruits such as *āmalaka* or in using it for sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*). Regarding food preparations such as oil-cakes from which the essence has been extracted, or those that have been melted down, or churned curds, and so forth—if consumed intentionally, one should consume *yāvaka* for three nights; if unintentionally, for half that time. After vomiting, one should drink clarified butter (*ghṛta*). The same applies to living beings prior to the five-clawed animals. If one eats food that lacks the *vaiśvadeva* offering or is not prepared near the sacred fire, or if one eats *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), cakes (*apūpa*), fried cakes (*śaṣkulī*), honey, or meat in vain—that is, without a proper purpose—there is a fast if done unintentionally; if intentional, three nights. One who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), however, should perform either the *kāya* penance or a three-night fast. Having eaten from a Śūdra’s vessel, a broken vessel, or a common pot, there is a fast and the consumption of *pañcagavya*. If done intentionally, three nights. For eating from a broken bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*), the *kāya* penance is required. For eating from broken vessels and the like, one should drink *pañcagavya*, or clarified butter, or *brāhmī*. Having eaten from the leaves of the *vaṭa*, *arka*, *aśvattha*, *kumbhī*, *tinduka*, *kovidāra*, or *kadamba* trees, one incurs the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. A householder who eats from the leaves of creepers, *palāśa*, lotus, or other trees should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. A forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) and an ascetic (*yati*) who eat from them incur the fruit of the *cāndrāyaṇa*. Others incur the same for eating from lotus leaves.
Now, regarding eating food that is defiled by actions such as being handed with the hand, or eating from a person who should not be eaten from:

in that regard, for eating food given by hand, eating in the presence of a Brāhmaṇa, eating in a defiled row, or eating by force from the hand of one unworthy of the row or a Śūdra, or [drinking] water [from such a hand], if done unintentionally, there is a night-fast (*nakta*); if intentional, a fast (*upavāsa*) and the consumption of *pañcagavya*. The same applies when honey, molasses, vegetables, cow’s milk, salt, or ghee are given by hand.
Or if one has a foot placed upon a seat, or is even half-covered by a garment; [in these cases, the penance is the same].
Having eaten food blown upon with the mouth, one should perform the Kṛcchra Sāntapana penance.
Now, regarding the Śrāddha meal:

Regarding food offered with the ancestors (pitr) and others in mind, there are three types of *śrāddhas*. Among them, during the ten-day period (*antardaśāha*) and on the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha*), there are nine *śrāddhas*. From the eleventh day until the end of the first year, there are sixteen *ekoddiṣṭa* rites; these nine mixed with the former are called "mixed" (*miśra*). The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is also mixed. Those performed thereafter are "ancient" (*purāṇa*). The *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day is mixed with the nine. In that case, due to the gravity of the penance (*prāyaścitta*), there is also a gravity of fault (*doṣa*). Some say the initial *ekoddiṣṭa* is independent; nevertheless, the rules, penances, faults, and punishments for both would apply. Even so, regarding the nine *śrāddhas* connected with impurity (*sūtaka*), one must perform a *kāya* penance upon eating. For the *ekoddiṣṭa* on the eleventh day, one should perform a *kāya* or a *pādona-kāya*. On the twelfth day or in the first month, one should perform only a *pādona-kāya*. In the second month, the third fortnight, the less-than-six-month period, and the less-than-one-year period, one should perform half a *kṛcchra*. In the third month and so on, until the end of the year, in the *sapiṇḍana*, and in the first annual rite (*ābdika*), one should perform a fast (*upavāsa*) or a *pāda-kṛcchra*. For every subsequent year and in ancient rites, one should eat only at night (*nakta*). Regarding a Guru, for the sake of wealth, in a nine-day *śrāddha*: three nights for the first, and two nights for the second. From the twelfth day onwards, two nights. From the second month onwards, a fast; from the third month onwards, *nakta* or *pañcagavya*. Or, for every year and in other ancient rites, six *prāṇāyāmas*. At a *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, three *prāṇāyāmas*. In those same cases, for one who eats without desire or is habitually devoted to recitation (*japa*), half of that is required. In *śrāddhas* for Kṣatriyas and others, the penances should be performed in sequence, doubled, tripled, or quadrupled. In times of non-distress, for a nine-day *śrāddha*, a *cāndrāyaṇa* or a *kāya*; from the twelfth day onwards, only a *kāya*; from the second month onwards, a *pādona*; from the third month until the end of the year and in the *sapiṇḍana*, three nights or half a *kāya*; in the first annual rite, a quarter *kāya*; for the annual rite, a fast. For a Kṣatriya, however, in a nine-day *śrāddha*, a *cāndrāyaṇa*; in the first monthly rite, a *cāndrāyaṇa* and a *parāka*; from the twelfth day onwards, a *parāka*; in the first, second month, or third fortnight, etc., a *mahāsāntapana*; from the third month onwards, a *kāya*; in the first annual rite, a *pādona*; for the annual rite, half; for the ancient rite, a quarter. For a Vaiśya, these same vows are increased by half. For a Śūdra, they are doubled. Alternatively, in a nine-day *śrāddha*, two *cāndras* or a *sārdha-cāndra*; from the twelfth day onwards, only a *sārdha-cāndra*; in the second month, third fortnight, etc., a *cāndra*; from the third month onwards, a *parāka*; in the year, a *mahāsāntapana*; for the annual rite, a *sāntapana*. In the case of those who died by the hands of Caṇḍālas, snakes, Brahmins, or beasts with fangs, by lightning, by falling, by poison, by hanging, or by fasting—sinners, thieves, outcasts, and those whose food is forbidden—one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa* for the nine-day *śrāddha*. In the first monthly rite, a *cāndrāyaṇa* and a *parāka*. From the twelfth day onwards, only a *parāka*. In the second month, third fortnight, etc., an *atikṛcchra*. From the third month onwards, a *kāya*; in the year, a quarter; for the annual rite, a fast. This applies even when eating in the presence of such persons if done for the sake of wealth. For those excluded from the row (*apāṅkteya*), in the eleventh-day *śrāddha*, a "child-*cāndrāyaṇa*" (*śiśu-cāndra*) is prescribed. An ascetic (*yati*), one under a vow (*vratin*), or a student (*brahmacārī*), having eaten food from one in impurity or at a nine-day or monthly *śrāddha*, having performed the stated penance, should further perform three nights, one fast, three *prāṇāyāmas*, and consume clarified butter (*ghṛta-prāśana*), then complete the remainder of his vow. In times of non-distress, however, a *kāya*, three nights, one night's fast, six *prāṇāyāmas*, and consuming *pañcagavya* are added. In case of repetition, double the *kṛcchra* and so forth. In *śrāddhas* where raw food (*āma*) or gold is intended, half or a quarter of the respective penances mentioned above apply. Alternatively, in times of non-distress, for a *āma-śrāddha*, one who is unable should perform a *kāya* or a *taptakṛcchra*. For a *hema-śrāddha*, three nights and a *kāya*. For an intended *śrāddha*, a fast and three nights. If by chance one eats at *ekoddiṣṭa* *śrāddhas* for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras that are interrupted by impurity, the penances are *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, *taptakṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa* respectively. From the twelfth day onwards, one should reduce the penance by a quarter each time. In cases of great interruption, however, three nights and so forth. Regarding a Guru, a fast, *nakta*, and six, three, or *prāṇāyāmas* apply. In times of non-distress, all this is doubled. In the case of very learned men (*atiśrotriya*) or ancient rites where no specific expiation is mentioned, one becomes pure by drinking water ten times while reciting the *Gāyatrī*. Thereafter, one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) as appropriate. Having eaten unintentionally or in times of distress at a *cūḍā-homa*, before the *namakarana*, at the *jātakarman*, at an ancillary *śrāddha* (*aṅga-śrāddha*), during impurity or even when not in impurity, at a name-giving *śrāddha*, at the end of the *cūḍā-homa*, at the *caula-śrāddha*, at the *sīmanta*, at the *soma* sacrifice, at the *ādhāna*, or at the *brāhmaudanika* rite, one should perform a *sāntapana*. If intentional and in times of non-distress, a *cāndrāyaṇa*. In other sacraments (*saṃskāras*), a fast is always required, or three nights in times of non-distress. A girl given to another after being promised to someone else is a *punarbhū
Now, regarding the impurity of consumption caused by possession:

In that regard, regarding the eating of food at a sacrifice performed by one who is not learned in the Vedas (*aśrotriya*), at a sacrifice offered by a village priest, or at a sacrifice offered by a woman or a eunuch;
