or at the meal of a king’s domestic chaplain, a royal servant, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra; or at the meal of those who keep goats, sheep, or buffaloes, of a village headman, or of a ruler of land; or at the meal of thieves, singers, carpenters, usurers, or those established in a consecration; or at the meal of a miser, one bound in fetters, one accused of a crime, an unchaste woman, a hypocrite, a physician, a tailor, an astrologer, one intoxicated, one angry, one afflicted by disease, or a courtesan; or at the meal of those who live by dogs, chariots, liquor, women, or hunting; or of the cruel, those who eat leavings, the fierce, the outcast, or the slanderous; or of a butcher, a weaver, a fuller, a merchant, or an ascetic; or of one who has violated his vows (*vrātya*), a blacksmith, a bell-founder, one who lives by trees or horses, or sellers of ghee, milk, oil, salt, or molasses; or of those who constantly tend fires, the sick, bell-ringers, poisoners, weapon-makers, or those who destroy the livelihood of Brahmins, cows, or gods; or of flute-players, drunkards, prostitutes, heretics, those who live by their wives, or those born in the reverse order of castes such as Sūtas; or of blacksmiths, the ungrateful, those who sell merit, Soma, or their own souls; or of those whose livelihood is litigation, hatred, the stage, or goldsmithing; or of distillers of liquor, washermen, hunters, or those with dogs; or of fraudulent actors, dancers, the husband of a low-caste woman, or those who tolerate an adulterer in their house; or of those conquered by women, gamblers, teachers of Śūdras, priests for Śūdras, or those who have abandoned their duty toward their wives; or of village priests, those who serve low-caste women, merchants, those who carry burdens on their backs, or servants; or of those who have taken a bride while the elder brother is unmarried, those who have married before their younger brother, those who marry before their younger brother, or those who give a younger sister in marriage before the elder; or of those who marry a remarried woman, those who marry a younger sister while the elder is still unmarried, those who live by spinning wheels or oil-pressing, those who live by fortune-telling, those who live by birds, those who cross the sea, or those with missing or redundant limbs; or of those who abandon their mother, father, son, teacher, or the sacred fire; or of those who use false measures, those who sell counterfeit gold, daughters, or women, or those who sell truth; or of tin-workers, leather-workers, smiths, tailors, or those who live by the sons of widows; or of those who eat from the vessels of others, those who have no offspring, those who guard their teacher’s wife, those who administer poison, or those who live by soup; or of those who live by childbirth, butchers, potters, or painters; or of those who cause confusion of castes, those who destroy hermitages, thieves, those who practice useless penance, or those who perform useless sacrifices—when standing on the path of such sinners, the penance for eating their alms-food is the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. For eating the food of these [sinners] who have not performed expiation, or for officiating at their sacrifice, giving to them, or accepting gifts from them; likewise for the food of those with deformed nails or black teeth, of Brahmins who eat the food of Śūdras, or Śūdras who eat the food of Brahmins—all of whom are those whose food is unfit to be eaten; or at a public water-stall (*prapā*), at a sacrificial session (*sattra*), at a *Soma* sacrifice, or at a funeral rite on the eleventh day (*ekādaśāha-śrāddha*); or food that is tainted, or looked upon by a wicked person, a learned man who is disgusted, or a great sinner; or food touched by a dog, smelled by a cow, licked by a bird, or requested by many people with anger or astonishment; or food touched by the foot, treated with contempt, or served without honor; or food passed around repeatedly, or the leavings of a woman or a Śūdra, or meat not prepared for a purpose, or food belonging to one in a state of birth or death impurity (*sūtaka*), or food belonging to a deceased person—if one eats the food of any of these, or if one intentionally consumes semen, feces, or urine, the penance is three nights of fasting. In case of repetition, a *Kṛcchra* penance is required. If intentional and repeated, an *Atikṛcchra*; if repeated, a *Taptakṛcchra*. For those who have maintained celibacy and so forth, the penances are *Taptakṛcchra*, *Cāndrāyaṇa*, and a second consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*). For extreme repetition, one should subsist on milk for two, three, six, nine, or twelve nights, or perform a *Cāndrāyaṇa*. For excessive repetition, an increased *Cāndrāyaṇa* is prescribed. In times of distress, one fast for one, two, three, or four days. In extreme distress, one performs three, six, nine, or twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). For raw grains, a bath suffices. For the food of a Brahmin, a single meal per day. For improper conduct or wicked conduct, eating only at night. For one who merely calls himself a Brahmin (*brāhmaṇabruva*), a bath and the recitation (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. The same applies to the food of those who hate their guru, teacher, fire, Dharmaśāstra, cows, or Brahmins, and to the food of those who have strayed from their Vedic branch (*śākhāraṇḍa*). For those forcibly enslaved by unchaste women, the accursed, Mlecchas, Cāṇḍālas, or robbers; or for killing cows and other animals; or for cleaning the leavings of such persons; or for eating their food; or for eating the dung of camels, donkeys, pigs, and the like; or for sexual union with their women; or for eating the food of those who have lived for a month among such people—the penance is a *Kāya* penance. For one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), a *Cāndrāyaṇa* or a *Parāka* penance is required. For one who has lived among them for a year, a *Cāndrāyaṇa* and a *Parāka* are both required.
Now, regarding the consumption of food during the period of impurity caused by birth or death:

In that regard, regarding the impurity (*āśauca*) of the twice-born (*dvija*), those of the same caste (*savarṇa*) shall observe a fast or a three-night penance. If a Brāhmaṇa has eaten unintentionally during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, he should perform one, two, or three nights of fasting respectively. In case of repetition, however, he should perform one, three, five, seven, or nine nights of fasting; or, in case of repetition, he should perform thirty-two or one hundred and eight breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). If it was intentional, then in all cases he should perform the *Sāntapana*, *Kāya*, *Mahāsāntapana*, or *Cāndrāyaṇa* penances, or the consumption of *pañcagavya*. Or, he may perform one, two, three, or four *Kāya* penances. In case of intentional repetition, he should perform the *Kāya*, *Kṛcchra*, *Taptakṛcchra*, and *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Or, in case of repetition, he should observe the *Yāvakavrata* (subsisting on barley-gruel) for one, two, three, or six months. In extreme distress, he may perform twelve, thirty, sixty, or one hundred breath-restraints. The same applies to a Kṣatriya during the impurity of a Vaiśya or a Śūdra, and to a Vaiśya during the impurity of a Śūdra. During the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya should perform one hundred and eight recitations (*japa*) or observe a night-fast. For a Vaiśya during the impurity of a Kṣatriya, it is the same. During the impurity of the twice-born, a Śūdra must bathe. During the impurity of a Śūdra, a Śūdra must bathe and consume *pañcagavya*. Upon touching a Śūdra, there is bathing if one has sipped water (*ācamana*), and *pañcagavya* if one has drunk. For a student (*brahmacārin*) and others, there is a fast, one hundred recitations, and *pañcagavya*; or a three-night fast with one thousand recitations and the addition of *pañcagavya*. Some say that birth-impurity (*jātāśauca*) is to be treated as lighter. The same applies to the impurity of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). One should not touch someone who has eaten during a period of impurity until they have evacuated their bowels. The expiation for that should be performed once the impurity has passed, because as long as the eaters remain impure by the mere act of eating once, they lack the eligibility [for rites]. Eating in the house of such a person requires a night-fast or a full fast. Regarding a *Kāpālika* or food and drink belonging to a *Kāpālika*, one should perform the *Kāya* penance or half of it respectively. In case of repetition, it is doubled; if intentional, tripled; if intentional repetition, quadrupled; and in case of extreme repetition, a *Cāndrāyaṇa* or half of it. The same applies to sexual intercourse with his women. In case of extreme repetition, a year-long *Kṛcchra* is required. If the food of an outcast (*patita*) is available, one should abandon it and perform an *Atikṛcchra*. There is no fault for an *Agnihotrī* engaged in a food-distribution (*annasatra*) if the food is raw (*āma*); but if it is cooked (*pakva*), he should subsist on barley-gruel for one or three nights, or perform twelve or twenty-four breath-restraints. Having taken the sacred fire and established it within himself (*samāropa*), if one ceases from the five sacrifices (*pañca-yajña*) and lives off the cooking of others, he should perform the five sacrifices after abandoning reliance on another's cooking and refrain from giving gifts; he should feed the gods and ancestors every fortnight or every month. For one who does not offer the ancestral rite (*śrāddha*) to them, if it is not repeated, a *Cāndrāyaṇa* is required. However, for eating the food of one habitually practicing forbidden acts other than those previously enumerated, there is a day’s fast. In case of repetition for a year, a *Parāka* penance is required. What is prescribed here applies specifically to a Brāhmaṇa; in that case, for a Kṣatriya, a quarter less is to be assigned, for a Vaiśya, half, and for a Śūdra, a quarter. For the women of those respective castes, half the penance applies; for menstruating women, exactly what is prescribed for each specific case should be performed.
Thus concludes the penance for eating forbidden food. Now follows the penance for acts causing loss of caste and so forth.

For acts causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), if committed intentionally, one should perform the *mahāsāntapana* penance; if unintentionally, the *kāya*. For acts causing mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), one should subsist on barley gruel (*yāvaka*) for a month, or perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. For acts rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), one should perform the *kṛcchra* or *atikṛcchra*. For acts causing defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*), one should perform the *mahāsāntapana* or the *taptakṛcchra*. Having caused a donkey or similar animal to carry a Brāhmaṇa, or having accepted wealth from a censurable person, one should perform half a *kṛcchra*. In these cases, for women, the penance is half; however, for those who are menstruating, that which is prescribed for each specific case must indeed be performed. Thus end the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*).
Now follows the miscellaneous expiations (prakīrṇaprāyaścitta).

In that regard, having mounted a vehicle yoked with donkeys or camels and traveled a distance, or having bathed naked, or having eaten, or having had intercourse with one’s own wife during the day—one shall become pure by immersing oneself in water while clothed and performing *prāṇāyāma* (breath control). If done unintentionally, a mere bath suffices. However, for actually riding a donkey, the penance is double. Having addressed a Guru with "hum" or a Brahmin with "thou," or having defeated a Brahmin through deceitful speech, or having bound him with a garment, one shall quickly appease him and fast. For repetition, the fast lasts three nights. If one raises a staff to strike a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; for actually striking him, an *atikṛcchra*; for causing blood to flow, a *kṛcchra-atikṛcchra*. If the blood flows internally or the skin is pierced, a *kṛcchra*; if a bone is broken, an *atikṛcchra*; for cutting off a limb, a *parāka*. If struck with the foot, one shall fast, bathe, and appease him; for merely touching him with the foot, one shall simply appease him. If one is distressed and voids excrement or urine in water or fire when not near a body of water, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on and touching a cow. If done intentionally, one shall fast and bathe with one's clothes on. For repetition or if not distressed, a *taptakṛcchra* is required. For the omission of *śrauta* or *smārta* rites, a fast is prescribed. Afterward, the specific expiation mentioned for each case, such as an *iṣṭi* sacrifice, must also be performed. If one who is healthy sleeps during the day after sunrise, he shall stand during the day reciting the *Sāvitrī* and fast. If he sleeps at sunset, he shall stand during the night reciting the *Sāvitrī* and not eat. For the omission of duties such as bathing, a fast or the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* one hundred and eight times is prescribed. For the omission of a *Snātaka*'s vows, such as wearing worn-out or dirty clothes, a fast or the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* one hundred and eight times is prescribed. For the omission of any one of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) when not ill, a fast is required; for a wealthy man, half a *kṛcchra*. The same applies to the omission of the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) on festival days (*parvan*) by one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), and likewise for the omission of approaching one’s wife during her season (*ṛtu*). If a man burns his second wife with the *vaitānika* (sacrificial) fires while his first wife is still living, it is equal to drinking liquor (*surāpāna*). If out of anger one says of one’s own wife, "She is unapproachable," the penance for the various castes is nine *kṛcchras*, six, three, and one-night fasts respectively. For eating without having bathed, etc., a fast and daily recitation are required. If one gives or causes others to give food unequally to those seated in a single row out of affection or other motives, or if one solicits such, a *kāya-kṛcchra* is required. For one who blocks a waterway, one who obstructs a maiden’s marriage, and one who shows partiality in honor toward equals, the penance is a *cāndrāyaṇa*. If a Soma-drinking Brahmin smells the scent of a liquor-drinker, he shall immerse himself in water, perform three *prāṇāyāmas* or the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times, and consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*). One who does not drink Soma shall do so without immersion in water; for others, it is simply a *prāṇāyāma* without mantras. For the smell of intoxicants, half of that. For directly smelling liquor, it is equal to drinking it. If smelled unintentionally, three *prāṇāyāmas* suffice. For smelling intoxicants, or the smell of feces, urine, carnivorous animals, or putrid odors, three *prāṇāyāmas* are required. Upon seeing them, one *prāṇāyāma*. Upon touching them, a bath and consuming clarified butter. Upon touching liquor, a bath and consuming the *pañcagavya*. Upon smelling a corpse, three *prāṇāyāmas* in water; if not a Soma-drinker, not in water; for others, *prāṇāyāmas* without mantras. Having drunk water from a vessel that once held dried liquor, one should subsist on *yāvaka* (barley-gruel) for a fortnight. For water from a liquor vessel, milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three nights. For water from a vessel where stale water stood, milk boiled with *gandhapuṣpī* for six days. For water from a vessel that held dried intoxicants, *yāvaka* for seven nights. In other cases, half of the aforementioned penance. A relative degree of severity should be applied based on the intensity of the taste of liquor or intoxicants. For vomiting, a *cāndrāyaṇa* or *kāya-kṛcchra* is required. Having drunk water defiled by feces and the like, a *sāntapana* for two days. If the taste is perceived, a quarter-*kṛcchra*. If the face is touched by droplets of liquor, feces, or urine, one should wash it with earth and cow dung and drink *pañcagavya*. Having given, touched, or received liquor, one should bathe and drink *kuśa*-water for three days. One who is entitled to bathe on occasions such as the *saṃkrānti* (sun’s passage), if he eats or drinks, he should recite the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times. For contact with a Śūdra or similar, a fast; for contact with a Caṇḍāla or similar, a three-night fast or a *kāya-kṛcchra*. For contact with a washerman or similar, half of that. For touching one who has touched them, a fast or a three-night fast. For failing to perform the daily bath and eating, a fast or a three-night fast. In all cases of occasional baths, the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times or twelve *prāṇāyāmas* are additional requirements. Upon touching impure things, dogs, or other untouchables, if one eats or drinks, a three-night fast is required for a householder; if intentional, a six-night fast. For one observing a vow, a *kāya-kṛcchra* or *cāndrāyaṇa*. If one touches a Caṇḍāla or similar without bathing before eating, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is required. For touching a washerman or similar at the end of a meal, if intentional, a *kāya-kṛcchra* after bathing. For touching a dog, crow, or similar while not bathing before eating, a three-night fast if intentional. If one eats or drinks after the occasion for bathing has arisen, a *sāntapana* for three nights. For eating without sipping water (*ācamana*), the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* one hundred and eight times. For eating, a fast. If excrement is discharged after beginning to eat but before the *āpośana* (sipping water), one should bathe outside with one's clothes on and perform six *prāṇāyāmas*. If there is an emission of feces while eating, one should perform purification, fast, and drink *pañcagavya*. If one becomes impure while eating, one should drop that morsel on the ground and bathe. If one eats that morsel, a fast is required. If one eats all of it, a three-night fast. If feces or the like fall on the head of one who is eating, one should discard the food, bathe in a river, and perform three *prāṇāyāmas*. If one touches a *sagotra* (kinsman) while eating, one should abandon the food. By touching water, one is purified. If one touches a non-*sagotra* while eating, purification comes simply by ceasing the meal. (*If two people of the same caste touch each other while eating, purification comes simply by ceasing.*) If
Thus concludes the miscellaneous expiations.

Now, if one who is arrogant does not perform the penance for a great sin (*mahāpātaka*), then all his *sapiṇḍas* and kinsmen, having dressed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*) and loosened their topknots, should, on the evening of a "empty" lunar day (*riktātithi*), outside the village, pour out a water-filled jar brought by a female slave, saying in the presence of a teacher: "You are dead to us. [144] Then, without looking back, they should touch water and enter the village. Thereafter, they should exclude him from all religious duties, avoiding conversation and other social interactions. If, through negligence, conversation or the like occurs unintentionally, he should remain for one night reciting the *Sāvitrī*. If intentional, for three nights. In case of repetition, there is degradation (*pātitya*) after a year. Then, when he has performed the penance and returned, the *sapiṇḍas* should bathe with him in holy water and, at a holy place and time, facing a holy direction, pour out a jar full of water, saying: "You are ours again. Thereafter, he becomes pure once he has given fodder to cows and they have eaten it. If he does not perform the penance again, he remains excluded from social dealings. The abandonment and readmission of women and those who have fallen (*patita*) is similar; however, having built a hut near the main house, one should provide food for the maintenance of life and soiled clothing, and protect them while depriving them of luxuries. For women as well, the causes of falling include the commission of great sins (*mahāpātaka*), minor sins (*upapātaka*), repeated secondary sins (*anupātaka*), and especially approaching a man of lower caste, causing abortion, and even for a non-Brāhmaṇa woman, the killing of her husband. For those who have approached a disciple, a teacher, or a person censured by the teacher, the penance is likewise. For Kṣatriyas and others, one should state the penance after consulting a Brāhmaṇa. For women and Śūdras, the instructions should be given excluding the recitation of mantras and fire-offerings (*homa*). Breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) without mantras should be prescribed in all cases. Recitation and the like are for those habituated to performing sacrifices and rituals; for others, however, recitation and the like apply. For those who merely bear the name, the ignorant, the poor, and those who do not study, austerity alone is prescribed. One whose fault is known by people other than the perpetrator is one of "renowned fault" (*vikhyātadoṣa*); such a person, even if learned, should quickly perform the vow of penance approved by the assembly (*parṣad*). In that assembly, there should be Brāhmaṇas who know the Veda and Dharma, numbering from one to a thousand or more as appropriate, excluding those who are excessively superior. The fee for the assembly (*parṣaddakṣiṇā*) should be a hundred thousand cows or more, down to some small amount, according to the number of *kṛcchra* penances, or simply the satisfaction of the assembly. Having bathed once with his clothes on, remaining silent, and while still wet, having given the fee to the assembly, confessed his sin, and accepted the penance and its vow, he should bathe again and perform the vow. The assembly should say: "If it were not equal to that [sin], speak! If he speaks without knowing, that entire sin falls upon him. If he performs it without the consent of the assembly, he must double it. To preserve his hair, he should perform double the penance. Shaving is not desired for learned Brāhmaṇas and women.
Thus concludes the section on public penance in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. Now follows the section on secret penance:

In that regard, one who has committed an offense other than those for which a specific agent is designated should perform a secret penance (*rahasya-prāyaścitta*) when the fault is unknown. An ignorant person, however, having learned of the secret penance through another source, should perform it in secret. For women and Śūdras, it is the same, with the exception of *japa* (recitation) and *homa* (fire-oblation). Where no specific food is mentioned, milk and similar substances are to be understood. Where no specific time is mentioned, a year and so forth are intended. Where no specific place is mentioned, mountains and the like are to be understood as prescribed by Gautama. In the case of *japas*, the seer (*ṛṣi*), deity (*devatā*), meter (*chandas*), and application (*viniyoga*) must be known. For the unintentional killing of a Brāhmaṇa: fasting for three nights, submerged in water, one should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa-sūkta*—"Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca"—three times. At the end of the three nights, having given a milch cow, one becomes pure. If unable to give a cow, one becomes pure by performing sixteen breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) accompanied by the *Vyāhṛtis* every day for a period of time. In the case of repetition, one established in the vow for thirty nights, exhausted by breath-restraints, should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa*; thus one is purified from mortal sins (*mahāpāpa*). If intentional, one should go out either east or north, bathe, wear clean clothes, and at the water's edge, having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), with wet clothes once and the hand purified once, facing the sun, one should recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* a hundred times in the morning, a hundred at midday, a hundred in the afternoon, and an unlimited number when the stars have risen. One should drink a handful (*prasṛti*) of barley-gruel. From seven nights for minor sins (*upapāpa*), twelve nights for those equal to mortal sins, and twenty nights for mortal sins, one is purified. The same applies to the intentional repetition of other mortal sins. In the case of killing a Brāhmaṇa devoid of qualities, one should go out either east or north and offer eight thousand oblations into a blazing fire. The same applies to the instigator and the actual perpetrator. In the case of killing one possessing qualities, the killer devoid of qualities must fast for three nights, bathe at the three periods of the day, and recite the *Aghamarṣaṇa* three times. The same applies to the instigator and the consenter. For the causal agent (*nimittakartṛ*), there is a threefold recitation of the *Aghamarṣaṇa*. This is to be understood as stated in the Smṛtis. This entire collection of penances should be reduced by one-fourth when applied to a woman engaged in sacrifice, a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya, an *Ātreyī* woman, the wife of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), a pregnant woman, or an embryo whose sex is unknown. Alternatively, having fasted for a day and night, or having observed a night-fast, one should emerge [from the water] and offer forty oblations of clarified butter—five for each of the eight mantras beginning with "To the body-hairs, Svāhā!"—thus completing the rite.
Thus concludes the penance for killing a Brahmin and other such offenses.
Now follows the penance for drinking liquor:

In that regard, if one intentionally drinks *paiṣṭī* liquor once, or drinks *gauḍī* or *mādhvī* liquor repeatedly, one should fast for three nights and offer forty oblations of clarified butter with the verses of the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* hymns. If one is unable to fast for three nights, one should recite daily for a month sixteen times any one of the following: "May [the fire] burn away our sin" (*apa naḥ śośucad agham*), "The Vasisthas [praise] the Dawn with hymns" (*prati stomebhir uṣasaṃ vasiṣṭhāḥ*), "May there be protection for us from the great [goddesses]" (*mahitrīṇām avostu*), or "Come now, let us praise Indra" (*etonvindraṃ stavāma*). If the intentional act involves a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), this should be done daily for a year, along with an oblation using the mantras beginning with "Of the sin committed by the gods" (*devakṛtasyainasaḥ*). Alternatively, one may perform the recitation of the mantra "Obeisance indeed to the fierce one, obeisance to win over" (*nama id ugraṃ nama āvivāsa*). In the case of repeated commission of a mortal sin, however, one should remain composed and follow a cow for a year, subsisting on alms while reciting the *Pāvamānī* verses. The same applies when there is a combination of mortal sins.
Thus concludes the penance for drinking liquor.
Now follows the penance for stealing gold.

In that regard, one who steals the gold of a Brāhmaṇa shall be purified by standing in water while reciting the *Ekādaśarudra* hymns and fasting for three nights; or else, covered in ashes and sleeping on a bed of ashes, he shall be purified from the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, the drinking of liquor, the theft of gold, and violating the Guru’s bed. However, for stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa who is utterly devoid of merit, he should recite once the hymn beginning with *asya vāmasya palitasya hotuḥ*. He should also recite the six verses addressed to the gods (*daiva-ṣaḍṛca*) beginning with *yaj jāgrato dūram udaiti daivam*, as well as the *Śivasaṃkalpa* hymn. The same applies to the theft of gold of a quantity less than this [one *suvarṇa*], and likewise for those who are abettors or instigators.
Thus concludes the penance for stealing gold.
Now follows the penance for violating the Guru’s bed.

In that regard, a minister who has approached the wife of his guru shall fast for three nights and, having performed the recitation (*japa*) and the fire-oblation (*homa*) forty times of the sixteen-verse hymn beginning with "The Thousand-headed Puruṣa" (*Sahasraśīrṣā Puruṣa*), he shall be purified upon giving a milch cow at the conclusion. This same rule applies to the drinking of *surā* liquor or the theft of gold. Alternatively, one who has violated the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*) shall be purified in a month by reciting daily sixteen times either the hymn beginning with "Haviṣyāntam ajaram," or the hymn beginning with "Na tam aṃho na duritam," or the hymn beginning with "Iti vā iti me manaḥ," or the hymn beginning with "Sahasraśīrṣā Puruṣaḥ. If the act was intentional, there shall be the *Śākala-homa* with the mantras beginning with "Devakṛtasyainasaḥ. For the repetition of a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), there shall be a hundred-thousand-fold oblation (*lakṣahoma*) of sesame seeds with the *vyāhṛtis*. However, for approaching a woman who has committed adultery, one shall be purified by reciting once the hymn beginning with "Haviṣpāntam," or the *Pāvamānī* verses, or the *Janadapa*, or the *Vālakhilyas*, or the *Nivit-praiṣas*, or the *Vṛṣākapi*, or the *Hotṝn*, or the *Rudras*. In cases of secondary sins equal to violating the teacher’s bed, a quarter less [of the penance] should be applied; in cases of sins equal to mortal sins, half less should be applied everywhere in this manner. And regarding association with a mortal sinner, whichever person has associated with whom, that person shall perform the very same penance as the latter; such is the rule for violating the teacher’s bed.
Thus concludes the expiation for the great sins (mahāpātaka).

For minor offenses (*upapātaka*), one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) performed in secret; or for a mortal sin (*mahāpātaka*), four hundred breath-restraints; for a heinous sin (*atipātaka*), three hundred; for a secondary sin (*anupātaka*), two hundred; and for a minor offense, one hundred. In all cases, it is doubled for habitual practice, tripled for intentional acts, and quadrupled for intentional habitual practice. For miscellaneous minor sins (*prakīrṇaka-upapāpa*), the breath-restraints are one-fourth of the prescribed number. Alternatively, in the case of a manifest minor offense where three *cāndrāyaṇa* penances are required, there should be one thousand breath-restraints. Or else, for a mortal sin, there should be one hundred thousand recitations of the *gāyatrī*; for a heinous sin, three-quarters; for a secondary sin, half; for a minor offense, a quarter; and one-fourth of that again for miscellaneous sins. Alternatively, for a mortal sin, there should be a fire-oblation (*homa*) of one hundred thousand sesame seeds accompanied by the *gāyatrī* or the *vyāhṛtis*; for heinous sins and the like, it is reduced by a quarter and so forth.
Thus ends the section on secret penances in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. Now follows the definition of the *kṛcchra* penances:

In this context, the duties that constitute the limbs (*aṅga*) of the vow (*vrata*) are the *yamas* and *niyamas*. The ten *yamas* are: celibacy (*brahmacarya*), compassion (*dayā*), forbearance (*kṣānti*), charity (*dāna*), truthfulness (*satya*), absence of crookedness (*akauṭilya*), non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), non-stealing (*asteya*), gentleness (*mādhurya*), and self-restraint (*dama*). The ten *niyamas* are: bathing (*snāna*), silence (*mauna*), fasting (*upavāsa*), sacrifice (*ijyā*), Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), restraint of the generative organ (*upasthanigraha*), service to the teacher (*guruśuśrūṣā*), purity (*śauca*), freedom from anger (*akrodha*), and vigilance (*apramāda*). Regarding the *Sāntapana Kṛcchra*: on the previous day, one should fast; then, having combined cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*), and water infused with *kuśa* grass, one should drink it and fast on the following day. This two-night rite is the *Sāntapana Kṛcchra*. When one fasts on the previous day and on the following day worships these [substances] himself with mantras, offers oblations with mantras, and consumes them with mantras, it is known as the *Brahmakūrca*. Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and *kuśa* water are known as the *Pañcagavya*. Regarding these: the urine of a copper-colored cow is to be taken; the dung of a white cow; the milk of a yellow cow; the curd of a blue cow; and the clarified butter of a black cow. Alternatively, all may be from a Kapila (tawny) cow. If none of these colors are available, any color may be used. The measure is eight *māṣas* for cow urine, sixteen *māṣas* for cow dung, twelve *māṣas* for milk, ten *māṣas* for curd, eight *māṣas* for clarified butter, and half of that for *kuśa* water. One should take the cow urine with the *Gāyatrī*, the cow dung with "gandhadvārām," the milk with "āpyāyasva," the curd with "dadhikrāvṇaḥ," the clarified butter with "tejo 'si śukram asi," and the *kuśa* water with "devasya tvā. Having offered this *Pañcagavya* into the fire with seven-leafed *kuśa* grass whose tips are unbroken and which is white in color, using the verses ending with "irāvatī," "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," and "mānastoke śaṃvatī," one should stir the remainder of the offering with the syllable *Oṃ*, consecrate it, draw it out, and drink it with that same [mantra]. One should drink it with a middle-sized *palāśa* leaf, a lotus leaf, a golden vessel, a copper vessel, or by means of the *brahmatīrtha*. This, together with the fire-oblation, is to be understood as the *Brahmakūrca*. However, a woman or a Śūdra, having had it prepared by Brahmins, should drink it silently. When the *Brahmakūrca* is practiced for three nights, it is the *Yatisāntapana*. The *Sāntapana Kṛcchra* lasting seven days consists of drinking each of the following—cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and *kuśa* water—on successive days, followed by a fast for one night. These [penances] are to be applied according to one's capacity and other factors; the same applies to subsequent cases. The *Mahāsāntapana*, however, involves repeating each of the six substances—cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and *kuśa* water—for three days each, thus lasting fifteen days. Alternatively, the *Mahāsāntapana* lasts twenty-one nights: one repeats each of the six substances—cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and *kuśa* water—for three days, followed by a three-day fast. The *Yati-mahāsāntapana* occurs when each of the six substances, beginning with cow urine, is practiced for two days each. The *Taptakṛcchra* consists of drinking hot milk, clarified butter, and water on successive days, followed by a fast for one night. Alternatively, the *Taptakṛcchra* lasts twelve nights by practicing four things—hot water, steam, milk, and clarified butter—three times each. In that case, one should drink three *palas* of water, two *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of clarified butter. The amount of hot water and steam is merely enough to complete the three-night period. The *Pādakṛcchra* consists of eating once a day (*ekabhakta*), eating only at night (*nakta*), eating only what is obtained unsolicited (*ayācita*), and fasting (*upavāsa*). In the case of eating once a day, there are either fifteen or twenty-six mouthfuls (*grāsa*). At night, there are either twelve or twenty-two. In the case of eating only what is unsolicited, there are exactly twenty-four. All mouthfuls should be the size of a hen’s egg or the size that can enter the mouth; there is an option between these two views based on one's capacity. Or rather, the *Pādakṛcchra* is as follows: three days of eating once a day is the *Pādakṛcchra* to be given to a Śūdra; three days of eating at night is the *Pādakṛcchra* for a Vaiśya; three days of eating only what is unsolicited is the *Pādakṛcchra* for a Kṣatriya; and three days of fasting is the *Pādakṛcchra* for a Brāhmaṇa—such is the settled rule. The *Ardhakṛcchra* would consist of the two parts of eating only what is unsolicited and fasting. The *Pādonakṛcchra* would consist of the three parts of eating once a day, eating only what is unsolicited, and fasting. The *Prājāpatyakṛcchra* consists of eating once a day, eating at night, eating only what is unsolicited, and fasting, repeated three times in direct order or three times in reverse order, for children or the sick. For those who are capable, the *Prājāpatya* may consist of three days of eating once a day, three days of eating at night, three days of eating only what is unsolicited, and three days of fasting, or in reverse order. The *Atikṛcchra* involves eating only as much food as fills the palm of the hand, not a fixed number of mouthfuls. Alternatively, if one eats only a single mouthful on the day of eating, this is the *Atikṛcchra* for a capable person; the rest is as before. The *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra* lasts twenty-one nights of subsisting on milk. Alternatively, for a capable person, subsisting on water for twelve nights constitutes the *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. In the *Parāka*, there is a fast for twelve days. In the *Saumyakṛcchra*, one should consume oil-cakes (*piṇyāka*), boiled rice, the scum of boiled rice, buttermilk, water, and barley meal (*saktu*) over five days respectively, and fast on the sixth day. The quantity of the oil-cakes and so forth should be merely enough to sustain life. Or the *Saumyakṛcchra* may consist of three days of oil-cakes, barley meal, and buttermilk, followed by a fast on the fourth day. As for the *Cāndrāyaṇa*: starting from the first day of the bright fortnight, one increases the mouthfuls by one each day—the size of a peacock’s egg—until there are fifteen mouthfuls on the full moon day. Then, starting from the first day of the dark fortnight, one decreases the mouthfuls by one each day, resulting in a fast on the new moon day; this is the *Yavamadhya* (barley-shaped) *
Thus ends the definition of the Kṛcchra, Cāndrāyaṇa, and other penances.
Now, the general rules for the Cāndrāyaṇa:

Bathing should be performed three times or twice a day; in the *taptakṛcchra* penance, it is performed once. In every instance of bathing, having performed the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) and the recitation of the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn and so forth, one should emerge from the water and perform the worship of the Sun (*sūryopasthāna*) with a solar mantra or the *Sāvitrī*. Thereafter, one should recite auspicious mantras and the *Gāyatrī* eight thousand or a hundred times, according to one's capacity. The four types of alms—barley-gruel, milk-rice, curd, and clarified butter—as well as food consisting of roots, fruits, tubers, and other sacrificially pure items (*haviṣya*), are thus described. Having consecrated that sacrificial food with the mantra "Āpyāyasva," one should consecrate the morsels of food with the *Gāyatrī*. Now, the substitute rites (*pratyāmnāya*) will be explained:

For a *prājāpatya* penance, one should give a cow, or the price of a cow, or the gift of a cow, or the price of a cow; and that price of a cow should be given as one *niṣka*, half a *niṣka*, or a quarter of a *niṣka*. In case of extreme inability, one may give half of that, or land, wealth, grain, clothing, and so forth of equivalent value, or provide a meal for twelve Brahmins, or give an amount of land, wealth, grain, clothing, and so forth equal to that, or perform a complete recitation (*pārāyaṇa*) of a *saṃhitā*, or perform ten thousand recitations (*japa*) of the *Gāyatrī*, or a thousand *tila* oblations, or perform two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) according to one's capacity. Depending on the inability to provide food for a cow and so forth, these requirements increase twofold, threefold, fourfold, fivefold, or sixfold. In place of a fast, one may provide a meal for one Brahmin or give an amount of wealth, grain, clothing, and so forth equal to that; and there is an increase of twofold and so forth according to capacity. Alternatively, one thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī* or twelve breath-restraints should be performed according to capacity. In place of a *cāndrāyaṇa*, eight *prājāpatyas* are required; in a *taptakṛcchra*, six; and in an *atikṛcchra*, three should be performed. However, in cases where [the penance] is easily accomplished, three *cāndrāyaṇas* should be performed; in a *taptakṛcchra*, two and a half *kāyas*; in an *atikṛcchra* and a *mahāsāntapana*, two *kāyas*; and in a *parāka*, five or three *kāyas* should be performed.
Now, the substitution for sacred fords (tīrtha) in place of difficult penances (kṛcchra) will be stated:
"In the Veda, at a sacred ford, in a deity, in a sacrifice, in a medicinal herb, and in a guru—
whatever kind of mental disposition one maintains, such will be the accomplishment."
A sacred field, fire, water, deities, Brahmins, cows, teachers, and pilgrimage sites are said to be purifiers;
they cleanse through dwelling there, performing oblations, bathing, worship, and by the nourishment of anger.
Now, regarding the substitution for all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) according to the Purāṇas, a brief scriptural basis is stated:
"The gods Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva; Indra, Agni, Yama, Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Yakṣa, Soma, Guha, and the Gaṇas."
These, having themselves become sacred fords, attained perfection through those fords:
the Manus, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Maruts, and the Anilas.
The Viśvedevas, the Tuṣitas, the Sādhyas, the Nāgas, the Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas—
these and many other deities attained perfection through the sacred fords (tīrthas).
The Bhṛgus, Aṅgirases, Agastya, Viśvāmitra,
Atri, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and other great-souled ones attained their power through sacred fords (tīrthas).
Hariścandra, Nala, Vainya, Purukutsa, Purūravas, Sagara, Kārtavīrya, and others obtained their kingdoms through sacred fords (tīrthas).
Indrabhairava, Rāma, and others, as well as the great sages such as Gautama,
removed sins such as the killing of a Brahmin solely through sacred fords.
Viśvāmitra, along with his sons, cast off his great sin by means of penance at a sacred ford; having attained the status of a Brahmin despite the curse of Vasiṣṭha’s son, he was purified.
Having made even Triśaṅku—a caṇḍāla—a brahmin, he performed the sacrifice for him;
and by that very body, he caused him to enter the heavenly world.
Without fasting for three nights or more, without visiting sacred fords,
and without giving gold and cows, one is born as one known as poor.
One who visits sacred fords without performing vows, fasts, kṛcchra penances, and the like,
and without giving food, horses, clothing, and so forth, will certainly be born poor.
Likewise, in the Devīpurāṇa:
"The Pāṇḍavas, for the sake of attaining sovereignty and for the pacification of their misfortunes,
[were instructed] by Śrīkṛṣṇa, Nārada, Vyāsa, Śrīkaṇṭha, Indrāja, and Lomaśa."
Likewise, led by Mārkaṇḍeya, Pulastya, Aja, and the Seven Sages,
they performed ascetic penances with devotion for twelve years each.
The story beginning with "The holy places performed [the rite]" and so forth is heard in the Purāṇa,
concerning the high-souled ascetic Viśvanātha, who was free from all latent impressions (nirbīja).
From the age of twenty until the end of his hundredth year, he constantly frequented sacred pilgrimage sites,
traveling in the company of many companions who were learned in numerous Smṛtis and Purāṇas.
The entire fruit of the sacred ford has been declared,
which was not even accomplished by Mārkaṇḍeya, Aja, Hanumān, Jāmbavat, Romaśa, and others.
The entire fruit of visiting sacred fords is said to be equal to the merit of the rite of gifting a cow;
likewise, at the end of the Dvāpara age, Vyāsa [compiled] the Purāṇas for men of short lifespans.
Having contracted [the boundaries] from the end of winter in the southern region, one should conduct the legal proceedings;
for there dwell spirits, ghosts, piśācas, ancestors, and brahmarākṣasas.
Even today they still say that the sacred ford (tīrtha) was effective for such a difficult purpose:
"The Sūta, though a Śūdra, was formerly a knower of the Purāṇas; through the sacred fords he then became a Brāhmaṇa."
He said to his disciples, "Indeed, establish pilgrimage sites marked with syllables."
They spoke to Viśvakarman, and Viśvakarman, the all-knowing,
caused his disciples to perform the difficult syllables and limbs [of the ritual] at all sacred fords (tīrthas).
Even today, marks indicating difficult syllables are seen here and there; when the numerical values of the letters are not understood, another method is stated.
An expert in the Purāṇas and Smṛtis, for the sake of attaining the fruits of the holy sites (tīrthas) proclaimed by Viṣṇu,
has spoken this for the benefit of the world, wherein even that which is difficult to reach is described.

In the *Purāṇas*, the *Smṛtis*, and the *Tīrthakalpas*, the fruits of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are described as being equal to the gift of a cow, ten cows, a hundred cows, or the merit of a thousand cows; equal to the fruit of the *Agnihotra*, the fruit of meritorious sacrifices (*iṣṭi*), the fruit of a *Yajña*, or the fruit of an *Aśvamedha*; as destroying minor offenses (*upapātaka*), major offenses (*pātaka*), and great offenses (*mahāpātaka*); and equal to the fruits of fasting, a three-night fast, the *Kṛcchra*, the *Cāndrāyaṇa*, a fortnightly fast, a monthly fast, a six-monthly fast, or a yearly fast. Setting aside such commendatory exaggerations (*arthavāda-praśaṃsā*), the fruits of the sacred fords have been stated here by establishing the corresponding *Kṛcchra* penances according to the fitness of each case. The compilers of *Tīrthasaṃgrahas* have likewise stated this. We state them in the same way for those unable to perform physical *Kṛcchra* observances, so that they may avoid falling into sin (*pātitya*). Among these, bathing in the Bhāgīrathī is equal to six years of *Kṛcchra* for those who have traveled sixty *yojanas*. For every increase of one *yojana* in the journey, the *Kṛcchra* increases by half. Formerly, the rivers were presided over by the Seven Mothers (*Saptamātṛkā*) due to fear of Rākṣasas. When the fear had passed, they became goddesses again. Consequently, in the dry riverbeds, the Bhāgīrathī flowed in seven colors and in seven streams. Bathing once in the seven Gaṅgās at those places where Viṣṇu-Gaṅgā and the other Seven Mothers reside is equal to a quarter-*Kṛcchra*. At Prayāga, it is double that. The same applies at Gaṅgādvāra and the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean. In Vārāṇasī, the Gaṅgā is extremely difficult to reach; its merit at the edge of the ocean cannot be calculated. In Vārāṇasī, a great offense (*mahāpātaka*) does not enter; one who dies there is indeed liberated. Regarding all pilgrimages, the distance is reduced by six, four, or two *yojanas* depending on differences in foreign lands, differences in languages, or obstructions by great mountains or great rivers. Bathing in the Yamunā is equal to twelve *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled twenty *yojanas*. At Mathurā, it is double. Bathing in the Sarasvatī is equal to four years of *Kṛcchra* for one who has traveled forty *yojanas*. At Prabhāsa and Dvāravatī, it is double. In these two rivers, for every increase of one *yojana* in the journey, the *Kṛcchra* increases by a quarter. Bathing in the divine rivers such as the Dṛṣadvatī, Śatadru, Vipāśā, Vitastā, Śarāvatī, Maruvṛddhā, Asiknī, Madhumatī, Payasvatī, and Ghṛtavatī is equal to thirty *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled fifteen *yojanas*. Bathing in divine rivers such as the Candrabhāgā, Vetravatī, Śarayū, Gomatī, Devikā, Kauśikī, Nityajalā, Mandākinī, Sahasravaktrā, Paunaḥpunyā, Pūrṇapuṇyā, Bāhudā, Vāruṇī, and Gaṇḍakī is equal to sixteen *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled twelve *yojanas*. At the mutual confluence of these rivers, the fruit is that of the "Three Rivers" (*Trinadī*). In other great rivers flowing to the ocean, the fruit is six *Kṛcchras*. In large lakes (*mahānade*), the fruit is half that of a great river. In the Śoṇa and Mahānada, the fruit is half that of the Gaṅgā. In ordinary rivers, the fruit is half that of a river. In the Vairocana rivers, the fruit is half that of a great river. At the *Puṣkara* holy sites, it is equal to Prayāga. The same applies at Saṃnihatyā. At Māhiṣmatī and similar places, an *Homa* performed in a fire that is constantly visible yields tenfold merit. Having visited Gayā, the Mahānadī, Seturāmeśvara, Someśvara, Bhīmeśvara, Śrīraṅga, Padmanābha, Puruṣottama, Naimiṣa, Badaryāśrama, Puṇyāraṇya, Dharmāraṇya, Kurukṣetra, Śrīśaila, Mahālaya, Kedāra, Puṣkara, Rudrakoṭi, the Narmadā, Āmrātakeśvara, Kubjāmra, Kokāmukha, Prabhāsa, Vijayeśa, Purīndra, Pañcanada, Gokarṇa, Śaṅkukarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Dvāravatī, Māyā, Avantī, Gayā, Kāñcī, Śālagrāma, Śambhalagrāma, Kambalagrāma, and other such fields of liberation (*muktikṣetra*), one obtains the fruit of bathing at Gayā. Vārāṇasī is indeed superior to all of them. Even for one who dies at Mahāprayāga, there is liberation. Death at any other Prayāga is merely a seed for liberation. Bathing in the Narmadā is equal to twenty-four *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled twenty-four *yojanas*. At the confluence with the Kubjikā, it is double. At Muktitīrtha, it is fourfold. In the Tāpī, it is equal to ten *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled ten *yojanas*. In the Payoṣṇī, it is equal to eight *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled eight *yojanas*. At their confluence, it is double. In the Godāvarī, it is equal to three years of *Kṛcchra* for one who has traveled sixty *yojanas*. There, bathing in the eleven *Tīrthas* at the thirty *yojana* mark, whether in the direction of the current or against it, is equal to sixty *Kṛcchras*. At the confluence with the Vañjarā at Prayāga, it is double that. At Saptagodāvarī and Bhīmeśvara, it is triple. At Kuśatarpaṇa, it is equal to Gayā. In the Vañjarā, it is equal to twelve *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled twelve *yojanas*. In the Godāvarī, from the point of separation to the edge of the ocean, it is sixfold. In the Praṇītā, it is equal to four *Kṛcchras* at four *yojanas*. In the Pūrṇā, it is half that at half that distance. In the Kṛṣṇāveṇī, it is equal to fifteen *Kṛcchras* at fifteen *yojanas*. In the Tuṅgabhadrā, it is equal to twenty *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled twenty *yojanas*. At the Paṃpā, it is double that. At Hārihara, it is triple. In the Bhīmarathī, it is equal to ten *Kṛcchras* for one who has traveled ten *yojanas*. At the confluence with the Kakudmatī, it is equal to fifteen *Kṛc
The measure of an *aṅgula* is said to be eight barley grains placed horizontally, or three rice grains placed vertically; twelve *aṅgulas* constitute a *vitasti*.
Two *vitastis* make one *aratni*; from that, a *kiṣku*; from that, a *dhanus*.
Two thousand *dhanus* make one *krośa*, and four *krośas* make one *yojana*.
They declare a region of one and a half *gavyūti*s to be one *yojana*;
the learned know a *gavyūti* to be measured by five thousand *dhanus*.

The observances for pilgrimages include eating but one meal a day, sleeping on the ground, celibacy except during the fertile period, and so forth. At a sacred site (*tīrtha*), one should perform bathing, recitation (*japa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and the like. In the case of a deity, one should perform the offering of water (*arghya*), water for the feet (*pādya*), unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), perfumes, worship, and so forth; such rules regarding the substitution of rites at sacred sites are to be applied. This being the case, one should act in such a way that the mind becomes purified. However, one who goes for the sake of another receives a sixteenth part of the merit. One who goes incidentally (*prasaṅgena*) receives half the fruit. One who reaches a sacred site by chance (*anuṣaṅgeṇa*) and bathes receives only the fruit of the bath, not the fruit of the pilgrimage itself. For the sake of one's father, paternal uncle, grandfather, great-grandfather, maternal uncle, father-in-law, or those whom one supports; for the sake of a teacher (*guru*), preceptor (*ācārya*), or sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*); for the sake of their wives; or for the sake of one's mother’s sister or father’s sister—one receives an eighth part of the merit oneself after bathing. A son performing [the rite] directly for his parents receives a fourth part of the merit.
A husband and wife, as well as co-wives, obtain half the fruit from one another;
for those who seek [the fruit], there is a reduction in the reward—such is the nature of the fruit of service.

During the two months beginning with Karkaṭaka (Cancer), the great rivers flowing to the ocean remain continuously in their menstrual state (*rajasvalā*). Among them, however, the Bhāgīrathī, Gomatī, Candrabhāgā, Sarasvatī, Sindhu, Mahānadī, and Śarayū remain in their menstrual state for three nights. Those small streams that dry up during the summer season and are filled again by rains become *rajasvalā* at the end of ten days.

Small streams (*kulyā*), minor rivers, and major rivers remain in a state of impurity (*rajasvalā*) for seven days, a fortnight, or a month respectively. In the case of small reservoirs such as ponds, wells, and tanks that contain little water and lack old (standing) water, they remain impure for three nights. Therefore, bathing, libations (*tarpaṇa*), and other rites should not be performed there because of their impurity; however, there is no prohibition for those who reside on the banks. The Sarasvatī, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and all rivers are never impure. It is said in the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas* that wherever the words "Gaṅgā," "Yamunā," or "Sarasvatī" appear, the defect of impurity does not apply there. Furthermore, even for those not residing on the banks, there is no defect of impurity during the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* ceremonies, the ritual bath at the conclusion of a vow (*vrata-snāna*), or during lunar and solar eclipses. All small streams (*kṣudranadī*) are not considered impure.
Thus concludes the procedure for visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Now, in place of the twelve-year vow and other such observances required for the great sins (*mahāpātaka*), the *prājāpatya* and other penances, as well as their substitutes, are described:

In that regard, regarding the twelve-year penance (*dvādaśavārṣika*), if one calculates one *prājāpatya* for each of the twelve days, then thirty-six hundred and sixty *prājāpatyas* result for the twelve-year penance. Therefore, for a major sin (*mahāpātaka*) committed once unintentionally, one should perform three hundred and sixty *kāyās*. If unable to do that, one should give thirty-six hundred cows, or their value; or, as the price of the cows, one should give according to one's capacity thirty-six hundred *niṣkas*, or half-*niṣkas*, or quarter-*niṣkas*. If even giving the value is impossible, one should perform that many fasts (*udavāsa*). If unable to do even that, one should perform thirty-six hundred thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī* mantra, calculated by taking ten thousand recitations for each *prājāpatya*. Or, one should perform three hundred and sixty complete recitations of the Vedas (*vedapārāyaṇa*). Or, that many thousands of *tila*-oblations. Or, two hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Such substitutes for *kṛcchra* penances should be applied with a count of three hundred and sixty for major sins. For heinous sins (*atipātaka*), in place of the nine-year vow (which is one-quarter less than the twelve-year vow), two hundred and seventy *kāyās* should be performed. If unable to do that, the gift of cows and so forth should be performed. For minor sins (*anupātaka*), in place of the six-year vow, one hundred and eighty *kāyās* [should be performed], and the same number of cows and so forth. When there is a plurality of minor sins, the three-year vow should be performed. In its place, for the three-year vow, ninety *kāyās* should be performed, and the same number of cows and so forth. For each individual minor sin, a three-month vow is prescribed; in its place, seven and a half *kāyās* are the substitute, and the same number of cows and so forth. In the case of the cow-killing vow consisting of three nights accompanied by the gift of eleven bulls, however, eleven and a half *kāyās* [are required], and the same number of fasts and so forth. In the month-long milk-vow, two and a half *kāyās* are the substitute, and likewise for the month-long *pañcagavya* vow. In the *parāka* vow, three *kāyās* are the substitute, and likewise for the *sāntapana* vow lasting seven days, half a *kāya* [is the substitute], and so on. Regarding miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇaka*), a *prājāpatya* should be calculated by assigning a quarter or other fractions; or, since a *prājāpatya* consists of six fasts, it should be calculated according to one’s capacity.
Now, all the expiations shall be described.

In that regard, concerning many various sins other than the *mahāpātakas* (great crimes), such as those committed unknowingly (*ajñāta*) and so forth, a person who is extremely virtuous and utterly detached, being unable to perform a penance for each individual cause, should perform a six-year *kṛcchra* or one hundred and eighty *prājāpatyas*. Or, he may perform the substitution (*pratyāmnāya*) of cows and the like in that same number. In the case of repetition, it is double; if intentional (*matyā*), triple; if intentional with repetition, fourfold. In the case of extreme repetition or continuous repetition, it is fivefold. In the case of repetition over a long period, it is sixfold. Regarding very numerous miscellaneous minor sins (*prakīrṇaka-kṣudrapāpa*) committed unintentionally, if one is unable to perform a penance for each cause, one should perform a one-year *kṛcchra* or thirty *prājāpatyas*. Or, one may perform the substitution of cows and the like in that same number. In the case of repetition, it is double; if intentional, triple; if intentional with repetition, fourfold. In the case of extreme repetition or continuous repetition, it is fivefold. Likewise, in the case of repetition over a long period, it is sixfold. For minor sins committed unknowingly, if one is unable to perform a penance for each cause, one should perform a *kṛcchra*, an *atikṛcchra*, and a *cāndrāyaṇa*. Or, one may perform twelve *prājāpatyas* in place of those; or they say one may perform half of that (six) in place of them. Or, one may perform the substitution of cows and the like in the place of the *kṛcchra* in that same number. In the case of repetition, it is double; if intentional, triple; if intentional with repetition, fourfold. In the case of extreme repetition or continuous repetition, it is fivefold. Likewise, in the case of repetition over a long period, it is sixfold. This set of four penances is for the highest class of person. For the middle class, it is double; for the lowest class, it is triple. Even for those whose great meritorious or demeritorious acts of sacrifice (*iṣṭa*) and public works (*pūrta*) have not been impaired—such as the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the teacher (*ācārya*), and the patron (*yajamāna*)—there shall be a universal penance (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) known as *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa*. In place of that, they say one may perform twelve *prājāpatyas* or half of that (six).
Thus ends the procedure for all expiations in the Smṛtyarthasāra.

In all cases where no specific expiation has been mentioned, the *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances should be applied according to suitability, either collectively or individually. For minor secondary offenses (*upapāpa*), a fast or a three-night vow should be applied according to suitability. For very minor offenses, twelve or six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) should be applied according to suitability. For women and Śūdras, the breath-restraints are performed without mantras. Alternatively, gifts of food sufficient for a man’s meal, or the offering of the *hantakāra* (the first portion of a meal), should be applied; or likewise, the giving of wealth, grain, and so forth, should be performed. In the case of a *homa*, an oblation should be made with the mantra: *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā*. If a limb of the ritual action is omitted, there should be a recitation (*japa*) of *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ* one hundred and eight times. If there is a lapse in silence (*vāgyama*), one should remember Viṣṇu or Śiva. To ensure that what was done unknowingly is complete and not deficient, one should remember Acyuta or Śambhu.
I bow to that Infallible One, by whose remembrance and by whose utterance of His name, whatever is deficient in penance, sacrifice, ritual acts, and the like, immediately attains completeness.
Whatever may fall away from the sacrifices through ignorance or greed, that becomes complete simply by the remembrance of Viṣṇu; such is the Vedic revelation.
Thus says the *Padmapurāṇa*.

Thus ends the section on the rules for all expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. The measure of a *niṣka*: According to the concordance between worldly usage and the scriptures, a *niṣka* consists of forty *māṣas*. Half of that is twenty; half of that is ten. In the case of a *suvarṇa*, if one is unable to provide that, silver may be used instead. Eight *prājāpatyas* constitute one *cāndrāyaṇa*; six (or seven) [of those] constitute a *taptakṛcchra*; three [of those] constitute an *atikṛcchra*. In this manner, thirty *prājāpatyas* are required for a year-long vow (*abdavrata*).

Thus ends the section on expiation (*prāyaścitta*) in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*, composed by Śrīdhara Ācārya— a performer of sacrifices and knower of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, son of Viṣṇu Bhaṭṭopādhyāya, the great Maheśvara and lord of the Nāgas named Viśvāmitra.
